issues.title: Limited visibility and confidence in CoCounsel Next scale testing and readiness
issues.description: Service management has limited visibility into CoCounsel Next scale testing, which is currently owned and run by product engineering. Scale tests are being referred to as 'load tests' and typically run for about two hours, which may not be sufficient to represent real production behaviour. There are concerns that scale tests are not staying ahead of increasing beta usage and that problems appear when simulating higher loads (e.g., double wave one for anticipated wave two). The service management scale program is not being used, and the service management team lacks confidence that CoCounsel Next is prepared for GA or even higher beta usage.
issues.impact_assessment: Because scale testing is controlled by product engineering with limited transparency, service management cannot properly assess operational readiness or ensure sufficient capacity and stability prior to General Availability. The current short-duration load tests may fail to reveal issues that would surface under sustained production load. Evidence of problems when attempting to simulate higher waves of beta usage suggests that performance and reliability risks may materialize if GA is pursued without robust, long-running scale tests. This threatens GA timelines and risks customer-facing instability.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Dependent on product engineering scale tests and potential engagement of the Service Management Scale Team; affects CoCounsel Next GA readiness and AI EASY operational guardrails.
issues.resolution: Engagement with the AIESE team to discuss scale testing concerns and agree a plan to address. As of 11 May 2026, Jenkins, Justin P. (TR Technology) confirms he has access to scale testing meetings and results, but the adequacy of the testing approach and alignment with service management expectations are still being actively worked.
issues.source_file_name: Operational Readiness — CoCounsel Next Product Launch - Scope & requirements.docx

issues.title: Agent Core rollback runbook too complex for SRE/GCC to execute quickly
issues.description: The current rollback runbook for the Agent Core component of CoCounsel Next is highly complex. Service management (including SRE and GCC) is concerned that, in a production incident, the steps will be difficult to follow quickly and safely, which undermines the requirement that rollback be fast and easy to execute when customers are impacted.
issues.impact_assessment: Rollback is a critical control for protecting customers during production incidents. If the Agent Core rollback procedure remains complex, SRE and GCC staff may struggle to execute it under time pressure, increasing the risk of prolonged customer impact, errors during rollback, or reliance on product engineering to intervene. This undermines the Service Mgmt - Change/Release milestone’s goal of having rollback that service management can execute independently by the 24 June 2026 beta release and may necessitate limiting who can perform rollbacks or altering the interim support model.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on CoCounsel Next product engineering leadership (including Singh, Chetan and Matisse, Viola) to agree on acceptable rollback complexity, resourcing for simplification work, and any interim support arrangements; affects the Service Mgmt - Change/Release milestone and beta readiness for June 24, 2026.
issues.resolution: Run through the current Agent Core rollback runbook in an upcoming Thursday gameday session with the CoCounsel Next engineering team to demonstrate the complexity and agree on next steps, then either (a) simplify the rollback procedure to a form that SRE/GCC can execute confidently, or (b) explicitly accept short-term risk by having product engineering own rollback through beta, with a dated plan to deliver a simplified, service-management-usable rollback runbook before GA.
issues.source_file_name: CoCo Next - Service Management Bi Weekly.docx

issues.title: Service management lacks adequate communication and planning visibility for CoCounsel Next
issues.description: Service management has limited visibility into CoCounsel Next planning and day-to-day decisions. Many discussions occur in Slack with restricted membership (e.g., only specific individuals such as Dante De Luca and Jenkins, Justin P. have access), and there are few or no ongoing project planning meetings involving service management. The AI EASY approach intentionally uses different communication tools and restricted channels, which reduces transparency for the broader service management team.
issues.impact_assessment: The lack of structured communication and visibility impairs service management's ability to identify risks, track progress toward GA, and ensure operational readiness. Without consistent updates on scale testing, milestones, and decisions, service management cannot reliably define or verify minimum guardrails, increasing the risk of misalignment and last-minute surprises before GA.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on CoCounsel Next product and engineering teams sharing information via meetings or communication channels (e.g., Slack). Affects service management readiness, guardrails definition, and coordination with AI EASY leadership.
issues.resolution: Identify a contact from the AI ESE program who can provide the engagement that we require to adequately plan Service Management tasks to support the GA launch.
issues.source_file_name: Operational Readiness — CoCounsel Next Product Launch - Scope & requirements.docx

issues.title: Traditional go/no-go sign-off model unclear under AI ESE approach
issues.description: Under the AI ESE model, it is unclear whether there will be formal go/no-go or sign-off meetings involving service management, product engineering, and other stakeholders prior to CoCounsel Next GA. Service management expects some form of multi-team sign-off but does not currently know if or how this will occur for CoCounsel Next.
issues.impact_assessment: Without a clear go/no-go decision process, CoCounsel Next could be promoted to GA without service management's confirmation that operational guardrails and requirements are met. This undermines governance, increases the risk of unapproved changes reaching production, and may result in post-release incidents that could have been mitigated through formal readiness checks.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Dependent on AI ESE program leadership, service management leadership (e.g., LeBlanc, Wil), and CoCounsel Next product leadership defining and agreeing a GA sign-off process.
issues.resolution: This issue will be resolved when the list of requirements/guardrails is finalized.
issues.source_file_name: Operational Readiness — CoCounsel Next Product Launch - Scope & requirements.docx

dependencies.title: Service management visibility into CoCounsel Next communications and scale results
dependencies.description: Effective operational readiness for CoCounsel Next depends on service management having adequate visibility into project communications and scale test results, many of which currently occur in restricted Slack channels or informal meetings.
dependencies.dependent_on: CoCounsel Next product and engineering teams granting appropriate Slack access or establishing shared meetings and reporting mechanisms, and continuing to include service management in scale testing meetings and result reviews.
dependencies.consumer: Service management team (including SREs and GCC staff)
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delayed or limited visibility reduces service management's ability to identify issues early, contribute to planning, and validate readiness before GA, potentially leading to late discovery of operational risks.
dependencies.mitigation: Request broader Slack access for key service management stakeholders, schedule regular joint meetings, and ensure key updates are summarized via shared channels or project documentation. As of 11 May 2026, Justin Jenkins has access to scale testing meetings and results; remaining work focuses on improving broader communication and planning visibility.
dependencies.source_file_name: Operational Readiness — CoCounsel Next Product Launch - Scope & requirements.docx

dependencies.title: Enterprise security governance (ISRM and BISO) engagement for CoCounsel Next GA
dependencies.description: CoCounsel Next GA readiness depends on enterprise security governance teams, including ISRM and the assigned Business Information Security Officer (BISO), performing required security scanning, validating remediation of findings such as HTTP-to-HTTPS changes, and formally confirming that security non-negotiables are met before GA.
dependencies.dependent_on: ISRM and the designated BISO for CoCounsel Next to complete security scanning, review results, confirm remediation of issues like non-secure internal protocols, and provide GA security sign-off.
dependencies.consumer: Service management team and CoCounsel Next product engineering leadership
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If ISRM scanning or BISO engagement is delayed or absent, required security changes (e.g., HTTP-to-HTTPS remediation) may not be validated before GA, potentially blocking GA approval, creating compliance gaps, or forcing last-minute changes that jeopardize stability and launch timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Include the presence of an assigned BISO and completed ISRM security scanning as explicit items in the non-negotiable operational readiness checklist. If these conditions are not met, GA readiness will be flagged Red in executive reporting and product engineering will be required to resolve the gap before proceeding.
dependencies.source_file_name: Operational Readiness — CoCounsel Next Product Launch.docx

dependencies.title: Datadog synthetics depend on MFA being disabled for CoCounsel Next bot accounts
dependencies.description: The ability to run Datadog synthetic tests for CoCounsel Next key scenarios across multiple bot accounts depends on multi-factor authentication (MFA) being disabled or bypassed for those specific bot accounts. Currently MFA prompts block synthetics from running automatically.
dependencies.dependent_on: Identity/authentication team responsible for configuring MFA policies on CoCounsel Next synthetic bot accounts
dependencies.consumer: Service management monitoring team (including Ureño, Jose (TR Technology) and Jenkins, Justin P. (TR Technology))
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If MFA remains enabled for synthetic bot accounts past the beta release on 24 June 2026, Datadog synthetics will not provide full automated coverage, limiting early detection of functional or performance regressions and reducing confidence in CoCounsel Next’s monitoring posture during beta.
dependencies.mitigation: Use a single bot account without MFA as a temporary workaround to run synthetics while pursuing MFA exemptions for additional accounts, and complement synthetics with real usage data analysis and manual checks until full multi-account synthetics can be enabled.
dependencies.source_file_name: CoCo Next - Service Management Bi Weekly.docx

decisions.title: Use shared Azure DevOps (ADO) project and RAG-scored epics as central tracker for CoCounsel Next operational readiness
decisions.description: The project will use a shared Azure DevOps (ADO) project and board as the central tracker for CoCounsel Next operational readiness. Epics will be organized under high-level categories such as change/release and incident management (based on the service management guardrails document). Features and tasks will be nested under these epics. Each epic will carry a RAG status to represent GA readiness along that dimension, and stakeholders will review and update these statuses in a weekly call, with the intention that all epics are Green by the end of August.
decisions.rationale: A single ADO project with structured epics, features, and tasks provides a shared, transparent view for ISRM, service management, product engineering, and platform engineering to coordinate CoCounsel Next operational readiness work and track progress toward GA. RAG statuses on epics allow quick assessment of readiness across multiple dimensions and align with executive reporting expectations.
decisions.options_considered: Continue tracking readiness items in static documents and separate backlogs per team (service management ways-of-working backlog, product engineering backlog in Linear), versus using a shared ADO project as the central connective backlog; defer structuring until after GA.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Service management visibility into CoCounsel Next communications and scale results; Consolidate CIO requirements and deliverables for CoCounsel Next operational readiness; Review service management guardrails list with CoCounsel Next product engineering leadership.
decisions.source_file_name: CoCo Next - Ops readiness check in 2 of 2.docx

milestones.name: ISRM - Establish AI Security Governance Model
milestones.description:
Scope

Establish a standardized AI security governance model to ensure all AI capabilities are consistently assessed, reviewed, monitored, and remediated across the lifecycle. This includes defining intake criteria for security reviews, executing secure AI assessments on new features, and enabling operational monitoring and remediation processes to manage risk in production.

milestones.name: ISRM - Achieve Compliance Readiness
milestones.description:
Scope
Assess CoCounsel’s current security posture against applicable regulatory and AI-specific standards to identify control gaps and establish a clear baseline for compliance readiness. This includes performing structured gap assessments against SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, and ISO 42001 frameworks.

Business Outcomes
Clear understanding of current compliance posture across key frameworks
Early identification of control gaps impacting audit and certification readiness
Improved ability to prioritize remediation efforts based on risk and compliance impact
Increased confidence from leadership in readiness for regulatory and audit requirements
Stronger alignment with industry standards for AI and security governance

milestones.name: Service Mgmt - Ownership & Support
milestones.description:
Purpose
This ensures that every service in CoCounsel Next has a clear, named owner, a functioning on-call rota, and a documented escalation path. When something goes wrong in production, there should never be any ambiguity about who responds.
Scope
• Service ownership — a named owner and assignment group (Eng, SRE etc.) recorded for every service
• On-call rota — defined, published, and kept current
• Escalation path — specific named individuals documented and accessible to anyone who might need them

milestones.name: ISRM - Enable CoCounsel Customer Trust & External Assurance
milestones.description:
Scope

Enable CoCounsel to effectively communicate its security, legal, and operational posture to customers by providing clear, consistent documentation and ensuring alignment across Customer Trust, Product Engineering, and Labs. This includes delivering core artifacts and preparing responses to anticipated customer questions.

milestones.name: Service Mgmt - Change/Release
milestones.description:
Purpose

Ensures that all changes to the CoCounsel Next production environment — whether code deployments, infrastructure changes, or feature flag modifications — are tracked, owned, and reversible. It is the highest priority milesonte for GA readiness.

Scope

•  Deployment tracking — every production deployment has a corresponding ServiceNow change record and a named owner

•  Feature flag governance — flag changes are auditable and owned

•  Rollback capability — the Service Management team can execute a rollback independently, without engineering support

Out of Scope

The mechanics of how deployments are built or automated (this sits with Engineering). This milestone is concerned with process, ownership, and documentation around changes — not the technical implementation of the pipeline itself.

Dependencies

•  Engineering team to confirm deployment process and provide SM access to execute rollbacks

•  ServiceNow team to confirm change record process and any integration requirements

milestones.name: Service Mgmt - Incident Management
milestones.description:
Purpose

Ensures that when something goes wrong in production, the team knows about it immediately, knows what to do, and has practiced doing it. It covers the flow from alert to incident, the runbooks needed to respond, and a hands-on gameday to validate readiness.

Scope

•  ServiceNow integration — all production issues result in a tracked incident, whether via manual or automated alert-to-incident flow

•  Runbook library — documented, peer-reviewed response guides for the top anticipated failure scenarios

•  Gameday — a hands-on rehearsal of incident response, not a theoretical discussion

Out of Scope

Monitoring and alerting configuration (covered in the Monitoring / Alerting) assumes alerts exist and focuses on what happens after one fires.

Dependencies

•  Monitoring / Alerting — alerts must exist before the incident flow can be validated

•  ServiceNow team — to confirm incident creation process and access

•  Engineering team — to participate in gameday and review runbooks for accuracy

milestones.name: CIO Deliverables/requirements for rollout finalised
milestones.description: Across CIO (ISRM, SM, Platform Engineering) identify the deliverables, dependencies and requirements to support the CoCo Next rollout.  These will form the 'plan' for delivery.

milestones.name: Service Mgmt - Scale & Stability
milestones.description:
Purpose
This ensures CoCounsel Next has been tested at realistic load levels, that known breaking points and capacity risks are understood and tracked, and that an ongoing process exists to review and adjust as usage grows.
Scope
• Load testing — CoCounsel Next load tests run concurrently with LSM scale tests, at expected and near-term peak load
• Capacity risk tracking — Mercury limits and other major risks are understood, documented, and owned
• LSM Scale Team engagement — approach and capacity validated with the LSM Scale Team
• Ongoing review — periodic review of production usage and behaviour, with tests adjusted accordingly

milestones.name: ISRM - Drive Production & Launch Readiness for AI Capabilities
milestones.description:
Scope
Ensure AI capabilities are ready for General Availability (GA) by addressing key operational risks and establishing minimum security and operational standards for launch. This includes remediating critical protocol issues and defining ISRM guardrails to support consistent and secure AI ESE launches.

Business Outcomes
Reduced risk of security issues at product launch
Improved consistency and control across AI capability releases
Clear expectations for Product Engineering on security and operational requirements
Increased confidence from leadership in GA readiness
Stronger alignment between ISRM and product teams on launch standards

entities.name: IA Remediations
entities.okrs: CIO1a - Deliver an improved and market leading product experience for our customers

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

**Scope:** The IA Remediations project establishes consistent visibility, ownership, and governance for CIO-owned Internal Audit remediation items so that commitments are actively managed within CIO processes and delivery risks are surfaced early. This matters because unresolved audit findings and late extensions increase control risk, regulatory scrutiny, and the likelihood of enterprise-level escalation.

**Current Status:** Overall status is Red, driven by incomplete remediation plans for items due 30 Jun 2026. Of 20 CIO-owned findings, 4 are closed. Of the 16 remaining open items, 3 are past due with no recovery plan and 9 have not yet started – 5 of which are due in 2026.

## Path to Green

-   Submit all extension requests – respective remediation owners, coordinated by Shannon/Program Manager by 10 Jun 2026.
    
-   Establish formal recovery plans for all past-due items – respective remediation owners, coordinated by Shannon/Program Manager by 19 Jun 2026.
    

## Milestones

-   10 Jun 2026 - Submit and obtain decisions on all required extension requests for remediation items that cannot meet their current due dates
    
-   19 Jun 2026 – All open remediation items have assigned owners and active recovery plans
    
-   30 Jun 2026 - Complete remediation and closure activities for Protecht issues 1016488 “Governance of BU Managed Accounts” and 1028549 “Unused GCP Accounts”.
    
-   31 Aug 2026 – Complete remediation and closure activities for Protecht issue 1016563 “Absence of a Deny List Capability”

risks.title: Ownership gaps for Internal Audit remediation items may delay completion
risks.description: The May 20, 2026 CIO Internal Audit Remediations baseline report identifies ownership gaps for some of the 17 open Internal Audit remediation items. Where accountable owners are ambiguous or not yet assigned, remediation activities may not be actively driven, leading to delays and increased likelihood of items becoming past due and requiring escalation.
risks.impact_description: If ownership gaps persist, remediation items may not progress as planned, causing more items to become past due. This can increase audit finding exposure, trigger enterprise-level escalations, damage the CIO organization’s control environment reputation, and undermine the project’s purpose of improving visibility, ownership, and governance over Internal Audit remediation activities.
risks.mitigation: Assign and confirm accountable owners for all remediation items with owner ambiguity, as part of the Path to Green. Use the baseline inventory and portfolio snapshot to identify items without clear ownership and ensure they are explicitly assigned within the CIO organization.
risks.source_file_name: May 2026 CIO Exec Summary Monthly Report.docx

risks.title: Resource constraints may prevent timely completion of Internal Audit remediations
risks.description: The baseline report lists resource constraints as a key risk theme for the CIO organization’s open Internal Audit remediation items. Limited availability of staff or competing priorities may prevent remediation work from starting or progressing, particularly for items not yet started and those requiring extensions.
risks.impact_description: If resource constraints are not addressed, remediation activities may be delayed, more items may become past due, and extension requests may increase. This can result in failure to meet Internal Audit commitments, heightened regulatory and audit scrutiny, and possible enterprise-level escalation, undermining the objective of improving governance and risk management.
risks.mitigation: Use the portfolio snapshot and remediation progress tracking to identify items at risk due to resource constraints, prioritize critical remediations, reallocate or augment resources where possible, and submit extension requests for items that cannot meet current due dates.
risks.source_file_name: May 2026 CIO Exec Summary Monthly Report.docx

risks.title: Past due remediation items may remain unresolved or lack recovery plans
risks.description: The CIO Internal Audit Remediations report notes that there are past due items; two are close to closure and three require recovery plans. If these items are not promptly closed or given formal recovery plans, they may remain overdue and continue to expose the organization to control and compliance risk.
risks.impact_description: If the past due items are not closed quickly or placed on credible recovery plans, audit commitments will continue to be breached, increasing exposure to repeat findings, negative Internal Audit reporting, and potential enterprise-level escalation. This will undermine the project goal of ensuring past-due and at-risk items are identified early and addressed through CIO processes.
risks.mitigation: Close the two past due items that are close to closure and establish recovery plans for the remaining three past due items, as defined in the Path to Green. Monitor these items closely in monthly reports until they are fully remediated or formally extended.
risks.source_file_name: May 2026 CIO Exec Summary Monthly Report.docx

risks.title: Remediation items due June 30, 2026 may miss their deadlines due to incomplete plans or pending owner responses
risks.description: Several remediation items are coming due by the end of June 2026. The baseline report notes that some of these, including specific items, have not started and have owner responses pending or require extensions. Without confirmed remediation plans and timely owner engagement, these items may not be completed by their June 30, 2026 due dates.
risks.impact_description: If items due June 30, 2026 are not completed on time, the CIO organization will fail to meet agreed Internal Audit remediation deadlines. This increases audit exposure, may necessitate reactive extension requests, and could result in escalation at the enterprise level, directly conflicting with the project’s objective of surfacing delivery risks before they become overdue issues.
risks.mitigation: Confirm remediation plans for all items due June 30, 2026 and obtain owner responses for items not started. For items that cannot meet their current due dates, submit formal extension requests ahead of June 30, 2026. Monitor progress through the monthly portfolio snapshot and escalate if completion by the due date is unlikely.

risks.title: Required extensions for remediation items may not be submitted in time
risks.description: The baseline report states that five remediation items require or are likely to require extensions, but no formal extension requests have been submitted as of May 2026. risks.impact_description: If necessary extensions are not submitted and approved before due dates, the organization will register overdue audit commitments and may be seen as non-compliant with Internal Audit expectations. This increases the likelihood of negative audit reporting, enterprise-level escalation, and additional scrutiny on CIO governance processes.
risks.mitigation: Identify all remediation items that require or are likely to require extensions and submit extension requests for all items that cannot meet current due dates, as specified in the Path to Green. Track the status of each extension request and ensure approvals are obtained before due dates.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

**Scope:** ICFR Transformation is modernizing the internal control over financial reporting operating model by standardizing SOX processes, simplifying the control universe, and consolidating tooling so that evidence, workflows, and reporting are consistent and sustainable at scale. This matters because current fragmented processes and tools increase compliance cost, dilute governance, and extend testing and audit cycles.

**Current Status:**

Three of eight near-term milestones are complete; five are in progress against May-June 2026 targets. Finance and Technology scope boundaries are confirmed; the control universe rationalization is underway and on track and the self-assessment process pilot program in Protecht is live and receiving positive feedback.

Overall status is Green, driven by timely completion of foundational governance and tooling decisions that de-risk subsequent design and migration work.

## Path to Green

The program is on track against milestone targets, so the focus is on mitigating the top risk of limited stakeholder availability by scheduling key design and approval workshops well in advance and using formal governance forums to keep decisions moving when individual participants are unavailable.

## Milestones

-   12 Jun 2026
    
    -   Present future tooling ecosystem to SteerCo
        
    -   Present 2026 scope to audit committee
        
    -   Walk through updated standard controls proposal with PWC
        
-   30 Jun 2026 – Full launch of self-assessment process program in Protecht
    
-   31 Mar 2027 - Complete ICFR Transformation implementation and transition to steady-state ICFR governance.

risks.title: Tool duplication and fragmented adoption across ICFR tooling ecosystem
risks.description: Multiple tools (Protecht, ADO, SharePoint, legacy repositories, DoubleCheck) currently support overlapping ICFR activities without a clear target-state architecture, risking continued duplication and fragmented adoption even after the transformation.
risks.impact_description: If tool duplication persists, control data may remain fragmented, evidence and testing results may be inconsistent, reporting may lack integrity, and users may experience confusion over system-of-record responsibilities, undermining efficiency, governance, and audit readiness.
risks.mitigation: Define explicit system-of-record roles for each tool, design an integration architecture, select and implement a clear future-state tooling model (Protecht-led or complementary integrated), and develop a repository retirement and migration plan to consolidate control lifecycle data.

risks.title: Change fatigue among control owners participating in ICFR transformation
risks.description: Control owners are already subject to multiple initiatives and may experience change fatigue as new ICFR processes, controls, tooling, and certifications are introduced.
risks.impact_description: If change fatigue grows, control owners may disengage, reduce quality of execution, or revert to legacy practices, leading to inconsistent control performance, incomplete evidence, and failure to sustain the new operating model over time.
risks.mitigation: Simplify control patterns where possible, introduce automation and continuous monitoring to reduce manual burden, provide clear guidance and reusable templates, and sequence changes to avoid overloading control owners during critical periods.

risks.title: PwC may refuse to use internal ICFR tools for audit interactions
risks.description: The external auditor (PwC) has previously been hesitant to use internal tools, and may continue to resist adopting Protecht or related platforms for evidence requests and status updates.
risks.impact_description: If PwC does not use internal tools, audit requests may remain email-based and ad hoc, leading to poor visibility, repeated evidence capture, unclear ownership, and additional administrative effort, and may limit the value of the new ICFR workflow and reporting capabilities.
risks.mitigation: Design and implement a controlled Excel-based exchange model for PwC status updates that integrates into internal workflows, maintain disciplined internal request intake and tracking, and agree on a structured interaction model with PwC early in the program.

risks.title: Over-scoping of ICFR due to conservative posture
risks.description: The organization may continue to define an overly broad ICFR scope, including excessive controls and application coverage, due to conservative risk and audit postures, despite transformation efforts to rationalize.
risks.impact_description: If over-scoping persists, the control universe may remain larger than necessary, driving unnecessary compliance cost and complexity, extending testing and remediation cycles, and making the framework harder to sustain and defend.
risks.mitigation: Apply materiality-led scoping criteria, document risk-based rationale for inclusion/exclusion decisions, align scoping logic with external auditor expectations, and obtain CDA approval for scope changes to avoid conservative drift.

risks.title: Non-integrated access systems and third-party portals may weaken access governance
risks.description: Some systems are not integrated with SailPoint and rely on manual processes or third-party portals, creating potential gaps in provisioning, certification, and deprovisioning controls within the ICFR scope.
risks.impact_description: If non-integrated access systems remain unmanaged, there may be inconsistent or delayed deprovisioning, incomplete access reviews, and increased risk of unauthorized access that could impact ICFR control effectiveness and audit outcomes.
risks.mitigation: Define and implement compensating access controls, establish exception governance for non-integrated systems, design measurable deprovisioning controls, and incorporate these systems into the Access Governance Modernization workstream.

risks.title: Inconsistent evidence quality across ICFR controls
risks.description: Evidence supporting ICFR controls may vary in quality, completeness, and standardization, which can undermine audit readiness and increase rework during testing and external reviews.
risks.impact_description: If evidence quality remains inconsistent, auditors may challenge control effectiveness, additional testing and rework may be required, and compliance cycle time may increase, undermining one of the core objectives of the transformation.

risk_owner.name: Quality Reviewer role / Control Design Authority

mitigation_plan_owner.name: Quality Reviewer role / Track G Lead (Shannon)

risks.mitigation: Define standard evidence patterns and requirements, embed evidence standards into workflow and templates, establish a quality review function to validate sufficiency, and provide reusable job aids and training to control owners.

risks.title: Program sprawl and excessive stakeholder model may dilute focus and slow decisions
risks.description: The ICFR transformation program may expand its scope or stakeholder base excessively, resulting in complex governance, slow decision-making, and blurred accountability.
risks.impact_description: If the program becomes overly broad with too many stakeholders, decision cycles may lengthen, priorities may become unclear, and delivery of key workstreams could be delayed or under-resourced, impacting achievement of year-1 outcomes and overall objectives.
risks.mitigation: Maintain a lean core team and a small, decision-capable Control Design Authority; define clear roles and decision rights; use structured decision forums; and manage scope through formal change control to avoid uncontrolled expansion.

risks.title: Limited stakeholder availability may delay ICFR design and implementation
risks.description: Key finance, operations, business, compliance, IT, and audit stakeholders may not have sufficient time to participate in workshops, reviews, and approvals, which could slow or stall the design, validation, and implementation of the modernized ICFR operating model.
risks.impact_description: If stakeholder availability is limited, critical design decisions may be delayed, future-state processes may not reflect operational reality, implementation timelines could slip, and the project may miss ICFR reporting and audit timelines, reducing the effectiveness and credibility of the transformation.
risks.mitigation: Plan and schedule workshops well in advance, secure Sponsor and leadership support to prioritize stakeholder time, use focused, time-boxed sessions, provide asynchronous review options, and track attendance and decisions through a formal governance cadence to keep momentum even when some stakeholders are unavailable.

risks.title: Competing business priorities may reduce participation from control owners and functional leads
risks.description: Control owners and functional leaders may prioritize other initiatives or operational demands over participation in the ICFR transformation activities, reducing timely engagement in design, testing, and adoption.
risks.impact_description: If key control owners and functional leaders do not engage, the project may deliver designs that lack buy-in, suffer from delays in approvals and adoption, and face implementation issues that compromise the effectiveness and sustainability of the new ICFR framework.
risks.mitigation: Escalate prioritization needs through the Sponsor and business leadership, clearly communicate project value and regulatory importance, align project milestones with business calendars, and incorporate ICFR tasks into performance objectives for key leaders and control owners.

risks.title: Inconsistent existing documentation may increase effort required for assessment and standardization
risks.description: Current SOX and ICFR documentation is inconsistent in quality, format, and completeness, which may increase the complexity and effort needed to perform current-state assessment, gap analysis, and standardization.
risks.impact_description: If documentation inconsistency is higher than anticipated, timelines for assessment and rationalization may extend, resource requirements may increase, and some controls or processes may be misinterpreted, leading to potential gaps in the future-state framework and additional rework.
risks.mitigation: Define clear documentation standards upfront, prioritize critical processes and high-risk areas for early review, allocate dedicated resources for documentation clean-up, and use templates and guidance to drive consistency during remediation of existing materials.

risks.title: Change resistance may slow adoption of new ICFR processes, templates, and tools
risks.description: Control owners, process teams, and other stakeholders may resist changes to established ICFR processes, documentation standards, and tooling, slowing adoption of the future-state operating model.
risks.impact_description: If change resistance is significant, the project may achieve only partial adoption, leading to inconsistent execution, mixed evidence quality, and limited realization of efficiency and governance benefits, as well as potential audit challenges.
risks.mitigation: Implement structured change management and communication plans, deliver role-based training and office hours, highlight quick wins, involve stakeholders in design decisions through governance forums, and use leadership sponsorship to reinforce expectations and accountability.

risks.title: Technology dependencies or approval delays may impact implementation timing for system enablement
risks.description: If supporting technology changes, integrations, or new tools require extended architecture, security, or procurement approvals, implementation of system-enabled ICFR capabilities may be delayed.
risks.impact_description: Delays in technology decisions or approvals could push back deployment of tooling for control repository, workflow, evidence management, and reporting, resulting in prolonged reliance on fragmented legacy tools and limiting the ability to achieve the desired automation and transparency within the project timeline.
risks.mitigation: Engage enterprise architecture, security, and procurement teams early; define and agree tooling decision criteria; prepare required documentation in advance; and schedule governance checkpoints to obtain timely approvals for Protecht/ADO and related integrations.

assumptions.title: Required stakeholders will be available for ICFR transformation activities
assumptions.description: Finance, operations, business, compliance, IT, and audit stakeholders will be available to support workshops, reviews, and approvals required for the ICFR transformation program.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The program relies on cross-functional expertise and decision-making; without active stakeholder participation, design and implementation cannot proceed effectively.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Stakeholder availability is typically constrained, but given Sponsor backing and the regulatory importance of ICFR, it is reasonable to assume that critical participants will prioritize involvement once schedules and expectations are clearly communicated.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If key stakeholders are repeatedly unavailable, secure delegate representation, adjust schedules, escalate to leadership for prioritization, or narrow scope to areas with engaged ownership while planning a later wave for others.
assumptions.validation_method: Track actual attendance and participation in early workshops and governance meetings; escalate gaps through Sponsor and leadership if patterns of non-participation emerge.

assumptions.title: Scope decisions and design principles will be confirmed in a timely manner
assumptions.description: Key scope decisions and design principles for the ICFR operating model will be confirmed quickly enough to maintain project momentum.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The program is structured around phases and workstreams that depend on clear, agreed scope and design principles to proceed without rework.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The creation of a Control Design Authority and explicit governance expectations for Sponsor approval are intended to streamline decision-making, making it reasonable to assume that scope and design principles will be confirmed within agreed timelines.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If decisions are delayed, escalate to the Sponsor and CDA, time-box discussions, adopt provisional decisions for pilots, or de-scope contentious elements to avoid blocking the entire program.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor timing of key governance decisions versus planned milestones; review decision log for aging items and resolution timelines.

assumptions.title: Existing SOX documentation and process information will be accessible for review
assumptions.description: Existing SOX documentation, testing artifacts, and process information will be available and accessible to the project team for assessment and rationalization.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Current-state assessment and gap analysis depend on access to existing control documentation and testing records across tools and repositories.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current ICFR and SOX operations rely on these documents, indicating that they exist and are used; the main risk is access permissions and completeness, but a high level of availability is expected.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If documentation is missing or inaccessible, engage system owners to restore or grant access, prioritize recreation for high-risk areas, and adjust timelines to allow for targeted documentation reconstruction.
assumptions.validation_method: Attempt access to key repositories and sample documents early; confirm permissions and completeness with document owners and audit teams.

assumptions.title: Funding and resourcing for approved scope will be made available
assumptions.description: Budget and human resources needed to execute the approved ICFR transformation scope will be provided by the organization.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The project has been chartered as a strategic initiative, implying alignment to funding and resourcing plans.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Regulatory and governance importance of ICFR modernization increases the likelihood of funding approval, but competing enterprise priorities could still impact allocations, so confidence is moderate rather than absolute.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If full funding is not secured, prioritize highest risk and value workstreams, phase implementation over longer timelines, or seek additional funding through governance channels.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm allocated budget and headcount against the approved charter; review funding approvals and staffing assignments during mobilization.

assumptions.title: Sponsor and business leadership will actively support adoption and decision-making
assumptions.description: The Sponsor and business leadership will provide active support for adoption of new processes and tools and will participate in timely decision-making throughout the project.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Effective transformation requires visible leadership support to drive adoption, resolve conflicts, and prioritize ICFR work among competing initiatives.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Formal Sponsor approval and alignment with broader modernization and governance priorities indicate strong leadership interest, making ongoing support reasonably likely.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If leadership engagement declines, escalate through governance forums, highlight regulatory and risk implications, and adjust communications to better align with leadership needs and priorities.
assumptions.validation_method: Observe Sponsor and leadership participation in steering meetings, approvals, and communications; track escalations and their resolution times.

assumptions.title: Control universe can be reduced from ~751 to approximately 600 controls
assumptions.description: It is feasible to rationalize the current control universe of approximately 751 controls to a more focused set of around 600 controls without compromising ICFR effectiveness.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Preliminary analysis indicates over-scoping and overly granular or duplicative controls, suggesting rationalization opportunities.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Experience in similar programs often reveals rationalization opportunities; however, constraints from auditors or regulatory interpretations may limit the extent of reduction, so confidence is moderate.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the control universe cannot be reduced as much as planned, focus on simplifying execution, automating key controls, and improving evidence quality to reduce operational burden without significant reduction in control count.
assumptions.validation_method: Perform detailed control rationalization analysis (Track C), including mapping to risks and processes, and review proposed reductions with CDA and external auditors.

validation_owner.name: Track C Leads (Veronica G for business processes, Mark Brady for ITGC)

assumptions.title: Application scope can be reduced through materiality-led scoping
assumptions.description: The in-scope application population for ICFR can be reduced by applying materiality and risk-based scoping criteria.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Current discussions and observations suggest that application scope may extend beyond what is necessary for material financial reporting risks.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Preliminary discussions indicate that some applications are conservatively included; however, external auditor alignment is required to confirm reductions, leading to moderate confidence.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If application scope cannot be materially reduced, focus on standardizing and automating controls across the existing application set and implement more efficient testing and evidence processes to offset the complexity.
assumptions.validation_method: Conduct a formal ICFR scoping and risk assessment (Track B) based on financial statement line items, materiality thresholds, and system dependencies, and validate with external auditors.

assumptions.title: Selected controls can be shifted from per-application to domain/platform or process-level design
assumptions.description: It will be possible to redesign selected controls from a per-application or per-product basis to domain, platform, or process-level controls.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Current-state controls show app-centric design that may not be necessary when risks can be managed at higher levels, reducing duplication.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The nature of many ITGCs and process controls lends itself to higher-level design, but technical and organizational constraints, as well as auditor expectations, will influence feasibility, hence moderate confidence.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If shifting controls proves infeasible in some areas, maintain necessary application-level controls while focusing on standardization and automation to limit incremental overhead.
assumptions.validation_method: Identify candidate controls during Track C rationalization, design higher-level controls, and review with CDA, process owners, and auditors to confirm acceptability.

validation_owner.name: Track C Leads (Veronica G and Mark Brady)

dependencies.consumer: Platform & Tooling (Track A) and overall ICFR Transformation design
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in the tooling decision will postpone configuration, migration, and integration work, risking delay of control rationalization and reporting improvements.
dependencies.mitigation: Complete capability assessments within the first 6 weeks, establish time-bound decision governance, and define interim use of existing tools if needed.

decisions.title: Future-state ICFR tooling model selection
decisions.description: Determine whether the enterprise will adopt a Protecht-led consolidation model, where Protecht becomes the primary platform for control repository, self-assessment, certification, testing results, issue tracking, and reporting, or a complementary integrated model where Protecht is the enterprise ICFR repository while ADO and SharePoint are used as the primary workflow and evidence repositories for control execution.
decisions.rationale: A clear tooling model is required to eliminate fragmentation, define system-of-record boundaries, improve workflow clarity, and enable integrated reporting and evidence management.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Protecht-led consolidation replacing DoubleCheck and reducing reliance on fragmented repositories; 2) Complementary integrated model with Protecht as ICFR repository and ADO/SharePoint as workflow and evidence tools.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependent on Protecht capability deep-dive, ADO usage assessment, and defined decision criteria; impacts Platform & Tooling (Track A) and migration planning.

decisions.title: ICFR Transformation governance structure and track lead model
decisions.description: Confirm the ICFR Transformation governance structure, including the Steering Committee, Program Steering Group, Control Design Authority (CDA), program coordination roles, and named leads for Tracks A–G (Platform & Tooling, ICFR Scoping & Risk Assessment, Control Rationalization, Ownership & Certification, Access Governance, Continuous Control Monitoring, and Change Management & Adoption).

decision_owner.name: Executive Sponsors (Andrea Blatter and Jason Escaravage)

decisions.rationale: A formalised governance structure with clearly defined executive sponsors, program coordinators, CDA membership, and track leads is required to ensure accountable decision-making, coordinated delivery across seven concurrent transformation tracks, and effective oversight of ICFR modernization activities.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Supports existing dependency 'Cross-functional coordination for process changes' by defining accountable leads and governance forums across Finance, IT, Internal Audit, Compliance, and business control owners.

objectives.description: Program PMO: Govern delivery across all seven ICFR transformation tracks, including milestones, RAID (risks, actions, issues, decisions), and consolidated reporting under Steering Committee oversight.

Track A – Platform & Tooling: Define the target-state ICFR tooling architecture and govern all platform decisions, including the Protecht vs. ADO model, the auditor request workflow, and the 360° reporting layer.

Track B – ICFR Scoping & Risk Assessment: Refresh the enterprise ICFR compliance scope using materiality, business process analysis, and system dependency mapping, and align the resulting scope posture with PwC.

Track C – Control Rationalization: Reduce and rationalize the ICFR control universe from ~751 controls to a defensible, risk-based set and shift from per-application to domain and platform-level control design patterns.

Track D – Ownership & Certification: Define clear accountability for every ICFR control—from Design Authority through to Certifier—and implement a formalized quarterly certification cycle in Protecht.

Track E – Access Governance: Strengthen access governance across SailPoint-integrated and non-integrated systems, including defined exception handling for third-party portals and a measurable governance cadence.

Track F – Continuous Control Monitoring (CCM): Build a prioritized CCM capability by identifying practical, data-supported automation use cases and evaluating the right platform to scale monitoring beyond manual testing.

Track G – Change Management & Adoption: Ensure ICFR transformation changes in process and tooling are effectively adopted and sustained through targeted communications, role-based training, and adoption measurement.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

**Scope:** The HIPAA Compliance Program delivers a centrally governed HIPAA control and oversight model for Thomson Reuters products, services, and enterprise functions, so the business can reduce regulatory, contractual, and reputational risk while remaining scalable. Outcomes include a HIPAA-aligned control framework, updated BAAs and breach processes, PHI inventories, and product-specific assessments and remediation across priority offerings such as HighQ, SIU, Legal Tracker, Contract Express, CLEAR, and CoCounsel.

**Current Status:**

Of 9 defined product and process milestones, 1 is complete, 7 are in progress with zero schedule variance, and 1 is slated to begin next mont. All June 2026 deliverables remain aligned to their 30 Jun 2026 targets. The Contract Express final HIPAA gap assessment was delivered 3 Jun 2026. CoCounsel FedRamp and v.2 Commercial HIPAA assessment is scheduled to complete on 15 Jun 2026.

Overall status is Green, driven by key product assessments and remediations tracking to plan with no material schedule slippage

## Path to Green

The project is green. The top mitigation focus is on executing SIU and Legal Tracker remediation to meet their 30 Jun 2026 and 31 Dec 2026 deadlines respectively, with progress monitored via Protecht and any delays escalated through the SteerCo to protect year-end compliance commitments.

## Milestones

-   15 Jun 2026 - Finish CoCounsel FedRamp and v.2 Commercial HIPAA assessment
    
-   30 Jun 2026 - Complete HighQ HIPAA remediation, SIU Professional Services remediation of most gaps, and the CLEAR HIPAA assessment for CLEAR, CLEAR Batch, and CLEAR Investigate.
    
-   30 Sep 2026 - Complete deep-dive data handling assessments for additional Professional Services groups
    
-   31 Dec 2026 - Complete all remaining SIU Professional Services HIPAA remediation, deliver Legal Tracker remediation for its year-end HIPAA deadline, and update HIPAA breach notification requirements in legal notification playbooks

risks.title: Inadequate or outdated HIPAA policies, BAAs, training, and breach notification processes
risks.description: Policies, contract templates (BAAs/BASAs), training procedures, and breach notification playbooks are being reviewed and updated as part of the HIPAA program. Until updates are complete and rolled out, there is a risk that current materials may not reflect the desired future state or regulatory expectations.
risks.impact_description: If outdated or incomplete policies, contract templates, training, or breach notification procedures remain in use, employees and customers may receive inconsistent or incorrect guidance. This could lead to misaligned BAAs, inadequate training coverage, or mishandled breach/disclosure events, resulting in compliance gaps or adverse regulatory findings.

raised_by.name: HIPAA Compliance Program Scope document and April 23, 2026 Status Report

risks.mitigation: Continue updating the HIPAA compliance program charter, BAAs, HIPAA Privacy Notice, training procedures, and breach notification requirements. Distribute updated notices and templates (e.g., U.S. health plan HIPAA Privacy Notice issued in February 2026; updated BAAs delivered to suppliers and customers), assign and monitor training completion, and embed updated requirements into legal notification playbooks.

risks.title: Competing priorities may limit product and operational teams’ capacity for HIPAA assessment and remediation
risks.description: Product and operational teams may have limited bandwidth due to competing priorities, which could constrain their ability to participate in HIPAA assessments, scope validation, and remediation work.
risks.impact_description: If teams cannot allocate sufficient time and resources to HIPAA activities, assessments and remediation may be delayed or incomplete. This could result in extended periods of noncompliance, missed project milestones, delayed implementation of controls, and increased risk exposure for TR and its customers.

mitigation_plan_owner.name: Program Manager for HIPAA Compliance Program

risks.mitigation: Establish program governance with a SteerCo to drive accountability, prioritize HIPAA workstreams, and secure leadership support for resource allocation. Clearly communicate expectations to product and operational teams, integrate HIPAA activities into planning cycles, and track progress through program artifacts such as milestones, timelines, and RAAID logs.

risks.title: Variability in product architectures and data flows may prevent a single uniform HIPAA solution
risks.description: Products and services differ in architectures, data flows, and contractual commitments, which may make it difficult to implement a single standardized HIPAA compliance solution across all in-scope areas.
risks.impact_description: If a one-size-fits-all approach is pursued but proves infeasible, some products may end up with misaligned or ineffective controls. This variability could lead to uneven compliance levels, increased complexity in monitoring and audits, and potential gaps where specific product risks are not adequately addressed.

mitigation_plan_owner.name: R&C and Privacy in coordination with Product/Engineering

risks.mitigation: Develop a business-aligned control framework that distinguishes between enterprise-level controls and product-specific requirements. Tailor remediation plans to each product’s architecture and data flows while maintaining common control objectives, and leverage lessons learned from early assessments (e.g., HighQ, SIU, Legal Tracker) to build reusable patterns.

risks.title: Phased implementation may extend beyond initial project window
risks.description: The need for phased implementation across multiple products and services means that full HIPAA compliance maturity may require stages beyond the initial project timeline (2025-07-07 to 2027-12-31).
risks.impact_description: If the program cannot achieve full maturity within the initial project window, some products may remain partially compliant, with incomplete remediation or monitoring. This could necessitate extended funding, increase program management complexity, and leave residual compliance and operational risks unaddressed for a longer period.

mitigation_plan_owner.name: Program Manager for HIPAA Compliance Program

risks.mitigation: Plan and communicate a phased roadmap that clearly identifies which capabilities and products will be addressed in each stage, including post-project activities. Secure long-term sponsorship and funding for ongoing compliance work, and embed HIPAA guidance into the broader product compliance framework to support ongoing scalability.

risks.title: Unclear decisions on signing BAAs/BASAs during discovery and remediation phases
risks.description: The program has not yet finalized decisions on whether to sign BAAs/BASAs for in-scope products during the discovery phase or before remediation is complete, and whether to unwind existing contracts for products without valid PHI use cases.
risks.impact_description: If decisions about BAAs/BASAs are not clarified, sales and legal teams may take inconsistent positions, either accepting excessive risk by signing agreements prematurely or missing revenue opportunities by declining deals. Existing contracts may also remain in place where TR cannot or should not support PHI, exposing the company to contractual and compliance risk.

raised_by.name: HIPAA Compliance Program Scope document (Critical Decisions sections)

risks.mitigation: Use the SteerCo to define and approve a clear decision framework for BAAs/BASAs, including conditions under which they can be signed during discovery or remediation, and any time limits. Determine criteria and processes for unwinding contracts where there is no valid PHI use case. Communicate this guidance to Sales, Commercial Excellence, and Customer Trust teams as part of the broader awareness campaign.

risks.title: Lack of clarity from FedRamp-based HIPAA assessments for C-Track and Case Center
risks.description: For C-Track and Case Center, Fortreum conducted assessments within the FedRamp space, but the reports did not provide clear remediation guidance for identified HIPAA gaps.
risks.impact_description: Without clear remediation guidance, the product teams may be uncertain how to address HIPAA gaps, delaying remediation and limiting the ability to confidently issue BAAs. This could stall sales opportunities, leave compliance gaps unaddressed, and increase regulatory and contractual risk.

risk_owner.name: Product owners for C-Track and Case Center

risks.mitigation: R&C and Privacy will review the Fortreum assessment results, interpret the findings, and provide detailed remediation guidance to the C-Track and Case Center teams before BAAs are issued. Align the remediation steps with the HIPAA control framework and track them through Protecht or equivalent tooling.

risks.title: Potential gaps in SIU Professional Services remediation execution
risks.description: Although the SIU Professional Services HIPAA assessment is complete and a remediation plan has been developed, remediation is staged through the end of 2026, and not all gaps will be resolved by mid-2026.
risks.impact_description: If planned SIU remediation activities are delayed or not fully implemented, SIU services may remain partially noncompliant while being sold under BAAs, exposing TR to compliance and contractual risk. Extended timelines also increase the window during which issues could result in incidents or audit findings.

mitigation_plan_owner.name: SIU Professional Services remediation project lead

risks.mitigation: Execute against the defined remediation plan with milestones targeting completion of most gaps by the end of Q2 2026 and all gaps by the end of 2026. Monitor progress via Protecht or program dashboards, escalate delays to the SteerCo, and adjust resources as needed to meet deadlines.

risks.title: Legal Tracker remediation year-end deadlines
risks.description: The Legal Tracker HIPAA assessment is complete, and remediation planning is underway with deadlines expected by year-end.
risks.impact_description: If Legal Tracker remediation is not fully planned and implemented by the year-end deadline, Legal Tracker may continue to operate with HIPAA gaps, affecting its ability to support existing and new customers under BAAs and potentially exposing TR to compliance and contractual risk.
risks.mitigation: Finalize the remediation plan and hold regular working sessions between Privacy and product engineering teams to track implementation. Align the timeline with the year-end completion target and escalate any blockers to the SteerCo.

risks.title: Existing BAAs may have requirements for PHI ingestion and breach notification.
risks.description: Privacy is currently identifying and reviewing existing BAA’s to ensure tools have been properly scoped for ingestion of PHI and flagging contracts with breach notifications requirements less than 5 days with ISRM and Customer Trust.
risks.mitigation: Privacy reviewing existing BAAs to ensure compliance

assumptions.title: Product managers and business owners will participate in scope validation and use-case review
assumptions.description: The program assumes that product managers and business owners will actively participate in validating HIPAA scope and reviewing use cases where PHI may be processed.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Accurate identification of in-scope products and PHI use cases requires detailed knowledge held by product managers and business owners, and the program is designed around their engagement.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The corporate culture and governance model generally require product and business owner involvement in compliance projects; however, competing priorities could limit their availability, so this assumption is reasonable but not guaranteed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If engagement is lower than expected, escalate to segment and functional leadership, leverage SteerCo authority to mandate participation, and consider dedicating central resources or business analysts to perform additional discovery in under-engaged areas.
assumptions.validation_method: Track participation of product managers and business owners in scope workshops, assessments, and reviews; confirm that each product with potential PHI use cases has documented input from its owner.

validation_owner.name: Program Manager for HIPAA Compliance Program

assumptions.title: Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance will continue to provide centralized guidance
assumptions.description: The project assumes that existing support functions, specifically the Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance, will continue to provide centralized guidance for HIPAA compliance activities.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The future-state HIPAA compliance framework and oversight model rely on these functions to define controls, policies, and monitoring, and they are already acting as central guidance providers.
assumptions.validity_explanation: These functions are integral to enterprise risk and privacy governance and are already leading aspects of the HIPAA program, making it highly likely they will continue to provide guidance throughout the project.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If centralized guidance capacity is reduced, appoint interim leaders or expand responsibilities of existing officers (e.g., interim HIPAA Compliance Officer) and consider external advisory support to maintain momentum.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm that Privacy Office and Risk & Compliance maintain dedicated roles for HIPAA and continue participating in SteerCo, program design, and assessments.

assumptions.title: Leadership sponsorship from the Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer will remain in place
assumptions.description: The project assumes that the Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer will continue to sponsor the HIPAA Controls Enhancement Program.

owner.name: Chief Operating & Technology Officer and Chief Legal Officer

assumptions.rationale_basis: Executive sponsorship is critical to secure funding, resources, and cross-functional participation for a multi-year HIPAA program.
assumptions.validity_explanation: While executive sponsorship is currently strong, leadership priorities can shift over a multi-year period, so continued sponsorship is likely but not guaranteed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If sponsorship weakens, seek formal endorsement from broader executive leadership (e.g., RC, O&T, Legal leadership), present risk and compliance implications, and adjust program scope to focus on highest-risk areas while attempting to regain executive support.
assumptions.validation_method: Review SteerCo membership and confirm ongoing participation and approvals from the sponsoring executives; monitor whether their directives continue to support the program.

assumptions.title: Contractual obligations imposing HIPAA-like requirements can be identified and included in scope
assumptions.description: The project assumes that contractual obligations (BAAs/BASAs or BAA-like clauses) that impose HIPAA or HIPAA-like requirements on products not directly regulated will be identifiable and can be incorporated into scope assessments.
assumptions.rationale_basis: To ensure comprehensive coverage, the program must account for contractual obligations beyond strictly regulated HIPAA products, and this requires being able to identify such obligations in contracts.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial contract searches have begun and data dumps are being produced, indicating feasibility; however, contract complexity and legacy agreements may make it difficult to ensure 100% coverage.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If comprehensive identification proves difficult, prioritize high-risk segments (e.g., healthcare, insurance, GLLF) and implement forward-looking controls such as standardized BAA templates and contract intake processes to better capture future obligations.
assumptions.validation_method: Complete contract searches for BAAs/BASAs and BAA-like clauses, validate findings against proposed in-scope products, and confirm with legal and commercial teams that the coverage is comprehensive.

assumptions.title: Funding and staffing will be sufficient to execute assessments and initial control enhancements
assumptions.description: The program assumes that funding and staffing levels will be adequate to complete HIPAA assessments, gap analyses, and initial control enhancement roadmaps across in-scope products and services.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The scope of assessments and remediation (including external advisory support) requires material investment and dedicated resources over multiple years.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Some funding and staffing have already been secured, but future phases and remediation costs may require additional approvals, creating some uncertainty.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If funding or staffing constraints arise, re-prioritize assessments and remediation to focus on highest-risk products and obligations, leverage external advisors selectively, and seek incremental funding with clear justification based on risk reduction and contractual requirements.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor budget approvals, actual spend, and staffing assignments against the planned assessment and remediation roadmap.

assumptions.title: Steering Committee (SteerCo) and program governance will be established and effective
assumptions.description: The program assumes that a SteerCo with representation from key functions (Commercial Excellence, GCO, O&T, Product, Finance, etc.) will be formed and will effectively drive accountability and decision-making.

owner.name: HIPAA Program Sponsor and Program Manager

assumptions.rationale_basis: The complexity and cross-functional nature of HIPAA compliance requires a governance body to prioritize work, resolve trade-offs, and oversee risk decisions.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial steps toward governance (identifying membership and scheduling kickoff) are underway, but effectiveness will depend on ongoing engagement and clarity of mandate.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If SteerCo participation or effectiveness is weak, refine the charter, seek stronger executive sponsorship, adjust membership, or institute smaller working groups with delegated authority for operational decisions.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm SteerCo formation, membership, charter, and regular meeting cadence; evaluate whether key decisions and escalations are being handled through this forum.

assumptions.title: Scope of in-scope products can be accurately determined based on upload capability and known PHI use cases
assumptions.description: The program assumes that focusing on products with upload capabilities and known PHI-related patterns will allow accurate determination of which products and services are in-scope for HIPAA.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Upload capability is a primary driver of whether customers can input PHI, and initial surveys have identified specific patterns (interaction with clients of customers, matter/document management, billing products).
assumptions.validity_explanation: The approach is aligned with how customers typically supply PHI (through file uploads and similar mechanisms), but edge cases or indirect data flows may still exist.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If gaps emerge during audits or data handling reviews, expand the scoping methodology to include additional criteria (e.g., integrations, logs, support channels) and revisit products initially deemed out of scope.
assumptions.validation_method: Compare scope results against contract data (BAAs/BASAs), customer use cases, and findings from data handling reviews to confirm that no significant PHI-processing products are overlooked.

validation_owner.name: R&C and Privacy in partnership with Product

assumptions.title: Planned HIPAA assessments (HighQ, SIU, Legal Tracker, Contract Express, CLEAR, CoCounsel, etc.) will be completed on current timelines
assumptions.description: The program assumes that the scheduled HIPAA assessments for key products will be completed as planned (e.g., HighQ remediation by June 30, 2026; SIU gaps mostly remediated by end of Q2 2026; Legal Tracker by year-end).
assumptions.rationale_basis: Program planning and stakeholder expectations are built around these timelines for assessments and remediation.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current progress suggests timelines are achievable, but dependencies on external advisors, internal resources, and product priorities introduce uncertainty.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If assessment timelines slip, adjust remediation priorities, communicate revised timelines to stakeholders, and consider allocating additional resources or simplifying scope for initial phases.
assumptions.validation_method: Track assessment milestones, deliverable dates, and remediation plan approvals for each product against the program schedule.

## Executive Summary

**Scope:** TR Government Baseline Compliance delivers a single, enterprise-approved compliance standard across in-scope government-facing products, based on NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, 45 additional TR privacy controls, and applicable HIPAA requirements. This will reduce security and regulatory risk, unlock government sales opportunities, and establish a repeatable framework to demonstrate control maturity to government and public-sector customers.

**Current Status:** Overall, the status is Green. The critical funding milestone (2027 EPC case) was presented to the Executive Committee 26 May 2026 and is progressing on plan with zero schedule variance.

## Path to Green

The project is currently green. The primary risk to maintaining this status is the 2027 EPC funding approval. The committee may approve less than the full 2027 budget ask. Should partial funding be confirmed, the PMO will present a revised prioritized scope and adjusted schedule, ranking products in order of criticality to protect the highest-value deliverables within the available budget.

## Milestones

-   15 Sep 2026 - Detailed project plan and resource plan baselined; in-scope product list finalized
    
-   15 Oct 2026 - Kick off sessions completed with all in-scope product groups
    
-   31 Dec 2027 - TR Government Baseline Compliance delivered across all in-scope products

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

This program is migrating all HighQ applications from 13 third‑party colocation sites into Azure so those facilities can be decommissioned and associated dilapidation and closure activities completed, reducing external data center dependence and cost. The outcome is a fully cloud‑hosted HighQ footprint with all legacy colos exited once client data retention obligations are met.

To date, 0 of 13 sites have been fully migrated and shut down against a target of 13 of 13 by 31 Dec 2026, with 11 sites planned for completion by 30 Sep 2026 and the remaining 2 sites (SG1 and SG2 in the UK) completing by 31 Dec 2026 due to contract and data‑availability requirements. All key milestones retain their planned or latest‑estimate dates, and no schedule variance has been recorded on the core migration and decom submission activities.

Overall status is Green, driven by a defined migration and closure schedule that incorporates client requests for extended data availability at SG1 and SG2 while still achieving full exit of the 13 colos by 31 Dec 2026. Tracking progress of all sites closely to ensure no slippage.

## Path to Green

All HighQ sites are now trending as Green.

The primary mitigation focus is on managing migration‑phase issues or client date changes by working closely with business stakeholders to assess impact and adjust individual migration windows so that colo exit dates and cost exposure remain within the current 2026 plan.

## Milestones

-   Complete the final client migrations to Azure and the associated monitoring period for all 13 HighQ sites by 31 Dec 2026, achieving 100% migration and shutdown of the legacy colos.
    
-   Submit decommission requests for all HighQ sites following the final migrations so that 100% of decoms are lodged by 30 Sep 2026.
    
-   Complete dilapidation and closure activities for all HighQ third‑party sites, including SG1 and SG2, by 31 Dec 2026.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Sydney DC Exit Project is delivering the full migration of business applications out of the Sydney colo and completing dilapidation works so the site can be exited and ongoing data centre costs removed. This enables consolidation onto strategic platforms and reduces operational risk from aging on-premise infrastructure.

So far 0 of 4 migration batches have been completed, with Batch 1 (covering 25% of BU applications) in progress on its planned schedule from 01 May 2026 to 31 Oct 2026. Remaining batches are defined with a final batch target of 100% of BU applications migrated by 31 Mar 2027, followed by closure activities by 31 May 2027 against a program end date of 30 Jun 2027.

Overall status is Green, driven by migration activities starting on the planned dates and a clear phased path to reach 100% application migration before colo closure.

## Path to Green

The primary risk is dependency on VMware and Solaris migrations, which could delay colo exit and increase running costs, so the team is reviewing and sequencing VMware migration plans and build requirements to keep the overall 30 Jun 2027 exit date whole.

## Milestones

- Complete review of VMware migration plans and related issues by 27 May 2026.
- Complete Migrating Apps Batch 1 (25% of BU applications) by 31 Oct 2026.
- Complete Migrating Apps Batch 4 (targeting 100% of BU applications migrated from Sydney colo) by 31 Mar 2027.
- Complete dilapidation and colo closure activities by 31 May 2027.
- Exit the Sydney colo and transition to steady-state operations by 30 Jun 2027.
