## Executive Summary

The Payments Unification – Stripe Program is consolidating Thomson Reuters’ fragmented PASS and SAP-based payment and fraud platforms into a unified Stripe architecture across Canada and US Legal. This enables capabilities such as default AutoPay, 3DS authentication, unified notifications, and Enterprise Data Lake reporting driving reduced operational complexity, improved regulatory control, and consistent payment experiences across SSP, eStores, IVR, and related channels.

For **Canada Phase 2.1**, System Integration Testing (SIT) is in progress with **10 of 37 end-to-end test cases completed** and **17 currently in execution**. SIT experienced a **7-day delayed start**, with completion now forecasted for **June 12, 2026** (vs. June 5 baseline).

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) commenced on **June 1, 2026**, with **66 business test cases identified and in execution**, tracking to the planned completion date of **July 2, 2026**.

**Overall program status remains GREEN**, with delivery progressing through SIT and UAT, schedule variance contained, and key scope and architectural decisions locked.

* * *

## **Path to Green (Focus Areas)**

While delivery remains on track, current SIT findings reinforce the need for stronger **upfront requirement maturity and cross-system integration alignment** to minimize downstream rework and improve execution efficiency.

* * *

## **Key Risks & Observations**

### **1\. Integration & Technical Alignment**

-   Gaps in **Stripe vs. non-Stripe payment handling** across hybrid flows
    
-   **Legacy system compatibility constraints** impacting end-to-end workflows
    
-   **Data synchronization challenges** across Stripe, SAP, and downstream systems, requiring webhook-based event handling
    

Result: Design adjustments required to align **SAP-driven processing with Stripe’s event-based (webhook) architecture**

* * *

### **2\. Requirement Maturity & Scope Clarity**

-   **One-time payment scenarios** required refinement during SIT
    
-   **Micro-deposit handling** reclassified from defect to **scope/design gap**
    
-   **Customer notification requirements (EN/FR)** not fully defined upfront
    

Result: Several SIT defects were reclassified as **requirement or design gaps**, increasing rework during testing

* * *

## **Current Status & Mitigation**

-   Code fixes for identified issues **implemented and deployed (June 2, 2026)**
    
-   SIT team actively **retesting impacted scenarios**
    
-   Issues are **contained within SIT phase** with no current impact to overall program milestones
    

**Focus:**

-   Drive closure of remaining SIT defects
    
-   Ensure stability prior to UAT scale-up
    
-   Prevent recurrence through improved governance in upcoming phases (US Legal)
    

* * *

## **Key Milestones**

-   **SIT Completion (Canada 2.1):** June 12, 2026
    
-   **UAT Completion (Canada 2.1):** July 2, 2026
    
-   **Canada 2.1 Go-Live:** July 11, 2026
    
-   **US Legal 2.2 – Requirements & Refinement:** June 30, 2026
    
-   **Program Completion:** June 30, 2027

risks.title: Banking regulation and fraud compliance requirements for direct debit may not be identified in time
risks.description: Targeted research into banking regulation and fraud compliance for direct debit (bank accounts) versus credit card processing has not yet been completed. The project team needs explicit direction on what billing details and controls must be implemented in customer-facing systems (UI) for bank-account workflows, including fraud response requirements and how bank-account handling must differ from card workflows.
risks.impact_description: If the regulatory and fraud-compliance requirements for direct debit are not identified and confirmed in time, the Stripe-based banking/direct debit capabilities for Canada may be designed or implemented in a non-compliant way. This could lead to regulatory breaches, the need for significant rework of UI and process flows, delays to go-live for direct debit features, or forced disablement of bank-account payment options. It could also require disruptive changes for customers if bank-account workflows must later be altered, and may expose Thomson Reuters to legal and financial penalties.
risks.mitigation: Rachel Torgerson will engage Treasury to obtain guidance on applicable banking regulations for Canada and the required controls for direct debit versus credit card processing. A compliance owner will be identified to provide authoritative requirements for billing details, fraud response, and differentiating bank-account workflows from card workflows. The outputs of this research will be incorporated into the business and technical requirements for the Stripe program before finalizing designs for direct debit flows.

risks.title: 3DS enforcement posture for Canada may remain undefined after standard 3DS adoption
risks.description: Following the decision to adopt standard 3D Secure (3DS) redirect implementation for Canada (WI 1189631), a follow-on decision is required to define how aggressively Thomson Reuters will enforce 3DS (e.g., build and release deactivated versus activated). This includes decisions on redirect and callback handling in DCP eStores and SSP and how 3DS is used across flows.
risks.impact_description: If the 3DS enforcement posture (e.g., always-on, risk-based, or initially deactivated) is not clearly defined, the program may implement 3DS capabilities without a consistent business strategy. This could result in inconsistent customer experiences across channels, suboptimal fraud and authorization outcomes, and potential rework to change configurations post-implementation. It may also create uncertainty for channel teams (DCP eStores, SSP) about required UI and redirect behaviors and could delay rollout if disagreements arise late in the cycle.
risks.mitigation: Schedule and conduct a decision meeting between business and architecture to define the desired 3DS enforcement posture for Canada, including whether 3DS is released initially deactivated or activated and under what conditions. Document the decision and ensure it is reflected in configuration, channel implementation guidance, and rollout plans. Confirm that redirect and callback patterns are fully supported in DCP eStores and SSP regardless of the chosen enforcement level.

assumptions.title: All recurring direct debit bank accounts for Canada are treated as business accounts with no special UI fields
assumptions.description: For Canada recurring direct debit setup in GuestPay and SSP journeys, no special UI fields (such as a personal vs. business account indicator) will be added. All accounts are assumed to be business accounts, and PAD (Pre-Authorized Debit) requirements are covered via Autopay Terms & Conditions required by RBC Bank.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Existing direct debit arrangements via RBC Bank and SAP have historically been set up as business accounts, with compliance requirements addressed through terms and conditions rather than additional UI fields. The business prefers to avoid complicating the user interface unless required by regulation.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The decision log records that no special UI fields are required because all accounts will be treated as business accounts and that PAD requirements are handled contractually through Autopay Terms & Conditions. This aligns with prior implementations via RBC and SAP where mandatory PAD elements were captured outside of the UI fields being discussed. However, this rests on regulatory interpretation that personal accounts are not in scope for this program or can be treated under the same contractual framework, which still needs to be reconfirmed in light of evolving regulations.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation shows that personal vs. business account differentiation or additional PAD-specific data must be captured, update the UI for GuestPay and SSP to add the required fields (e.g., account type selector, additional mandate data), adjust backend processing accordingly, and schedule targeted testing. Communicate changes to impacted channels and update customer-facing documentation.
assumptions.validation_method: Review RBC PAD requirements and internal compliance guidance for Canada to confirm whether additional fields are needed, and validate with Treasury or Compliance that treating all accounts as business accounts is acceptable.

assumptions.title: Stripe transactional data ingested into the Enterprise Data Lake will not contain PII or raw card/bank details
assumptions.description: The team agreed that all underlying Stripe transactional data will be ingested into the Enterprise Data Lake (EDL) using Fivetran with daily refresh, and that this data will not contain PII or raw card/bank details because all sensitive details are tokenized. Therefore, the data does not require special data classification beyond standard EDL processes.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Stripe’s tokenization model and Thomson Reuters’ design explicitly avoid storing raw card or bank account details in downstream systems. The EDL ingestion is planned to use Stripe’s APIs or exports that expose tokenized, non-PII identifiers rather than raw sensitive data, allowing use of standard EDL governance rather than a special classification regime.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The decision log documents explicit alignment that the ingested Stripe data will not contain PII or raw card/bank details and will follow standard EDL processes. Stripe’s architecture is designed around tokenization, and the project’s scope does not include storing raw payment instrument data in internal systems. With appropriate field-level selection when configuring Fivetran, the resulting dataset should remain non-PII. However, this depends on careful configuration and validation to avoid accidentally ingesting sensitive fields.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation reveals that sensitive data is present or could be ingested, reconfigure the Fivetran and Stripe extraction to exclude those fields, implement masking or tokenization at ingestion, and classify the affected datasets according to higher security standards. Temporarily restrict access to impacted datasets while remediation occurs and update data governance documentation and training to prevent recurrence.
assumptions.validation_method: Review the Stripe-to-EDL data mappings and Fivetran configuration to ensure that only tokenized, non-PII fields are ingested; perform a data sample inspection in a secure test or lower environment to confirm absence of raw card/bank details or direct PII and obtain sign-off from Security/Compliance.

assumptions.title: Validation of HRC (High Radius) for Canada 2.1 can be handled via UAT business testing only
assumptions.description: When the HRC workstream was delayed, the decision was made that no new HRC feature would be created for go-live, HRC would not be part of the July 11 go-live, and no technical or QA feature work would be required. Validation was initially planned to be handled only via UAT business testing.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Given HRC’s exclusion from the Canada 2.1 go-live scope and the desire to minimize additional work on a delayed workstream, the team believed that limited validation through UAT business testing would be sufficient to confirm that existing HRC processes remained unaffected.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initially, the project assumed that excluding HRC from the Stripe go-live scope meant that minimal validation would suffice and that existing HRC processes were stable. However, ongoing discussions showed that stakeholders required more formalized validation and governance artifacts than UAT alone could provide.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If UAT alone is deemed insufficient, create a dedicated, lightweight HRC feature capturing current-state testing requirements, have business stakeholders review and confirm alignment, and obtain formal sign-off to close validation activities without adding new functional scope.
assumptions.validation_method: Use UAT business testing to exercise key HRC flows and confirm there are no regressions in the Pay by Phone feature or related processes.

assumptions.title: Default AutoPay implementation effort is small, manageable, and timing is flexible relative to Stripe go-live
assumptions.description: In deciding to implement Default AutoPay for the Canada Payments Program, it was confirmed as a business requirement with no opt-out approval workflow included. The meeting notes state that the effort is small and manageable, aligns with the US Legal approach, and can be delivered within the Stripe program or deferred without blocking Stripe go-live if required.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The Default AutoPay change is primarily a configuration and flow change rather than a net-new system build, and similar patterns have already been implemented in the US context. The team believes this can be implemented with limited engineering effort and scheduled flexibly.
assumptions.validity_explanation: During the decision meeting, Ryan and other stakeholders confirmed that Default AutoPay effort is small and manageable and that it aligns with an existing US Legal approach. Because the same pattern is being reused, it is reasonable to assume a limited incremental effort. However, integration nuances with Canada-specific flows or dependencies on other Stripe program changes could still increase complexity, so this remains an assumption until detailed design and implementation are complete.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If implementation proves larger or more complex than expected, re-prioritize Default AutoPay delivery relative to other scope, consider phased rollout, or fall back to a configuration that maintains Bill To options while delaying full Default AutoPay behavior. Communicate any changes to stakeholders and adjust change management and training materials accordingly.
assumptions.validation_method: Refine the implementation plan and estimates for Default AutoPay, confirm alignment with engineering leads, and validate against actual effort as work progresses. Compare with the US implementation to ensure scope parity and complexity assumptions are accurate.

decisions.title: Agnostic email template alignment for payment emails
decisions.description: Boomi will send an agnostic payment acknowledgement email for SSP, OC, IVR, and other channels when a Stripe payment_intent webhook is received. A unified email template has been agreed, and the business will provide the French-language version and failure-payment customer communication verbiage. Email notifications are aligned across channels and systems.

decision_owner.name: Cindy Gregoire; Rachel Torgerson; Kristen Ackerman

decisions.rationale: The existing SSP payment template is specific to a single system and cannot be reused across all channels. An agnostic template and common rules for when emails are sent are required to align architecture and business expectations and to unblock Boomi technical refinement.
decisions.options_considered: Use the existing SSP payment email template versus creating a new, unified agnostic template triggered from Boomi upon Stripe webhooks; determine whether to send acknowledgement on payment_intent.created versus payment_intent.succeeded; determine handling of failure and refund notifications.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Boomi / ESC / SAP / DCP / SSP / Salesforce / Conga email notification flows; Stripe payment_intent webhooks; Boomi Level 2 support processes; ESC postback behavior.

decisions.title: Provide business-level breakdown of IVR transaction volumes for Canada to support PCI Pal decision
decisions.description: The program acknowledged a set of dropped business requirements related to IVR transaction volumes for Canada and recorded these changes in the Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog. Formal business acknowledgement of the dropped requirements has been provided.
decisions.rationale: Certain IVR-related business requirements were deemed unnecessary or out of scope for the Canada Payments Program. Formal acknowledgement and documentation were needed to ensure shared understanding of scope reduction and to support PCI Pal-related decision-making.
decisions.options_considered: Retain the IVR-related business requirements for Canada versus dropping them and recording the change in the Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog; PCI Pal scoping for Canada; IVR transaction volume analysis.

decisions.title: Business requirements updates for Canada (including approval of SAP_1_R28 shared payment method requirement)
decisions.description: Multiple Canada business requirements from the Stripe Requirement Master were categorized as dropped, newly added, or changed. Notably, requirement SAP_1_R28, allowing customers to use the same payment method for autopay across multiple payer accounts, was approved. Several requirements were reclassified as non-functional or technical, and multiple BAU reconciliation and reporting requirements were dropped from the program scope.

decision_owner.name: Kristen Ackerman; Mathew Varghese; Rachel Torgerson; Vivek Y

decisions.rationale: Stripe-based architecture changes make some SAP capabilities obsolete (e.g., SAP settlement for Canada), and several listed items are non-functional or BAU activities rather than business requirements. The business wants to allow shared payment methods across payer accounts, and duplicate payment method detection in Stripe would conflict with this desired behavior.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain existing SAP behavior preventing shared payment methods and keep all original requirements versus approving SAP_1_R28 to allow shared payment methods across accounts, dropping settlement- and reconciliation-related requirements that are BAU, and reclassifying monitoring and security requirements as non-functional or technical.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Stripe_Requirement Master.xlsx; Payment Phase 2-1 Business Requirement Changelog.xlsx; SAP settlement process for Canada; Stripe settlement processing; Stripe duplicate detection/fingerprint capabilities.

decisions.title: Dropped chatbot business requirements for Canada
decisions.description: All chatbot-related business requirements for Canada (SAP_1_R7, SAP_1_R10, SAP_R3_R11, SAP_R3_R14) were dropped from the Canada Payments Program scope, and the chatbot payment experience for Canada is out of scope for Phase 2.1.
decisions.rationale: There is no chatbot or chatbot-based payment experience for Canada in the current scope. Maintaining chatbot requirements would misrepresent the solution scope and create unnecessary delivery expectations.
decisions.options_considered: Retain the chatbot-related requirements presuming a future chatbot experience versus declaring all chatbot payment requirements out of scope for Phase 2.1 and updating the business requirement documentation accordingly.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Stripe_Requirement Master.xlsx; Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog; Canada chatbot or digital payment experiences.

decisions.title: Dropped mid-term modification (order capture) requirement for Canada (SAP_1_R27)
decisions.description: The Canada mid-term modification business requirement SAP_1_R27, allowing agents to change a submitted order and initiate payment with existing stored payment details, was dropped from the program scope.
decisions.rationale: Following discussions between Sue Monjeau and the Order Management team, mid-term modification via reuse of stored payment details was deemed not relevant for payment processing in the target scope, making the feature unnecessary for the Stripe program.
decisions.options_considered: Implement the mid-term modification capability to allow agents to reuse stored payment details for modified orders versus dropping the requirement as not relevant to current business scenarios.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Stripe_Requirement Master.xlsx; Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog; Order Management processes for Canada.

decisions.title: Release handling and aggressiveness for 3DS enforcement in Canada
decisions.description: A decision is required on whether 3D Secure (3DS) support for Canada will be built and released in a deactivated state or built and released activated, and what level of enforcement aggressiveness TR will adopt for 3DS. This item tracks the need for a follow-on decision after agreeing to adopt standard 3DS redirect implementation.
decisions.rationale: While the decision to adopt standard 3DS redirect implementation (WI 1189631) has been made, the business has not yet defined how aggressively to enforce 3DS at launch. The enforcement posture affects customer experience, risk management, and engineering scope, so a dedicated decision is required.
decisions.options_considered: Build 3DS support and release it deactivated initially versus build 3DS support and release it activated with defined enforcement rules; possibly adjust enforcement levels over time.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Work item 1189631 (standard 3DS redirect implementation); DCP eStores (Print and Product); SSP; bank account / PAD redirect patterns; business and architecture alignment on 3DS posture.

decisions.title: Dropped renewal business requirements for Canada
decisions.description: Canada renewal business requirements SAP_1_R23, SAP_1_R24, SAP_1_R25, and SAP_1_R26, which involved using existing card or bank details for renewal payments by customers or agents, were dropped from scope. The renewal payment experience for Canada remains aligned to the existing model (autopay or invoice and one-time payment outside SSP).
decisions.rationale: In the current SSP model for Canada there is no interactive renewal payment experience; renewals are handled either via autopay or through invoicing and one-time payments outside SSP. Maintaining renewal flows using stored payment details in SSP would conflict with this model and introduce unnecessary complexity.
decisions.options_considered: Introduce interactive renewal flows in SSP leveraging stored card/bank details versus dropping the renewal requirements and keeping the existing autopay/invoice-based approach.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Stripe_Requirement Master.xlsx; Payments Phase 2.1 Business Requirement Changelog; SSP renewal and subscription flows for Canada.

decisions.title: Direct debit UI fields for Canada direct debit compliance
decisions.description: For Canada recurring direct debit (bank account) setup, no special UI fields are required to distinguish personal versus business bank accounts. All accounts will be treated as business accounts, and PAD (Pre-Authorized Debit) requirements are covered via Autopay Terms & Conditions required by RBC Bank for both GuestPay and SSP journeys.
decisions.rationale: Existing RBC Bank PAD processes and Autopay Terms & Conditions are sufficient to meet compliance requirements without introducing additional UI fields to distinguish personal and business accounts. Simplifying the UI reduces complexity while staying compliant.
decisions.options_considered: Add specific UI fields to capture whether a bank account is personal or business and any extra compliance-related fields versus assuming all accounts are business accounts and relying on RBC PAD requirements embedded in terms and conditions.
decisions.dependencies_linked: RBC Bank PAD requirements; Autopay Terms & Conditions; GuestPay and SSP bank account journeys for Canada.

decisions.title: Research on banking regulation and fraud compliance controls for direct debit vs credit cards
decisions.description: The team needs a decision, informed by research with Treasury and compliance, on what regulatory and fraud-related controls and customer data must be collected for bank-account-based direct debit versus credit card processing. This includes defining how bank-account workflows differ from card workflows to remain compliant and minimize customer impact when bank account changes are required.

decision_owner.name: To be confirmed (compliance owner; interim follow-up by Rachel Torgerson)

decisions.rationale: Introducing direct debit capabilities via a credit card vendor requires clarity on regulatory obligations and fraud response processes, which differ from card-only processing. Lack of guidance could lead to non-compliant workflows or poor customer experience when addressing bank-account-related fraud.
decisions.options_considered: Rely on existing card-based compliance controls for bank accounts versus defining differentiated controls and data collection for direct debit in collaboration with Treasury and compliance owners.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Treasury guidance on Canadian banking regulations; compliance ownership for direct debit; fraud response processes for bank accounts versus credit cards.

decisions.title: Default to AutoPay versus continued support of "Bill To" in Canada Payments Program
decisions.description: Default AutoPay will be implemented as a business requirement for the Canada Payments Program. Bill To will continue only within defined exceptions; no opt-out approval workflow is included. The decision is final, though delivery timing can be flexible if needed and does not block Stripe go-live.

decision_owner.name: Rachel Torgerson; Kristen Ackerman; Sue Monjeau

decisions.rationale: The program’s strategic direction is to favor AutoPay while still accommodating necessary exceptions. Implementing AutoPay as default aligns with US Legal’s approach and can be delivered with small, manageable effort within the Stripe program without blocking go-live.
decisions.options_considered: Option A – AutoPay default with Bill To allowed only for defined exceptions; Option B – support both AutoPay and Bill To broadly as customer/rep choice; Option C – deprecate Bill To in Canada and move to AutoPay-only or equivalent pattern.
decisions.dependencies_linked: SAP and SSP billing configuration; rep-led ordering flows; Finance and Collections policies; AutoPay email/SMS notifications; US Legal’s billing approach.

decisions.title: Adopt 3DS for Canada with Stripe for customer-entered credit card flows
decisions.description: Thomson Reuters will adopt 3D Secure (3DS) with Stripe for customer-entered credit card payment flows in Canada (eStores, SSP, Chatbot) as part of Payment Program Phase 2.1. The decision is to implement 3DS immediately rather than defer. 3DS does not apply to direct debit or MOTO (rep/agent) flows.
decisions.rationale: Adopting 3DS immediately improves fraud prevention and authorization outcomes while addressing cross-functional concerns from Product, Risk, and Compliance. Deferring 3DS would delay these benefits and require a later retrofit of customer experiences and architecture.
decisions.options_considered: Option A – immediate 3DS adoption for Phase 2.1 customer-entered credit card flows; Option B – deferred 3DS adoption, for example targeting Q4 2026; maintain status quo without 3DS in the interim.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Payment Program 2-1 - Canada KDD for 3DS; Solution Architecture; 3DS redirect fallback implementation (return/returnTo URL handling) in eStores, SSP, and Chatbot; Stripe Radar or equivalent risk controls; monitoring of auth and conversion metrics.

decisions.title: Enterprise Data Lake (EDL) requirements for Stripe data
decisions.description: All underlying Stripe transactional data, excluding PII and raw card/bank details, will be ingested into the Enterprise Data Lake (EDL) via Fivetran. Data will be refreshed daily and will follow standard EDL classification processes without requiring special handling beyond tokenization-based protection.

decision_owner.name: Rachel Torgerson; Kristen Ackerman; Sue Monjeau; Sean Olsen

decisions.rationale: Full transactional data in the EDL enables comprehensive reporting and analytics while tokenization ensures sensitive payment data is not exposed. Using Fivetran standardizes ingestion and daily refreshes provide timely data for downstream consumers without additional classification overhead.
decisions.options_considered: Ingest only summarized or dashboard-level Stripe data versus ingesting full transactional Stripe data; use alternative ingestion mechanisms versus standardizing on Fivetran; different refresh cadences versus daily refresh.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Enterprise Data Lake platform; Fivetran ingestion pipelines; Stripe data schemas; internal consumers of Stripe payment data.

decisions.title: Move non-functional requirements (NFRs) to UAT spreadsheet for Canada new payment gateway scenario
decisions.description: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) related to the new payment gateway business scenario for Canada will be tracked within the UAT spreadsheet instead of separate artifacts, ensuring they are covered during testing.
decisions.rationale: Consolidating NFRs into the UAT plan simplifies testing governance and ensures non-functional expectations are explicitly validated during UAT rather than managed separately.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain NFRs in separate documentation versus integrating them into the UAT spreadsheet as part of the testing plan.
decisions.dependencies_linked: UAT testing plan for Canada new payment gateway; NFR coverage for the Stripe program.

decisions.title: Delayed HRC go-live and handling of existing Pay by Phone feature 1229417
decisions.description: High Radius / HRC will not be part of the July 11 go-live for Canada Phase 2.1. No new HRC feature will be created for go-live, and no technical or QA feature work is required. Validation of HRC will be handled via UAT business testing only.

decision_owner.name: Kristen Ackerman; Sue Monjeau; Cindy Gregoire

decisions.rationale: The HRC workstream is delayed and cannot align with the project’s July 11 go-live date. Excluding HRC from the go-live scope avoids introducing incomplete or unvalidated changes while still allowing validation of existing HRC processes through UAT business testing.
decisions.options_considered: Create a new HRC feature for go-live and attempt to align timelines versus excluding HRC from the July 11 release and validating current functionality through business UAT only.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Feature 1229417 (Pay by Phone); HRC workstream readiness; July 11 Canada Phase 2.1 go-live; UAT business testing plan.

decisions.title: Customer lists for QA and migration approach for Canada
decisions.description: The business will not manually provide a list of 100 customers for QA testing. There will be no partial or pilot migration for Canada. QA testing must rely on the data migration strategy instead of ad hoc customer lists.

decision_owner.name: Kristen Ackerman; Sue Monjeau; Cindy Gregoire

decisions.rationale: Relying on manual customer lists and partial migrations adds operational complexity and does not reflect the true production migration approach. Using the defined data migration strategy for QA ensures alignment between testing and actual rollout.
decisions.options_considered: Provide a manually curated list of customers and/or run a pilot/partial migration versus conducting QA solely based on the planned data migration strategy without ad hoc lists.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Canada data migration strategy; QA test planning; production cutover and migration approach.

decisions.title: HRC validation approach for Canada 2.1 using a dedicated testing feature
decisions.description: A lightweight HRC Feature (1264043) will be created solely to support validation and testing for Canada 2.1, confirming that existing HRC processes remain unchanged and function as expected as Stripe is rolled out. This feature introduces no new scope, functional changes, or go-live dependencies and exists only to anchor testing and formal sign-off.
decisions.rationale: Although HRC is excluded from Canada 2.1 go-live scope, stakeholders determined that UAT alone is insufficient to satisfy validation and governance needs. A minimal feature provides structured testing, documentation, and formal sign-off without expanding functional scope.
decisions.options_considered: Rely solely on UAT business testing for HRC validation versus creating a minimal dedicated feature to track validation requirements, tests, and sign-off.
decisions.dependencies_linked: High Radius / HRC processes; Feature 1264043; Canada 2.1 Stripe rollout; validation and governance sign-off requirements.

milestones.name: Payments Unification Canada 2.1
milestones.description:
The Payments Unification project aims to consolidate, streamline, enhance payment systems for improved efficiency and user experience.​ To begin this journey of consolidating our payment processor landscape to Stripe as a single strategic vendor – eliminating the need for the Payment Authorization Secure Server (PASS) to be a tokenization and authentication routing platform. Another goal is to replace our existing fraud detection infrastructure with the same single vendor (or vendor that provides a hosted fraud solution not requiring TR integration).​
Phase 2.1 – Canada Scope:
 Integrate Stripe payment processing for CANADA​
Conduct thorough testing and validation.​
Ensure compliance with regional requirements and timelines ​
Integrate with PCIPal to collect payment information and processing through Stripe, for payments initiated by customers thru IVR

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

**A. Scope:** To integrate Development, QA, Staging and Production environments into the TR Azure Cloud platform.

**B. RAG Status: GREEN – Key Success:** In alignment with the timeline agreed upon by our project stakeholders, cloud integration for all non-production environments (Dev, QA, UAT/Staging) was successfully completed by Q4 2025. We are now on track for the Production Cutover scheduled for June 20th, with planning calls already in place to ensure a smooth transition.

**C. Metric:** Azure Cloud integration is currently at 50% completion. The project team is confident that the remaining critical production integration will be completed by June 30, 2026.

**E. IMPORTANT UPDATE:** The SafeSend Leadership team has confirmed the production cutover date as June 20th, 2026, with a planned downtime of 6 to 12 hours. This has been strategically scheduled during the Juneteenth long weekend to minimize operational impact.

**F. SafeSend One: Overview of Cutover Details:**

-   **Change ID:** CHG0252111 (Currently in "New Phase" and will soon move to approval phase)
    
-   **Schedule:** June 20th, starting at 10:30 AM IST (12-hour window)
    
-   **Description:** The SafeSend team will perform a production cutover from the SS Azure Tenant to the TR LZ Azure Tenant.
    

## **Key Challenges & Mitigation Plans**

#### **A. Azure Quota Limitations Threatening Cutover Timeline**

**Issue Summary:**

-   Azure resource quotas in Central US and East US 2 regions are blocking progress.
    
-   Redis Enterprise instance creation is delayed due to exhausted compute SKU quota.
    
-   SQL Pool creation requires an additional 4,000 vCores, delaying testing and production preparation.
    
-   Temporary Redis SKU workaround is in place, but long-term issues persist.
    

**Recommendation/Mitigation:**

1.  **Use Reserved Capacity:**
    
    -   Reserved capacity guarantees resource availability but involves additional costs.
        
    -   Reserved capacity has been successfully used for critical workloads by Thompson Reuters in the past.
        
2.  **Retry Deployments:**
    
    -   Attempt deployments during off-peak hours, although resource availability cannot be guaranteed.
        

**Next Steps:**

-   **Action Owner: \[Pramod\]**
    
    -   Set up a call with Manir, Praful, and Suhas to discuss leveraging Azure's reserved capacity to bypass infrastructure constraints.
        
    -   Once workloads are running (e.g., after two months), reservations can be canceled if no longer required.
        

#### **B. JFrog Artifactory Issues Blocking CI/CD Pipelines**

**Issue Summary:**

-   Rate-limiting (429 errors) is affecting NuGet/.NET package downloads (~255 applications across 100+ daily PRs).
    
-   npm "metadata" issue is a permissions problem, preventing publishing to specific packages in the @sssuite-component-ui scope.
    

**Impact:**

-   Critical package-building issues must be resolved before June 1st to avoid project delays for the July delivery deadline.
    
-   Failure to address these issues promptly will block development and testing phases, jeopardizing the timeline.
    

**Mitigation: Rate-Limiting (429 Errors):** Add NuGet caching to build workflows to reduce traffic and errors.

risks.title: Cutover and rollback planning for production migration may be incomplete before migration window
risks.description: The RunBook_Prod sheet shows that cutover and rollback planning tasks (including detailed cutover steps and rollback actions for application, database, storage, and domain changes) are marked as 'Not yet Started'. These activities are essential to safely execute the production migration and to revert changes if issues occur.
risks.impact_description: If cutover and rollback plans are not fully defined, reviewed, and tested before the production migration window, the team may be forced to improvise during cutover. This can lead to extended downtime, confusion during incident handling, inability to cleanly revert to the pre-migration state, potential data corruption or data loss, and reputational risk if customer-facing systems remain unavailable or unstable.
risks.mitigation: Finalize a detailed cutover plan covering all steps for storage, SQL, Cosmos DB, APIM, Key Vault, and application deployment, including timings and responsibilities. Define and document a rollback plan covering re-deploying the Q1 release via Azure DevOps, reverting Key Vault secrets, undoing storage and database changes, and reversing domain changes via GoDaddy. Conduct at least one rehearsal of critical steps in a non-production environment to validate feasibility and timing, and ensure all stakeholders understand their roles during cutover.

risks.title: Production storage and table migrations may fail or overrun due to untested migration service setup
risks.description: Production storage blob and table migrations depend on deploying a migration service and VM/AKS-based tooling (AzCopy, scripts, jobs) during April 17–27, 2026. The RunBook_Prod notes that the service for storage migration needs to be deployed and that Ravindra must update the storage migration plan with prerequisites and tasks. If these prerequisites are not ready or adequately tested, the production storage migrations may fail or take longer than the planned window.
risks.impact_description: If the migration service, VM/AKS infrastructure, and scripts for storage and table migration are not properly set up and tested, data transfers may fail, stall, or run longer than expected. This can result in incomplete or inconsistent storage content in TR Azure, requirement for multiple re-runs, extended maintenance windows, potential data loss, and unavailability of application features that rely on blob or table storage during or after migration.
risks.mitigation: Implement and validate the full storage migration toolchain (VM, AKS, AzCopy-based scripts, configuration generation, failed-job handling) in non-production environments (Dev, QA, STG), leveraging the detailed POC steps already executed there. Update the production storage migration plan with all prerequisites and tasks, including change feed configuration, SAS-based transfers, delta container handling, and cleanup procedures. Schedule sufficient buffer in the production window, and pre-run trial migrations on a sample of production containers to validate performance and error handling before the full migration.

risks.title: Key Vault secret migration and validation may delay production deployment readiness
risks.description: In the RunBook_Prod, key vault secret migration tasks (creating target Key Vault, bulk secret migration, ATUM deployment, and secret validation) are all marked as 'Not yet Started'. Dev notes from earlier environments indicate that application deployment depends on Key Vault being updated and operational. If key vault tasks slip, production deployment readiness may be delayed.
risks.impact_description: If Key Vaults are not created and populated with correct secrets before production deployment, applications may fail to start or function correctly due to missing or incorrect configuration secrets (e.g., connection strings, API keys). This could block production cutover, require emergency changes during the migration window, or lead to post-migration incidents and rollbacks.
risks.mitigation: Create the target production Key Vaults and configure access as per TR standards, then use bulk migration tools or scripts (and ATUM) to populate secrets. Validate secret correctness with EMs and application owners before the migration window by running application readiness checks in a pre-production setup. Incorporate Key Vault readiness checks into the production runbook and treat them as mandatory gates before proceeding with application deployment.

risks.title: Incomplete CI/CD migration from Azure DevOps to GitHub Actions could impact non-production DevOps migration timeline
risks.description: The DevOps Migration Phase (Non-Prod) indicates that ADO to GitHub migration is in progress with several outstanding tasks such as bulk creation of CI/CD pipelines as GitHub Actions workflows, validation of builds and artifacts, and full end-to-end dry runs. Notes highlight constraints around JFrog version updates and limitations with variable group mapping, requiring conversion of variable groups into YAML files.
risks.impact_description: If the migration of CI/CD pipelines from Azure DevOps to GitHub Actions is not completed and validated before the non-production DevOps migration deadline (Q4 2025 / availability to developers in early February 2026), developers may be forced to continue using legacy pipelines or experience disruptions in build and deployment workflows. This can slow feature delivery, complicate production migration readiness, and increase operational overhead by maintaining dual tooling.
risks.mitigation: Finalize the design and implementation of GitHub Actions workflows for all CI and CD pipelines, including addressing JFrog version alignment and converting ADO variable groups to YAML-based configuration. Run all CI pipelines to generate artifacts and validate pushes to JFrog, verify test coverage, and perform end-to-end dry runs across CI, CD, CT, and CO stages. Address any issues in mapping test cases and service connections, and ensure developers are onboarded and trained on the new workflows before the planned non-prod DevOps migration date.

risks.title: Wildcard certificate and domain management constraints may impact SSL and customer subdomain strategy
risks.description: The QA and Dev runbooks note ongoing POCs for SSL certificates via Venafi and for adapting existing domains, as well as discussion around wildcard certificates for customer-specific subdomains (thousands of potential subdomains). TR standards typically do not accept wildcard certificates, requiring exceptions or design changes. Although one historical RAID entry indicates the team decided not to proceed with wildcard certificates, the broader production SSL and domain strategy (including potential migration from GoDaddy to AWS Route 53) still requires alignment and impact analysis.
risks.impact_description: If SSL and domain strategies (including handling of customer-specific subdomains) are not fully aligned with TR standards and implemented before production, the team may face blockers in obtaining required certificates, delays in domain configuration, or security policy exceptions. This may delay production cutover, force suboptimal workarounds, or require post-migration rework of customer access patterns and portal design.
risks.mitigation: Complete the Venafi-based certificate POCs, finalize the decision to avoid wildcard certificates for customer portals, and document the new design approach for handling customer access without wildcard certs. Coordinate with TR PKI, security, and domain management teams to confirm migration plans from GoDaddy to AWS Route 53 where applicable, and ensure required certificates and DNS records are provisioned and tested in non-prod before production cutover.

risks.title: Datadog training and integration may not be completed before production migration
risks.description: Datadog training is a prerequisite for setting up monitoring integrations for the new TR Azure subscriptions. Notes indicate that key tasks for Datadog IaC, RUM, and APM monitoring cannot be fully defined or executed until SafeSend and TR staff complete training and understand TR Datadog standards. If training and integration are delayed, monitoring for infrastructure and applications in the new TR Azure tenant may not be ready before or during production migration.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog training and integration are not completed before production migration, the project may go live without fully functional observability. This could lead to limited visibility into application and infrastructure health, slower incident detection, difficulty in troubleshooting migration issues, and increased risk of prolonged outages or performance degradation in production. Lack of compliance with TR monitoring standards could also trigger rework or governance escalations.
risks.mitigation: Arrange and complete Datadog training sessions for SafeSend and TR DevOps staff; use the documented TR Datadog integration procedures to configure log forwarding from Azure Log Analytics to Datadog and to enable RUM, APM, and infrastructure monitoring. Run a proof-of-concept to push application insights and metrics (including event logs) to Datadog in non-production, refine dashboards and alerts, and then apply the same configurations in production before the June 2026 production migration.

risks.title: Urgent Azure Quota Limitations Threaten Cutover Timeline: Escalations Underway with Microsoft for Redis and SQL Resources
risks.description:
•	Issue Summary: Azure resource quotas in Central US and East US 2 are blocking progress. Redis Enterprise instance creation is hindered by exhausted compute SKU quota despite Microsoft's efforts to increase it. 
•	SQL Pool creation requires an additional 4,000 vCores in both regions. Testing and production cutover preparation are delayed, with a temporary Redis SKU workaround in place, but the original issues persist.
risks.impact_description: Impacts the SafeSend One Production Pre-migration activites
risks.mitigation:
Recommendation/ Mitigation: Bill is explained that the inability to deploy the Redis cache is not due to a subscription quota issue, but rather a constraint in the overall capacity of the Azure data center. He emphasizes that increasing the subscription quota won't resolve the issue because the data center itself is at capacity for the required SKU. To guarantee deployment, the team has two options:

1.	Use Reserved Capacity: This option ensures availability of resources but involves additional costs. Reserved capacity guarantees deployment at any time but must be planned and approved by management. Bill notes that Thompson Reuters has successfully used reserved capacity for critical workloads in the past, such as during tax seasons.
2.	Retry Deployments: The team can keep attempting deployments during off-peak hours, but this is dependent on availability and cannot be guaranteed.

Bill clarifies that Microsoft support cannot provide an ETA for when capacity will become available because it depends on customer demand and deployment timing. However, he has escalated the issue to inquire if additional capacity might come online before the end of next month. Even if new capacity is added, it will still be consumed by other customers unless reserved.

Finally, Bill recommends that the team explore the reserved capacity process with their internal cloud cost team, which has experience with it. Corey Cox adds that setting up reserved capacity typically takes days, not weeks, which provides a clearer timeline for planning.
•	Next Action: [Pramod] to setup call with Manir, Praful, and Suhas to have internal discussion i.e using Azure's reserved capacity to bypass infrastructure constraints and secure the required SKU. Once the setup is complete and workloads are running (e.g., after two months), the reservation can be canceled if no longer needed.

risks.title: JFrog Artifactory Issues Blocking CI/CD Pipelines (Rate Limits & npm Metadata)
risks.description: Issue Summary: SafeSend Project team highlighted the criticality of resolving the package-building issue to ensure the project stays on track for its July delivery deadlines. Without this resolution, development and testing will remain blocked, jeopardizing the timeline. The team is trying to identify the right person to escalate or resolve the issue urgently
risks.impact_description: Impact: The team emphasizes the urgency of resolving the package-building issue before June 1st, as the next phase of work is set to begin on that date. Failure to address this issue promptly could significantly impact the overall project timeline
risks.mitigation:
Mitigation: Yesterday, [Prasanna] scheduled with Jfrog team/arch Team (Johannes, Julian and Brain)
1.	The rate-limiting (429) problem is real. It's confined to NuGet/.NET package downloads — 670,000 errors in the last 30 days, peaking at 294,000 in a single day — driven by ~255 .NET applications across 100+ daily PRs all pulling the same packages from JFrog with no caching on the runners. The fix is a workflow change on build side (add a NuGet cache), not a JFrog rate-limit increase.
2.	The npm publish "metadata" issue is actually a permissions issue. The same token publishes successfully nearly 6,000 times per month to other packages — it only fails on two specific packages in the @sssuite-component-ui scope, which have never been published successfully. A JFrog admin needs to extend the team's permission to cover that scope and or work through the self service portal to add the permission. The metadata reindex they requested won't help.
3.	Fixing #1 also solves a major transfer-cost problem. SafeSend's traffic is 99.997% downloads (~4 TB/week) vs. uploads (~122 MB/week), and the NuGet caching fix should remove roughly 3.1–3.5 TB/week of egress — about 80% of their total JFrog traffic — while making the 429s disappear as a side effect. One change, three wins: their builds get faster, their errors stop, and our bill drops.

entities.name: Digita Virtual Office AVD/Azure Migration (DVO)
entities.okrs: In Progress

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Digita Virtual Office AVD/Azure Migration is moving the UK Digita Virtual Office workload from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop in Azure UK, using patterns established for Virtual Office US. This is required to avoid renewed Citrix licensing, align to the AVD strategy, and complete migration before tax blackout windows and the November 2027 Citrix license expiry.

To date, 1 of 8 defined milestones is complete (Project Discovery and Planning) and 1 is in progress (Non-Prod Planning, Environment Setup), with 6 remaining in planned status against a program end date of 30 Jun 2027. Discovery finished on 27 May 2026, two days ahead of the 29 May 2026 plan, and the Non-PROD environment build is tracking to its planned completion on 06 Jul 2026 with no reported variance.

Overall status is Green, driven by early completion of discovery and non-production infrastructure build progressing to the current plan while key scheduling risks are already identified and being mitigated.

## Path to Green

The program remains Green by tightly aligning the detailed schedule to UK tax blackout windows and the November 2027 Citrix license expiry, and by monitoring delivery against interim dates for Non-PROD completion in 2026 and PROD cutover by April 2027 so any slippage can be escalated before it threatens those constraints.

## Milestones

- Project Discovery and Planning is completed as of 27 May 2026, ahead of the planned 29 May 2026 finish.  
- Non-Prod Planning and Environment Setup will complete with Non-PROD AVD infrastructure ready in Azure by 06 Jul 2026.  
- Non-PROD migrations, including associated testing, will complete by 09 Aug 2026.  
- Production migrations, including customer cutover to Azure Virtual Desktop, will complete by 02 May 2027.  
- Program close-out, including full transition to steady-state operations and alignment with the Citrix license exit, will complete by 30 Jun 2027.

risks.title: Production blackout windows may constrain migration schedule
risks.description: Production migration activities cannot occur during UK tax blackout windows (no PROD migrations between December 2026 and March 2027 / blackout noted as Nov 2026 to Mar 1 2027 in the charter). This reduces the available windows to complete the Digita Virtual Office (DVO) migration from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD).
risks.impact_description: If the project schedule is not aligned to the UK tax blackout windows, production migration waves could be delayed or blocked. This may force compressing remaining work into fewer windows, increase the risk of schedule overrun past Q2 2027, require additional coordination with business stakeholders, and potentially drive additional operational cost or extended dual-running of AWS and Azure environments.
risks.mitigation: Plan the overall migration timeline so that Non-PROD infrastructure and migrations are completed by Q3 2026 and PROD infrastructure is ready by October 2026. Schedule dry run migrations and final PROD cutover in allowable windows outside of the blackout period (e.g., PROD dry run by 2026-12-31 and PROD migration by 2027-04-01). Coordinate with business/product stakeholders to confirm exact blackout dates and embed these constraints in the detailed project plan and ADO milestones.

risks.title: Citrix license expiry may be reached before migration completes
risks.description: Thomson Reuters is not renewing the Citrix license for the Digita Virtual Office (DVO) environment, and the existing Citrix license expires in November 2027. The DVO migration from Citrix in AWS to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) must therefore be completed before the license expiry.
risks.impact_description: If the DVO migration to Azure Virtual Desktop is not completed before the Citrix license expiry in November 2027, the project could lose the ability to run production workloads on the existing Citrix platform. This could lead to service disruption for UK customers, emergency unplanned spend to extend or re-establish licensing, rushed and higher-risk cutovers, and damage to customer trust and regulatory compliance posture.
risks.mitigation: Align key milestones so that Non-PROD migration completes by July 31, 2026, Non-PROD testing by August 31, 2026, PROD infrastructure is ready by October 2026, and PROD migration completes by April 1, 2027. Monitor schedule progress against these dates, escalate slippage early, and maintain a contingency plan to negotiate a short-term Citrix extension only if absolutely required. Track this as a critical path risk in ADO and regular status reviews.

decisions.title: Potential dependency on CIAM migration for UK customers
decisions.description: There may be an external dependency to migrate UK Digita Virtual Office customers to CIAM, and this CIAM-related work must be completed prior to production migration to Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD). The exact dependency and timing are not yet fully confirmed.
decisions.rationale: Confirm whether CIAM migration for UK customers is a mandatory prerequisite for PROD cutover by engaging CIAM, Identity Management, and Product/Service Management teams. If mandatory, define and agree a CIAM migration plan and timeline that completes before the planned PROD migration (April 1, 2027). Track CIAM activities as a separate workstream with clear milestones and ensure they are included in the overall project critical path. Escalate any CIAM delays early and prepare interim access patterns if needed.

decisions.title: Start with baseline SQL MI sizing and scale dynamically based on usage patterns
decisions.description: Initial SQL Managed Instance sizing for the DVO migration will use a baseline configuration (e.g., 8-core instances), with the intention to scale dynamically based on real usage patterns observed during and after migration.
decisions.rationale: Due to limited historical benchmarks and uncertainty in accurately sizing ~7,200 databases, a baseline sizing strategy reduces upfront complexity and avoids significant over- or under-provisioning. Dynamic scaling based on observed usage provides flexibility and allows optimization over time while enabling timely progression to build and migration phases.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Attempt to fully validate and lock down precise SQL MI sizing before build based on limited historical data.
2) Use a baseline sizing approach (e.g., 8-core instances) and adjust dynamically as usage data becomes available (selected).
decisions.dependencies_linked: Sizing and capacity uncertainty issue; SQL Managed Instance constraints; Cloud Migration Factory execution planning.

## Executive Summary

VMware to Hyper-V Migration is delivering a full migration of VMware workloads to Hyper-V, including handling out-of-scope, suspect, and orphaned VMs and decommissioning all VMware infrastructure. This matters because Thomson Reuters must completely eliminate VMware from all datacenters by 30 Jun 2026 with no exceptions.

Overall status is Green, driven by VMware workload migration reaching 99% completion with only ESX host decommissioning remaining.

## Path to Green

The main remaining risk is delay in decommissioning all ESX hosts by 30 Jun 2026, mitigated through a dedicated decommission plan and close tracking against the hard VMware exit deadline.

## Milestones

- Complete all in-scope VMware virtual machine migrations to Hyper-V by 31 May 2026.
- Decommission all ESX hosts in all locations by 30 Jun 2026.
- Fully eliminate the VMware footprint and close the VMware to Hyper-V Migration project by 30 Jun 2026.
