dependencies.title: Build HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment within buffer to protect dependent activities
dependencies.description: The HighQ environment build has exhausted its schedule buffer; any delays will impact a range of dependent activities.
dependencies.dependent_on: HighQ engineering and infrastructure teams completing environment build
dependencies.consumer: All downstream HighQ Port Authority workstreams and integrations
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in environment build will directly push out all dependent testing, integration, and compliance activities, jeopardizing delivery timelines.
dependencies.mitigation: Actively track and manage this as a risk even though it is currently on track, ensuring rapid response to emerging delays.

dependencies.title: Select compliant antivirus scanning tool for HighQ (Sophos/SentinelOne/Defender)
dependencies.description: HighQ must identify an antivirus/malware scanning tool that meets FedRAMP FIPS 140-2/3 cryptographic requirements, evaluating options such as Sophos, SentinelOne, and Microsoft Defender. License procurement has been completed and verification of the selected option is in progress.
dependencies.dependent_on: Tool evaluation and compliance verification for Sophos, SentinelOne, and Defender
dependencies.consumer: HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment security posture
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If a compliant antivirus solution is not selected and verified in time, HighQ may need to make late changes to security tooling, impacting the engineering timeline and potentially delaying FedRAMP/HIPAA readiness and Port Authority commitments.
dependencies.mitigation: Continue evaluation and compliance verification of Sophos, SentinelOne, and Defender; license procurement has been completed and verification is in progress for the selected option(s). If no single tool meets requirements, explore alternate strategies based on Fortreum and security team guidance.

dependencies.title: Issuance of BAAs for C-Track and Case Center depends on remediation guidance
dependencies.description: Before Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) can be issued for C-Track and Case Center, Risk & Compliance and Privacy must provide detailed remediation guidance to the product teams based on the Fortreum FedRamp HIPAA assessment, which identified gaps but did not specify remediation steps.
dependencies.dependent_on: Risk & Compliance and Privacy remediation guidance for C-Track and Case Center
dependencies.consumer: C-Track and Case Center product teams and associated sales/commercial teams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If remediation guidance is delayed, BAAs cannot be issued for C-Track and Case Center, potentially delaying or preventing sales to customers requiring HIPAA-compliant solutions and impacting revenue and customer relationships.
dependencies.mitigation: In the interim, limit or defer HIPAA-related sales commitments for C-Track and Case Center, and prioritize development of remediation guidance for these products within R&C and Privacy workplans.

dependencies.title: Alignment with ICFR reporting timelines and audit calendars
dependencies.description: ICFR Transformation activities must align with existing ICFR reporting timelines, audit calendars, and regulatory compliance obligations.
dependencies.dependent_on: ICFR reporting schedule and external/internal audit calendars
dependencies.consumer: ICFR Transformation program
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Misalignment could cause conflicts with audit activities, increased rework, and potential compliance breaches.
dependencies.mitigation: Plan implementation waves around key reporting and audit milestones and coordinate timelines with Finance and Internal Audit.

dependencies.title: Budget and resource capacity constraints
dependencies.description: The pace and breadth of ICFR Transformation implementation are limited by available budget, resource capacity, and internal change bandwidth.
dependencies.dependent_on: Approved transformation budget and staffing availability across Finance, IT, Compliance, and business teams
dependencies.consumer: All ICFR Transformation workstreams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Insufficient budget or resources will slow implementation, reduce scope, or defer key improvements.
dependencies.mitigation: Phase scope based on priority, secure incremental funding as needed, and manage resource allocation across workstreams.

dependencies.title: Cross-functional coordination for process changes
dependencies.description: Process changes required by the ICFR Transformation must be coordinated across Finance, IT, Internal Audit, Compliance, and business control owners.
dependencies.dependent_on: Engagement and availability of Finance, IT, Internal Audit, Compliance, and business control owner stakeholders
dependencies.consumer: All process-focused ICFR Transformation workstreams
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Lack of coordination may lead to inconsistent adoption, conflicting practices, and delayed realization of benefits.
dependencies.mitigation: Establish clear governance forums, stakeholder engagement plans, and communication channels to coordinate changes.

dependencies.title: Sponsor re-approval for material changes
dependencies.description: Material changes to ICFR Transformation scope, timeline, or funding require Sponsor review and re-approval.
dependencies.dependent_on: Sponsor availability and governance process for change approvals
dependencies.consumer: ICFR Transformation program change control
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in sponsor re-approval could stall critical adjustments, causing schedule slippage or misaligned scope.
dependencies.mitigation: Maintain proactive communication with the Sponsor, prepare clear change cases, and schedule regular review checkpoints.

dependencies.title: Tooling model decision dependent on capability assessment
dependencies.description: Selection of the future-state ICFR tooling model (Protecht-led consolidation vs complementary integrated model) depends on an accelerated assessment of Protecht and ADO capabilities and defined decision criteria.
dependencies.dependent_on: Protecht capability deep-dive, ADO usage assessment, and agreed decision criteria
dependencies.consumer: Platform & Tooling (Track A) and overall ICFR Transformation design
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: Delays in the tooling decision will postpone configuration, migration, and integration work, risking delay of control rationalization and reporting improvements.
dependencies.mitigation: Complete capability assessments within the first 6 weeks, establish time-bound decision governance, and define interim use of existing tools if needed.

dependencies.title: Rightsline user-management APIs and re-platform completion for Alliant SailPoint onboarding
dependencies.description: Alliant SailPoint onboarding depends on the Rightsline vendor providing suitable user-management APIs and/or completing their internal re-platforming with a unified user-management layer. Currently, Rightsline exposes only business APIs (not suitable for identity lifecycle), operates a closed, vendor-controlled platform that prevents TR or third parties from building integrations, and is in the middle of a major re-platforming with no committed timeline.
dependencies.dependent_on: Rightsline vendor delivery of user-management APIs and unified user-management platform for Alliant
dependencies.consumer: SOX 404 SailPoint application onboarding program for Alliant
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If Rightsline does not deliver appropriate user-management APIs or complete the new unified platform in time, SailPoint cannot automate onboarding, provisioning, and deprovisioning for Alliant. This may delay Alliant onboarding into 2027, require duplicate integration work (current platform and again after migration), and leave SOX access controls for Alliant manual or fragmented.
dependencies.mitigation: Two main paths are under consideration: (1) Request Rightsline to build user-management APIs on the current setup and deliver by July 15, 2026, enabling SailPoint onboarding completion by end of Q3 2026 (noted as difficult due to vendor bandwidth); or (2) Defer Alliant onboarding until Rightsline completes its internal re-platforming and builds APIs on the new setup, accepting a likely 2027 timeline and planning interim manual controls.

decisions.title: Host HighQ and Contract Express in Azure GovCloud
decisions.description: The HighQ and Contract Express environments for the Port Authority program will be hosted in Azure GovCloud rather than commercial Azure.
decisions.rationale: Using Azure GovCloud aligns with FedRAMP requirements and government customer expectations for data residency and security.
decisions.options_considered: Commercial Azure versus Azure GovCloud for HighQ and Contract Express environments.

decisions.title: Use CoCounsel FedRAMP Moderate for Port Authority security requirements
decisions.description: To meet Port Authority contractual security requirements, CoCounsel will satisfy all security obligations by achieving FedRAMP Moderate authorization (anticipated completion in Q3 2026), without separate additional security work specifically for Port Authority.
decisions.rationale: Leveraging the existing FedRAMP Moderate program avoids duplicative work and ensures a standardized security posture that meets Port Authority expectations.
decisions.options_considered: Performing separate Port Authority‑specific security enhancements for CoCounsel versus relying on the broader FedRAMP Moderate authorization.

decisions.title: Layer privacy and HIPAA controls onto CoCounsel FedRAMP environment
decisions.description: CoCounsel will implement required privacy and HIPAA controls on top of its FedRAMP version to meet full Port Authority requirements, rather than maintaining separate implementations.
decisions.rationale: Extending the FedRAMP environment with privacy and HIPAA controls consolidates compliance into a single hardened environment and simplifies operations.
decisions.options_considered: Implementing privacy and HIPAA controls separately outside the FedRAMP environment versus layering them onto the FedRAMP CoCounsel platform.

decisions.title: Use product-level templates for privacy controls
decisions.description: For each privacy control, control templates will be maintained at the product level (one template per control per product) rather than a single shared template across products.
decisions.rationale: A single shared template approach, as used for FedRAMP, would be too time‑consuming for the Port Authority program timeline; product‑level templates provide flexibility while allowing reuse where possible.
decisions.options_considered: A single control template per control shared across products (FedRAMP-style) versus separate control templates per product for each privacy control.

decisions.title: Rely on CIAM FedRAMP for authentication
decisions.description: CIAM FedRAMP will be used as the authentication system. HighQ and Contract Express will reuse all FedRAMP systems, including the CIAM FedRAMP solution.
decisions.rationale: Reusing the existing CIAM FedRAMP solution leverages an already FedRAMP-audited component, reduces additional security work, and maintains consistency across products.
decisions.options_considered: Using CIAM FedRAMP for authentication versus deploying a separate or local account authentication solution for Port Authority.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Decision 0018 regarding local account support; dependency 0024 regarding CIAM requirements gathering.

decisions.title: Exclude CoCounsel integration from June Port Authority deliverable
decisions.description: CoCounsel integration is not required for the June Port Authority deliverable. CoCounsel will instead deliver with FedRAMP in Q3 2026.
decisions.rationale: Deferring CoCounsel integration to Q3 aligns its delivery with FedRAMP and reduces scope and risk for the June Port Authority milestone.
decisions.options_considered: Including CoCounsel integration in the June Port Authority deliverable versus deferring it to align with FedRAMP in Q3 2026.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel FedRAMP authorization dependency (0014) and broader CoCounsel HIPAA/privacy schedule decisions (0038, 0062).

decisions.title: Define critical HighQ features for June 30 Port Authority deliverable
decisions.description: For the June 30 Port Authority deliverable, the critical HighQ features are iSheets, Rule Builder, and Contract Express (document automation).
decisions.rationale: Focusing on iSheets, Rule Builder, and Contract Express ensures the HighQ government environment meets the core contractual requirements by the June 30 deadline.
decisions.options_considered: Various possible HighQ feature sets, including broader or narrower subsets, for the government version.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependencies on HighQ environment build and Contract Express integration; estimation exercises referenced in decisions 0027 and 0028.

decisions.title: Schedule HighQ Office Plug‑In for Q3 2026, not June deadline
decisions.description: The HighQ Office Plug‑In will be delivered as part of the Q3 2026 version and does not have an end‑of‑June deadline for the Port Authority project.
decisions.rationale: The Office Plug‑In is not critical to the June 30 Port Authority deliverable and can be deferred to reduce near‑term scope and risk.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the HighQ Office Plug‑In by June 30 versus deferring it to Q3 2026.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ Q3 2026 release planning and engineering capacity.

decisions.title: Do not support local accounts; rely on CIAM FedRAMP federated SSO
decisions.description: The Port Authority will use CIAM FedRAMP, which supports only federated SSO. Local username/password authentication will not be supported. No additional security work is required for the CIAM team for Port Authority because the CIAM solution has already passed FedRAMP audit. Some privacy controls may be implemented in CIAM FedRAMP in the second half of 2026 after FedRAMP ATO, subject to scope definition.
decisions.rationale: The CIAM FedRAMP solution was consciously designed for federated SSO only and has already passed FedRAMP audit; maintaining this model avoids additional work and preserves the FedRAMP boundary integrity.
decisions.options_considered: Supporting local account authentication for Port Authority versus requiring onboarding via federated SSO through CIAM FedRAMP.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CIAM FedRAMP solution and FedRAMP privacy controls scoping with James Pena and Jenna Perrin.

decisions.title: Move HighQ to Azure GovCloud
decisions.description: HighQ will be moved to Azure GovCloud for the government version.
decisions.rationale: Hosting HighQ in Azure GovCloud aligns the product with FedRAMP and government customer requirements and is consistent with decisions made for other products in the program.
decisions.options_considered: Retaining HighQ in commercial Azure versus moving to Azure GovCloud.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ environment build dependency (0060) and FedRAMP/HIPAA-related decisions such as 0040 and 0052.

decisions.title: Keep separate commercial and government systems for HighQ and Contract Express
decisions.description: There will be two systems for each application: one commercial system, which remains as it is today, and a separate government system maintained independently from the commercial version.
decisions.rationale: Separating commercial and government systems simplifies compliance and operational boundaries for FedRAMP/HIPAA and Port Authority requirements.
decisions.options_considered: Maintaining a single unified system for both commercial and government use versus running separate commercial and government systems.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Azure GovCloud hosting decisions (0008, 0011) for HighQ and Contract Express and FedRAMP Moderate planning (0026).

decisions.title: Defer FedRAMP Moderate independent assessment for HighQ and Contract Express
decisions.description: HighQ and Contract Express will implement the technical work needed to achieve FedRAMP Moderate level security by June 30, 2026, to meet Port Authority requirements, but an independent third‑party FedRAMP Moderate assessment will only be performed later when they formally pursue FedRAMP Moderate authorization.
decisions.rationale: Port Authority requires a FedRAMP‑equivalent security posture but does not require an immediate formal FedRAMP Moderate assessment; deferring the assessment reduces near‑term cost and schedule pressure while still delivering the necessary technical controls.
decisions.options_considered: Completing a full independent FedRAMP Moderate assessment by June 30 versus implementing the technical controls by June 30 and deferring the formal assessment.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Security control implementation for HighQ and Contract Express and future FedRAMP PMO involvement for templates (0029).

decisions.title: Decide on subset of features for government HighQ
decisions.description: It was agreed that, following estimation exercises targeted for February 6, 2026, a decision would be made regarding whether the government version of HighQ will deliver a subset of features and, if so, which features will be included or excluded.
decisions.rationale: Understanding the effort and constraints first via estimation allows an informed decision on which HighQ features can be delivered in the government environment by the required timelines.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the full HighQ feature set for government versus delivering a subset of features tailored to Port Authority needs and resource constraints.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Estimation exercises for HighQ; follow‑on action to share list with April Jones.

decisions.title: Decide on subset of features for government Contract Express
decisions.description: It was agreed that, following estimation exercises targeted for February 6, 2026, a decision would be made regarding whether the government version of Contract Express will deliver a subset of features and, if so, which features will be included or excluded.
decisions.rationale: Estimation results are needed before committing to a specific subset of Contract Express features for the government environment.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the full Contract Express feature set for government versus delivering a subset of features tailored to Port Authority requirements and capacity.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Estimation exercises for Contract Express; follow‑on action to share list with April Jones.

decisions.title: Do not complete control templates for each security control prior to FedRAMP certification
decisions.description: The team will not complete a control template for each security control as part of the Port Authority program. When HighQ and Contract Express pursue FedRAMP certification, the FedRAMP PMO will own the control templates.
decisions.rationale: Deferring control template creation reduces workload and focuses the program on implementing necessary controls rather than duplicating FedRAMP PMO responsibilities.
decisions.options_considered: Creating control templates for each security control during the Port Authority program versus relying on the FedRAMP PMO to own templates during formal certification.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Security control implementation for HighQ and Contract Express; future FedRAMP PMO engagement.

decisions.title: Run Contract Express as a separate service, not hosted inside HighQ
decisions.description: Contract Express will not be hosted or run inside HighQ; it will operate as an independent system even in the government environment.
decisions.rationale: Separating Contract Express reduces architectural coupling and simplifies security and operational boundaries, especially under FedRAMP and Port Authority constraints.
decisions.options_considered: Hosting/embedding Contract Express inside HighQ versus running Contract Express as a standalone service.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ–Contract Express integration patterns and environment design.

decisions.title: Exclude HIPAA compliance for WL and PL at launch
decisions.description: HIPAA compliance is not in scope for Port Authority for Westlaw (WL) and Practical Law (PL) at launch because customers cannot upload information into these products unless additional upload capabilities are added later.
decisions.rationale: Since no PHI will be uploaded, WL and PL do not need HIPAA compliance for the initial Port Authority scope, reducing unnecessary work.
decisions.options_considered: Including WL and PL in scope for HIPAA compliance versus excluding them due to lack of PHI upload capabilities.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Product feature set for WL/PL; any future features enabling data upload could change scope.

decisions.title: Remove CoCounsel data migration tool from Port Authority scope
decisions.description: The CoCounsel data migration tool is removed from the Port Authority scope. Port Authority users will not require migration of previously uploaded documents; they can re‑import items as needed since they will retain access to the commercial instance.
decisions.rationale: Accounts have confirmed that migration of uploaded data from the commercial to the FedRAMP environment is not required, so removing this work reduces scope and complexity without impacting user outcomes.
decisions.options_considered: Including a CoCounsel document upload migration tool in scope versus relying on users to re‑import documents from the existing commercial instance.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel FedRAMP deployment and user access to the commercial CoCounsel environment.

decisions.title: Scope product integrations for CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in (HighQ focus only)
decisions.description: For the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in, HighQ is the only required product integration for the Port Authority deliverable. CoCounsel and Legal Tracker integrations will be disabled and should not be available.
decisions.rationale: Limiting integrations to HighQ minimizes scope, reduces security and compliance complexity, and focuses on the required integration for Port Authority.
decisions.options_considered: Enabling multiple product integrations (HighQ, CoCounsel, Legal Tracker) in the Outlook Add‑in versus restricting the integration to HighQ only for the Port Authority deployment.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and HighQ FedRAMP/HIPAA environment.

decisions.title: Set delivery date for Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in (HighQ integration) to Q3 2026
decisions.description: The Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in, with HighQ integration only, is required by the Q3 go‑live and is not required for June 30, 2026, as it does not impact data ingestion.
decisions.rationale: Deferring the Outlook Add‑in to Q3 avoids overloading the June 30 milestone with non‑critical functionality that does not affect data ingestion or compliance.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering the Outlook CoCounsel Web Add‑in by June 30 versus delivering it for the Q3 go‑live.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ Q3 go‑live timeline and CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in development.

decisions.title: Defer CoCounsel privacy control delivery for Port Authority to 2027 (superseded by later decision)
decisions.description: The CoCounsel privacy control delivery for Port Authority will be delayed until 2027, alleviating 2026 funding constraints while still meeting customer contractual needs. FedRAMP and HIPAA work will continue as originally planned. CoCounsel estimates for this deferred work will be included in the 2027 EPC funding asks.
decisions.rationale: Deferring privacy controls to 2027 reduces 2026 funding pressure while preserving the ability to meet overall contractual obligations by extending the delivery timeline.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering CoCounsel privacy controls in 2026 versus deferring their delivery to 2027 while continuing FedRAMP and HIPAA work.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Later decision 0062, which updates the CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy control delivery timeline; CoCounsel FedRAMP and HIPAA remediation schedules.

decisions.title: Set CoCounsel HIPAA remediation and privacy control implementation timeline to Q1/Q2 2027 (later updated)
decisions.description: With the delay in CoCounsel privacy control delivery, it was decided that CoCounsel would have until Q1/Q2 2027 to deliver, with the expectation that HighQ is FedRAMP certified for integration by then and CoCounsel privacy controls are in place at integration time.
decisions.rationale: Aligning CoCounsel privacy control implementation with HighQ’s FedRAMP certification and integration schedule provides a realistic timeframe and consistent security posture.
decisions.options_considered: Completing CoCounsel work in 2026 versus extending delivery into Q1/Q2 2027.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ FedRAMP certification schedule; CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy control implementation; later updated by decision 0062.

decisions.title: Clarify that TDE/TFE is not a Port Authority contractual requirement for HighQ
decisions.description: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) and Transparent File Encryption (TFE) are not Port Authority contractual requirements for HighQ. They are being pursued to meet HIPAA expectations and Thomson Reuters’ internal “reasonable and appropriate” risk posture. Port Authority requirements are satisfied as long as encryption is FIPS 140‑2 validated and data at rest and in transit are protected.
decisions.rationale: Separating contractual requirements from internal and HIPAA expectations clarifies priorities and ensures Port Authority obligations are met without mandating TDE/TFE for contract compliance.
decisions.options_considered: Treating TDE/TFE as mandatory for Port Authority contractual compliance versus treating them as internal/HIPAA‑driven enhancements while still meeting Port Authority encryption requirements via FIPS‑validated encryption.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ encryption implementation decisions and HIPAA compliance planning; cryptography dependency 0051.

decisions.title: WL FedRAMP does not require HIPAA compliance at launch
decisions.description: For the WL FedRAMP environment, no PHI will be uploaded by the client; therefore, HIPAA compliance is not required at launch.
decisions.rationale: Since WL FedRAMP will not process PHI at launch, pursuing HIPAA compliance would be unnecessary for the initial release, conserving resources.
decisions.options_considered: Making WL FedRAMP HIPAA compliant for launch versus omitting HIPAA compliance due to absence of PHI uploads.
decisions.dependencies_linked: WL FedRAMP feature set and data ingestion capabilities.

decisions.title: Use Privacy SharePoint as system of record for privacy control documentation
decisions.description: The authoritative copy of privacy control documentation will be stored on the Privacy SharePoint page. While this is the system of record, teams may continue to store architecture documents, ADO artifacts, and other related documentation in their usual internal repositories.
decisions.rationale: Centralizing privacy control documentation in a dedicated SharePoint repository improves governance and traceability while allowing teams to maintain supporting artifacts where they normally work.
decisions.options_considered: Using multiple distributed repositories with no single system of record versus designating the Privacy SharePoint page as the authoritative source for privacy control documentation.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Privacy workstreams across CoCounsel, HighQ, Contract Express, and Outlook Add‑in.

decisions.title: Reuse HighQ hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov for Outlook Add‑in
decisions.description: For the CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in on HighQ, the group agreed to reuse the HighQ hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov to maintain consistency, minimize scope changes, and meet project timelines. Improvements may be considered after the Port Authority project.
decisions.rationale: Reusing the existing HighQ hosting model reduces complexity, avoids new architectural risk, and supports meeting aggressive timelines.
decisions.options_considered: Designing a new hosting model for IAM/CoCounsel in Azure Gov versus reusing the established HighQ hosting model.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and HighQ Azure Gov environment.

decisions.title: Leverage existing HighQ standards and controls for IAM/CoCounsel deployment
decisions.description: The group agreed to leverage existing HighQ standards and controls for deployment, logging, and compliance for IAM/CoCounsel in order to align with FedRAMP/HIPAA requirements and reduce additional engineering effort.
decisions.rationale: Using proven HighQ standards reduces engineering workload and ensures consistency with FedRAMP/HIPAA practices already in place.
decisions.options_considered: Creating new deployment and logging standards for IAM/CoCounsel versus reusing HighQ’s existing standards and controls.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in deployment pipeline and compliance controls.

decisions.title: Exclude OpenAI/AI components from government Outlook Add‑in architecture
decisions.description: OpenAI/AI components will be excluded from the current CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture for government compliance; only HighQ and IAM microservices will be deployed.
decisions.rationale: Excluding AI components reduces compliance and security complexity and ensures a cleaner FedRAMP/HIPAA boundary for the initial government deployment.
decisions.options_considered: Including OpenAI/AI components in the government Outlook Add‑in architecture versus limiting the deployment to HighQ and IAM microservices.
decisions.dependencies_linked: CoCounsel for MS Outlook Add‑in architecture and FedRAMP/HIPAA scope.

decisions.title: Confirm thomsonreuters.com as the valid domain for public-facing URLs
decisions.description: The group confirmed that thomsonreuters.com will be used as the valid domain for public‑facing URLs, as required for DNSSEC and FedRAMP compliance.
decisions.rationale: Using thomsonreuters.com ensures alignment with DNSSEC and FedRAMP requirements and avoids complications with alternative domains.
decisions.options_considered: Using alternative domains versus standardizing on thomsonreuters.com for public‑facing URLs.
decisions.dependencies_linked: DNS configuration, FedRAMP compliance, and Outlook Add‑in public endpoint design.

decisions.title: Defer some HighQ application-level encryption work to post-June 30 and log risk in Protecht
decisions.description: The tech team proposed a layered encryption solution with proper access controls for HighQ, which the Privacy team accepted as sufficient for now. A formal risk entry will be logged in Protecht after April 7. Additional application-level work to further protect index and temporary files is acknowledged but intentionally deferred until after June 30, 2026, and will be tracked as a separate item.
decisions.rationale: The accepted layered encryption solution meets near‑term needs, allowing the June 30 milestone to be met while deferring more complex application-level work to a later phase.
decisions.options_considered: Implementing full application‑level protections for index and temp files before June 30 versus adopting a layered encryption approach now and deferring additional protections.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Cryptography dependency 0051; HighQ HIPAA and FedRAMP compliance work; Protecht risk tracking.

decisions.title: Do not adopt Plexus for HighQ and related projects at this time
decisions.description: The group decided not to adopt Plexus for HighQ at this time due to its lack of mature Azure cloud offerings and an associated budget ask that HighQ could not commit to. Plexus may be reconsidered in the future, but not while HighQ is simultaneously executing HIPAA/FedRAMP environment work and the DC exit project.
decisions.rationale: Introducing Plexus now would increase complexity and cost during a period when HighQ is already engaged in two major projects, offering insufficient benefit relative to the risk.
decisions.options_considered: Adopting Plexus for relevant security or compliance functions versus continuing with existing tools and approaches.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ HIPAA/FedRAMP environment project and DC exit project timelines.

decisions.title: Set CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy control implementation delivery to Q3 2026
decisions.description: CoCounsel HIPAA remediation and privacy control implementation will be delivered in Q3 2026. This decision was made in a meeting with Paul, Bill, and Maria on April 29 and communicated during the Weekly Sync on April 30.
decisions.rationale: Establishing a Q3 2026 delivery date aligns CoCounsel’s HIPAA and privacy work with overall program planning and revises earlier assumptions that had pushed some work into 2027.
decisions.options_considered: Delivering CoCounsel HIPAA and privacy controls in 2027 versus bringing delivery forward into Q3 2026.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Earlier decisions 0038 and 0039 regarding CoCounsel privacy control deferral; CoCounsel FedRAMP and HighQ FedRAMP integration timelines.

decisions.title: Proceed with sale of SIU Professional Services for Fraud Detect with approved BAAs
decisions.description: The HIPAA Assessment group (R&C and Privacy) recommended proceeding with the sale of SIU Professional Services for Fraud Detect using approved BAAs, subject to the completed assessment and defined remediation plan.

decision_owner.name: HIPAA Assessment Group (Risk & Compliance and Privacy)

decisions.rationale: The SIU Professional Services HIPAA assessment is complete and a remediation plan is in place, with most gaps scheduled for remediation by the end of Q2 2026 and all by year-end 2026, enabling the organization to proceed with sales under appropriate controls.
decisions.options_considered: Proceed with SIU Professional Services sales under BAAs versus delaying or restricting sales until all remediation is complete.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Execution of SIU Professional Services remediation plan; monitoring of remediation milestones; ongoing HIPAA oversight.

decisions.title: Adopt specific encryption settings for HighQ in Azure Government and track in Protecht
decisions.description: Key decisions were made regarding encryption settings for HighQ in Azure Government environments; these decisions will be logged as issues in Protecht for tracking and the approach will be reused for other products.

decision_owner.name: Risk & Compliance and Privacy in collaboration with HighQ engineering

decisions.rationale: Standardizing encryption settings in Azure Government and tracking associated issues in Protecht ensures consistent, auditable application of security controls and provides a model for other products.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain existing encryption configurations versus adopting a standardized set of settings for Azure Government and formalizing their tracking in Protecht.
decisions.dependencies_linked: HighQ HIPAA remediation plan; Protecht issue tracking configuration; future product assessments that will reuse the Azure Gov encryption approach.

decisions.title: Future-state ICFR tooling model selection
decisions.description: Determine whether the enterprise will adopt a Protecht-led consolidation model, where Protecht becomes the primary platform for control repository, self-assessment, certification, testing results, issue tracking, and reporting, or a complementary integrated model where Protecht is the enterprise ICFR repository while ADO and SharePoint are used as the primary workflow and evidence repositories for control execution.
decisions.rationale: A clear tooling model is required to eliminate fragmentation, define system-of-record boundaries, improve workflow clarity, and enable integrated reporting and evidence management.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Protecht-led consolidation replacing DoubleCheck and reducing reliance on fragmented repositories; 2) Complementary integrated model with Protecht as ICFR repository and ADO/SharePoint as workflow and evidence tools.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependent on Protecht capability deep-dive, ADO usage assessment, and defined decision criteria; impacts Platform & Tooling (Track A) and migration planning.

decisions.title: Decision on Alliant SailPoint onboarding timing and integration approach
decisions.description: Determine whether to proceed with SailPoint onboarding for Alliant on the current Rightsline platform by requesting user-management APIs, or to defer onboarding until Rightsline completes its internal re-platforming and unified user-management layer with suitable APIs.
decisions.options_considered:
Option 1: Request Rightsline vendor to build user-management APIs on the current platform and deliver them by July 15, 2026, enabling SailPoint onboarding completion by end of Q3 2026, acknowledging that the vendor currently lacks bandwidth and this may require duplicate integration work after their re-platform.
Option 2: Defer onboarding of the Alliant application until Rightsline completes its internal re-platforming and builds user-management APIs on the new setup, accepting that this may push onboarding into a 2027 timeline and planning for extended interim manual controls.

decisions.title: ICFR Transformation governance structure and track lead model

entities.name: Customer Success Enablement
entities.status: Customer Success Enablement will deliver a unified Salesforce‑based Customer Success platform using Certinia CS Cloud to replace Gainsight, consolidate CS workflows, and increase automation. The program will roll out in phases, starting with a minimum viable CS platform to get CS teams operational quickly, then progressing to optimized health scoring, deeper data integrations (e.g., Snowflake, Pendo, Eloqua, Gong), advanced automation, governance improvements, and foundational GenAI capabilities for CS use cases.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Customer Success Enablement is delivering a unified Customer Success platform on Salesforce using Certinia CS Cloud to replace Gainsight and centralize success plans, health, risk, and playbook execution. This matters because CS teams currently rely on fragmented, manual workflows that limit visibility, automation, and scalable value realization for customers.  

At the program level, 2 of 4 defined milestones are complete, with Gainsight decommission finished on 31 Mar 2026 as planned and vendor onboarding for Certinia completed on 31 May 2026, 2 days later than its 29 May 2026 plan. Within the constituent projects, the Gainsight Migration to GSI remains in progress against an unchanged 30 Jun 2026 target, while Certinia Wave 1 planning is running 20 days late versus the original 16 May 2026 target even as use case alignment is trending 4 days ahead of its 23 Jun 2026 plan and data migration is holding to a 13 Jun 2026 target.  

Overall status is Red, driven by delayed Wave 1 planning and unresolved design and data-quality dependencies that put July 2026 UAT and go-live dates at risk.  

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses on closing the critical Certinia Wave 1 gaps by timeboxing and resolving open design decisions and TAAP health score definitions before build, while running targeted data remediation sprints to stabilize subscription, hierarchy, and territory data ahead of UAT. In parallel, the program must secure additional coverage from the Certinia side to remove the single-point-of-failure risk and re-baseline the Wave 1 plan so that downstream build, UAT, and deployment activities can proceed with clear scope and realistic dates.  

## Milestones

- Complete Certinia Wave 1 sandbox Data Migration by 13 Jun 2026.  
- Complete Certinia Wave 1 Align Use Cases milestone by 19 Jun 2026.  
- Complete Gainsight Migration to GSI, including unified relationship view and data migration, by 30 Jun 2026.  
- Complete Certinia Wave 1 UAT by 16 Jul 2026 and overall Wave 1 project completion and go-live by 27 Jul 2026.  
- Complete the Customer Success Enablement program by 31 Dec 2026.

risks.title: Handling of 25K record loads may be constrained by Salesforce limitations and current one-time load approach
risks.description: There is a risk that the approach to handle 25K record loads, given Salesforce limitations and the decision to manage this as a one-time load in GSI via a Power BI dashboard query, may not scale or may be insufficient if larger or recurring loads are needed in the future.
risks.impact_description: If Salesforce limitations prevent efficient handling of high-volume record loads and the one-time load approach in GSI proves inadequate, the team may be unable to load or refresh large datasets reliably. This could result in incomplete or outdated relationship-level data, degraded reporting and customer health monitoring, increased manual workarounds, and potential disruption to Customer Success operations and analytics.
risks.mitigation: Continue discussions on how to handle 25K record loads within Salesforce limitations and future tool assessments. In the near term, manage the requirement as a one-time load in GSI using a Power BI dashboard query while evaluating longer-term options such as optimizing Salesforce data model and limits, introducing additional integration or ETL tooling, or adjusting load frequency and batch sizes.

risks.title: Single point of failure from Certinia side – Christina is covering both BA and SA roles

risks.impact_description: If Christina remains the single point of failure without backup, any unavailability (e.g., PTO, illness, bandwidth constraints) could halt requirements clarification, data mapping, HLD changes, and Success Plan migration activities. This may delay critical design and configuration decisions, slow issue resolution, increase the risk of errors due to workload, and ultimately impact the project’s ability to achieve a path to green status and meet planned build, UAT, and go-live dates.
risks.mitigation: Identify and assign at least one additional Certinia resource to provide backup coverage for BA and/or SA responsibilities currently handled by Christina; clearly define role split and ownership for key deliverables (requirements, data mapping, HLD updates, Success Plan migration); ensure knowledge transfer and documentation so work can continue if Christina is unavailable.

entities.name: CIAM Migrations
entities.status: CIAM Migrations is a multi‑year program to modernize and consolidate customer identity and access management across Thomson Reuters by moving all legacy IDP and SSO solutions to the CIAM platform. The program coordinates federated SSO migrations, local user migrations (such as ONESOURCE, OnePass and other products like SafeSend, etc), and enabling CIAM features to deliver a unified, secure, and simplified sign-in experience across products.
entities.okrs: Migrate 65% of all SSO customers by Dec 31, 2026 (all legacy IDPs). Migrate 100% of OnePass accounts (SSO and Local) to CIAM by Dec 31, 2026.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

**Scope:** CIAM Migrations is migrating all legacy customer identity providers onto the TR Account/CIAM platform so customers have a single secure login across Thomson Reuters products and legacy IDPs can be decommissioned. The program spans federated SSO migrations (5,771 connections), local user migrations and CIAM capabilities needed to support that migration.

**Current Status:** Overall status is Red, driven primarily by low customer engagement and agreement to CIAM migration timelines. While the 48% customer engagement rate is a big win, the trajectory remains far below the 2026 target to meet 65% of legacy SSO connection migrated.

Progress on federated SSO migrations remains very low, with only 0.4% completion toward the Q2 milestone of 22% of total SSO connections, but changes to the communication strategy has resulted in a 48% customer response rate. Local user migrations are more advanced, with 98% of OnePass local user accounts in forced migration, 95,000 SafeSend local users fully cut over to CIAM. ONESOURCE local user migrations are behind plan; basic auth and OData constraints are blocking a subset of tenants with resolution targeted by Jul 31.

## Path to Green

1.  Scale outreach: Increase email volumes (target: Jun 15).
    
2.  EOL communication: Deploy CIO-approved OnePass end-of-life notice after stakeholder sign-off (target: Jun 15).
    
3.  Re-baseline OKRs: Complete late-June federated SSO projection to formally reset the 65% target to align with the realistic migration ceiling identified in the May analysis. (target: Jun 30)
    
4.  Unblock tenants: Continue ONESOURCE basic-auth remediation and MFA cutovers to clear queued migrations and ensure no ready tenant is held back (complete Jul 31).
    

## Milestones

-   Jun 30 2026: 22% SSO connection migrated (1,256); 57 unblocked ONESOURCE MFA tenants migrate to CIAM
    
-   2 Jul 2026: Revised CIAM SSO migration OKRs baselined and approved
    
-   31 Dec 2026: Complete 65% of total SSO connection migrations (3,665 connections) and 100% of OnePass local user migration
    
-   30 Apr 2027: Complete 100% of all local and SSO migrations for ONESOURCE

risks.title: 65% 2026 CIAM migration target (including OnePass) may not be achievable with current customer engagement and outreach capacity
risks.description: There is a significant risk that the program will not achieve the 2026 objective of migrating 65% of legacy SSO connections to CIAM and completing the OnePass SSO migration. Current customer response rates remain extremely low (reported as below 0.5% progress in executive reporting), the outreach vetting process is slow due to difficulty identifying the correct CSM/Account Specialist for each account, and communications volume, while increasing, is still only in the hundreds of emails per month. Leadership is questioning whether the 65% + full OnePass target is realistic even under the optimistic assumption that 100% of customers agree to migrate, given constraints on team capacity, customer engagement, and sequencing across products (OnePass, SafeSend, OneSource, Legal Tracker, etc.).
risks.impact_description:
If the 65% migration target and full OnePass completion cannot be achieved by the end of 2026:
- The program will miss its primary OKR/metric communicated to CIO leadership and executives, undermining confidence in the SSO Migration plan.
- OnePass customers (especially large/complex GLF/MLF customers) may remain on legacy IDPs longer than planned, increasing operational overhead and extending support for legacy SSO.
- Co Counsel/Co Counsel Next adoption may be negatively impacted if key customers are not on CIAM, or timelines for those customers must be adjusted.
- The project may require formal re-baselining of scope and timelines, with potential downstream impact on the final June 2027 completion target.
- Additional unplanned escalation and governance effort will be needed to explain and manage missed targets with senior leadership.
risks.mitigation:
1) Near-term re-planning and projections:
- Conduct a 1–2 week exercise (by late May 2026) to build realistic projections by segment and product (OnePass, SafeSend, OneSource, Legal products, etc.) based on actual response rates and capacity.
- Identify which products and customer segments can realistically be migrated by end of 2026 and to what percentage, including specific expectations for OnePass vs other products.
- Re-evaluate projections again in mid-July 2026 after a new feature (allowing customers to migrate without bringing all products at once) is available, to see if that accelerates legal product migrations.

2) Increase and improve customer outreach:
- Increase the volume of vetted customer communications (targeting ~350–400 emails per month in the near term, growing to 500–600 per month as processes stabilize).
- Strengthen the language in initial and follow-up emails (including clearer end-of-life messaging for legacy IDPs and a more urgent but polite tone). Raul Bauza has already updated first and second email templates.
- Send more messages and follow up sooner and more often with customers, leveraging the new templates.

3) Improve vetting and account ownership processes:
- Continue work by Eduardo Cuevas, Hassan, and Adrian to reconcile CSM/account owner information from multiple systems and vet customer contacts so outreach goes to the right person.
- Maintain the practice of engaging CSMs/Account Specialists prior to outreach to ensure correct contacts and to support escalations.

4) Re-sequence and prioritize segments:
- Revisit prioritization of segments and products, seeking opportunities to compensate for slow or complex OnePass migrations by accelerating migrations in other products (e.g., SafeSend, OneSource) while still honoring previously communicated commitments to noisy/priority customers (e.g., GLF and MLF).

5) Governance and metric alignment:
- Use the late-May and mid-July projections to determine whether the 65% + full OnePass metric remains realistic; if not, prepare a proposal for adjusted OKRs and timelines for executive review.

risks.title: Hybrid TR Account / legacy SSO states from partial federation may create long-term security and technical debt issues
risks.description: To accelerate meeting migration targets, the team is considering a "partial federation" / multi-connection approach where customers are migrated off OnePass for specific legal or OneSource products, while other Thomson Reuters Account (TRA/CIAM) products for the same customer remain on local (non-federated) credentials. In this model, a single customer can be left in a hybrid state for an extended period (some users/products federated, others not). During the May 29, 2026 weekly status meeting, Peter Grigoriou and Jeff Olson noted that many customers may be comfortable remaining in this hybrid state, while Harvarinder Batth expressed concern that once such configurations are in place they may persist "for the next 10 or 20 years," effectively becoming long-lived technical debt and potentially creating security gaps if customers assume all access is federated and centrally controlled.
risks.impact_description:
If hybrid partial-federation states become widespread and long-lived:
- Customers may assume all Thomson Reuters applications are protected by SSO and their IdP deprovisioning, while in reality some products remain on local credentials, increasing the risk that offboarded users retain access to certain TR products.
- Security and compliance posture could be weakened, especially for regulated clients, if account lifecycle management is inconsistent across products.
- CIAM and SSO teams will carry significant long-term technical debt, requiring ongoing BAU projects to "clean up" and fully federate customers long after the formal SSO Migration program end date.
- Future funding and capacity will be required to complete these full-federation cleanups, competing with new feature work and potentially impacting Vinay's and other leaders' budgets.
- Confusion in internal and executive reporting may arise if migrations are counted as "complete" at the connection level while customers remain only partially federated in practice.

raised_by.name: Grigoriou, Peter (TR Technology) and Olson, Jeff (TR Technology), with concerns strongly voiced by Batth, Harvarinder S. (Operations & Technology)

risks.mitigation:
1) Define a clear policy for hybrid states:
- Document under what conditions partial federation / multi-connection configurations are acceptable as an interim measure and for how long.
- Ensure customers are explicitly informed of the implications of remaining partially federated (e.g., some products still using local accounts) and acknowledge this risk.

2) Track hybrid configurations as first-class objects:
- Extend CIAM/SSO tracking (e.g., migration spreadsheets and dashboards) to flag customers in hybrid states, including which products are federated and which are not.
- Treat hybrid customers as not fully "done" from a CIAM perspective, even if specific federated connections are counted toward the program’s migration metrics.

3) Plan a follow-on clean-up program:
- Assign the CIAM team to own a phased plan to move hybrid customers to fully federated states over time, potentially as BAU once the main SSO Migration program ends.
- Estimate effort and seek funding approval from leadership (e.g., Vinay, Marc) for this remediation work to avoid perpetual technical debt.

4) Limit use of hybrid patterns where feasible:
- Prioritize full-federation for new customers and for high-risk / high-value clients, using the hybrid approach primarily as a tactical tool to unblock specific migrations (e.g., legal products) where necessary.

5) Governance and reporting:
- Align executive reporting so that both connection-level migration counts and the number of customers still in hybrid states are visible, avoiding a false sense of completion while significant technical debt remains.

risks.title: Delay in SAP product team implementing CIAM-only onboarding for new accounts may expand OnePass footprint and create rework
risks.description: For Co Counsel customers interested in Anthropic MCP and related AI features, the long-term plan is that all new accounts will be created as CIAM-only by default, regardless of sales channel. Sales leaders (Kristine and Marie) agree with this direction, but the SAP product team (owned by Kyle in the Amy Hutsell group) has not yet committed to delivering the required feature to stop creating new OnePass accounts. In the interim (next ~1.5 months), new accounts continue to be created on OnePass, requiring manual migration before MCP can be enabled and adding operational overhead and noise. Although the OnePass team is planning to deliver an API in mid-June that SAP can leverage, SAP’s implementation timing remains uncertain.
risks.impact_description:
If the SAP product team does not implement CIAM-only onboarding for new accounts by end of Q2 2026:
- New Co Counsel Legal and related customers will continue to be provisioned on OnePass, increasing the number of accounts that must later be migrated to CIAM.
- Operational overhead will grow as support and CIAM teams must first onboard customers onto OnePass and then subsequently migrate them, instead of onboarding directly to CIAM.
- Inbound Anthropic MCP demand will generate more one-off migration requests that must be manually handled via the current intake process, increasing noise and delay.
- The OnePass legacy footprint will expand instead of contract, complicating achievement of 2026 and 2027 CIAM migration targets.
- Leadership priorities (including Andrew’s focus on MCP success) may be harder to meet if the underlying onboarding pipeline continues to create new legacy accounts.
risks.mitigation:
1) Drive OnePass API delivery:
- Ensure the OnePass team delivers the required API for CIAM-only onboarding to non-production over the coming weekend and to production in their bi-monthly release targeted for June 15, 2026.

2) Engage SAP product management:
- Work with Hassan to provide SAP product management (Kyle and the Amy Hutsell group) with clear requirements and technical details for consuming the new OnePass API.
- Use the current MCP-related operational pain and Andrew’s strategic priority for MCP/AI features as leverage to prioritize this feature on SAP’s roadmap and seek an explicit commitment date.

3) Escalate if necessary:
- If SAP does not commit to a near-term implementation date, escalate through Jason and, if needed, to Raghu/Andrew to reinforce the importance of stopping new OnePass account creation for MCP-related products.

4) Monitor net-new account creation:
- Track the number of new Co Counsel-related accounts created on OnePass each week and quantify the additional migration and support effort required.
- Use this data to reinforce the case for expedited SAP implementation.

5) Temporary guardrails:
- Where feasible, have sales and support teams manually steer new high-priority MCP customers toward CIAM onboarding paths, even before the SAP feature is live, to limit growth of the OnePass footprint in critical segments.

risks.title: Identity divergence and data master misalignment during CIAM migration for non-migrated ONESOURCE platform tenants
risks.description: When new users are created in ONESOURCE (OSP) tenants that have not yet been enabled for CIAM migration, the system automatically creates a parallel CIAM identity as part of a standardized backend flow. These two identities — OSP and CIAM — are independent with no enforced synchronization. If a user's email is subsequently changed in OSP but not in CIAM (or vice versa), the systems treat the updated email as a new, separate identity. This creates a compounding risk of duplicate identities, broken access, and data master misalignment — particularly once tenants are migrated and CIAM becomes the system of record.
risks.impact_description:
Duplicate or orphaned CIAM identities for the same user
Users losing access to ONESOURCE and other TR products post-migration
Loss of user history when profiles are incorrectly reassigned
Incorrect role/permission assignments persisting in CIAM
Admin confusion leading to unintended identity creation
Broader platform risk if other products exhibit the same behavior
risks.mitigation: ONESOURCE and CIAM team working on defining process and UX that will give users options to either update an existing account email, link to an existing email or create a new CIAM account with the email which will enforce controls.

risks.title: ONESOURCE products who leverage OData connections are unable to have users who license the product migrate
risks.description: There is no solution to migrate OData connectors to CIAM yet, putting the migration of customers using them at risk.
risks.impact_description: Customers using ONESOURCE products that rely on OData connections cannot migrate to CIAM until a compatible solution is available, delaying CIAM migration for those tenants and constraining the overall migration timeline.
risks.mitigation: ONESOURCE team to complete a POC and implement the approved pattern; CIAM team to accept the SAML assertions required for OData-based connections. POC has been completed and implementation work is in progress, targeting a June 2026 timeline for OData migration enablement.

risks.description: As the program enters large-scale migration (non-SSO and non-basic auth tenants), scaling execution across the customer base may be constrained by the need for stronger coordination among account managers, support teams, marketing, and other customer-facing organizations.
risks.impact_description: If coordination across account managers, support, marketing, and customer-facing organizations is insufficient, migration velocity may lag, leading to slower-than-planned adoption of CIAM, extended reliance on legacy authentication, and potential slippage of migration milestones.
risks.mitigation: Continue conducting and expanding one-on-one migration sessions led by Prajyoth and Eduardo; CIAM SSO team to schedule further sessions directly with account managers; improve customer guidance and readiness materials (Pendo guides, communications) to support coordinated outreach.

risks.title: Limited reliability of legacy IDP user metrics may undermine CIAM migration planning and tracking
risks.description: Some legacy IDPs, such as certain platforms referenced in the CIAM reporting appendix (e.g., Checkpoint and others), have historically provided limited or unreliable data on key metrics, including the number of users being migrated and the number of users per federated customer IDP. Obtaining this data, even upon request, can be challenging, and tracking it on an ongoing basis is likely to be complex and resource-intensive.
risks.impact_description: If reliable user and connection metrics cannot be obtained from legacy IDPs, the program will struggle to accurately quantify migration scope, track progress against the 65% federated migration OKR, and validate completion across multiple platforms. This could result in underestimating or overestimating remaining work, misallocating migration capacity across SSO and local user workstreams, and delaying decommissioning decisions for legacy IDP systems. It may also impair executive reporting and undermine confidence in program status across products such as OnePass, ONESOURCE, SafeSend, and other legacy IDP-based platforms.
risks.mitigation: Identify which legacy IDPs have the weakest usage and user-count data, and prioritize targeted data collection efforts for those platforms (e.g., one-off data extracts, log analysis, or customer self-reporting) to establish baseline metrics. Use alternative proxies (such as federated connection counts or license counts) where exact user counts are unavailable. Allocate specific analysis capacity within the CIAM program to maintain and update these metrics over time, and factor higher uncertainty ranges into migration planning and OKR tracking. Escalate systemic data gaps through program governance if they materially affect reporting or decision-making.

risks.title: Customer readiness for API user migration timelines
risks.description: API user migration work is funded and in development with the API Guild team (development targeted for Q4 2026 and migrations starting Q1 2027), but there is a concern that customers may not be ready to adopt the new API authentication timelines.
risks.impact_description: If customers are not ready when API migration capabilities become available (Q4 2026–Q1 2027), adoption of CIAM-based API authentication may be delayed, extending reliance on legacy authentication and leaving API users misaligned with the broader CIAM migration strategy.
risks.mitigation: Continue progressing API Guild development work funded by CIAM; plan customer readiness activities (communications, guidance, and timelines) ahead of Q1 2027 to prepare API customers for migration and align expectations with the new capabilities.

risks.title: Ping Federate performance and UI limitations may delay SSO configuration and CIAM migrations
risks.description: Ping Federate is exhibiting performance and UI issues when handling large numbers of configured URLs and connections. Pages listing thousands of customer URLs are taking a very long time to load and intermittently timing out, which in turn causes errors and delays when the customer SSO team attempts to configure new CIAM SSO connections or modify existing ones. These issues are affecting not only CIAM migration work but any customer SSO configuration activity that relies on Ping, and are causing setup cycles to take significantly longer than expected. Although a workaround exists and some remediation work is planned (including a change being deployed the night of June 5, 2026), there is a risk that these problems persist or recur, creating ongoing friction and delay in enabling SSO for CIAM migrations.
risks.impact_description:
If Ping Federate performance and UI limitations continue to cause timeouts and errors when configuring SSO connections:
- The CIAM/customer SSO team will require more calendar time and manual retries to configure each new connection, reducing throughput and increasing lead times for customer migrations.
- Customers may experience delays in getting their SSO configurations set up and tested, extending the overall migration cycle beyond the targeted 30-day window discussed with customers and leadership.
- Planned migration waves (especially for OnePass, legal products, and OneSource) may slip, putting additional pressure on the team to meet the 65% 2026 CIAM migration target.
- Broader customer SSO work (not only CIAM-related) may be hindered, potentially impacting other programs that rely on timely SSO setup.
- Confidence in the mediation/native architecture and in CIAM as a stable platform could be undermined if these operational issues are perceived as persistent platform instability.
risks.mitigation:
1) Work directly with Ping support:
- Maintain and escalate existing tickets with Ping Federate support to diagnose the root cause of UI timeouts and performance degradation when listing large numbers of URLs.
- Collaborate on configuration or product-level changes (e.g., paging, limits, UI optimization) to ensure administrative actions remain performant even at current and projected scale.

2) Implement interim technical workarounds:
- Apply the change planned for the night of June 5, 2026 to reduce the probability of timeouts in the short term.
- Where possible, avoid navigating high-volume UI views and instead rely on more targeted configuration paths or APIs.

3) Protect customer migrations from impact:
- Prioritize Ping-related work that directly unblocks in-flight CIAM customer migrations.
- Communicate realistic configuration timelines to the CIAM migration team so customer-facing expectations (e.g., “within 2–3 days after metadata URL is received”) remain credible.

4) Monitor and validate improvements:
- Track configuration lead times and error rates before and after Ping changes to confirm the issue is improving.
- If issues persist beyond June, prepare a contingency plan (e.g., additional tooling, scripting, or capacity) to avoid Ping becoming a sustained bottleneck for SSO setup.

5) Governance and reporting:
- Highlight Ping-related constraints in the weekly migration process efficiency workstream so leadership understands how much of cycle time is controlled by external platform behavior versus internal process.

risks.title: Anthropic MCP migration intake handled by single SME may create capacity bottleneck and weekend coverage gaps
risks.description: Anthropic MCP-related migration requests for Co Counsel Legal/Next are currently funneled through a single intake process that is being manually reviewed and actioned primarily by Harvarinder Batth. Requests arrive via a new form and require checking whether accounts are SSO or local, obtaining customer approval to migrate to CIAM, and then handing off to Kim for inclusion in nightly migration waves. There is no weekend/holiday coverage in place yet, and Harv is considering checking requests hourly or every two hours. Leadership explicitly called out that Harv is a potential single point of failure and that early in the process there could be 72-hour windows (e.g., long weekends) where customers receive no response. This could undermine the opportunity to capitalize on strong inbound demand from Anthropic MCP users who are "fish wanting to jump into the boat."
risks.impact_description:
If MCP migration intake remains dependent on a single SME with no backup and ad-hoc review cadence:
- Customers requesting Anthropic MCP enablement may experience multi-day delays in getting migration approvals and instructions, especially over weekends/holidays.
- Co Counsel support teams will continue to send ad-hoc emails to Harv, increasing noise and confusion about status.
- The program may miss a key opportunity to demonstrate fast, customer-friendly CIAM migrations for highly interested customers, weakening one of the few strong demand levers for CIAM.
- Leadership perception (including Andrew and Jason) of the CIAM/SSO team’s operational readiness for AI-related features may be negatively impacted.
- As MCP-related features expand beyond the initial small-firm cohort into larger SSO customers, the bottleneck could scale into broader delays and customer dissatisfaction.
risks.mitigation:
1) Define and document a clear internal MCP migration intake process, including steps to:
- Verify whether the requesting account is SSO or local.
- Contact the customer to obtain approval to migrate to TR Account (CIAM).
- Provide the customer with migration steps and MCP enablement instructions.
- Hand off approved account numbers to Kim by an agreed daily cutoff time for inclusion in nightly migration waves.

2) Distribute load across multiple team members:
- Have Harv, Hassan, Nick, and potentially Shannon share responsibility for reviewing form submissions in time-boxed slots (e.g., Harv at 9:00, Hassan at 10:00, Nick at 11:00, etc.) to avoid a single point of failure.
- Ensure that at least one backup reviewer is identified for long weekends/holidays so that requests do not sit unreviewed for 72 hours.

3) Set and communicate SLAs and cutoffs:
- Establish and communicate a clear daily cutoff time (e.g., 15:00) by which vetted account lists must be sent to Kim so she can compile and process them before end of day.
- Communicate to Co Counsel support and other stakeholders that requests received after the cutoff will be processed the next business day.

4) Train and onboard additional reviewers:
- Harv to record a walkthrough of processing the next few MCP requests and share written steps/process with Nick and others so they can take over reviews when Harv is unavailable.

5) Monitor early volume and adjust staffing:
- Track request volume and response times in the first few weeks; if inbound demand grows faster than expected, adjust reviewer coverage and consider involving Ops once supporting tools (e.g., Greg’s tool to identify SSO vs non-SSO) are available.

risks.title: HighQ product team deprioritization may leave ~700 legacy HighQ SSO connections unmigrated within CIAM program timelines
risks.description: During the June 5, 2026 status meeting, Harvarinder Batth and Eduardo Cuevas reported that the HighQ product team does not currently prioritize migrating their legacy SSO customers to CIAM. HighQ is not on OnePass and has approximately 600–700 legacy SSO connections that would need to be moved to TR Account (CIAM). The HighQ team is in the middle of two other migrations, faces resource constraints, and has recently encountered issues when migrating customers to CIAM/SSO, leading them to pause proactive outreach. They indicated that they intend to perform further analysis and only plan to restart planning at the end of Q3 2026, with no firm migration deadline or schedule. There is a risk that HighQ migrations slip beyond the life of the central SSO migration team or are indefinitely delayed, leaving a large block of connections on legacy SSO and undermining CIAM migration objectives.
risks.impact_description:
If the HighQ product team continues to deprioritize CIAM migrations and does not commit to a concrete timeline:
- Approximately 600–700 HighQ legacy SSO connections may remain on legacy IDPs beyond 2026–2027, directly reducing the proportion of connections migrated to CIAM and making the 65% (and eventual 100%) migration objectives harder or impossible to achieve.
- The central CIAM/SSO migration team may disband or significantly shrink before HighQ is ready, forcing HighQ to run a separate, ad hoc migration program without the benefit of shared tooling, templates, and experience.
- Customers using HighQ in combination with other TR products (e.g., Legal Tracker or other legal products) may remain in fragmented or hybrid identity states longer than planned, with inconsistent SSO experiences and potential security/compliance gaps.
- Leadership may need to re-baseline migration KPIs and communicate that a large, named product family (HighQ) will complete after the main SSO Migration program, increasing scrutiny and governance overhead.
- Future funding may be required to support a separate HighQ migration initiative, competing with other priorities and increasing total program cost.
risks.mitigation:
1) Clarify ownership and scope:
- Decide formally whether HighQ migrations are part of the central SSO Migration program scope or a separate product-led stream, and document this in program governance.

2) Engage HighQ leadership:
- Schedule a leadership-level discussion with the HighQ product director and key stakeholders (including Hassan and Marc) to review expectations, enterprise CIAM objectives, and the consequences of an open-ended delay.
- Seek a commitment from HighQ to a concrete analysis completion date (end of Q3 2026) and a draft migration plan with target start/end dates.

3) Set program constraints and expectations:
- Communicate clearly that central migration team support is expected to taper by end of 2026; if HighQ defers beyond that, they may need to run migrations predominantly with their own resources, with CSS/central team only providing connection-level support.
- Establish a notional deadline (e.g., Q4 2026 / Q1 2027) by which HighQ migrations should be substantially complete, subject to leadership approval.

4) Prepare for re-inclusion in the program:
- Temporarily exclude HighQ connections from the core 5,700-connection total used for CIAM program metrics, while tracking them separately as a distinct HighQ workstream.
- Maintain periodic check-ins with HighQ so their analysis and planning can feed back into the main program if they are ready sooner than expected.

5) Governance and escalation:
- Escalate to CIO/platform leadership if HighQ does not produce a credible plan by end of Q3 2026, including options such as mandated timelines or additional shared resources.

Feedback indicates issues with tone, short response timelines, time zone mismatches, and lack of coordination with local account teams. Delayed onboarding / migration scheduling
Reduced client satisfaction (especially Premium Care accounts)
Potential reputational impact to TR (white-glove experience expectations not met)
Increased operational overhead due to escalations and rework
Risk of inconsistent messaging across regions

Adjust tone to focus on benefits and partnership
Remove high-risk wording (e.g., “not optional”, “disruption”)

Targeted follow-up actions for large / strategic customers (June 5, 2026 status meeting):
- Monitor customer feedback on the updated templates; to date, only four customers (~0.7% of communications) have raised concerns, mostly large or strategic accounts.
- For large / sensitive customers (e.g., GLLF and UK strategic accounts), consider slightly modified wording and/or bespoke communications led by their CSMs to avoid misinterpretation of subject lines and deadlines (e.g., clarifying that dates refer to response deadlines, not hard migration cutover dates).
- Continue using the strengthened templates for the broader customer base given the materially improved response rate (~48% of contacted customers have now responded, versus ~15–20% in earlier weeks).

risks.title: Product-by-product (partial) SSO migrations may create long-term hybrid security and technical debt for CIAM
risks.description: During the May 29, 2026 OnePass–CIAM Migration Weekly Status Meeting, the team discussed accelerating SSO migration progress by enabling customers to migrate on a product-by-product basis (e.g., moving Legal Tracker or ONESOURCE SSO connections off OnePass to CIAM) while leaving other TR Account products for the same customer on local credentials or non-federated states. This "multi-connection" approach would allow counting those product connections as migrated for CIAM OKR purposes, even if the customer remains in a hybrid state where some users are federated and others are not. While this could improve near-term migration metrics, leadership (Harvarinder, Peter, Jeff) expressed concern that customers may assume deprovisioning and access controls are fully centralized when they are not, and that hybrid configurations may remain indefinitely due to funding and prioritization constraints, creating long-lived security and technical debt across products.
risks.impact_description:
If partial, product-by-product SSO migrations are widely adopted without a clear follow-on plan to consolidate customers into fully federated CIAM configurations:
- Customers may remain in hybrid states for many years, with some applications federated and others still using local credentials, increasing the risk of orphaned accounts and inconsistent access revocation when users leave an organization.
- Security expectations between TR and customers may become misaligned; customers could believe all TR products are centrally controlled when only a subset are, increasing exposure to unauthorized access and complicating incident response.
- The CIAM platform and product teams will carry significant long-term technical debt, with complex, inconsistent federation patterns across products and tenants that are harder to support, monitor, and audit.
- Future programs aiming to improve security posture or simplify customer experience may face higher costs and longer timelines to clean up hybrid states and complete full federation.
- Program-level reporting may overstate sustainable progress (counting connections as "migrated" while underlying security/control objectives are only partially met), reducing transparency for leadership and stakeholders across SSO Migration (proj-107) and Local User Migration (proj-109).
risks.mitigation:
Define and govern a controlled use of product-by-product (partial) migrations:
- Establish clear CIAM program guidelines for when partial federation is allowed (e.g., specific segments, temporary bridge for complex multi-product customers) and require documentation of the residual hybrid state for each such customer.
- Ensure all customers adopting partial migrations are explicitly informed of the implications (e.g., some products still using local credentials, deprovisioning not fully centralized) and acknowledge these trade-offs.
- Define a follow-up "cleanup" strategy owned by the CIAM program, including:
  * Target windows within which hybrid states should be resolved (e.g., 12–24 months after partial migration).
  * Criteria for prioritizing high-risk customers for full federation.
  * Integration of hybrid cleanup into BAU CIAM roadmap and funding plans.
- Enhance internal tracking so that program dashboards distinguish between fully federated migrations and partial (product-level) migrations, enabling leadership to see both OKR progress and residual security/technical debt.
- Coordinate with security and architecture governance bodies to review and endorse the partial migration approach and to set expectations for future remediation.

Pilot the multi-connection approach with a limited number of customers (e.g., Legal Tracker + ONESOURCE examples) and review lessons learned before broad rollout.

This will reduce throughput across the SSO Migration and ONESOURCE Local User Migration projects, cause the program to fall further behind schedule, and may require additional specialized resources or tooling. It could also create inconsistent customer experiences and complicate sequencing across platforms, delaying the retirement of legacy IDP systems and impacting the program’s strategic objective of unified CIAM.

Continue validating the scale and distribution of account and product complexity across the program and adjust sequencing so that migrations are ordered by account readiness. Use emerging capabilities such as the account merging feature and improved onboarding processes to handle complex accounts more efficiently, and consider adjusting plans or resource allocation for highly complex customers.
