assumptions.title: Sufficient June 2026 data will enable a realistic re-baseline of CIAM SSO migration OKRs by end of June
assumptions.description: The program is proceeding on the basis that, by the end of June 2026, enough data will have been gathered from current and upcoming SSO migration activities (including the ~84 customers engaged in May and subsequent June outreach) to support a realistic re-baseline of the CIAM SSO migration OKRs. During the May 29, 2026 status meeting, leadership agreed that the previously planned mid‑June (June 15) checkpoint would not provide adequate evidence, and that a later June decision point is needed to understand true cycle times from customer engagement to migration and sustainable engagement rates.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Initial projections show that current SSO migration throughput and engagement rates are insufficient to meet the 65% 2026 CIAM migration target, and there is significant uncertainty about actual average cycle times (e.g., 30 vs 45 vs 60+ days) from engagement to migration. Leadership previously scheduled a mid‑June reevaluation, but the ramp-up of the SSO Onboarding Team, process refinements, and the current small sample of engaged customers mean more runtime data is required to derive a realistic plan. Extending the re-baseline checkpoint to late June is assumed to provide a more representative dataset across products and customer segments.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The SSO Onboarding Team, communication templates, and booking tools are actively being refined, and outreach volumes are increasing. A four- to six-week window (late May through June) should be sufficient to observe whether these changes materially improve funnel conversion and throughput. However, engagement behavior can vary by region and product, and some customers may move more slowly than expected, so there remains a risk that June data will still be limited or skewed. Hence confidence is medium rather than high.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If June data proves insufficient or indicates that SSO migration throughput remains far below target, the program will: (1) escalate the need for stronger structural changes (e.g., additional SSO Onboarding capacity, expanded vendor support, or more aggressive customer policies such as firmer cutover timelines); (2) consider deferring the formal OKR re-baselining decision to July while clearly communicating interim expectations to leadership; and (3) potentially segment the OKR into sub-targets (by product or region) to better reflect realistic delivery patterns.
assumptions.validation_method: Analyze June 2026 SSO migration funnel metrics (number of customers contacted, responded, meetings scheduled, technical setup started, migrations completed) across key segments and products; compare observed average cycle times and engagement rates against the assumptions used in Harvarinder's projection model; prepare a revised projection and migration plan for late June leadership review and potential OKR re-baselining.

assumptions.title: Average time from customer engagement to migration completion is approximately 30–45 days
assumptions.description: Current migration projections assume that, once a customer has engaged (i.e., replied to outreach and started working with the SSO team), the end-to-end cycle to complete their migration is roughly one month. In the May 29, 2026 status meeting, Harvarinder Batth explained that the projection model assumes engaged customers are migrated within 30 days, but acknowledged this may actually be closer to 45 days or longer on average due to customer internal processes (coordinating IT resources, security reviews, data clean-up, user communication) and TR-side process gaps. This assumption underpins the monthly throughput estimates derived from the 84 currently engaged customers and future outreach plans.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The projection spreadsheet discussed by Harvarinder uses engagement rates (e.g., 25% in the first month, 15% in the second, then 10% thereafter) combined with an assumed 30-day cycle time from engagement to completion. This yields an upper-bound estimate of ~2,700–2,800 migrated connections in 2026 once adjusted for the corrected total connection count. The team needs a working estimate of cycle time to convert engagement numbers (e.g., current 84 engaged customers) into migration throughput for planning and for re-baselining the 2026 targets.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current evidence is limited and mixed: some smaller customers can migrate quickly, but larger or more complex customers (e.g., GLLF) face extended internal coordination, security review, and data clean-up requirements, as highlighted by both Peter Grigoriou and Harvarinder. The team is still refining processes and expects efficiency gains by late June, but until more data is collected, the true average cycle time remains uncertain.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency:
If analysis shows that the average cycle time is materially longer than 30–45 days:
- Update the projection model with the new empirically-derived cycle times and re-baseline the 2026 migration targets, communicating changes to leadership.
- Explore process and tooling changes to shorten cycle time (e.g., multi-connection support to decouple legal product migrations from broader TRA SSO changes, better customer-facing tools for data clean-up).
- Consider additional capacity (e.g., expanding Capgemini team) to handle more migrations in parallel.
- Further prioritize segments and products where shorter cycle times are achievable to maximize progress against revised targets.
assumptions.validation_method:
1) Track the 84 currently engaged customers through to completion, recording the date of first engagement, date of TRA SSO setup, and date of final migration for each.
2) Calculate the average and distribution (e.g., median, 75th percentile) of cycle times across this cohort by the end of June 2026.
3) Repeat the analysis monthly (July, August) to see whether process improvements shorten the average.
4) Use these empirical cycle times to update the projection model and re-baseline migration targets and throughput assumptions.

assumptions.title: Forced migration of local user accounts will drive adequate completion of individual user migrations
assumptions.description: The program assumes that forcing local user accounts into migration will result in most individual profiles being migrated without extensive manual intervention, despite some inactive or invalid user profiles.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Forced migration mechanisms are designed to encourage or require users to move to CIAM when accessing products, reducing the need for manual outreach and minimizing residual legacy accounts.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The high coverage of forced migration suggests that most active users will encounter the new CIAM flows. However, evidence already shows that many profiles remain unmigrated due to user behavior, so the assumption holds only if this residual segment is small enough not to materially affect program objectives.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If a large number of profiles remain unmigrated, the unmigrated profiles will be bulk migrated following completion of the SSO migrations.
assumptions.validation_method: Analyze migration completion rates at the profile level within forced-migration accounts and compare against target thresholds for program completion.

assumptions.title: Account and product complexity will remain manageable within current CIAM migration processes
assumptions.description: The program assumes that, although higher than initially anticipated, account- and product-level complexity can be addressed using current migration processes, tooling, and sequencing strategies without requiring major redesign of the CIAM migration approach.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The program has already started validating complexity and leveraging features like account merging and sequencing by readiness, which are expected to handle most complex scenarios.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Early indications are that account complexity is higher than anticipated, but the program is actively validating the scale and distribution and deploying new features aimed at addressing it. Until data shows that these measures are insufficient, leadership is treating complexity as manageable within the existing framework.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: CIAM feature being developed to allow product by product migration of SSO connections.
assumptions.validation_method: Release of feature

assumptions.title: Expanded SSO Onboarding Team capacity from April 27 will enable recovery of migration throughput
assumptions.description: The program assumes that onboarding the remaining five SSO Onboarding Team members starting April 27 will significantly increase federated migration throughput and help close the Q1 migration gap, contributing to an overall move from Red toward Green.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Program plans to "go to green" rely on the SSO Onboarding Team consistently completing more federated connection migrations than originally projected, which requires additional headcount to be fully operational.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The expanded team is committed and scheduled, and the onboarding process already exists. However, the actual ramp-up speed and productivity of new members remain unproven until several bi-weekly cycles of operation are observed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: We will monitor communication and migration rates during the month of May and re-evaluate timeline the first week of June to determine if additional acceleration is necessary.
assumptions.validation_method: Measure federated migration and communications, tracking the number of completed migrations per period and comparing against targets required to close the Q1 gap.

assumptions.title: 65% of legacy SSO connections can be migrated to CIAM by end of 2026 by de-emphasizing complex OnePass customers and compensating with other products
assumptions.description: The program is proceeding under the assumption that the 65% migration target for 2026 can still be achieved even if some large/complex OnePass customers (e.g., GLF/MLF) are not fully migrated by year-end, by accelerating migrations in other products and segments such as SafeSend, OneSource, and other legal products. The idea is that these products may be able to move faster and partially compensate for delayed or incomplete OnePass migrations, potentially resulting in a mix where OnePass is not 100% complete but overall CIAM migration still reaches approximately 65%.
assumptions.rationale_basis: In the meeting, Harvarinder stated he still has confidence that 65% can be achieved, but not including full OnePass completion, and suggested compensating by pushing more migrations through other products (e.g., SafeSend with ~300 connections, OneSource, other products) that may be more willing to move faster based on different communication approaches.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current leadership sentiment acknowledges that the original plan likely overestimated customer response rates and did not fully account for non-responsive customers. However, there is some evidence that other products (e.g., SafeSend, OneSource) may be easier to move and a new feature is expected to unlock faster partial migrations for legal products starting in Q3. Because these levers are not yet fully validated and rely on customer behavior, confidence is moderate rather than high.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency:
If analysis in late May and July shows that the 65% target cannot be met even with compensating migrations:
- Prepare a revised set of OKRs/metrics for executive approval, potentially reducing the 2026 percentage, decoupling OnePass completion from the 65% metric, or shifting some scope into 2027.
- Further re-sequence segments, focusing on highest-priority customers (e.g., GLF/MLF and Co Counsel Next candidates) even if overall percentage remains lower.
- Consider additional measures to improve customer engagement (e.g., stronger end-of-life enforcement, more aggressive escalation, or alternative outreach channels) to raise migration throughput.
assumptions.validation_method:
1) A 1–2 week projection exercise across segments and products to quantify realistic 2026 migration volumes.
2) A follow-up re-evaluation in mid-July 2026 after the new "partial migration" feature is available and early adoption data is observed.
3) Comparison of actual monthly migration throughput versus the projections to confirm whether compensating migrations are materializing.
assumptions.source_file_name: Sync on CIAM Migration timeline and metrics.docx

assumptions.title: Customer outreach volume can scale to approximately 400–600 vetted migration emails per month
assumptions.description: Planning assumptions for the SSO Migration program currently presuppose that the team can ramp and sustain a significantly higher volume of vetted customer communications, reaching roughly 350–400 emails per month in the near term and 500–600 per month in subsequent months, as data processes and account ownership identification improve.
assumptions.rationale_basis: In the meeting, Harvarinder and Eduardo noted that March outreach volume was around 100 emails, April around 200+, and that in the last week alone they sent approximately 80–90 emails. They discussed a trajectory where May might reach ~400 emails, June ~500, and subsequent months 500–600, assuming vetting and data processes are streamlined.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The team is already trending upward from ~100 to 200+ emails per month and has recently sent ~80–90 emails in a single week, indicating that a few hundred emails per month are feasible. However, vetting bottlenecks (e.g., identifying correct CSM/Account Specialist contacts across multiple systems) and limited data access still constrain growth, so sustained 500–600 emails per month is plausible but not yet proven.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency:
If outreach volume cannot reach or sustain 400–600 vetted emails per month:
- Prioritize outreach to highest-impact segments and customers (e.g., GLF/MLF, Co Counsel Next prospects, upcoming migration waves) rather than broad coverage.
- Seek additional data analysis and operations support to increase vetting throughput (e.g., temporary staffing, automation, better dashboards).
- Explore alternative outreach and escalation mechanisms (e.g., leveraging sales/CSM campaigns, webinars, or account reviews) that do not rely solely on direct emails.
- Re-calculate migration throughput and adjust 2026 targets accordingly, escalating to leadership if capacity remains a hard constraint.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor monthly counts of vetted initial and follow-up outreach emails sent and compare them against the 400–600 per month target; correlate outreach volume with available vetted customer lists and vetting throughput to determine whether capacity and processes can sustain the planned scale.
assumptions.source_file_name: Sync on CIAM Migration timeline and metrics.docx

assumptions.title: Co Counsel Next enablement can proceed without requiring CIAM migration as a strict prerequisite for existing Co Counsel Legal customers
assumptions.description: The CIAM/SSO migration and Co Counsel Next product enablement plans are being discussed under the assumption that existing Co Counsel Legal customers can begin using Co Counsel Next without first being migrated to CIAM. The rationale is that these customers already have access and can be given a feature flag to enable Co Counsel Next, avoiding additional friction and delays from making CIAM migration a prerequisite.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Harvarinder explained that existing Co Counsel Legal customers already have access and that Co Counsel Next is effectively a new feature/skin enabled via a feature flag. Requiring CIAM migration as a prerequisite for these customers may introduce significant data clean-up and friction, potentially slowing time to market. There is active discussion with leadership (e.g., Marc) about whether CIAM should remain a prerequisite for these customers.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The current design indicates that Co Counsel Next can be enabled as a feature within the existing product, and leadership believes that many customers already have access with their current registration keys. However, there are concerns about customer friction, data clean-up, and perception of past access issues. Until more evidence is gathered, confidence remains moderate.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency:
If it is determined that CIAM migration must be a prerequisite for Co Counsel Next for existing Co Counsel Legal customers:
- Re-sequence the CIAM migration plan to prioritize co-counsel-related customers ahead of other segments.
- Coordinate carefully with Co Counsel Next go-to-market plans to minimize delays and communicate clearly with affected customers.
- Provide additional resources for data clean-up and migration support for these customers to shorten the prerequisite migration phase.
- Reassess CIAM migration capacity and timelines to ensure that prioritizing these customers does not critically undermine overall migration targets.
assumptions.validation_method: Ongoing product and architecture review between CIAM leadership and Co Counsel Next product leadership (including Marc and Hassan) to determine whether enabling Co Counsel Next without CIAM introduces unacceptable risk or experience issues; evaluation of early customer experiences and support incidents for customers enabled on Co Counsel Next without prior CIAM migration.
assumptions.source_file_name: Sync on CIAM Migration timeline and metrics.docx

assumptions.title: Customer agreement rates will be sufficient to meet CIAM migration timelines
assumptions.description: Program planning assumes that a high enough proportion of customers will engage and agree to proposed migration timelines so that the CIAM Migrations program can achieve its projected migration volumes and schedule.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The program must migrate large numbers of customers from legacy IDPs to CIAM within specific timeframes. This requires customers to respond to outreach and agree to migration dates, so the plan is built on expected engagement rates.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current data from the April 18 – May 1, 2026 reporting period shows overall engagement of approximately 40% following outreach, but only 0.38% of all active federated connections have been migrated. This indicates that, while some customers are engaging, agreement rates and follow-through remain well below what is required to hit program targets. The program is strengthening communication (including a proposed OnePass End-of-Life statement), accelerating account vetting to reach 100% of OnePass customers, and involving Customer Account Managers sooner. These steps may improve agreement rates, but until trend data over several cycles is available, the assumption remains fragile.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If customer agreement rates remain insufficient despite enhanced communications and earlier Customer Account Manager involvement, the program will need to further increase incentives and communication touchpoints, re-sequence migrations to focus more heavily on highly responsive customers and products (e.g., SafeSend, ONESOURCE, other legal products), and re-baseline program timelines and OKRs to realistic engagement levels. Leadership may also need to consider introducing stronger measures such as firmer end-of-support timelines for legacy IDPs.
assumptions.validation_method: Track the percentage of customers who respond and agree to proposed timelines over multiple outreach cycles and compare against planned engagement assumptions.

assumptions.title: CIAM federated user migrations will proceed based solely on customer agreement without a forced migration date
assumptions.description: The program is currently planning federated (SSO) user migrations under the assumption that customers will agree to proposed migration timelines and that there will be no firm forced-migration date. All federated user migration timelines are therefore contingent on customer agreement, and customers are not obligated to accept any specific date.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The CIAM program has not yet defined or communicated a forced cutover date for federated migrations away from legacy IDPs such as OnePass. Current strategy relies on gaining customer agreement through outreach, strengthened communications (including proposed OnePass End-of-Life messaging), and expanded SSO Onboarding Team capacity rather than enforcing unilateral migration deadlines.
assumptions.validity_explanation: As of the April 18 – May 1, 2026 status reporting period, all federated migration timelines explicitly state that they assume customer agreement and that there is no forced migration date. However, ongoing low engagement and the risk of missing the 65% migration OKR may drive leadership to adopt firmer measures in future, such as setting mandatory cutover dates in conjunction with End-of-Life communications for legacy IDPs. Until such a decision is made, the program continues to operate under a voluntary, agreement-based model.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If it becomes clear that an agreement-only approach will not achieve program objectives in time, the program may need to propose and implement one or more forced migration dates (tied to End-of-Life/End-of-Support timelines for legacy IDPs) and adjust customer communications accordingly. This would involve coordinated stakeholder alignment, updated legal and customer messaging, and a re-baselined migration plan reflecting mandatory cutovers.
assumptions.validation_method: Review program governance and communications decisions to determine whether a forced migration date is introduced (e.g., OnePass End-of-Life approval including a mandatory cutover).

issues.title: Program-level issue: Low customer engagement and agreement on CIAM migration timelines
issues.description: Customer engagement and agreement on CIAM migration timelines remains significantly below what is required to support the CIAM Migrations program schedule. In the most recent period, the SSO Onboarding Team sent 96 customer outreach emails and received only 13 responses, and overall engagement following outreach is reported at approximately 40%. Because there is no forced-migration date for many federated (SSO) migrations, progress is heavily dependent on customers responding and agreeing to proposed timelines. At current engagement levels, the program is unlikely to achieve its migration goals within the targeted timeline.
issues.impact_assessment: Low customer engagement and limited agreement on CIAM migration timelines is constraining both federated (SSO) and local user migration throughput across products (e.g., OnePass, ONESOURCE, SafeSend). The program’s overall RAG schedule status remains Red, and key OKR metrics (0.38% of total active federated connections migrated) indicate significant underperformance relative to plan. Without a material increase in customer responses and timeline commitments, the CIAM Migrations program will not achieve its 65% 2026 migration target or complete OnePass migrations on the planned schedule, driving extended parallel operation of legacy IDPs and delaying retirement of those platforms.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Dependent on customer engagement and agreed timelines for CIAM migrations; relies on Customer Account Manager participation, SSO Onboarding Team capacity, and approval of OnePass legacy IDP end-of-life communications.
issues.resolution: Implement a multi-pronged response focused on: (1) introducing stronger OnePass legacy IDP end-of-life and end-of-support communications (currently drafted and under internal review), (2) reducing the escalation timeline for involving Customer Account Managers from 4 weeks to 2 weeks, and (3) accelerating the volume and timing of customer outreach communications, including bringing forward communications to more customers. Program leadership will also monitor the ramp of the expanded SSO Onboarding Team through May and consider re-baselining timelines if federated migration volumes do not recover the Q1 shortfall.

issues.title: Program-level issue: Limited and unreliable user metrics from some legacy IDPs complicate CIAM progress tracking
issues.description: Some legacy IDPs (e.g., Checkpoint and similar platforms) have historically provided limited or unreliable data on key metrics, including the number of users being migrated and the number of users per federated customer IDP. Obtaining this information, even upon request, may present challenges, and tracking it on an ongoing basis is likely to be complex and resource-intensive.
issues.impact_assessment: Inconsistent or unreliable user metrics from certain legacy IDPs reduce the CIAM Migrations program’s ability to accurately measure migration progress by platform, reconcile user counts against OKR targets, and plan federated migration timelines. This introduces uncertainty into executive reporting and may mask emerging delivery risks if user volumes are materially higher than currently visible. It also increases manual effort required from product and analytics teams to assemble and validate data across platforms.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Affects migration progress reporting for the SSO Migration (proj-107) and overall CIAM Migrations OKRs; dependent on legacy IDP platform teams’ ability to supply or improve user metrics.
issues.resolution: Leverage platform and product teams to obtain the best-available metrics from legacy IDPs, prioritize data improvements for high-volume platforms, and clearly document any known gaps or assumptions in program-level reporting. Where precise user counts cannot be obtained, use conservative estimates and focus on tracking the number of federated connections migrated as a proxy while planning targeted data remediation for critical systems.

issues.title: Ping Federate UI performance issues delaying SSO connection setup
issues.description: Ping Federate is experiencing UI performance and timeout issues when loading pages with large numbers of configured URLs for customers, causing delays and intermittent errors during SSO connection setup. Administrators sometimes receive errors and must retry actions, slowing down configuration of CIAM/SSO connections for new and migrating customers.
issues.impact_assessment: The Ping Federate UI performance issue is directly slowing down the configuration of SSO connections required for CIAM migrations and for any new customer SSO setups. Administrators are encountering timeouts and errors when loading pages that list thousands of URLs, forcing retries and extending the time required to create or modify connections. This reduces throughput on the technical setup stage and may create a backlog, even when customers provide metadata URLs promptly. The issue affects all customers whose SSO connections must be configured via the affected Ping Federate instances, not just CIAM migration customers, and therefore has a broad operational impact.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Ping Federate platform performance; CIAM customer SSO configuration team; all CIAM/SSO migrations requiring new or updated connections.
issues.resolution: Work with Ping support and internal administrators to identify and remediate the root cause of the UI performance bottleneck (e.g., optimizing how large URL lists are rendered, adjusting timeouts, or restructuring configuration views). Implement interim workarounds discussed in the June 5, 2026 meeting during a planned maintenance window to keep configuration work moving while a permanent fix is developed.

issues.impact_assessment: Residual unmigrated profiles within accounts marked as forced migration create ambiguity in migration completion metrics and complicate closure of local user profile migration scope across platforms within the CIAM program.
issues.resolution: profiles will be bulk migrated to CIAM. It would be beneficial to clean these unmigrated profiles up prior to bulk migration - Program Manager is working with team to identify who can lead the clean up effort.

issues.title: Low customer response rate continues to impact CIAM migration progress
issues.description: Customer response to CIAM migration outreach remains below the level required to support the planned migration from legacy IDPs to TR Account (CIAM), though some improvements are being observed as outreach is accelerated and templates are strengthened.
issues.impact_assessment: The persistently low response rate continues to constrain the CIAM migration funnel. Even with increased outreach volume, insufficient customer replies make it difficult to schedule migrations and demonstrate progress against the 65% 2026 migration target. However, recent actions — including stronger first, second, and third emails and escalations via CSMs — are starting to show incremental improvements in responses, which may mitigate impact if sustained.
issues.dependencies_affecting: SSO Onboarding team’s outreach capacity; Customer Success Managers and Account Specialists for escalations; shared mailbox and tracking spreadsheet data quality.
issues.resolution: Increase the volume and cadence of outreach emails (currently ~80–90 per week), use updated first, second, and third email templates with stronger 'polite urgency' and clearer legacy IDP end-of-life messaging, send a third email for non-responders, and escalate to Customer Success Managers/Account Specialists when there is no response after the third email. Eduardo will also reconcile the shared mailbox with the tracking spreadsheet by May 20, 2026 to ensure response data is accurate.

issues.title: Difficulty Identifying Account Specialist / CSM Ownership for Customer Accounts
issues.description:
The project team is facing significant challenges identifying the appropriate Account Specialist (ASM) or Customer Success Manager (CSM) for each customer account requiring SSO migration follow-up and escalation.

The required account ownership information is spread across multiple systems and is not aggregated or centralized. Many of these systems support only specific customer segments, such as Corporates, Legal, and Tax, or sometimes only a single product area, such as Legal Tracker. As a result, the team is unable to easily determine the correct ASM or CSM contact for each account.

This has created a highly manual and time-consuming process, requiring the team to review accounts one by one and coordinate with multiple teams and data analysis resources to locate the correct account owner.
issues.impact_assessment:
The lack of centralized ASM/CSM ownership data is slowing down the escalation process for non-responsive customers and may delay customer engagement, migration scheduling, and overall execution of the SSO migration from the legacy IDP to TR Account (CIAM).

It also increases the operational burden on the project team and supporting teams, creating inefficiencies and risk of inconsistent or delayed follow-up.
issues.resolution:
To address this issue, the project team recommends the following actions:

Engage data owners and business segment teams:
Partner with representatives from Corporates, Legal, Tax, and product-specific teams to identify the authoritative sources for ASM/CSM ownership data.

Create a consolidated account ownership tracker:
Build a centralized working file or dashboard that aggregates ASM/CSM information from available systems and maps each customer account to the appropriate owner.

Assign data analysis support:
Secure dedicated support from data analysis experts to help extract, reconcile, and validate account ownership data across the different systems.

Define a repeatable lookup process:
Establish a standard process for identifying ASM/CSM ownership for each account, including clear escalation paths when ownership is missing, outdated, or conflicting.

Prioritize high-risk / non-responsive customers:
Focus initial ownership mapping efforts on customers who have not responded to migration communications or who are part of upcoming migration waves.

Identify long-term data governance needs:
Escalate the lack of centralized account ownership data as a broader operational gap and recommend a long-term solution for maintaining a single, reliable source of account ownership information.

decisions.title: Adopt multi-pronged strategy to improve CIAM migration outreach effectiveness
decisions.description: Leadership agreed that the CIAM migration program will simultaneously pursue four key strategies to improve customer engagement and migration progress: (1) send outreach emails to more customers (increasing volume), (2) follow up sooner and more frequently with non-responsive customers, (3) strengthen the language and tone of communications, including clearer legacy IDP end-of-life messaging to create urgency, and (4) re-segment and re-sequence migration priorities across products and customer segments to compensate for early slowness and adjust for low response rates.
decisions.rationale: Executive leadership has been concerned that reported metrics show poor progress and that initial plans were overly optimistic about customer response rates. A coordinated, multi-pronged approach is needed to increase engagement, accelerate migrations, and credibly demonstrate a 'path to green' while managing expectations about the 65% target and OnePass completion.

decisions.title: Conduct two-stage reevaluation of 65% CIAM migration target and OnePass completion
decisions.description: The team will conduct a two-stage reevaluation of the 65% CIAM migration target and OnePass completion goal. First, a 1–2 week exercise (by late May 2026) will produce realistic projections based on current response data, segment-by-segment analysis, and reprioritization of products (including potential compensation from Safesend, OneSource and other products if large/complex OnePass customers lag). Second, in mid-July 2026, the team will reevaluate the plan again using data from the new feature that allows customers to migrate without all products moving at once, assessing whether overall completion can reach approximately 90–95% of the original target.
decisions.rationale: Progress to date and very low response rates indicate the original plan may not be realistic, especially for large and complex OnePass customers. Leadership needs a more evidence-based assessment of whether the 65% target is achievable and what trade-offs (e.g., compensating with other products) are required, while also considering new feature capabilities that may accelerate legal product migrations later in the year.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain the 65% and full OnePass completion goals without reevaluation; immediately reduce targets based on early pessimism; delay any reconsideration until much later in 2026.

decisions.title: Define three CIAM migration workstreams with named leads

These workstreams will be tracked in the weekly status deck.
decisions.rationale: Discussion highlighted three major bottlenecks to achieving CIAM migration targets: readiness of vetted outreach lists, low customer response rates, and slow/complex migration execution. Formalizing these as workstreams with named leads and weekly tracking creates accountability and visibility into progress on each dimension.
decisions.options_considered: Continue treating these activities as implicit tasks without explicit workstreams or leads; focus only on customer engagement without separately tracking outreach readiness and process efficiency.

A fixed follow-up date ensures the leadership group reviews concrete data and projections rather than relying on early, incomplete observations from the first few weeks of the full team being in place.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

The Mergers, Acquisitions & Divestitures (MAD) program governs technology integration and separation for acquired and divested businesses so they can operate on Thomson Reuters platforms or exit TSAs without disruption, security gaps, or stranded cost. It delivers cloud landing, lead‑to‑cash enablement, and divestiture technology exit for assets such as SafeSend, Tic Tie Calculate, Signature Standalone, Time Base, Ochre, and Noetica.

Across the portfolio, 9 of 11 constituent projects are Green and 2 are Amber, with the overall program running through 31 Dec 2026. Key H1 2026 milestones are concentrated in June and July, including SafeSend production migration by 30 Jun 2026, SafeSend One lead‑to‑cash UAT and CS&S go‑lives in June–July 2026, and Project Ochre Cloud Migration Phase 2 completing on 29 Jun 2026, while some security and audit activities (e.g., Noetica ISRM critical findings remediation at 31 Jul 2026 and Additive ISRM audit attestations running 7 days late) indicate control work is lagging execution.

Overall status is AMBER, driven by unresolved data and platform integration dependencies in the SafeSend One program that threaten the July 2026 go‑live window.

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses on unblocking SafeSend One by finalising MDM and CIAM integrations ahead of June UAT, aligning CS&S and upstream workstream schedules to protect the 13 Jul and 27 Jul 2026 launches, and closing Noetica ISRM critical findings by 31 Jul 2026 so integration work can resume under an agreed, lower‑risk AWS and DR strategy.

## Milestones

- Complete SafeSend production migration and final Azure cloud integration for non‑production and production environments by 30 Jun 2026.  
- Complete SafeSend One Lead‑to‑Cash UAT by 11 Jun 2026 and the SSOne market/sales/support/SSP delivery tech release by 20 Jun 2026.  
- Deliver SafeSend One CS&S production go‑live on 13 Jul 2026 and enable SafeSend new sales on the CPSP stack by 27 Jul 2026.  
- Complete Project Ochre Cloud Migration Phase 2 from TR AWS to NewCo cloud, including overall migration and cutover, by 29 Jun 2026.  
- Close out remaining MAD integrations and divestiture technology exits, and transition all in‑scope assets out of MAD governance, by 31 Dec 2026.

risks.title: Incomplete or incorrect Noetica application access lists
risks.description: Application lists collected for Noetica users may be incomplete or inaccurate if they are captured as infrastructure inventories rather than user access requirements and job-profile-based usage.
risks.impact_description: If this risk occurs, the project may base reimage and access configuration on incomplete or incorrect application lists, leading to missed critical tools for specific roles, repeated rework to fix access issues, and extended disruption for Noetica teams during the integration.
risks.mitigation: 1) Obtain user access requirement lists rather than generic infrastructure inventories. 2) Collect application usage by job profile (e.g., product, engineering, developer) instead of only per individual, to ensure a complete view of critical tools per role.

risks.title: Disaster recovery replication may conflict with Noetica customer contractual and data-isolation commitments
risks.description: Implementing a DR strategy that replicates private customer data across regions or into shared locations may conflict with Noeticas existing contractual commitments and data-isolation guarantees (e.g., one AWS account per customer for isolation). While the current proposal is to keep replication within each customers AWS account, there is still uncertainty about how this aligns with what has been agreed with customers and documented in contracts.
risks.impact_description: If the chosen DR replication approach violates contractual terms or perceived isolation guarantees, customers may object to the architecture, require contractual changes, or raise legal/compliance concerns. This could delay DR implementation, force costly redesigns, damage customer trust, and expose Thomson Reuters/Noetica to legal or regulatory scrutiny. Conversely, if DR is delayed or watered down to avoid these concerns, resilience gaps may persist and increase operational risk.
risks.mitigation: 1) Zachery to document the DR architecture explicitly stating that replication remains within each customers AWS account but across regions (no centralized shared account), highlighting how isolation boundaries are preserved. 2) Circulate this document to Ash and Donny, and route to Tom and Sabrina for legal/contractual and customer-facing review. 3) Tom and Sabrina to confirm whether the proposed architecture is compatible with existing contracts and customer expectations and identify any customers needing explicit communication or approval. 4) If any contractual gaps are found, adjust DR architecture or update contractual language as appropriate before implementation. 5) Ensure any customer communication clearly explains that data remains in their account, with encryption and key management controls maintained, and that replication is solely to enhance resilience.
risks.source_file_name: Noetica - Cold Standby DR Strategy Discussion – Requirement & Path Forward.docx

risks.title: Urgent Azure Quota Limitations Threaten Cutover Timeline: Escalations Underway with Microsoft for Redis and SQL Resources
risks.description:
•	Issue Summary: Azure resource quotas in Central US and East US 2 are blocking progress. Redis Enterprise instance creation is hindered by exhausted compute SKU quota despite Microsoft's efforts to increase it. 
•	SQL Pool creation requires an additional 4,000 vCores in both regions. Testing and production cutover preparation are delayed, with a temporary Redis SKU workaround in place, but the original issues persist.
risks.impact_description: Impacts the SafeSend One Production Pre-migration activites
risks.mitigation:
Recommendation/ Mitigation: Bill is explained that the inability to deploy the Redis cache is not due to a subscription quota issue, but rather a constraint in the overall capacity of the Azure data center. He emphasizes that increasing the subscription quota won't resolve the issue because the data center itself is at capacity for the required SKU. To guarantee deployment, the team has two options:

1.	Use Reserved Capacity: This option ensures availability of resources but involves additional costs. Reserved capacity guarantees deployment at any time but must be planned and approved by management. Bill notes that Thompson Reuters has successfully used reserved capacity for critical workloads in the past, such as during tax seasons.
2.	Retry Deployments: The team can keep attempting deployments during off-peak hours, but this is dependent on availability and cannot be guaranteed.

Bill clarifies that Microsoft support cannot provide an ETA for when capacity will become available because it depends on customer demand and deployment timing. However, he has escalated the issue to inquire if additional capacity might come online before the end of next month. Even if new capacity is added, it will still be consumed by other customers unless reserved.

Finally, Bill recommends that the team explore the reserved capacity process with their internal cloud cost team, which has experience with it. Corey Cox adds that setting up reserved capacity typically takes days, not weeks, which provides a clearer timeline for planning.
•	Next Action: [Pramod] to setup call with Manir, Praful, and Suhas to have internal discussion i.e using Azure's reserved capacity to bypass infrastructure constraints and secure the required SKU. Once the setup is complete and workloads are running (e.g., after two months), the reservation can be canceled if no longer needed.

risks.title: JFrog Artifactory Issues Blocking CI/CD Pipelines (Rate Limits & npm Metadata)
risks.description: Issue Summary: SafeSend Project team highlighted the criticality of resolving the package-building issue to ensure the project stays on track for its July delivery deadlines. Without this resolution, development and testing will remain blocked, jeopardizing the timeline. The team is trying to identify the right person to escalate or resolve the issue urgently
risks.impact_description: Impact: The team emphasizes the urgency of resolving the package-building issue before June 1st, as the next phase of work is set to begin on that date. Failure to address this issue promptly could significantly impact the overall project timeline
risks.mitigation:
Mitigation: Yesterday, [Prasanna] scheduled with Jfrog team/arch Team (Johannes, Julian and Brain)
1.	The rate-limiting (429) problem is real. It's confined to NuGet/.NET package downloads — 670,000 errors in the last 30 days, peaking at 294,000 in a single day — driven by ~255 .NET applications across 100+ daily PRs all pulling the same packages from JFrog with no caching on the runners. The fix is a workflow change on build side (add a NuGet cache), not a JFrog rate-limit increase.
2.	The npm publish "metadata" issue is actually a permissions issue. The same token publishes successfully nearly 6,000 times per month to other packages — it only fails on two specific packages in the @sssuite-component-ui scope, which have never been published successfully. A JFrog admin needs to extend the team's permission to cover that scope and or work through the self service portal to add the permission. The metadata reindex they requested won't help.
3.	Fixing #1 also solves a major transfer-cost problem. SafeSend's traffic is 99.997% downloads (~4 TB/week) vs. uploads (~122 MB/week), and the NuGet caching fix should remove roughly 3.1–3.5 TB/week of egress — about 80% of their total JFrog traffic — while making the 429s disappear as a side effect. One change, three wins: their builds get faster, their errors stop, and our bill drops.

risks.description: Transferring Noetica AWS accounts into the Thomson Reuters (TR) AWS organization requires decomposing AWS Control Tower and Identity Center usage at the Noetica org root, recreating OUs, and changing the account provisioning model. The Noetica team highlighted multiple technical concerns: heavy dependency on Control Tower and Identity Center, IAM role and org ID dependencies, CloudFront/WAF behavior, GPU capacity reservations, logging aggregation, and the lack of an easy rollback path if issues occur. Identity Center was called out as a major blocker because it must run at the org root, which conflicts with TR’s current FedRAMP constraints. If these complexities are underestimated or not fully mitigated, the org transfer project may cause subtle production breakages or stall indefinitely.
risks.impact_description: If the technical complexity and architectural blockers around Control Tower and Identity Center are not fully addressed, the Noetica AWS org transfer could (a) introduce subtle failures in IAM roles, org ID–dependent automation, CloudFront/WAF behavior, and GPU capacity reservations, leading to production incidents; (b) result in extended outages or degraded performance for Noetica customers due to misconfigured access or infrastructure; (c) leave the migration half-completed with no straightforward rollback, increasing operational risk and support burden; or (d) cause the entire transfer initiative to stall, delaying cost savings, security integration, and alignment with TR standards.

raised_by.name: John Willis / Donny Yung / Ash Alam (Noetica infrastructure and security leaders)

risk_owner.name: Bleninger, Zachery (TR Technology, Cloud Solutions Architect)

mitigation_plan_owner.name: Bleninger, Zachery (TR Technology, Cloud Solutions Architect)

risks.mitigation: 1) Zach Bleninger to document all outstanding technical risks and dependencies for the AWS org transfer, including Control Tower decommissioning, Identity Center constraints, IAM/org ID dependencies, CloudFront/WAF configuration, GPU capacity reservations, CI/CD impacts, quotas, and logging aggregation. 2) Schedule and conduct a deep-dive SME working session focused on these technical workstreams (Identity, Control Tower decomp, CI/CD, WAF, quotas) with TR Platform Engineering and Noetica infra/security leads. 3) Design a phased migration approach that includes non-production pilots, explicit success criteria, and a tested rollback plan before any production account transfer. 4) Evaluate alternatives or mitigations for Identity Center’s org-root requirement within TR’s FedRAMP constraints (e.g., replacement patterns, scoped access models). 5) Only commit to production cutover dates after SMEs agree that critical blockers are addressed and pilot results are acceptable.

risks.title: Board-level pressure to realise AWS cost savings may drive an overly aggressive Noetica AWS org transfer timeline
risks.description: TR leadership and the board are exerting pressure to realise AWS cost savings (~26% forecast) by moving Noetica accounts into the TR AWS organization quickly. While this transfer enables enterprise discounts and premium support, the Noetica team and product leadership emphasised the need to avoid derailing the product roadmap and to manage significant technical risks around Control Tower/Identity Center, security, and contracts. There is a risk that schedule pressure leads to an aggressive migration timeline that does not allow for adequate design, testing, and risk mitigation.
risks.impact_description: If board-level cost-savings pressure forces an accelerated AWS org transfer without sufficient technical due diligence and alignment with the Noetica roadmap, the project could (a) disrupt Noetica’s product development and customer commitments due to resource diversion to migration; (b) increase the likelihood of outages or degraded service quality caused by rushed identity, networking, or infrastructure changes; (c) damage trust between Noetica and TR technology/leadership if the migration is perceived as prioritising cost over stability; and (d) still fail to deliver expected savings if technical blockers (e.g., Identity Center, contracts) are encountered late and require rework or deferral.
risks.mitigation: 1) Use Noetica’s in-flight cost-optimisation work (already yielding ~31% MTD reduction) as an immediate lever to demonstrate savings while a careful AWS org transfer plan is developed. 2) Noetica to share a detailed cost-optimisation summary by the agreed date (end of Thursday) so leadership can see short-term savings independent of org transfer. 3) Zach Bleninger to document a balanced set of options that explicitly trade off speed, risk, and roadmap impact, including phased or partial migration scenarios. 4) Schedule a deep-dive SME session to decompose technical workstreams and produce realistic effort/timeline estimates before committing to firm dates. 5) Reconvene the full group with cost data, roadmap clarity, and a phased recommendation, and socialise this with leadership to set expectations that stability and roadmap protection are non-negotiable constraints.

risks.title: Starting pilot device reimage without full security and access alignment
risks.description: The project may begin the pilot reimage of Noetica devices before application lists, access paths, security, and ZPA configurations are fully aligned, which could reduce confidence from the Noetica Security team and cause avoidable issues.
risks.impact_description: If this risk occurs, the pilot may experience significant access and security issues, eroding Noetica Security’s confidence in the integration approach, creating rework to fix early problems, and potentially delaying broader rollout while trust is rebuilt.
risks.mitigation: 1) Delay the pilot until application lists are complete and access paths are validated. 2) Align security configuration, ZPA settings, and access controls across TR and Noetica before executing the pilot.

risks.title: Lack of implemented cold standby DR strategy for Noetica customer data
risks.description: The agreed cold standby disaster recovery (DR) strategy for Noetica—replicating customer private data from S3 buckets to a paired AWS region—may not be implemented in time (or at all), leaving Noetica workloads without a documented and tested DR option outside their current region. This is particularly relevant as Noetica integrates with other Thomson Reuters products that may have tighter SLAs and resilience expectations.
risks.impact_description: If a cold standby DR strategy is not implemented, a regional outage or data loss event in the primary AWS region could result in prolonged or total loss of access to Noetica customer data and services. This could lead to breach of SLAs, inability to support integrated TR products, reputational damage with customers who expect enterprise-grade resilience, and potential regulatory or contractual scrutiny around lack of disaster recovery capabilities.
risks.mitigation: 1) Zachery to draft a written proposal / architecture decision record describing the cold standby DR approach (S3 replication to a paired region per customer account, plus optional coverage for RDS and OpenSearch where required). 2) Circulate the proposal to the core group (including Ash, Donny, Noah) and route it to Tom and Sabrina for review and sign-off, ensuring contractual and customer expectations are addressed. 3) Donny to confirm with the product/firm library team whether full recovery is possible from S3 alone or if RDS/OpenSearch backups are also required, and feed this back into the DR design. 4) Once approved, define and agree a concrete implementation timeline (targeting H2) with Noetica engineering and security. 5) Track progress and implementation as a defined work item so the risk can be closed once DR replication is in place and validated.

assumptions.title: Phase 1 cloud migration completes in time to enable Phase 2 and dependent work
assumptions.description: Assumption that Phase 1 cloud migration (Colo to TR AWS Cloud for BRS and CV Mail) will complete on the planned dates (e.g., BRS by 2026-03-09 and CV Mail by 2026-03-24), enabling Phase 2 cloud migration, domain transfer, DNS hosting migration, and other downstream activities.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The HL Milestones show Phase 1 migrations for BRS and CV Mail as largely complete with specific cutover dates, and dependencies such as Phase 2 cloud migration and domain/DNS activities are scheduled assuming Phase 1 will be finished by early March 2026.
assumptions.validity_explanation: As of the latest updates, BRS AWS migration tasks are all marked Complete with a final cutover date of March 9, 2026. CV Mail AWS migration, including QA/Staging and Prod execution, is also reported as Complete with revised dates accepted. These completed tasks demonstrate that the assumption that Phase 1 would be delivered in early March has largely held true, making it a valid basis for planning subsequent work.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If any remaining Phase 1 activities slip, adjust Phase 2 schedule and prioritize critical workloads for earlier migration. Consider parallelizing some preparation for Phase 2 (e.g., CICD pipeline base structure, inventory and design work) so that the impact of minor Phase 1 delays on overall TSA timelines is minimized.
assumptions.validation_method: Track completion status of Phase 1 tasks in the HL Milestones (BRS AWS and CVMail AWS lines) and confirm Go-Live dates with the cloud migration team.

assumptions.title: ADO migration will be completed before Phase 2 cloud migration
assumptions.description: Assumption that migration of data from TR ADO to BRS ADO will be completed before Phase 2 cloud migration due to financial and other dependencies.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The RAIDD log lists a dependency that ADO migration should be completed before Phase 2 cloud migration because of financial dependencies. Project planning schedules ADO migration during April–May 2026, ahead of the overall Phase 2 completion date of June 29, 2026.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The ADO migration work item is scheduled for 2026-04-01 to 2026-05-29, with ownership assigned and TechM involved from the TR side. However, there are notes that vendor contract timing and start date are still to be confirmed, meaning the assumption is reasonable but not yet fully validated.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If ADO migration cannot be completed before Phase 2, defer non‑critical ADO-related scope from Phase 2 or implement temporary read‑only access to TR ADO for the buyer until migration completes. Re-sequence Phase 2 cutovers to prioritize environments that are less dependent on historical ADO data.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm ADO migration start and completion dates against the HL Milestones and verify that required data (e.g., development ticket history) is present and usable in BRS ADO before Phase 2 cutovers.

assumptions.title: Domain transfer must complete before DNS hosting migration and O365/email migrations
assumptions.description: Assumption that ownership transfer of key domains (e.g., bigredsky.com, cvmailuk.com, cvmail.com.au, cvmail.net) can be completed before DNS hosting migration and before Office 365 / email migrations that depend on the new DNS setup.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Project notes describe domain ownership transfer as a prerequisite for DNS hosting migration and subsequent O365 migrations. The HL Milestones show detailed steps for domain transfers (Phase 1) followed by a separate Phase 2 DNS hosting migration, and O365 migrations are noted as dependent on domain/email setup.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Multiple domain transfer tasks are already marked Complete, including bigredsky.com.au, bigredsky.au, cvmail.au, and cvmail.net. A combined task to transfer bigredsky.com, cvmailuk.com, and cvmail.com.au is scheduled through 2026-04-10 with active follow‑up reported. Given this progress and clear sequencing, it is reasonable to assume remaining transfers will complete ahead of DNS and O365 work.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If any critical domain transfer is delayed, delay dependent DNS hosting migration and email migrations for that domain while proceeding with unaffected domains. Implement temporary mail forwarding or aliases using existing TR infrastructure during the TSA to maintain service continuity until ownership transfer is complete.
assumptions.validation_method: Track completion of each domain transfer task in the HL Milestones and confirm registrar ownership change plus internal DNS updates before proceeding to Phase 2 DNS hosting migration and O365 cutovers.

assumptions.title: Office 365, SharePoint, and OneDrive migrations will complete successfully within TSA timelines
assumptions.description: Assumption that migration of user email (M365), SharePoint, and OneDrive data to the buyer’s environment can be completed using the chosen tools and vendor within the TSA period, after domain and email setup are finished.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Planning notes describe O365 migration as typically straightforward and handled by the O365 migration team, with a defined migration tool (AvePoint Fly) and third‑party provider (Troppus). Detailed phases (pre‑migration setup, identity/object mapping, pre‑stage and delta migration, cutover, validation and cleanup) are already scheduled.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The project has an agreed migration tool (AvePoint Fly), a migration vendor (Troppus), and documented progress showing completion of early phases and substantial work on pre‑stage/delta migration. However, Phase 4 (cutover) and Phase 5 (validation/cleanup) are not yet started and are tied to broader milestone readiness, so while the approach is sound, there remains schedule and coordination risk.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If migration appears unlikely to complete by TSA end, prioritize critical user mailboxes and high‑value SharePoint/OneDrive content for early cutover, extend O365 migration windows where possible, and if necessary arrange temporary continued TR access for a subset of users or data until final validation is complete.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor execution and completion of each migration phase in the HL Milestones and obtain confirmation from Neel and the buyer’s IT that all required mailboxes and data have been successfully migrated and validated.

assumptions.title: NewCo will have cloud and DNS infrastructure ready in time for Phase 2 migration and DNS hosting cutover
assumptions.description: Assumption that the buyer (NewCo) will set up the necessary cloud environments and DNS infrastructure (including name servers and any Cloudflare/CloudFront integration) in time to support Phase 2 TR AWS to NewCo cloud migration and DNS hosting migration within planned dates.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The Phase 2 cloud migration plan and DNS hosting migration plan both rely on NewCo having its own cloud infrastructure and DNS servers ready. Notes state that DNS hosting migration cannot start until Phase 2 cloud migration infrastructure is in place and that NewCo must set up DNS servers and related records.
assumptions.validity_explanation: While project notes indicate Danny is actively engaged in planning and that NewCo is moving forward with other technical capabilities, there is also explicit feedback that Phase 2 may not meet a May 31 date due to infrastructure readiness concerns. This suggests partial progress but not yet confirmed readiness, making the assumption plausible but not secure.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If NewCo infrastructure is not ready, pursue: (1) temporary extension of TR hosting for critical workloads; (2) phased migration where components can move to any ready NewCo environments while others remain on TR; and (3) revisiting TSA scope/costs to cover extended hosting and support until NewCo is fully ready.
assumptions.validation_method: Obtain firm dates and readiness confirmation from Danny and NewCo technical leads (e.g., Vish, Parvathi) for cloud environment availability and DNS/server configuration, and verify with test deployments and DNS record changes prior to production cutover.

assumptions.title: Cold standby DR implementation for Noetica will be delivered in H2 2026
assumptions.description: Planning for the Noetica integration assumes that the cold standby disaster recovery (DR) solution (S3 multi-region replication, and any additional components such as RDS/OpenSearch where required) will be designed, approved, and implemented during the second half of 2026 (H2).
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the meeting, Zachery and Kiran referenced H2 as the targeted timeframe for DR implementation, with the expectation that design documentation, reviews, and customer/contract checks will be completed beforehand.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The H2 timeline was agreed at a high level but remains dependent on completion of design documentation, contractual review, and customer communications. Until those prerequisites are completed and resourcing is confirmed, the H2 date is a planning assumption rather than a committed schedule.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If it becomes clear that H2 implementation is not achievable, update the risk register to reflect extended exposure, adjust integration plans and SLAs accordingly, and consider an interim, lower-effort backup posture (e.g., enhanced intra-region backup and recovery procedures) while a full multi-region DR implementation is rescheduled.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm by mid-2026 that a detailed DR implementation plan, including specific milestones and resourcing, has been baselined and approved; verify through program plans and DR work items that implementation is scheduled in H2.
assumptions.source_file_name: Noetica - Cold Standby DR Strategy Discussion – Requirement & Path Forward.docx

assumptions.title: Noetica customers will accept intra-account multi-region replication of their private data for DR
assumptions.description: It is assumed that Noetica customers, who were originally provided strong isolation guarantees through a one-AWS-account-per-customer architecture, will accept multi-region replication of their private data within their own AWS account (e.g., S3 and possibly RDS/OpenSearch replication) for disaster recovery purposes, provided isolation and encryption controls remain in place.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Donny stated that, from a technical and security perspective, intra-account multi-region replication is feasible and comparable to how other applications manage private customer data, and expressed a belief that customers would be understanding of this for backup purposes. However, he also noted the need for someone closer to customers and contracts (e.g., Tom and Sabrina) to confirm acceptability.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The proposed DR strategy keeps data within the same customer-owned AWS account and aims to preserve existing security controls, suggesting minimal change in data control and isolation. However, explicit customer and legal confirmation is still pending, so confidence remains moderate rather than high.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If customers do not accept intra-account multi-region replication, explore alternatives such as (1) contract updates explicitly permitting DR replication, (2) customer-selectable DR options with documented trade-offs, or (3) a more limited DR posture (e.g., enhanced intra-region backups only) paired with transparent risk acknowledgement.
assumptions.validation_method: Tom and Sabrina to review the proposed DR architecture and compare it against contractual language and customer commitments; where necessary, discuss the approach with key customers and document their acceptance or required changes.
assumptions.source_file_name: Noetica - Cold Standby DR Strategy Discussion – Requirement & Path Forward.docx

assumptions.title: Noetica environments can be fully recovered from S3 (and minimal additional) backups
assumptions.description: The DR design assumes that Noeticas core customer environments can be fully reconstructed primarily from S3 backups (raw documents) and, if necessary, a minimal set of additional data sources (e.g., RDS snapshots and OpenSearch snapshots), without requiring complex or bespoke recovery flows beyond those backups.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the discussion, Donny indicated that customer data is split across S3 (raw documents), OpenSearch (processed/chunked data), and RDS (linking and metadata), and that he believes OpenSearch content can be recreated from S3 and RDS. He committed to validate with the team that handles the firm library functionality to confirm the exact recovery requirements.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The current architecture already separates raw and derived data and uses managed services with snapshot capabilities, making it reasonable to expect that an appropriate combination of S3 and managed-service snapshots can support full recovery. However, detailed confirmation of dependencies and data flows is still outstanding.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If it turns out that additional data sources or services must be replicated or backed up to achieve full recovery, expand the DR scope to include those elements (e.g., multi-region RDS snapshots, OpenSearch snapshot replication to S3), and update timelines and cost estimates accordingly. If the required scope becomes too complex for initial implementation, prioritize a minimal viable DR scope with clearly documented limitations and a follow-on enhancement plan.
assumptions.validation_method: Donny to consult the product/firm library team to confirm whether complete reconstruction is possible from S3 alone or if RDS/OpenSearch data must also be replicated or backed up across regions; document the confirmed data recovery model in the DR architecture proposal.
assumptions.source_file_name: Noetica - Cold Standby DR Strategy Discussion – Requirement & Path Forward.docx

assumptions.title: Snyk scanning issues will be resolved or manually bypassed in time to avoid delays to SIGSA and TTC non‑prod and production cloud integrations
assumptions.description: Project planning assumes that the current Snyk scanning issues in the SafeSend/TTC codebase will either be fully resolved by the ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev team or, if not, that a manual intervention process will be approved and executed (within 1–2 days) so that SIGSA and TTC non‑production cloud integrations can complete in Q1 2026 and production cloud integration planning can start on schedule.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Non‑production cloud integration for SIGSA and TTC must complete in Q1 2026 to keep SafeSend One production in Q2 and SIGSA/TTC production in Q3 on track. Automated Snyk scanning is a prerequisite for promotion, so the team planned on either timely resolution of the Snyk issue or an approved manual workaround.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The risk log shows that the Snyk scanning risk was managed with direct involvement from the ISRM security team and a clearly defined contingency of manual intervention. The risk entry is marked as resolved by 2026-02-26, indicating that either the automated scanning was restored or an acceptable workaround was implemented in time, confirming the assumption held true for planning purposes.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If automated Snyk scanning cannot be restored promptly, proceed with the agreed manual intervention process (1–2 days) to perform required security checks and unblock deployments, while coordinating with ISRM and project leadership to document approvals and ensure compliance.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor progress of ISRM-Platforms-Security-Dev work on the Snyk issue and confirm either successful restoration of automated scans or completion of the manual intervention process; verify that SIGSA and TTC non‑production integrations complete by Q1 2026 and that production planning starts as scheduled.

assumptions.title: Noetica cloud migration to Thomson Reuters landing zone will occur in 2028 and is out of near-term scope
assumptions.description: Planning for the Noetica integration assumes that any large-scale cloud migration or landing zone change (e.g., moving core Noetica workloads from their current AWS architecture into a standardized Thomson Reuters landing zone) will not occur until 2028. Current work in the Technology CIO workstream is therefore focused on nearer-term items such as network integration, minimum viable controls (MVCs), disaster recovery design, and AWS account transfer/billing alignment, without attempting a full cloud migration in the current planning horizon.

owner.name: Bleninger, Zachery (TR Technology, Cloud Solutions Architect)

assumptions.rationale_basis: During the April 30, 2026 weekly sync, Milind asked whether there was any planned cloud migration that would be demanded alongside network integration. Zachery responded that cloud migration is planned for 2028, and the group treated this as sufficiently distant that it does not need to be actively planned now. This establishes 2028 as the informal target for any major cloud migration activity.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The statement about a 2028 cloud migration target was made in a live integration governance forum without objection and was treated as a long-term horizon by multiple participants. However, it has not been formally captured in a signed roadmap or governance decision, and TR strategic priorities could change, so confidence is moderate rather than high.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If plans change and cloud migration for Noetica is required earlier than 2028, update the integration scope, create dedicated migration risks, and establish a separate migration workstream with its own funding, resources, and milestones instead of folding migration into existing DR/network/account-transfer efforts. Re-baseline timelines and capacity to avoid overcommitting current teams.
assumptions.validation_method: Review TR and Legal portfolio cloud roadmaps and integration plans annually (or upon major strategic changes) to confirm that 2028 remains the target for Noetica cloud migration. Validate with Zachery, Milind, and Kiran that no earlier migration initiatives have been approved that would affect Noetica.
assumptions.source_file_name: Noetica Integration Technology CIO  Workstream Mtgs -- Weekly Sync.docx

assumptions.title: Pre-created AWS account model will be a viable replacement for Control Tower-driven per-customer account creation for Noetica
assumptions.description: It is assumed that, after moving Noetica accounts into the TR AWS organization and removing Control Tower at the org level, Noetica will still be able to operate effectively by using a model where TR pre-creates batches of AWS accounts in Noetica OUs, and Noetica's automation and deployment pipelines are adapted to consume these pre-existing accounts for new customers instead of creating accounts via Control Tower on demand.
assumptions.rationale_basis: In the April 30, 2026 meeting, Zachery proposed that, because Control Tower cannot be retained at the TR org level without FedRAMP/access complications, TR would "inflate batches" of AWS accounts in the Noetica OUs based on expected customer demand (e.g., 5–10 accounts for upcoming customers). Ash noted that current pipelines assume Control Tower-driven account creation and that they would need to assess changes to automation. This proposal forms a working assumption that adapting to pre-created accounts is feasible.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Conceptually, using pre-created accounts is a common pattern in large organizations, and TR has existing mechanisms to do so. However, Noetica's current automation, SCP layout, and on-call access patterns are built around Control Tower and may require non-trivial refactoring. Since these changes have not yet been designed or tested, confidence is only moderate.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If testing or design review shows that pre-created accounts are not a viable operational model, explore alternatives such as: (1) constrained use of Control Tower within the TR org under FedRAMP-compliant access controls, (2) a hybrid model where some Control Tower features are replaced by custom automation built by TR and Noetica, or (3) deferring the account transfer until a more robust solution is identified. In parallel, work with AWS account teams to revisit contractual options (e.g., extending TR discounts/support to Noetica's existing org) if technical constraints make account transfer too risky.
assumptions.validation_method: Document the proposed pre-created account model in Zachery's AWS org/account transfer proposal and have Noetica's engineering and automation teams review it. Prototype or dry-run the updated automation pipeline against a small set of pre-created accounts to confirm that customer onboarding and deployment can be performed without Control Tower. Capture results and go/no-go decision in the integration design review.
