assumptions.title: Short-term Noetica-led AWS cost optimisation can substantially reduce spend and ease timing pressure on AWS org transfer
assumptions.description: Planning for the Noetica AWS org transfer assumes that Noetica’s own cost-optimisation efforts (e.g., rightsizing OpenSearch and other infrastructure, tuning usage, and exploring savings plans) can deliver substantial near-term AWS savings (on the order of ~30%) so that TR can demonstrate meaningful cost reduction without immediately completing the complex org transfer into the TR AWS organization.
assumptions.rationale_basis: In the meeting, Donny Yung reported that Noetica has already achieved approximately 31% month-to-date AWS cost reduction through rightsizing (OpenSearch and other components) and expects further savings from additional tuning and potential savings plans. He advocated maximising these optimisations first while longer-term architecture and migration paths are defined, in order to avoid derailing the product roadmap and to reduce pressure to rush the org transfer.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Concrete MTD savings provide strong early evidence that optimisation is effective, but it is not yet proven that these levels can be sustained or further improved without impacting performance or roadmap priorities. Market conditions, workload growth, or unforeseen technical limits could reduce the achievable savings, so confidence is moderate rather than high.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If optimisation does not continue to deliver meaningful or sustainable savings, increase focus on alternative cost levers such as (a) carefully scoped, phased AWS org transfer steps that target high-value accounts first, (b) renegotiating discounts or support arrangements that do not require full org transfer, or (c) deprioritising lower-value features or projects to free up capacity for migration work. In parallel, escalate a revised, risk-aware migration plan to leadership to align expectations on achievable timing and risk profile.
assumptions.validation_method: 1) Noetica to produce and share a detailed AWS cost-optimisation summary (baseline vs current, initiatives, and forecast) by the agreed near-term date. 2) Track monthly AWS spend trends for Noetica accounts over the next 1–2 quarters to confirm that optimisation is delivering and maintaining targeted savings. 3) Use this data in leadership communications and migration planning to confirm that short-term savings are sufficient to support a more deliberate transfer timeline.

assumptions.title: Shifting Noetica customer renewals to standard TR contracts from June 1 will reduce some current contractual constraints on AWS architecture and integration options
assumptions.description: The integration planning assumes that, starting June 1, Noetica customer renewals moving onto standard TR contracts will reduce certain existing contractual constraints (e.g., strict single-tenant commitments and bespoke terms), thereby providing greater flexibility for future AWS org, security, and DR architecture decisions compared to legacy Noetica contracts.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the discussion on security and contract impacts (single-tenant customer contracts, Cognito pools, logging aggregation, security tooling), Sharon Smelter clarified that from June 1, Noetica customer renewals will move to standard TR contracts. This was positioned as a factor that may ease some of the contractual constraints currently influencing technical options for integration and DR.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The expectation is grounded in how TR typically standardizes contracts to support shared platforms, but actual customer renewals and negotiations may still result in exceptions or special terms, especially for large or sensitive customers. Until several renewals have been completed and analysed, the extent of constraint reduction is uncertain.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If standard TR contracts do not significantly reduce constraints, integration planning should (a) explicitly catalogue which contractual terms remain limiting for AWS org transfer and DR design, (b) prioritise technical patterns that comply with the strictest remaining requirements, and (c) consider targeted contract amendments or customer-specific DR options where needed. Additionally, adjust timelines and scope for AWS org transfer and DR implementation to reflect the added complexity of operating under heterogeneous contractual obligations.
assumptions.validation_method: 1) Legal and commercial teams to review the standard TR contract language being applied to Noetica renewals and compare it to current Noetica customer commitments relevant to AWS tenancy, region, and data handling. 2) As renewals occur after June 1, track any customer objections or carve-outs that preserve existing constraints. 3) Confirm with Sabrina and TR legal/commercial leads whether the new contracts materially widen the range of technically permissible integration/DR patterns.

dependencies.title: Resolution of AWS Identity Center and FedRAMP constraints to enable Noetica AWS org transfer
dependencies.description: The proposed transfer of Noetica AWS accounts into the Thomson Reuters AWS organization depends on resolving architectural and compliance constraints related to AWS Identity Center and FedRAMP. Identity Center currently must run at the AWS org root, which conflicts with TRs existing FedRAMP-boundary policies and makes a straightforward reuse of Noeticas current Control Tower/Identity Center setup infeasible. Without a resolved pattern for Identity and Control Tower decommissioning, the org transfer remains high risk and difficult to roll back.

owner.name: Bleninger, Zachery (TR Technology, Cloud Solutions Architect)

dependencies.dependent_on: Definition and approval of an AWS Identity Center and Control Tower decommissioning pattern that complies with TR FedRAMP boundary policies while supporting Noetica account and access management needs
dependencies.consumer: Thomson Reuters Cloud Solutions Architecture and Noetica technology integration workstream
dependencies.impact_if_delayed: If Identity Center and Control Tower constraints are not resolved, Noetica AWS accounts cannot be safely transferred into the TR AWS organization without high risk of subtle breakages (IAM role/org ID dependencies, CloudFront/WAF behaviour, GPU capacity reservations, logging and security tooling integrations) and limited rollback options. This would delay realization of ~26% AWS cost savings and postpone alignment with TR security and audit controls.
dependencies.mitigation: Conduct a focused SME design exercise (including TR Platform Engineering, Security, and Noetica infrastructure/security leads) to evaluate alternative identity and account-governance patterns that do not require Identity Center at the TR org root, such as pre-created accounts with updated CI/CD pipelines, alternative SSO/role-assumption flows, or staged/partial migrations. Validate proposed patterns against FedRAMP requirements and document a recommended approach for leadership review before executing any org transfer steps.

This includes validating ISRM expectations, confirming whether TPRM assessments are required, and ensuring appropriate data protection and endpoint controls are in place before access is granted.

decisions.title: Use Paymetric for SafeSend payments until Stripe is aligned
decisions.description: SafeSend will continue to use the current BAU Paymetric payment solution for its migration and launches, and will migrate to Stripe later in alignment with the broader Unification Payment program and CPSP timelines.
decisions.rationale: The Unification Payment program’s Stripe delivery timeline is not aligned with the 2026 SafeSend migration delivery dates; attempting to align SafeSend with Stripe now would create an unmet dependency and delivery risk.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Align SafeSend migration with Stripe delivery timeline under the Unification Payment program.
2) Proceed with SafeSend migration using existing BAU Paymetric and move to Stripe later with the rest of CPSP (selected).
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to CPSP Stripe risk R003 in the RAID log, where the Stripe project plan is not aligned with SafeSend target delivery dates.

decisions.title: Phase SafeSend One and Digital Sales & Self-Serve business launches
decisions.description: SafeSend One business launch will proceed ahead of Digital Sales and Self-Serve launches, with Digital capabilities following once foundational platforms and processes are in place.
decisions.rationale: Phasing launches ensures that foundational capabilities, including self-serve, are in place before Digital Sales and Self-Serve go live, reducing delivery risk and improving stability at launch.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Launch SafeSend One and Digital Sales & Self-Serve together.
2) Phase the launches so Digital Sales & Self-Serve follow after foundational lead-to-cash delivery (selected).
decisions.dependencies_linked: Impacts Digital workstream roadmap and dependencies on lead-to-cash (L2C) foundational deliverables planned for July 2026.

decisions.title: Set TTC Digital Sales & Self-Serve business launch target to January 2027
decisions.description: SSOne and TTC Digital phased deployment was agreed, with TTC Digital Sales & Self-Serve business launch targeted for January 2027, with a possibility to bring it forward into Q4 2026 if Digital commitments are met by June 2026.
decisions.rationale: Separating the TTC Digital launch provides additional time to deliver and stabilize core lead-to-cash capabilities and allows Digital teams to commit to a realistic delivery schedule, while retaining flexibility to pull the date forward if feasible.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Align TTC Digital Sales & Self-Serve launch with July 2026 L2C deliverables.
2) Target January 2027 for TTC Digital launch, with option to bring into Q4 2026 if commitments are met (selected).
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to Digital workstream scope, TTC digital rollout timing, and integration budget planning for 2026, as well as RAID risk regarding TTC scope, design, and schedule alignment with July 2026 deployment.

decisions.title: DKIM keys validated and configured for Salesforce email forwarding

decisions.title: Migrate Time Base from Jira to Azure DevOps and retire Jira

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

AI Reimagine (CIO) is delivering an end‑to‑end AI transformation across CIO, combining coding agents, AIOps, AI‑driven service management, and Datadog hygiene to reduce operating costs and shift teams from manual execution to exception management. The program matters because it underpins an O&T mandate to reimagine how work gets done while unlocking multi‑million‑dollar efficiency and stability benefits across Tier 1 services.  

Three program‑level “POV and Benefits Unlock” milestones run through 2026, with the Q2 tranche targeted for 30 Jun 2026 and subsequent waves through 31 Dec 2026; however, critical enablers are running behind, including SM AIOps’ POV milestone now tracking to 29 May 2026 versus a 31 Mar 2026 plan and Datadog Hygiene’s incident‑correlation MVP pushed from 30 Apr to 12 Jun 2026. Multiple key workstreams remain Amber or Amber‑to‑Green, and value‑case execution gaps persist, such as Comm Eng’s use‑case plan not yet covering the committed $3.3M benefits and DevOps / ITIL value‑realization roadmaps still in progress beyond their May 2026 targets.  

Overall status is Amber, driven primarily by incomplete and delayed value‑capture roadmaps and underpinning AIOps and DevOps milestones that are needed to turn pilots into measurable, program‑level savings.  

## Path to Green

The path to Green focuses on locking value‑capture and scale plans by completing the 2026 VC realization roadmaps for DevOps and ITIL, closing Comm Eng’s $3.3M benefits gap with additional use cases, and landing the Datadog Hygiene correlation MVP and SM AIOps POV so that Legal Tracker, GTM4, CIAM, and follow‑on applications can be onboarded to a repeatable, metric‑driven AIOps model.  

## Milestones

- Complete Q2 POV & Benefits Unlock (CCE AI coding agents, initial AIOps onboarding, and PLE agents proofs of value) by 30 Jun 2026.  
- Deliver the ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP to production by 12 Jun 2026, enabling reliable monitor‑to‑incident analytics for Datadog Hygiene and AIOps measurement.  
- Finalize ETS Service Desk Automation platform readiness by completing Agent Chat Vayusphere replacement on 19 Jun 2026 and delegated Service Desk knowledge base migration by 30 Jun 2026.  
- Confirm 2026 benefits and enablement outcomes across ETS and ISRM by completing ETS Discovery & Benefits 2026 on 30 Jun 2026 and ISRM InfoSec point‑solution deliveries on 31 Dec 2026.  
- Complete the overall AI Reimagine (CIO) program by 30 Dec 2027, including all coding agents, AIOps, service management, platform engineering, and ETS automation workstreams.

risks.title: Loopio tool GenAI expectations misaligned and AI feature enablement delayed
risks.description: There is a risk that expectations for Loopio’s GenAI capabilities are misaligned and AI feature enablement is delayed due to contract negotiations and configuration uncertainty. Until AI functionality is activated, the CT team must perform more manual work.

risks.title: Unresolved ServiceNow CI–service association behaviour may block cutover from Datadog incidents
risks.description: During the May 12, 2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, the team observed that ServiceNow is not associating services with the correct CIs for large applications such as Legal Tracker. Internal analysis suggests that a configurable limit of approximately 1,000 CIs per service causes additional CIs to be handled via dynamic CI groups, which in turn prevents correct service association and grouping. ServiceNow’s consultant (Doug) indicated there are “traverse rules” that might address this but needs to consult CMDB experts. Until a clear recommendation and fix are in place, the Legal Tracker product team considers this a showstopper for disabling Datadog-direct incident creation.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow continues to mis-associate or partially associate CIs to services due to the current service–CI association behaviour, AIOps cannot reliably determine which service is impacted by an event or alert for large applications. For Legal Tracker, this would mean that incidents created by AIOps could lack correct service context or rely on dynamic CI groups, undermining routing, impact analysis, and leadership reporting. As a result, Legal Tracker stakeholders will not agree to cut over from Datadog-direct incident creation, delaying the POV completion, delaying onboarding of subsequent products, and prolonging reliance on legacy workflows.
risks.mitigation: ServiceNow’s consultant Doug will escalate the CI/service association issue to their CMDB experts to review the current configuration, including the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit and available traverse rules. Together with the TR CMDB team, they will: (1) determine whether the association limit can be safely tuned without degrading ServiceNow performance; (2) design appropriate traverse rules or alternative modelling (e.g., hierarchical services) to support large applications like Legal Tracker; and (3) validate the chosen approach in a lower environment before promoting changes to production. In parallel, Jot will log this as a formal blocker in status reporting, and Talia will escalate via email and stakeholder channels (including Eric and John) to ensure it receives high priority attention from ServiceNow and the CMDB team. Cutover from Datadog-direct incidents for Legal Tracker will be deferred until a recommended and tested fix is in place.

risks.title: Incorrect priority and severity mapping from Datadog to ServiceNow incidents
risks.description: Priority and severity values from Datadog monitors are not yet consistently or correctly mapped into ServiceNow alert and incident fields. Severity has sometimes been populated from unexpected payload fields, custom test fields exist, and the mapping between Datadog alert_priority/alert_type and ServiceNow severity, impact, urgency, and priority is still being designed. If this is not resolved before enabling automated incident creation, incidents may be mis‑prioritized.
risks.impact_description: Mis‑prioritized incidents (e.g., P1 issues created as P3, or minor warnings created as P1) will distort SLAs, paging, and escalation. Major Incident processes could be flooded with false majors or miss real ones. This will reduce trust in the AIOps solution, force manual reprioritization, and may cause teams to resist adopting event‑driven incident creation.
risks.mitigation: Define and document a definitive mapping: use Datadog monitor priority (P1–P5) as the authoritative input, add custom impact and urgency fields on the alert record, map monitor priority into those fields via event rules, and customize the incident-creation subflow to derive incident priority solely from those values. Validate mapping with test payloads and a parallel run comparing new incidents to historical ones before turning off legacy Datadog incident creation.

risks.title: Lack of monitoring governance and standardized thresholds across products
risks.description: There is no centralized event management practice or monitoring governance. Platform Engineering publishes Datadog policies on SharePoint but does not audit or enforce them. Thresholds and configurations vary by product; 80% of monitors are synthetics with product‑specific thresholds, and 75% of GCC events come from one product (HighQ). Many teams do not understand event threshold concepts (informational/warning/critical).
risks.impact_description: Without standardized thresholds, tagging, and governance, noisy or misconfigured monitors will continue to flood Event Management and produce inconsistent event classification across products. AIOps capabilities (filtering, correlation, prioritization) may be overwhelmed or misused, leading to limited noise reduction, poor comparability between services, and difficulty onboarding new teams into the AIOps model.
risks.mitigation: Define and implement a monitoring governance model: standardize thresholds where feasible (infrastructure monitors), define enterprise guidelines for synthetic thresholds, establish tagging standards (including Asset Insight ID, service tags, and TR_‑prefixed custom tags), and create an auditing mechanism to flag non‑compliant monitors. Use Legal Tracker as a pilot to refine policies before scaling to other Tier 1 products such as HighQ.

Mitigation date: TBD as this is an on ongoing planning and knowledge transfer effort.

risks.title: Departure of key AIOps architect (Chris Rutherford) may impact continuity and governance
risks.description: During the 30-Apr-2026 regular sync, Jot and the team thanked Chris Rutherford and noted that he would not be on the project from the following day. Chris has been the primary architect and leadership liaison for the ServiceNow AIOps/Event Management design, including incident priority behaviour, governance model, onboarding approach, and alignment with the Datadog hygiene programme. His departure creates a risk that architectural context, design rationale, and decision history may be lost or diluted, slowing future rule changes, onboarding of new products, and governance maturation.
risks.impact_description: Without Chris’s ongoing involvement, the team may struggle to maintain a consistent architectural vision and governance approach for AIOps. Questions about incident priority tuning, standard rule sets, and onboarding patterns could take longer to resolve; decisions may be revisited without full context; and onboarding of additional products “aggressively” (as planned) may slow or diverge from the intended cookie-cutter model. This could delay achieving scale benefits, increase rework on rules and standards, and reduce leadership confidence that AIOps is being guided by a clear owner.
risks.mitigation:
1) Ensure a structured handover of architectural and governance responsibilities from Chris to designated internal owners (e.g., Paul as programme lead, Prastuti and Vinay on the platform side, and Jot for project coordination).
2) Treat Doug’s in-progress training videos and configuration documentation as critical artefacts and complete them on the agreed timeline, capturing rule designs, priority behaviour, and onboarding patterns in a single reference.
3) Explicitly assign a new technical architecture lead for AIOps/Event Management within TR and communicate this to all stakeholders and vendors.
4) Review open design decisions and risks that had Chris as owner or key contributor, and confirm updated ownership and next steps so that work does not stall when onboarding new products “aggressively.”

risks.title: High concentration of noise from HighQ overshadowing other Tier 1 services
risks.description: 75% of GCC monthly events come from a single product (HighQ) out of ~50 Tier 1 products. If this concentration of noise is not addressed, it will continue to dominate GCC workload and may mask important events from other services, even after Event Management is enabled.
risks.impact_description: HighQ’s excessive alert volume may consume much of GCC and AIOps analysis capacity, leaving less focus on other services and skewing correlation and reporting. Important issues in other Tier 1 products could be delayed or overlooked, undermining fairness and effectiveness of the event management rollout.
risks.mitigation: Treat HighQ as a specific remediation target in the monitoring governance program: review and rationalize its monitors, apply stricter thresholds and suppression for noisy synthetics, and consider product‑specific filtering and correlation rules. Use HighQ data as a pilot to demonstrate volume reduction and incorporate lessons into broader standards before onboarding all Tier 1 products.

risks.title: Datadog and ServiceNow event volume and storage constraints
risks.description: There are concerns about the volume of events if all Datadog accounts send events into ServiceNow. While Datadog does not charge egress fees, ServiceNow storage is finite (e.g., ~4TB per instance), and high event volume could consume storage and impact performance if retention and filtering strategies are not defined.
risks.impact_description: If too many raw events are ingested without filtering and reasonable retention policies, ServiceNow databases may grow rapidly, potentially degrading performance or forcing unplanned data purges. Budget discussions with ServiceNow may be triggered, and the team might need to rework the architecture (e.g., move some correlation back to Datadog).
risks.mitigation: Engage the ServiceNow account team to confirm event storage limits, recommended retention periods, and cost implications. Implement lifecycle rules to purge older events while retaining alerts and incidents for reporting. Decide on a scoped ingestion strategy (starting with Legal Tracker and a subset of monitors), and only expand the number of sources and products once event filtering and correlation are proven to reduce noise.

risks.title: Teams without Event Management access losing visibility during cutover
risks.description: Not all operational teams (e.g., Major Incident team) currently have access to the Event Management module and dashboards. If the legacy Datadog–driven incident creation is disabled before those teams have alternative visibility, they may not see or manage critical events during and after cutover.
risks.impact_description: Major Incident and other central teams could lose timely visibility into critical alerts and incidents, delaying triage, page-outs, and communications. This would directly increase MTTA/MTTR and could cause missed SLAs for high-priority services like Legal Tracker.
risks.mitigation: Run legacy and new integrations in parallel for at least 24 hours while verifying parity, and only decommission the legacy path once all necessary operational teams have appropriate access to Event Management or alternate views. As part of cutover planning, review and adjust role assignments so Major Incident and other key groups can see grouped alerts, incidents, and AIOps dashboards. Following the 12 May 2026 regular sync, extend this to ensure GCC managers and operators (e.g., Rajendran’s team supporting Legal Tracker) are explicitly granted Event Management access before they are expected to monitor alerts, so that Legal Tracker and GCC can align their support model around the event-first view.

risks.title: CI binding from events/alerts to CMDB CIs may not work reliably
risks.description: Despite existing CIs in the CMDB with matching names, ServiceNow’s out‑of‑the‑box CI identification and binding logic is often failing to associate incoming Datadog events/alerts with the correct CI records.
risks.impact_description: If CI binding continues to fail, alerts and incidents generated by Event Management will not be accurately tied to infrastructure or application CIs. This will reduce the value of correlation, service impact analysis, and reporting, and could cause confusion during incident triage (wrong CI, or no CI attached). It may also block some auto‑remediation flows that depend on CI context and erode stakeholder confidence in the AIOps solution.
risks.mitigation: Doug and the ServiceNow team will analyze why out‑of‑the‑box CI identification is not working despite seemingly matching CI names and host attributes. They will review event payload mappings, identification rules, and any missing attributes (e.g., host vs. FQDN vs. CI name). Legal Tracker and GCC will provide additional event samples (including synthetic tests) to validate host/CI mappings. Where needed, adjust event rules or identification logic, and document any required payload standards back to Datadog (e.g., always sending host rather than FQDN).

risks.title: Legal Tracker monitor priorities and severities may not align with TR standards needed for AIOps
risks.description: Legal Tracker’s Datadog monitors currently have impact, urgency, and priority configured in Terraform, but those settings may not align with the TR incident priority matrix or with what AIOps expects to calculate severity/priority in ServiceNow.
risks.impact_description: If Legal Tracker monitors are not using severity/priority consistently with TR standards, the incidents created by AIOps may have inappropriate impact/urgency, leading to mis‑prioritized work (e.g., too many high‑priority incidents or true P1s classified lower). This could reduce trust in the new solution and require rework after go‑live.
risks.mitigation: Andrea and the Legal Tracker team will review all monitors in Terraform to ensure severity and priority reflect actual business impact and urgency, aligning with TR’s incident priority matrix. They will work with Luis and GCC to confirm how these values map into ServiceNow AIOps, and adjust monitor configurations where needed. This review will be incorporated into the onboarding checklist for Legal Tracker before final incident‑creation cutover.

risks.title: Agent chat interaction visibility model may not support desired multi-agent access
risks.description: Jakub requested investigating whether the same interaction conversation can be available to multiple agents at once, which is not the default behavior of Advanced Work Assignment (AWA). Current understanding is that supervisors/managers can join ongoing interactions, but it is unclear whether the system can be configured so different agents can pick up the same interaction, or if timing parameters (e.g., 1-minute search interval) must be adjusted instead.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow and AWA cannot be configured to support the desired level of multi-agent access to a single interaction, or if timing parameters for agent search are not tuned, agent collaboration workflows may be constrained. This could limit the ability for multiple agents to assist on complex cases, slow handoffs, and impact response times. Alternatively, aggressive parameter changes (e.g., very short search windows) without careful testing could destabilize routing behavior.
risks.mitigation: 1) Investigate ServiceNow and Advanced Work Assignment documentation and configuration options to confirm whether an interaction can be surfaced to multiple agents concurrently and under what conditions (e.g., supervisor join vs re-queueing). 2) Evaluate alternative approaches such as adjusting the default 1-minute agent search window to shorter intervals (e.g., 10–15 seconds) and enabling supervisor join capabilities for complex cases. 3) Prototype the desired behavior in DEV/QA and review with Jakub to confirm it meets operational needs. 4) If true multi-agent access is not feasible, document the chosen interaction handling model and ensure HCL is trained on expected behavior and escalation paths.

risks.title: Production go-live before Event Management configuration and plugins are stable
risks.description: Event rules, respond rules, CI binding logic, and some plugins/scheduled jobs in upper environments are still under active revision. Doug has had to rebuild event rules from scratch due to conflicting behaviors, and some plugins in cloned environments require repair. There is pressure to meet the April 1, 2026 go‑live date for AIOps Event Management.

This could disrupt operations, undermine confidence in the new solution, and require emergency fixes in production.
risks.mitigation: Delay full go‑live of automated incident creation until: (1) event rules and respond rules are cleaned up and only approved rules are migrated; (2) required plugins and scheduled jobs are repaired in upper environments; (3) Datadog webhook payloads are standardized; and (4) a 24‑hour (or longer) dual‑run period validates behavior. Implement a change freeze so only Doug modifies AIOps event and alert rules until configuration is finalized, and prepare a clear checklist and ownership map for production enablement.

risks.title: Event forwarding between ServiceNow production and lower environments will function for test data
risks.description: The team is planning to use ServiceNow’s event forwarding from the production instance to dev and QA so that lower environments receive representative Datadog event traffic for testing rules and correlation without needing separate Datadog integrations for each environment.
risks.impact_description: If event forwarding between the production and lower environments does not function reliably, dev and QA will not receive representative production event traffic. This will limit the team’s ability to safely test new event rules, correlation logic, and responder rules using real-world data, increasing the risk that problematic configurations are promoted directly to production or that rule tuning is delayed.
risks.mitigation: Enable the event forwarding configuration in production, trigger Datadog events into the SNOW prod instance after webhook cutover, and confirm that corresponding events appear in dev (and subsequently QA) according to the expected schedule. If forwarding proves unreliable, fall back to (1) pointing Datadog test webhooks directly to dev/QA for specific monitors, or (2) manually injecting sample events into lower environments for rule testing. Coordinate with Doug to adjust or repair event management plugins if out-of-box forwarding behaviour is defective.

risks.title: Agent capacity and presence configuration may overload or mis-route chats
risks.description: Advanced Work Assignment (AWA) agent presence and capacity settings are not yet properly configured. Many agents appear as "available" indefinitely (even after being inactive for long periods), and default capacities (e.g., number of parallel chats per agent) are effectively unset or inconsistent. This can cause the system to treat long-inactive agents as available capacity and over-assign chats beyond reasonable limits.
risks.impact_description: If agent presence and capacity configurations remain unoptimized, chats may be routed to agents who are actually offline or no longer on shift, leading to long customer wait times and abandoned chats. Agents who are online can be overloaded with too many concurrent chats, impacting quality and agent experience. Misrouted or stuck chats will undermine confidence in the new agent chat solution and may force manual interventions, slowing adoption and putting service KPIs at risk.
risks.mitigation: 1) Define standard capacity limits per agent (e.g., 5 concurrent chats/incidents as discussed) and configure these limits consistently across all pilot agents. 2) Investigate whether there is an out-of-the-box or script-based mechanism to automatically mark agents offline after a defined period of inactivity or after logout; if available, implement and test it. 3) Review historical presence data (e.g., agents still showing available after weeks) to validate that the new configuration works as expected. 4) Coordinate with Gandikota, Srinu to deploy configuration changes across DEV/QA and PROD environments to keep them aligned. 5) Monitor queue utilization and agent feedback during the pilot to refine capacity and presence thresholds before broader rollout.

risks.title: Delayed monitor and tag standardization for GTM4 and SIAM may slip AIOps onboarding timelines

This will delay onboarding for these early adopter products, push out the MVP / early adopter milestone, and limit the evidence base beyond Legal Tracker for demonstrating AIOps value. risks.title: Missing Service Associations in AIOps-generated incidents may delay Datadog cutover

As of 12-May, this is called out as an LT blocker and work-in-progress item owned by Doug, with the project explicitly stating that Datadog direct incident creation cannot be cut off until the service association issue is resolved.
risks.impact_description: If impacted services continue to be missing from or incorrectly populated in AIOps-generated incidents, the team will be unable to safely disable Datadog’s direct incident creation for Legal Tracker. This will prolong the dual-run period, maintain duplicate/parallel incidents, and delay full realization of AIOps benefits such as reduced incident volume and improved routing. It may also erode stakeholder confidence if incidents lack correct service context, complicating impact assessment and communications during incidents.

Doug and Yash to (1) analyze current CI and service-mapping logic used by Event Management and incident creation flows; (2) update mapping rules so that service associations are derived correctly from Datadog payload fields (e.g., Asset Insight ID, service tags) and CI bindings; (3) validate behaviour on recent Legal Tracker incidents to confirm services populate as expected; and (4) only after consistent service association is confirmed, plan and execute the cutover step to disable Datadog-driven incident creation for Legal Tracker. risks.title: FedRAMP governance and plugin enablement may constrain or delay AIOps usage in regulated environments

risks.title: Lack of standardized Datadog monitor configuration and observability governance may hinder AIOps rollout
risks.description: Datadog monitors across Thomson Reuters are owned by many different teams without a single centralized observability practice. Priority, severity, tags, and other configuration standards are inconsistently applied, and many monitors are configured primarily for escalation convenience (e.g., over‑using P1/P2).
risks.impact_description: Without consistent monitor configuration and centralized ownership, the payloads feeding ServiceNow Event Management will vary widely in quality and semantics. This threatens the accuracy of correlation, severity/priority calculation, and CI binding, and will make it difficult to apply generic rules at scale. It also increases the overhead of onboarding each product and may require significant cleanup or refactoring later.
risks.mitigation: (1) Establish GCC as the central practice owner for event management and observability, working with Platform Engineering and product teams; (2) align the Datadog hygiene programme that Mike Krause is running with the requirements of AIOps, so payload and monitor configuration standards are unified; (3) define and publish TR‑wide standards for monitors (priority/severity usage, tags, asset IDs, service and CI tagging) that support ServiceNow AIOps; (4) consider progressively migrating monitors to "monitoring as code" (Terraform) for centralized management where feasible; and (5) incorporate monitor‑configuration checks into the onboarding checklist for each application before enabling AIOps for them.

risks.title: Infeasibility of effective governance with 110+ Datadog organizations
risks.description: The team questioned whether effective governance is feasible with over 110 Datadog organizations. The group agreed that governance is significantly harder at this scale and that deeper analysis and architectural discussion are required to determine a sustainable governance model.
risks.impact_description: If governance remains fragmented across 110+ Datadog organizations, it will be difficult to enforce standards, perform consistent audits, implement hygiene guardrails, and track compliance. This could lead to persistent noise, inconsistent alert quality, uneven incident detection, and slower progress toward enterprise‑wide observability maturity.
risks.mitigation: Schedule a dedicated governance and architecture session to assess options for managing or consolidating Datadog organizations, define a governance operating model that can scale (including standards, audit mechanisms, and ownership), and incorporate the chosen approach into the Datadog Hygiene roadmap.

risks.title: Insufficient Datadog monitor metadata blocks scalable cleanup
risks.description: Tax, Corporate, and Legal teams have indicated that current Datadog inventory exports do not include critical metadata such as "who created the monitor", "who the monitor is assigned to", and "when the monitor last fired". Dominique reported that Tax explicitly called this a "showstopper" for performing ongoing cleanup of monitors without Asset IDs. Without this metadata, teams cannot efficiently group, prioritize, or assign remediation work across hundreds or thousands of monitors.
risks.impact_description: If richer Datadog monitor metadata is not made available in inventory and analytics (e.g., Power BI) in the near term, product and engineering teams (starting with TRTA Tax, Corporate, Legal/HighQ) will be unable to run scalable, targeted monitor cleanup campaigns. Cleanup will either stall or require labor-intensive manual investigation of each monitor, delaying remediation of Asset ID coverage gaps and alert hygiene issues. This will slow Phase 1 outcomes, extend periods of noisy or low-quality monitoring, and reduce stakeholder confidence in the Datadog Hygiene program’s ability to support teams with actionable data.
risks.mitigation: Eric Sand will extend the Datadog inventory refresh script to pull full monitor metadata from the Datadog API, including creator, assigned/owned-by details, last-fired timestamps, environment tags, and other grouping attributes, and surface these fields in the Datadog inventory Power BI report. Eric is already in touch with LJ, who has built a "Datadog Jacker" tool that pulls alert metadata, evaluates tagging compliance, and supports bulk tag updates for two Datadog accounts; Eric will reuse or integrate LJ’s approach where possible to accelerate delivery. Once enhanced metadata is available in reports, the core team will share updated views with Tax, Corporate, Legal/HighQ so they can group monitors by owner and last-fired date and resume continuous cleanup of monitors lacking Asset IDs or required tags.
risks.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

risks.title: Single-occurrence Datadog alerts remaining as orphan alerts without incidents
risks.description: ServiceNow AIOps is currently configured so that incidents are only created after grouping multiple alerts. During the 11 May 2026 sync, Luis noted that some alerts are left as 'orphans' because they only occur once and therefore never become part of a multi-alert group that triggers incident creation. Until expectations are clarified with the Legal Tracker team and configuration is adjusted, there is a risk that valid single-occurrence alerts will not generate incidents, reducing visibility into certain issues.
risks.impact_description: If single-occurrence alerts remain as orphan alerts that never create incidents, the Legal Tracker support team and GCC may miss issues that only fire once (for example, short-lived but impactful failures). This will lead to gaps in incident records, incomplete service-impact reporting, and potential delays in triage and remediation when teams rely on incidents as their primary work object. It may also reduce confidence in the AIOps model if stakeholders discover problems that were visible as alerts but never escalated to incidents.
risks.mitigation: Work with the Legal Tracker product team (Elizabeth and Andrea) to review a sample set of orphan alerts and agree on which types must always generate incidents, even if they occur only once. Based on this feedback, adjust Event Management configuration so that certain alert types or severities (for example, critical P1/P2 alerts, or specific monitor scopes) can create incidents on first occurrence, while less critical alerts continue to rely on grouping. Validate the updated behaviour over several days with Legal Tracker and GCC, ensuring no critical alerts remain orphaned and that incident volume remains manageable.

risks.title: Out-of-the-box event and alert rules may not cover all Legal Tracker scenarios
risks.description: The team intends to start with mostly out‑of‑the‑box ServiceNow event rules and a very small number of TR‑specific rules (around three). Some known scenarios, such as monitors triggering on multiple hosts, are not fully addressed yet and cause sub‑optimal grouping.
risks.impact_description: If key Legal Tracker use cases are not adequately covered by the event rules and alert correlation, different issues could be grouped into a single alert (e.g., same monitor on multiple hosts), or too many alerts could be created. This would reduce clarity for GCC and Legal Tracker operations and could either hide problems or generate excess noise.
risks.mitigation: Use out‑of‑the‑box rules as the baseline for MVP but plan iterative refinement. Luis will adjust event rules (e.g., message keys) to avoid grouping alerts from the same monitor across different hosts where that is undesirable, and will test these changes in dev/QA using simulated events. Only once behaviour is acceptable will rules be promoted to production. For edge cases not covered by generic rules, design narrowly scoped TR‑specific rules while avoiding over‑customization.

risks.title: No clear ownership and governance model for Event Management could recreate Datadog ‘mess’
risks.description: There is currently no formally established owner for ServiceNow Event Management and AIOps governance; without this, different teams may create and modify rules, payloads, and processes inconsistently, similar to the fragmented situation in Datadog today.
risks.impact_description: If Event Management governance is not defined, teams may implement their own rules and changes without control, leading to inconsistent correlation, rule conflicts, and a "free-for-all" configuration state. This undermines the platform’s reliability, complicates support, and increases the risk of regressions when new products are onboarded.
risks.mitigation: Propose and agree that GCC will own Event Management practice and governance across TR, in partnership with Platform Engineering and ServiceNow platform owners. Define roles for central rule configuration vs. permitted local customization (e.g., event super-users), establish change governance for event/alert rules (including how to test in lower environments), and agree that non-compliant teams can have their configuration rights reduced. Consult ServiceNow on governance patterns used by other customers. Following the April 21, 2026 lessons-learned session, implement an interim hypercare model where a core team (including Prastuti, Vinay, Chris and GCC representatives like Luis) rapidly addresses configuration issues and rule changes, while Chris, Prastuti and Vinay design a durable role and access model (e.g., event management admin persona and controlled SRE roles) to avoid both over-centralization and ‘Wild West’ configuration as more products onboard.

risks.title: Poor KB/runbook quality limiting AI-driven remediation and playbooks
risks.description: Existing knowledge base articles and runbooks are fragmented, often stored in Azure DevOps wikis, and of uneven quality. The project intends to use ServiceNow AIOps (LEAP, Now Assist) and playbooks for automated or assisted remediation, which depend heavily on reliable KB content and standardized runbooks.
risks.impact_description: If KB and runbook content is not consolidated and improved, AI capabilities and playbooks will have limited material to learn from and recommend. Automated remediation and agent assist features may produce weak or incorrect guidance, reducing trust in the platform and limiting the shift from manual to automated L0 remediation. The project may achieve correlation but fail to realize remediation and MTTR reduction benefits.
risks.mitigation: Identify top recurring incident scenarios (starting with Legal Tracker infrastructure and CPU/disk cleanup workflows), migrate SOPs from Azure DevOps into ServiceNow knowledge bases, and standardize runbook formats. Enable LEAP on incident data, review generated automation opportunities, and create corresponding Flow Designer playbooks integrated with existing GitHub Actions and Azure Runbooks. Treat KB/runbook uplift as a prerequisite workstream for advanced AIOps phases.

risks.title: Datadog → ServiceNow production connectivity may not be working at go‑live
risks.description: OAuth / webhook connectivity from Datadog production to the ServiceNow production event table may fail (401 errors or authorization issues), preventing events from being ingested when the webhook endpoint is cut over to production.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog cannot authenticate to the ServiceNow production instance, no Datadog events will be ingested into Event Management. This will block testing of plugins, grouping, and event forwarding, and could delay or prevent the AIOps go‑live for Legal Tracker. Operations would have to continue relying solely on existing Datadog→SNOW incident integrations and would lose the benefits of correlation and alerting in SNOW.
risks.mitigation: Yash and Luis are jointly troubleshooting the OAuth and webhook configuration for the production instance: (1) verify and correct the OAuth access token URL to use the production SNOW instance, (2) confirm client ID and client secret values and update the Datadog auth method, (3) add any missing OAuth scopes as seen in the working dev configuration, (4) if necessary, create a new auth method in Datadog and re‑bind the webhook, and (5) engage Doug from ServiceNow to review SNOW‑side configuration and SMC logs if 401/authorization errors persist. Use test monitors in Datadog prod to validate end‑to‑end event receipt in SNOW prod before full cutover.

risks.title: Insufficient Legal Tracker event volume for tuning event rules and correlation
risks.description: Current Legal Tracker monitors are only sending a small number of events (e.g., 40–50) into the ServiceNow dev event table, far below the true number of monitors (~900+). This provides too little variety and volume to reliably design and test event rules, alert grouping, and CI binding before go‑live.
risks.impact_description: If the team does not have representative event samples from all key Legal Tracker monitors, they cannot properly analyze data behaviour, define generic vs. application‑specific event rules, or validate CI binding and out‑of‑box correlation. This may lead to poorly tuned rules, missed correlations, incorrect incidents, or delays to the planned end‑of‑March / early‑April go‑live for Legal Tracker in AIOps/Event Management.
risks.mitigation: Have the Legal Tracker team (Elizabeth and Andrea) systematically trigger test alerts for all key monitors and synthetics. Where possible, script bulk simulation by cloning monitors that point only to the dev webhook, so no production incidents are created. Coordinate with Yash so that simulated events are captured and analyzed in SNOW dev to understand different alert types, payload patterns, and CI/host identifiers before finalizing event rules and response rules.

risks.title: Machine-learning-based alert grouping may incorrectly group unrelated alerts and erode trust in AIOps
risks.description: ServiceNow’s machine-learning-based alert grouping is currently grouping unrelated alerts (e.g., a synthetic and an infrastructure monitor) into a single group for Legal Tracker, apparently based on CI relationships. Andrea and Luis observed at least one recent example where the impacted services differed but the alerts were still grouped, and Luis confirmed this grouping did not come from the TR-defined rules but from ServiceNow’s ML logic. If ML continues to group unrelated alerts, Legal Tracker and GCC will not be able to rely on alert groups to understand issues, and teams may push to disable AI features entirely, undermining the value of AIOps.
risks.impact_description: If ML-based alert grouping continues to behave unpredictably and combines unrelated alerts: (1) alert groups and resulting incidents may misrepresent the underlying problems, confusing Legal Tracker SREs and GCC; (2) operators may have to drill into individual alerts and incidents to understand what is actually happening, increasing workload and MTTR; (3) Legal Tracker and GCC will lose trust in AIOps, treating it as "not a reliable product" and resisting full onboarding; (4) stakeholders may insist on disabling ML features to avoid bad groupings, which would remove a core AIOps benefit (AI-driven incident reduction) and reduce the business case for further rollout; and (5) inability to demonstrate safe, beneficial AI usage will make leadership wary of expanding AIOps (including to FedRAMP applications).
risks.mitigation: Luis will collect concrete examples of incorrect ML-based groupings (such as the synthetic + monitor example raised by Andrea) and review them with Doug to confirm whether ServiceNow’s AI/ML grouping is still active and how it is making decisions (e.g., via CI relationships). Together, they will (1) analyse current ML configurations and correlation patterns, (2) determine whether ML grouping should be tuned (e.g., adjusting CI-relationship rules, thresholds, or training data) or temporarily disabled for Legal Tracker until behaviour is acceptable, and (3) design a validation plan using the AIOps dashboards to show how ML grouping reduces incidents without introducing mis-groupings. Only after this tuning and validation will the team encourage Legal Tracker and GCC to rely on ML-based groups for day-to-day operations.

risks.title: Loss of AIOps program lead may impact configuration and governance continuity
risks.description: Chris Rutherford, the ServiceNow / Platform Engineering leader and de facto program lead for the SNOW AIOps implementation, is leaving the project as of the end of April 2026. Chris has been a key architect for event management design, incident priority behaviour, and governance decisions. His departure may slow decision-making on rule changes, governance models, and onboarding patterns for new products, especially while Legal Tracker is still stabilising and additional products are preparing to onboard.
risks.impact_description: If responsibilities held by Chris Rutherford are not effectively transitioned, the project could experience delays in refining event rules, incident priority logic, and governance standards; slower responses to new issues raised by product teams (e.g., Legal Tracker, future early adopters); and reduced clarity on the long-term AIOps operating model. This may delay Legal Tracker stabilisation, slow onboarding of subsequent products, and increase dependency on the external ServiceNow consultant for platform decisions, potentially impacting schedule and cost.
risks.mitigation: Formalize a transition plan for Chris Rutherford’s responsibilities by: (1) identifying successor owners for platform configuration and governance decisions (e.g., Prastuti Khanna and Vinay Kumar for ServiceNow platform, Paul Berry for program governance); (2) ensuring Chris’s design decisions and rationale are captured in written standards and the AIOps configuration reference document that Doug is preparing; (3) confirming that open risks and actions where Chris is owner are reassigned to named TR staff; and (4) using the regular AIOps sync to validate that new issues (e.g., incident priority mismatches, onboarding patterns for new products) have clear internal owners rather than relying on Chris post-departure.

risks.title: Agent Chat + IVR integration requirements not yet defined with HCL
risks.description: Agent Chat enablement and IVR/voice integration (Amazon Connect) are critical to replacing the current chat channel. Requirements must be aligned with HCL to confirm minimum capabilities required without heavy customization.
risks.impact_description: Agent Chat enablement and IVR/voice integration (Amazon Connect) are critical to replacing the current chat channel Vayushpear that HCL is using. Requirements must be aligned with HCL to confirm minimum capabilities required without heavy customization.
risks.mitigation: Use the OOTB “live chat handoff from Virtual Agent in Microsoft Teams” story as the Phase 1 baseline, then capture deltas as follow‑on stories with HCL (what agents must see, VIP handling, handoff behavior).

risks.title: (Now Assist) Share Point Indexing failed
risks.description: SharePoint indexing is not functioning as expected for Now Assist. A ServiceNow support case has already been raised. Case coordination is ongoing between Krish Prashanth and the ServiceNow team. No update was available at the time of the meeting
risks.impact_description: SharePoint indexing is not functioning as expected for Now Assist which will result in failure of capturing the data
risks.mitigation: Follow up with ServiceNow on the support case, obtain status update, confirm resolution plan, and communicate progress to the core team

risks.title: [PE14] Agentic CD Pipeline Generation Automation: AI Model context window limitation impacts Cumulus Agent scalability
risks.description: The current AI model used for the AI‑assisted Cumulus pipeline creation tool has a 1,000‑file context window limitation, which may restrict its ability to accurately process and validate large or complex repositories. This constraint presents a risk to the reliability, scalability, and completeness of pipeline generation and validation as the solution evolves beyond the current POC scope.
risks.impact_description: If the context window limitation is not addressed, the AI‑assisted pipeline creation tool may fail to fully analyze larger codebases or complex repository structures, produce incomplete or inaccurate pipeline definitions, require increased manual intervention (reducing expected productivity gains), and limit the solution’s ability to scale for broader enterprise adoption. This would delay progression beyond POC and weaken the business value case for MVP and Scale phases.
risks.mitigation: Engage the Tiger Team to assess architectural or design patterns that mitigate context size constraints (e.g., repository chunking, staged analysis, or selective context loading).

risks.title: Insufficient reviewer knowledge to work through Loopio library content review
risks.description: There is a risk that reviewers lack sufficient product and content knowledge to effectively review and maintain the Loopio content library.
risks.impact_description: If reviewer knowledge remains insufficient, content library reviews may be incorrect or inconsistent, leading to outdated or inaccurate content in Loopio and reducing the effectiveness and trustworthiness of responses provided via the Customer Trust platform.
risks.mitigation: Assess reviewer knowledge, align roles accordingly, and expand the set of subject-matter experts (SMEs) contributing to Loopio. Update the library content knowledge base regularly to keep data current.

risks.title: ServiceNow integration — automation ownership and readiness for Cocounsel Legal
risks.description: CoCounsel is awaiting ServiceNow standard CHG template creation and CHG management configured within deployment pipelines. Cumulus automation hooks are in place; however, ServiceNow templates must be finalized and approved by the ServiceNow core team to complete onboarding.  (Owners: LSM CM + LSM RM + Cocounsel Legal SRE)
risks.impact_description: Delays in ServiceNow integration may block standardized change management workflows and delay delivery timelines.
risks.mitigation: Align with the ServiceNow core team on required templates and approvals; align with LSM CM, LSM RM, and Cocounsel Legal SRE on timelines to migrate and test standard change templates within pipeline.

risks.title: Discover additional opportunities to close financial gap
risks.description: The current set of identified PLE Point Solutions (e.g., ADO Assist) may be insufficient to close the remaining gap to PLE financial targets, with limited additional use cases identified to date.
risks.impact_description: If additional opportunities are not discovered in a timely manner, PLE may fall short of committed financial targets, requiring re‑baselining or reliance on higher‑risk assumptions.
risks.mitigation: Initiate a structured discovery effort across PLE teams to identify incremental, high‑impact point solutions; prioritize use cases with short time‑to‑value and clear benefit attribution.

risks.title: Materia DORA metric accuracy and trustworthiness (multi-repo lead time mapping)
risks.description: Lead-time metrics are correct for single repos but multi-repository services still have incomplete commit-to-deploy correlation (e.g., missing/ambiguous commit SHA mapping), which can skew DORA reporting in Port/IDP.  (Owners: Materia SRE + Materia Engineering)
risks.impact_description: Misleading readiness signals could drive incorrect gate decisions or erode stakeholder confidence, slowing adoption and scaling.
risks.mitigation: Run parallel validation against known deployments, document assumptions, and implement multi-source aggregation/custom hooks where needed; delay enforcement decisions until metrics pass validation criteria.

risks.title: Roadmap pressure to onboard additional products before pilot maturity
risks.description: Stakeholders are requesting additional app onboarding before the pilot has stabilized templates, validation criteria, and automation, creating pull to scale ahead of demonstrated repeatability.
risks.impact_description: Context switching and overcommitment could dilute focus, increase defects, and slow time-to-green for the core platform.
risks.mitigation: Communicate entry criteria for new apps, share a phased scaling plan (pilot → validate → template → expand), and provide periodic executive checkpoints on readiness metrics

risks.title: Cocounsel Legal MFE bundling + QA cycle limits Diamond Lane
risks.description: CoCounsel MFEs ship as bundled release sets with multi-day QA/code-freeze validation and heavy UI E2E testing; MFEs aren’t reliably independently releasable due to container/dependency coupling. Current Diamond Lane eligibilty evaluation design doesn't support bundles with multiple different release versions for each app.  (Owners: CoCounsel Legal Eng + QA/Release Mgmt)
risks.impact_description: Original scope of repos cannot be validated for release as a deployment bundle with current DL evaluation design or rearchitecting of software dependencies; threatens OKR timelines if enablement is defined as demonstrated deployment behavior change specifically for MFEs
risks.mitigation: Pursue Diamond Lane work on backend services (llmproxy) better suited for isolated release; Continue enhancement efforts for MFEs - formalize push-button secrets/config workflow; pursue incremental integration-test improvements to reduce manual QA dependencies.

risks.title: ServiceNow CIservice association behaviour may block cutover from Datadog incidents
risks.description: During the May 12, 2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, the team observed that ServiceNow is not associating services with the correct CIs for large applications such as Legal Tracker. Internal analysis suggests that a configurable limit of approximately 1,000 CIs per service causes additional CIs to be handled via dynamic CI groups, which in turn prevents correct service association and grouping. ServiceNows consultant (Doug) indicated there are traverse rules that might address this but needs to consult CMDB experts. Until a clear recommendation and fix are in place, the Legal Tracker product team considers this a showstopper for disabling Datadog-direct incident creation.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow continues to mis-associate or partially associate CIs to services due to the current serviceCI association behaviour, AIOps cannot reliably determine which service is impacted by an event or alert for large applications. For Legal Tracker, this would mean that incidents created by AIOps could lack correct service context or rely on dynamic CI groups, undermining routing, impact analysis, and leadership reporting. As a result, Legal Tracker stakeholders will not agree to cut over from Datadog-direct incident creation, delaying the POV completion, delaying onboarding of subsequent products, and prolonging reliance on legacy workflows.
risks.mitigation: ServiceNows consultant Doug will escalate the CI/service association issue to their CMDB experts to review the current configuration, including the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit and available traverse rules. Together with the TR CMDB team, they will: (1) determine whether the association limit can be safely tuned without degrading ServiceNow performance; (2) design appropriate traverse rules or alternative modelling (e.g., hierarchical services) to support large applications like Legal Tracker; and (3) validate the chosen approach in a lower environment before promoting changes to production. In parallel, Jot will log this as a formal blocker in status reporting, and Talia will escalate via email and stakeholder channels (including Eric and John) to ensure it receives high priority attention from ServiceNow and the CMDB team. Cutover from Datadog-direct incidents for Legal Tracker will be deferred until a recommended and tested fix is in place.

risks.title: Legal Tracker AIOps implementation fails to deliver incident reduction and customer value
risks.description: Despite Legal Tracker being the pilot product, AIOps/Event Management is not yet delivering the expected reduction in incidents or operational value. As of the April 21, 2026 lessons-learned session, Legal Tracker remains on a 1:1 Datadog alert-to-incident model in production, grouping rules have recently been configured in a way that adds little value (e.g., grouping by Asset Insight ID only), critical data prerequisites (Datadog tags, assignment groups, CMDB CI state) are still being remediated, and clear success criteria and ownership for rule maintenance are only now being defined. If this continues, the Legal Tracker team may not adopt Event Management as a new way of working, and the pilot will not demonstrate the promised benefits for broader rollout.
risks.impact_description: If Legal Trackers AIOps implementation does not achieve meaningful incident reduction and better grouping (e.g., grouping by API/service and assignment group), the Legal Tracker team will continue to work from noisy 1:1 incidents, undermining the core business case. This will erode stakeholder confidence (particularly Elizabeths team), make it harder to justify onboarding additional products, and may force the organization to fall back to legacy Datadog-driven workflows. Time and budget already invested in Event Management may be perceived as sunk cost with limited return, and leadership may question further AIOps investment.
risks.mitigation:
1) Explicitly define and document success criteria for Legal Tracker with the product team (Elizabeth), focused on grouping related alerts (e.g., 20 API alerts to one incident) by API/service and assignment group and measurable incident reduction.
2) Update ServiceNow AIOps grouping rules to use API name and TR-standard tags (environment type, AAID, and assignment group) rather than grouping primarily by Asset Insight ID; Doug has already added API name to the grouping rule and will iterate based on Legal Tracker feedback.
3) Complete Legal Tracker Datadog monitor/tag hygiene: Andrea and Luis to finish adding required tags (environment type, primary support group, API name) in Terraform and deploy changes, with status reported back to Elizabeth.
4) Engage the CMDB team (e.g., Ragash, Kavi) to remediate Legal Tracker CIs that are incorrectly marked as retired and perform a focused data readiness dry run so CI binding and impacted services populate correctly.
5) Use a short hypercare period with daily checks (Doug + TR core team) to validate alert grouping and incident creation behaviour and adjust rules quickly until Legal Tracker confirms value.
6) Only after Legal Tracker confirms incident-reduction benefits, use this configuration as a reusable baseline for onboarding the next set of products.

risks.title: Significant Asset ID coverage gaps in Datadog monitors
risks.description: Based on a February snapshot, about 25% of Datadog monitors lack an associated Asset ID. The team highlighted this as a critical data quality gap and a priority risk, and noted the need for a repeatable approach and ongoing inventory refresh to improve Asset ID coverage.
risks.impact_description: If Asset ID coverage remains low, it will be difficult to tie alerts to specific assets, services, and configuration items. This undermines ownership clarity, incident routing, impact analysis, and automation opportunities. It also weakens correlation between Datadog alerts and ServiceNow incidents, reducing the effectiveness of dashboards and remediation prioritization.
risks.mitigation: Establish a recurring Datadog inventory refresh that includes Asset ID fields, validate the accuracy of inventory exports, define minimum data completeness and validity requirements for Asset ID and service associations, and create a prioritized remediation backlog for monitors without Asset IDs. Track remediation outcomes for prioritized services and implement a data quality operating rhythm to prevent regression.

risks.title: Machine learning-based 'group text' alert grouping may incorrectly combine or misclassify alerts
risks.description: ServiceNow AIOps is applying machine learning ('group text' type) to group alerts based on similarities in alert descriptions. For Legal Tracker, many alert descriptions share similar text patterns, which has led to at least one case where unrelated alerts were grouped together unexpectedly. Because the ML model is tuned on existing data and technical teams are only now learning how to adjust its behaviour, there is a risk that machine learning-based groupings will over-group or mis-group alerts before the configuration and operating model are fully established.
risks.impact_description: If machine learning-based 'group text' grouping continues to combine alerts incorrectly, Legal Tracker (and later other products) may see unrelated issues collapsed into a single group or important alerts hidden within large, noisy groups. This will reduce triage clarity for SREs and product teams, risk delayed detection of genuine incidents, and undermine stakeholder confidence in AIOps correlation. As more products are onboarded, incorrect ML groupings could scale across services and make it harder to interpret alert queues and incident linkages.
risks.mitigation: Doug will document and provide detailed instructions to the TR technical team (Luis and colleagues) on how to inspect and tune the machine learning-based 'group text' grouping configuration in ServiceNow AIOps. The technical team will (1) review current ML groupings affecting Legal Tracker; (2) adjust relevant parameters or model settings so that legitimate similarities are used without over-grouping; (3) establish an operating procedure where product teams (e.g., Legal Tracker) flag odd 'group text' groupings to the technical AIOps team; and (4) incorporate ML grouping review into ongoing monitoring and onboarding playbooks so that future products have their grouping behaviour validated and tuned early.

risks.title: Duplicate or inflated incident volumes during AIOps and Datadog parallel run
risks.description: When AIOps/Event Management starts creating incidents from alerts while the existing direct Datadog→ServiceNow incident integration is still active, the same underlying issues may result in multiple incidents or an increased incident count during the transition period.
risks.impact_description: If both the legacy Datadog incident integration and the new AIOps‑driven incident creation are active, the Legal Tracker support team and GCC may receive additional incidents for the same events. This will increase operational workload, complicate triage, and skew incident metrics and reporting (e.g., MTTR, volume trends). It may also confuse stakeholders if they see multiple incident records for a single problem.
risks.mitigation: Define a clear cutover strategy and time‑boxed UAT: (1) initially limit AIOps to event → alert correlation in production and perform full incident creation in QA using prod‑like data, (2) run a side‑by‑side comparison of incidents generated directly from Datadog vs. AIOps over ~2 weeks to validate that AIOps produces the right incidents and fewer of them, (3) once satisfied, either disable incident creation in Datadog for Legal Tracker (via Terraform or update scripts) or introduce a control in ServiceNow that prevents incidents from being created via the old route for Legal Tracker services, and (4) communicate expected temporary metric distortion to incident reporting owners (e.g., Mike Krause) and Legal Tracker stakeholders.

risks.title: Delayed and non-compliant enablement of AIOps/Event Management in FedRAMP environment
risks.description: During the 11 May 2026 sync, AD asked about enabling AIOps/Event Management in the FedRAMP environment for high-noise FedRAMP applications (including HighQ). Tim Roe confirmed that no AIOps/Event Management work has yet started in FedRAMP and that an assessment is required to mirror enterprise configuration while complying with FedRAMP processes, approvals, and licensing constraints. There is also a need to ensure AI-related configurations (such as do not share data for AI training) are correctly set, as in the enterprise instance.
risks.impact_description: If AIOps/Event Management is not enabled in the FedRAMP environment in a timely and compliant manner, high-noise FedRAMP applications (including HighQ) will continue to generate excessive alert volumes without the benefit of AIOps grouping and suppression. This will limit the programs ability to demonstrate noise reduction for a key subset of services, delay benefits for FedRAMP customers, and risk misalignment with FedRAMP compliance requirements if modules are enabled without appropriate oversight. Conversely, if technical teams proceed without proper FedRAMP governance, there is a risk of non-compliance related to data handling, AI training settings, or licensing, which could trigger security, audit, or legal concerns.
risks.mitigation: Tim Roe will (1) review all AIOps/Event Management modules and configurations that were enabled in the enterprise ServiceNow instance and prepare a plan to mirror only the necessary components in FedRAMP; (2) coordinate with a designated FedRAMP representative (e.g., Dev Key or Pete France) and a project management resource to ensure all required FedRAMP processes, approvals, and licensing considerations are addressed; (3) consult with Vinay to ensure that AI training-related configurations (such as disabling data sharing for AI training) are explicitly set in FedRAMP, matching enterprise settings; and (4) report back to AD and Talia with an initial assessment and proposed enablement timeline. A FedRAMP representative will be added to ongoing AIOps governance meetings to maintain compliance oversight.

risks.title: ServiceNow event forwarding limits may cause loss of forwarded events for Datadog-based testing
risks.description: ServiceNow event forwarding from production to lower environments (dev/QA) is configured with both a daily limit and a one-hour time window. HiCase feedback from ServiceNow Support indicates that forwarding does not backfill historical events and respects these limits. During the 30-Apr-2026 regular sync, Yash highlighted that this combination introduces a risk that some Datadog events will not be forwarded (for example, older events outside the one-hour duration or when daily forwarding thresholds are reached), which could lead to missing test data in dev/QA or incomplete visibility if forwarding is used operationally.
risks.impact_description: If the per-day and one-hour forwarding limits are hit or if events fall outside the configured window, lower environments may not receive a representative set of Datadog events. This will reduce the team’s ability to test and tune event rules and correlation in dev/QA, may create confusion when events seen in production are not visible in lower environments, and could cause missed defects in rule logic. If forwarding is later relied upon for any operational troubleshooting, missing events could also impair analysis.
risks.mitigation: Doug will review the ServiceNow HiCase response in detail and work with Yash to (1) confirm the exact semantics of the per-day and one-hour forwarding limits; (2) evaluate whether a dedicated forwarding configuration can be created that targets only Datadog-originated events to minimise volume; (3) adjust forwarding schedules and limits where possible to reduce the chance of hitting caps; and (4) if limits cannot be relaxed sufficiently, design an alternative approach for lower-environment testing (e.g., direct Datadog webhooks to dev/QA or scripted sample event injection) so that dev/QA receive predictable test data without relying solely on forwarding.

risks.mitigation: Focus pilot on application only releases and rely on circuit breaker capabilities to stop unhealthy deployments in the near term; align with Materia engineering on plans for expanded feature flag use; ensure post-deployment validations page out on degraded customer experience.

Worksoft’s own AI capabilities are limited, and any AI agent would have to be built within Worksoft itself. A replacement tool (e.g., Tosca) is now being actively considered to address this constraint.
risks.impact_description: If Worksoft continues to block third-party LLM integration and no viable replacement tool is selected and implemented, the majority of Core regression tests (~85%) will remain unable to benefit from AI agents. This would significantly constrain AI-driven test automation and productivity gains in Core, leaving only the ~15% of tests using Selenium and Playwright able to leverage AI. The CE5 Testing Tools use case may fall short of adoption and efficiency targets, and the overall CE AI Reimagine benefits could be materially reduced. If a replacement such as Tosca is chosen and implemented, the risk could be reduced for all QE practices except the contact center, which would remain an exception.

In parallel, progress evaluation of replacement tools: Sumathi is currently assessing Tosca as the primary contender for a Worksoft replacement and has committed to return with findings by mid-June (Tuesday/Wednesday of next week). Ensure her assessment explicitly considers AI advancements and coverage for QE practices so that any replacement supports AI agents. If a viable replacement is confirmed, move forward with a migration plan that transitions Core regression suites off Worksoft (with the only exception likely being the contact center), quantify the cost/risk/timeline, and track adoption in the AI testing dashboard once implemented. Escalate outcomes and recommendations to leadership to support a broader Core regression test tool strategy.
