risks.title: ServiceNow incident reopen behaviour and incident number changes may cause confusion and reporting issues
risks.description: ServiceNow Event Management is currently configured so that when a new alert group matches a previously closed incident, the platform reopens that incident and, in some observed cases, changes the incident number and unlinks/links alerts between incidents. This is out-of-the-box behaviour tied to alert grouping windows and incident-respond rules, but it is unfamiliar to Legal Tracker and GCC teams, who are used to static incident numbers and non-reopened incidents from the legacy Datadog→incident flow. The team considers the current deterministic incident-priority patch and this reopen behaviour an MVP to allow Legal Tracker to proceed, but has not yet decided whether this should become the long-term standard.
risks.impact_description: If ServiceNow continues to reopen incidents and change incident numbers when subsequent alert groups arrive, Legal Tracker and other product teams may find incident history and tracking confusing. Historical analysis, SLA reporting, and major-incident reviews could be impacted if incident numbers are reused or altered, and if resolution notes and timelines are overwritten or merged across multiple alert bursts. Operators may lose trust in AIOps-generated incidents, and incident management leadership (e.g., Mike, Dominique) may raise concerns about data integrity and the ability to perform accurate trend and compliance reporting. This could slow adoption of Event Management, require manual workarounds, or force the team to disable some out-of-the-box behaviours after multiple products have already been onboarded.
risks.mitigation: Doug will investigate the current incident-respond and alert-grouping behaviour with ServiceNow experts to understand why incidents are being reopened and incident numbers changed when new alert groups arrive, including the unlinking/linking of related alerts. Options to be evaluated include: (1) adjusting the default 30-minute grouping window or related properties so that new alert bursts create new incidents instead of reopening closed ones; (2) changing configuration to prevent incident-number changes while preserving linkage between alerts and incidents; and (3) retaining out-of-the-box behaviour but clearly documenting it as a standard way of working and training teams accordingly. In parallel, TR will use dev/QA as a "laboratory" to experiment with non-deterministic, AIOps-native behaviour (dynamic impact/urgency and grouping) without affecting production, and will involve Legal Tracker stakeholders (Elizabeth, Andrea) and incident management (e.g., Mike, Dominique) in reviewing the preferred long-term pattern before applying any permanent configuration changes across products.

risks.title: ServiceNow incident reopen and incident number change behaviour may confuse teams and distort reporting
risks.description: In the current AIOps/Event Management configuration, ServiceNow may reopen closed incidents and, in some cases, change the incident number when new alerts are grouped into existing alert groups. Legal Tracker stakeholders (Elizabeth and Andrea, via feedback to Luis Jorge) have observed that grouped alerts can reopen a previously closed incident and that the related incident number can change when alert links are updated. This behaviour is driven by default ServiceNow grouping and respond rules (e.g., 30-minute grouping window and incident creation on alert-group creation) and is not aligned with the team’s existing ways of working or reporting expectations.
risks.impact_description: If incident reopen and incident-number-change behaviour remains as currently observed, GCC and product teams like Legal Tracker may find incident histories confusing, struggle to track resolution chronologies, and lose confidence in AIOps-generated incidents. Historical reporting and trend analysis (e.g., incident counts, MTTR, repeat incidents) could be distorted if incidents are repeatedly reopened or renumbered when new alerts arrive. This may increase resistance to working from alerts and incidents in Event Management, slow adoption of the new operating model, and force teams to rely on legacy Datadog-driven incidents or manual workarounds.
risks.mitigation: Analyse the current ServiceNow incident-respond and grouping behaviour for Legal Tracker, focusing on scenarios where grouped alerts reopen closed incidents and cause incident number changes. Consult ServiceNow product/CMDB experts to confirm whether this is expected out-of-the-box behaviour or misconfiguration. Potential mitigations include: (1) tuning the alert-grouping window (e.g., shorter than the 30-minute default) to limit late regrouping; (2) adjusting respond rules so not all alert groups immediately create incidents, shifting more work to alert handling; and (3) clarifying or updating configuration so incidents are not renumbered when alert links change. In parallel, run a focused session with the Legal Tracker team to explain standard AIOps incident lifecycle behaviour, gather their requirements, and agree on a documented standard for when incidents may be reopened vs new incidents created.

risks.title: Conversational greeting and fallback workflow may miss 2026-05-07 commitment
risks.description: The team committed to having a more natural, conversational virtual agent greeting, closing, and fallback experience ready by 2026-05-07, based on feedback from leaders (including Marc) that the current Now Assist chat lacks greetings, closing messages, validation, and ticket number sharing. During the 2026-05-05 SNOWNAWA working session, Shariq highlighted that there has been "no meaningful progress" on these conversational workflows, ownership is unclear (who raises the story, what Ashima and developers are working from), and admin access to edit templates is constrained. Although predefined templates and out-of-the-box system topics exist, they are not yet configured to meet the desired experience. If these items are not implemented and tested rapidly, the team may miss the 2026-05-07 target it has "given ourselves" for fixing the greetings and related chat behaviors.
risks.impact_description: If the conversational greeting, closing, and fallback workflows are not implemented and validated by 2026-05-07, the virtual agent experience will remain non-conversational (no personalized greeting, no clear closing, weak error/fallback handling, inconsistent ticket number communication). This will directly contradict commitments made to Marc and other stakeholders, undermine confidence in Now Assist as a polished product, and may delay further pilot or rollout activities that assume a baseline conversational experience. It also increases the likelihood of additional rework after leadership feedback, consuming scarce developer and SME time during an already compressed window.
risks.mitigation:
1) Capture a concrete story with clear description and acceptance criteria for the conversational workflow (greeting, closing, error handling, and fallback messages), as discussed by Vinay and Shariq, using the existing "virtual agent" story template format.
2) Shariq, Mayank, and Prithwiraj will meet immediately after the 2026-05-05 team meeting to define the exact greeting and fallback prompts, including personalization (e.g., "Hey, <name>, how can I help you?"), and provide these to Vinay the same day.
3) Ensure appropriate admin access is granted (e.g., to Mayank or another designated admin) to edit or duplicate the greeting templates and system topics in the sandbox environment.
4) Ashima has scheduled a focused working session for the next day with Srinivasan, Vinay, and others to prioritize and implement the greeting and fallback changes, treating this as a working session rather than relying on daily, asynchronous feedback.
5) Run internal "beta" testing by Shariq, Mayank, and Prithwiraj on the updated experience before requesting Marc and other leaders to retest, iterating quickly on any issues identified in the session.
6) Track progress against the 2026-05-07 target explicitly and escalate immediately if development or access constraints threaten that date.
7) As of the 2026-05-07 Service Desk AI automation sync, the team has progressed two of the seven documented conversational topics (initial greeting scenario and handover flow) but Mayank reported test failures in key scenarios (e.g., user enters a problem statement directly without "hi" and receives no greeting or empathy message; handover confirmation flow not yet implemented). Additional UX requirements were agreed, including an empathy-style acknowledgement that references the user’s name where technically feasible, replacing drop-down topic selection with visible options for top topics, and capturing all feedback and status in a centralized Excel tracker that Ashima will create. Daily 9 PM IST standups will be used to track completion of the remaining topics and retesting.

risks.title: Onboarding products without monitors-as-code or bulk-update capability may delay rollout
risks.description: During the discussion, Elizabeth highlighted that Legal Tracker’s Datadog monitors are managed as code (Terraform/GitHub), which makes it easier to apply standardized changes (tags, priorities, handlers). Chris and Jot noted that effort estimates will differ for teams that do not manage monitors as code. Luis mentioned GCC has scripts to perform bulk operations against Datadog monitors but indicated this is a workaround and not the best long‑term approach. If new products lack monitors‑as‑code or bulk‑update capabilities, onboarding them to AIOps will require more manual changes per monitor (e.g., adding handlers, tags, correcting priorities), which could slow the rollout or result in inconsistent configurations.
risks.impact_description: If a product team’s monitors are not managed as code or cannot be updated in bulk, adding the required handlers, tags, and priority/severity standards for AIOps will be slower and more error‑prone. This may delay onboarding timelines, cause inconsistent or incomplete adoption of tagging and priority standards, and increase operational risk (e.g., some monitors sending events, others not; mis‑prioritized incidents). It could also constrain the pool of suitable early adopters, limiting the ability to scale beyond initial products like Legal Tracker, Steve’s team, and Liat’s team.
risks.mitigation:
1) As part of candidate selection, explicitly assess whether a product’s Datadog monitors are managed as code (e.g., in GitHub/Terraform) or at least can be bulk‑updated via GCC or platform scripts.
2) Prioritize near‑term onboarding for teams that already have monitors‑as‑code (e.g., Legal Tracker, and only proceed with Steve’s and Liat’s teams if they meet this criterion or accept the extra effort).
3) Where monitors are not in code, leverage existing GCC bulk‑update scripts to add handlers and standard tags, and document this as a temporary mitigation rather than the default approach.
4) Encourage and support product teams in migrating key monitors to monitoring‑as‑code over time, aligning with the Datadog hygiene programme.
5) Reflect this requirement in the standard onboarding checklist so teams understand the expectation before committing to an onboarding date.

risks.title: Alert-threshold hygiene may be misreported if synthetic monitors are not excluded
risks.description: Nick and Dominique discussed that a "large chunk" of monitors show no alert threshold configured. Dominique clarified that, based on review with Tax, many of these are synthetic monitors, for which a traditional threshold is not expected. Current counting and reporting of "monitors without thresholds" does not filter out synthetics, which can overstate the problem and distort hygiene metrics.
risks.impact_description: If synthetic monitors continue to be included in counts of "monitors without alert thresholds", the program’s analytics and dashboards will overstate threshold hygiene issues (e.g., reporting 20–30% of monitors as missing thresholds). This will mislead stakeholders about the true severity of the problem, cause remediation backlogs to prioritize the wrong monitors, and waste engineering time chasing expected configurations instead of genuine gaps. It may also undermine trust in Datadog Hygiene metrics and delay focused work on real threshold defects.
risks.mitigation: Update the Datadog inventory refresh logic, Eric’s Power BI reporting, and any related analytics to explicitly identify monitor type and filter out synthetic monitors when calculating metrics and backlogs for "missing alert thresholds". Confirm with Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ that the refined views correctly separate synthetic monitors from other monitor types, and adjust the monitoring hygiene metrics dictionary so threshold-related KPIs explicitly exclude synthetics unless a specific exception is defined.

risks.mitigation: Conduct a structured impact analysis of potential Datadog org consolidation options, including data retention, anomaly model behavior, and AI/MCP rate limits. Present options with clear risks and trade‑offs to stakeholders and only proceed with consolidation under a controlled migration plan that preserves critical data and service continuity.

risks.title: Agent queue management governance between TR and HCL not defined
risks.description: The process and ownership for managing agent chat queues (e.g., adding new hires to language queues like French or English) has not been defined. This can result in agents not receiving interactions they should handle, degraded service levels, manual workarounds, and dependence on ad-hoc TR changes. risks.mitigation: 1) Inventory current Advanced Work Assignment (AWA) queue configurations (e.g., language-specific queues such as French and English) and document the required update operations (add/remove agent, change capacities). 2) Align with TR stakeholders (e.g., Vinay, Prastuti) on whether queue administration will remain a TR-only function or if selected HCL members will receive controlled access. 3) Define and document a standard process (e.g., request form or workflow) for HCL to request queue changes, including SLAs, roles and approvals. 4) Communicate the agreed process and responsibilities to HCL leadership and frontline supervisors, and update any onboarding materials for new agents. 5) Periodically review queue membership changes to ensure the process is being followed and remains efficient.

This can lead to incorrect or confusing answers, reduced trust from end users and ServiceDeskLeads, and potential pushback on broader rollout. Extended delay could also create misalignment with other milestones (e.g., virtual agent enhancements and IVR integration) that assume refreshed, curated KB content is available.
risks.mitigation: 1) Lock in a concrete plan by the Tuesday following the long weekend (early May 2026) for how to execute the KB refresh, including scope (top ~100 KBs first), sequencing, and owners. 2) Use Bineesh’s Excel list (886 total, 539 'keep', AI-suggested top 100) as the working baseline and assign reviewers (ServiceDeskLeads SMEs, Rashid, and knowledge manager Prastuti) to specific KB subsets. 3) Agree a time-boxed initial pass focused on the AI-suggested top 100 KBs so these can be validated and updated quickly, while planning subsequent passes for the remaining 'keep' KBs. 4) Track progress against this plan in the PMO tracker and adjust related virtual agent/Now Assist milestones if delays arise. 5) Escalate resourcing conflicts (e.g., Shariq’s costing model work) to leadership if they threaten the agreed refresh schedule.
risks.source_file_name: SD Automation KB Articles Refresh planning and timelines.docx

risks.title: Zurich upgrade and dev freeze may cause loss or rework of recent virtual agent and agent chat changes
risks.description: The upcoming Zurich upgrade will introduce a dev freeze period (May 8 to June 8) and a clone from production into the development environment. During the May 11, 2026 sync, Vinay explained that to avoid losing in-flight development work (especially virtual agent conversational workflows, plugins, and configuration changes), developers must take backups of update sets before the end of Friday. Srinu confirmed that some changes are already captured in update sets, but others (such as plugin enabling or certain configuration options) are not; these will need to be documented and manually re-applied after the clone. If backups and documentation are incomplete, recent VA and Agent Chat work could be overwritten or require significant rework after the clone, impacting timelines.
risks.impact_description: If update sets are not properly exported and configuration-only changes are not documented before the Zurich upgrade clone, the clone from production could overwrite or remove recent development work on virtual agent conversational workflows, Agent Chat configuration, and related integrations. This would require developers (Srinu, Prashanth and others) to rediscover and re-implement these changes manually, consuming additional effort during an already constrained period and potentially delaying the May 15 conversational workflow target and other milestones. Incomplete backups could also cause inconsistencies between dev, QA, and future production deployments, increasing the risk of defects at go-live.
risks.mitigation:
1) Ensure all recent development work for virtual agent conversational workflows, Agent Chat, and related configurations is captured in ServiceNow update sets before the Zurich upgrade clone; Srinu and Prashanth to coordinate and export these update sets by end of day Friday.
2) For items not captured in update sets (e.g., plugin enablement, certain configuration options), document the exact steps and settings so they can be manually re-applied on the cloned dev instance.
3) After the clone, re-import and commit the saved update sets into the dev instance and re-apply documented configuration changes, verifying that all key VA and Agent Chat functionality still works.
4) Continue development and feedback changes in dev and QA during the prod change freeze, deferring only production promotions until after the upgrade window, as confirmed by Vinay.
5) Kiran to monitor progress and request status updates from Srinu and Prashanth on backup completion, highlighting any areas where rework is expected so they can be time-boxed and prioritized.
6) If significant rework is required post-clone, adjust internal timelines for non-prod testing and update the RAAID log and milestones accordingly.
risks.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

risks.title: Misalignment of Datadog default maturity scorecards with Thomson Reuters standards
risks.description: The team is exploring whether existing Datadog maturity scorecards can be used to measure observability maturity. Datadog’s default scorecards are generic and likely not aligned to Thomson Reuters’ internal observability and monitoring standards. If they are adopted without proper alignment or customization, measurements of maturity may be misleading or inconsistent across teams.
risks.impact_description: If generic Datadog scorecards are used without alignment, the program may report inaccurate or non‑actionable maturity levels. This could lead to false confidence, misdirected remediation efforts, difficulty comparing maturity across business units, and reduced credibility of the Datadog Hygiene Program’s reporting with executives.
risks.mitigation: Review Datadog’s default maturity scorecard capabilities with Platform Engineering, assess alignment effort vs. value, and either customize the scorecards to match Thomson Reuters standards or define a TR‑specific maturity model. Do not adopt the default scorecards for official reporting until alignment is validated.

risks.title: Reliance on temporary customizations for incident priority and CI binding instead of AIOps-native behaviour
risks.description: To meet Legal Tracker timelines, the team has implemented temporary workarounds: (1) disabling out-of-the-box ServiceNow incident priority calculation and deterministically passing Datadog monitor priority straight through to incident priority; and (2) implementing temporary CI matching logic so that CI binding appears to work, even though underlying discovery/CMDB issues are unresolved. These changes diverge from ServiceNow AIOps standard design and are intended as MVP patches.
risks.impact_description: If the project continues to rely on deterministic Datadog>incident priority and temporary CI-binding logic, AIOps will not leverage dynamic priority calculation based on CI importance, blast radius, and alert state. This undermines the core value proposition of AI-driven prioritization, risks misaligned incident impact/urgency, and may require significant rework later to unwind customisations across multiple onboarded products. It also risks masking underlying CI discovery issues, which could resurface at scale and delay onboarding of additional applications.
risks.mitigation: Treat the current deterministic priority and CI-binding behaviour as an MVP for Legal Tracker only. In parallel, (1) use dev/QA as a "laboratory" to re-enable AIOps-native, non-deterministic incident priority calculation and tune scoring (e.g., adjust thresholds so that priority is not raised too aggressively after only two alerts); (2) work with Yash and the discovery/CMDB team to identify and fix the root causes of failed CI binding rather than relying indefinitely on custom matching; (3) once tuned, plan a controlled switch back to out-of-the-box priority and CI-binding logic for Legal Tracker, validating behaviour with Legal Tracker and GCC; and (4) ensure that future products are onboarded against the standardized AIOps configuration rather than inheriting Legal Trackers temporary customisations.

risks.title: Copilot live agent handoff and transcript sharing may not meet requirements
risks.description: The team is pivoting to Microsoft 365 Copilot as the interim conversational front end, but the live agent transfer capability from Copilot into ServiceNow Agent Chat has not yet been implemented or tested. Mayank and Shariq emphasized that for a good user experience, the entire Copilot conversation (or at least a useful summary) must be handed over to the ServiceNow live agent so that the agent can see the history and context. Today, the live agent functionality sits fully on the ServiceNow side, and it is unclear whether Copilot can reliably pass conversation history into the ServiceNow interaction/incident or whether an additional topic/API must be built specifically for live agent transfer. Until this is designed and validated, there is a risk that the handoff will be incomplete or fail altogether.
risks.impact_description: If Copilot cannot reliably transfer conversation history to ServiceNow during live agent handoff, agents will receive chats without prior context, forcing customers to repeat information and degrading the user experience. This will undermine the key requirement that the handoff from Copilot to the service desk be seamless, may increase handle times, and could reduce trust in the new Copilot-based channel. It may also require rework of the Copilot design or additional custom integration between Copilot and ServiceNow, delaying rollout and potentially impacting call/deflection targets.
risks.mitigation:
1) Design and implement a specific live agent transfer flow for Copilot that captures the user conversation (or a summary) and passes it into the ServiceNow interaction/incident as part of the handoff.
2) Use lower environments (Dev1) to prototype this behavior, ensuring the ServiceNow live agent sees the full context.
3) Coordinate between Mayank (Copilot design) and the ServiceNow team (Prastuti and Vinay) to determine whether this can be achieved without custom APIs, or if a limited API-based integration is required only for live agent transfer.
4) Execute end-to-end tests of Copilot conversations that escalate to live agents, validating that agents can see transcript/summary content and that no data is lost.
5) Document any limitations (e.g., only summaries, not full transcripts) and incorporate them into the pros/cons comparison table that Shariq will prepare for leadership review.

risks.title: Dynamic language translation capability may be lost when moving from Now Assist to Copilot
risks.description: Jakub and Shariq highlighted that the current dynamic language translation feature (used in Agent Chat to support non-English users while routing to English-speaking agents) relies on Now Assist capabilities. As the team pivots to Copilot as the front-end conversational agent, it is unclear whether equivalent dynamic translation will be available or how it will be implemented. Prastuti confirmed that Now Assist is required for the current AI-based real-time translation. If an alternative solution is not put in place, the project could lose the ability to offshore non-English traffic to the main support center while still providing localized experiences to users.
risks.impact_description: If dynamic translation cannot be provided in the Copilot-based solution, non-English language support may be constrained. TR might be unable to route non-English interactions efficiently to centralized English-speaking support teams while maintaining a localized user experience. This would reduce potential savings from offshoring non-English languages to the main support center in India, limit call/chat deflection for non-English users, and weaken the business case that assumes multi-language support via AI translation.
risks.mitigation:
1) Inventory the current dynamic translation implementation with Now Assist and document exactly which components (LLM, configuration) provide real-time translation in Agent Chat.
2) Assess Copilot capabilities for dynamic translation in the context of the planned Teams-based Copilot agent, including whether Copilot can translate user inputs and agent responses in real time.
3) Engage ServiceNow and Microsoft contacts to understand supported patterns where Copilot and ServiceNow Agent Chat can jointly provide translation, or whether Now Assist must remain in the path for translation only.
4) Prototype one or two non-English flows end-to-end with Copilot as the entry point and ServiceNow Agent Chat as the backend, validating that translation works for both directions.
5) If equivalent translation cannot be achieved, update the options/pros-cons table (that Shariq and Mayank will prepare) to reflect this limitation and escalate to Marc and AD for a decision on whether to retain Now Assist for translation, adopt an alternative LLM, or accept reduced multi-language capability in the near term.

risks.title: Copilot-based solution may not preserve interaction linkage and history in ServiceNow
risks.description: Prastuti raised concern that, with Now Assist, conversational data is attached to the ServiceNow interaction and carried forward to incidents, enabling AWA-based features such as routing users back to the same agent within a time window. She noted that, with Copilot, TR will likely not store Copilot conversations as Virtual Agent conversations in ServiceNow by default. It is uncertain whether Copilot conversations will be linked to interaction/incident records in a way that preserves history and supports existing AWA capabilities (e.g., context-aware routing).
risks.impact_description: If Copilot conversations are not stored and linked to ServiceNow interaction and incident records, agents will lose access to historical conversational data associated with a case, and AWA will be unable to use this history for routing (e.g., trying to route repeat contacts back to the same agent within three days). This reduces the effectiveness of Agent Chat, complicates follow-up interactions, and may degrade the service desk experience compared to the current Now Assist-based approach.
risks.mitigation:
1) Define a data model for capturing Copilot conversations or summaries in ServiceNow, ensuring that they are attached to interaction and/or incident records similarly to Now Assist conversations.
2) Evaluate mechanisms (e.g., MCP server configuration, service account access) to write summaries or transcripts from Copilot into ServiceNow tables without violating security or compliance constraints.
3) Test repeat-contact scenarios (e.g., user contacts service desk multiple times within three days) to verify whether AWA can leverage this stored history and whether any existing features (such as routing to the same agent) continue to work.
4) If full parity with Now Assist is not feasible, document the reduced capability and include it in the options comparison that will be presented to leadership, so that any gaps are explicitly accepted or mitigated via process changes.

risks.title: Amazon Connect CTI URL misconfiguration may delay IVR demo and cutover
risks.description: During the May 11, 2026 Service Desk AI automation sync, Jakub and Saket reported an issue with the URL used by the Amazon Connect CTI integration: it currently opens an incident record populated with user details instead of an interaction record, whereas the desired behavior is to start from an interaction record. This misconfiguration is blocking completion of CTI testing and prevents scheduling the previously agreed Amazon Connect demo session for Wednesday. Saket stated that once the correct URL is provided and CTI testing is successful, the team will need an additional 2–3 business days to confirm testing, followed by approximately 10–14 days for the telco/ISP to change the external IVR numbers and perform cutover, with old numbers running in parallel for 2–3 weeks. Until the URL issue is resolved, these downstream steps cannot begin, putting IVR cutover timelines at risk.
risks.impact_description: If the Amazon Connect CTI URL continues to open incident records instead of interaction records, CTI testing cannot be completed and the planned Amazon Connect demo session for HCL/TR stakeholders will be delayed. This, in turn, delays finalizing IVR cutover dates and communicating new numbers to Thomson Reuters users. Because the telco/ISP requires roughly 10–14 days to implement number changes and old numbers will run in parallel only for a limited period, any slip in resolving the URL issue can cascade into delays for Avaya-to-Amazon Connect cutover and subsequent integration of Amazon Connect with Now Assist / Agent Chat. This would slow realization of voice deflection benefits and could necessitate re-planning of 2026 IVR-related milestones.
risks.mitigation:
1) Identify and correct the CTI integration URL so that Amazon Connect opens an interaction record in ServiceNow instead of an incident record; Kiran and Bineesh to coordinate with the appropriate ServiceNow and telephony contacts (as referenced in the email chain including Ragesh).
2) Engage ServiceNow support (potentially via Presto or another POC) to validate that the corrected URL and configuration align with best practices for CTI interaction handling.
3) Once the URL is fixed, have the CTI/telephony team complete end-to-end testing within 2–3 business days, confirming that SAP ID (numeric) entry by callers maps correctly to the alphanumeric names that agents use.
4) After successful testing, agree and document IVR cutover dates, ensuring the ISP/telco has at least 10 days (ideally 2 weeks) to implement number changes and that old Avaya numbers run in parallel with new Amazon Connect numbers for 2–3 weeks.
5) Communicate new IVR numbers and cutover timelines to HCL and Thomson Reuters users well in advance, so downstream dependencies (e.g., integration into Agent Chat and Virtual Agent) can proceed.
6) Track progress and blockers in the existing Amazon Connect / CTI integration action items and escalate if URL resolution exceeds the 2–3 business day window.
risks.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

risks.title: Delayed Playwright agent rollout in Core due to resource turnover
risks.description: In Core, the Playwright AI agent rollout is delayed because the automation engineer in Sumathi’s area resigned and a replacement FTE is only now being onboarded. Sumathi has requested time until mid-June to start the Playwright agent POC and subsequent implementation.
risks.impact_description: If the Playwright agent POC and rollout in Core are further delayed, only Selenium-based tests will benefit from AI assistance in the near term. This limits AI adoption to a subset of Core automated testing and slows overall efficiency gains, potentially impacting CE5 Testing Tools milestones and delaying benefits realisation from AI-enabled regression testing in Core.
risks.mitigation: Prioritise onboarding and ramp-up of the replacement automation FTE in Sumathi’s area and schedule the Playwright agent POC to start by mid-June. Ensure prerequisites (environments, test suites, access) are prepared in advance so that the POC and rollout can progress quickly once the engineer is productive. Track Core Playwright agent adoption explicitly in the testing AI dashboard once data becomes available.
risks.source_file_name: AI Use Case Progress_Updates - Weekly Check Ins (2).docx

risks.title: Conversational greeting and fallback workflow may miss 2026-05-15 target due to customization constraints and vendor dependency
risks.description: The team has committed to delivering a complete conversational virtual agent workflow (including greetings when users do not start with "hi", handover behavior, and other feedback items) by 2026-05-15. Current testing shows that if a user types a problem directly (e.g., "my Outlook is crashing") without greeting the VA, the system does not send any greeting before giving a solution, which is considered poor user experience. Initial review on the prior Thursday suggested that achieving the desired greeting behavior may not be possible purely with out-of-the-box configuration and might require customization. During the May 11, 2026 sync, Vinay cautioned that custom scripting inside Now Assist / Virtual Agent is high risk for future upgrades and generally not recommended without ServiceNow guidance. The team is now dependent on multiple working sessions with the ServiceNow vendor (planned from Tuesday to Friday) to determine whether the required behavior can be achieved via configuration or safe customization. Until this is resolved, progress on several of the eight conversational workflow requirements remains blocked, increasing the risk that the agreed May 15 date will slip.
risks.impact_description: If the conversational greeting, closing, and fallback workflows cannot be implemented without high‑risk customization, or if ServiceNow vendor guidance is delayed, the team may miss the 2026-05-15 target for completing all eight conversational feedback items. This would leave the current poor experience in place (no greeting when users jump straight into a problem statement) and contradict commitments to stakeholders such as Marc. It could delay promotion of any completed conversational changes to production (since Kiran and Jakub prefer a single batch move once all eight requirements are done), push back pilot timelines, and force rework if interim customizations break during the upcoming Zurich upgrade.
risks.mitigation:
1) Avoid high‑risk custom scripting in Now Assist / Virtual Agent where possible; prioritize configuration-based changes to greetings and handover flows.
2) Use the scheduled ServiceNow vendor working sessions (targeting 4 sessions between Tuesday and Friday) to review the specific greeting requirement where users do not start with "hi" and obtain explicit guidance on safe configuration vs customization options.
3) Vinay to document any proposed customization and validate with ServiceNow during these sessions before implementation.
4) Ashima to keep the tracker of eight conversational feedback items updated, reflecting that greeting behavior (feedback #1) remains in progress and handover (feedback #4) is now working, based on tests by Srinu and Mayank.
5) Kiran to coordinate and ensure the vendor sessions are scheduled and attended by the right team members (Vinay, Ashima, Mayank, Prithvi) and to relay the UX requirements back to ServiceNow.
6) Defer promotion of conversational workflow changes to production until all eight requirements are implemented and validated, to avoid multiple disruptive deployments during the Zurich upgrade window.
risks.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

risks.title: Copilot integration behavior may change after MCP server and Zurich upgrade adjustments
risks.description: AD noted that, as part of the Zurich upgrade, an MCP server is being set up in the dev environment and that this may change slightly the experience and outcomes of current Copilot–ServiceNow integration tests. Mayank acknowledged this and expects it to help, but there is still uncertainty about how the new MCP setup and Zurich upgrade will affect existing Copilot prototypes and configurations.
risks.impact_description: If the MCP server setup or Zurich upgrade materially changes how Copilot connects to ServiceNow (e.g., permissions, data access paths, authentication), previously successful Copilot prototypes may fail or behave differently. This could require rework of Copilot integration, delay testing timelines, or introduce new defects in ticket creation, status checks, and live agent transfer flows. It may also complicate comparison of pre- and post-upgrade behavior, making it harder to validate that Copilot meets project requirements.
risks.mitigation:
1) Document the current Copilot–ServiceNow integration architecture and configuration prior to enabling the MCP server and Zurich upgrade.
2) Coordinate between AD, Prastuti, Vinay, and Mayank to plan a controlled test window after the MCP server is enabled, focusing on key Copilot functions (KB retrieval, ticket creation, status check, and live agent transfer).
3) Compare behaviors and outcomes before and after the MCP server setup to identify any regressions or changes.
4) Adjust Copilot configuration and ServiceNow permissions as needed to align with the new MCP-based architecture.
5) Capture lessons learned into the upgrade and cloning playbook so that future environment changes do not unexpectedly break Copilot integrations.

risks.title: Agent chat dashboards and analytics requirements not yet defined
risks.description: HCL stakeholders requested dashboards to monitor agent chat performance (e.g., agent status, availability, queues in line). While the conversational analytics plugin can provide some out-of-the-box insights, custom dashboards must be built from scratch based on specific KPIs HCL wants to see. These KPIs and dashboard requirements have not yet been provided by HCL.
risks.impact_description: If agent chat dashboard and analytics requirements from HCL are not defined and implemented before broader rollout, TR and HCL will lack visibility into operational performance (e.g., agent availability, queue backlog, volumes). This can hinder proactive management of the service desk, make it harder to detect issues, and limit the ability to demonstrate value of the new agent chat solution to leadership.
risks.mitigation: 1) Request HCL to provide a prioritized list of desired KPIs and views for agent chat dashboards (e.g., agent status, availability per queue, queue lengths, interaction volumes). 2) Enable the conversational analytics plugin to leverage available out-of-the-box dashboards where helpful. 3) Design and build custom dashboards from scratch in ServiceNow based on the agreed KPIs, ensuring they align with AWA data structures. 4) Review prototype dashboards with HCL (e.g., Nitin, Mehwish) and TR stakeholders (e.g., Jakub) to validate that they meet operational needs. 5) Iterate based on feedback and deploy dashboards to production aligned with the pilot timelines.
risks.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF Daily Sync.docx

risks.title: Market‑Benchmarked Coding Efficiency Limits
risks.description: Coding efficiency improvements are market‑benchmarked at approximately 8–10%, making benefits planning and realization complex. Gains are incremental, distributed across multiple teams and tools, and not concentrated in a single measurable outcome, which complicates planning and value realization for the AI coding agents efficiency initiative.
risks.impact_description: Difficulty in quantifying, attributing, and realizing savings from coding efficiency improvements. Benefits may remain theoretical or be absorbed as additional delivery capacity rather than converted to measurable financial value. This will increase the challenge of demonstrating clear ROI to leadership and could erode confidence in coding efficiency as a defensible value lever for the PLE AI Reimagine program.
risks.mitigation: Shift success metrics from pure efficiency percentage improvements to capacity redeployment or avoided cost. Define clear benefit capture mechanisms (for example, reduced backlog growth and reduced contractor usage). Bundle incremental gains into aggregated benefit stories instead of reporting per use case. Apply risk‑adjusted benefit forecasting for coding efficiency use cases.
risks.source_file_name: Delete PLE_ AI Coding Agents Efficiency-RAAID-export.xlsx

risks.title: Insufficient engineering and architecture participation in the core working group
risks.description: The program raised the question of which engineering and architecture resources should be formally aligned to the core working group. Current attendees form the core team, but additional engineering participation is needed to provide sufficient implementation depth and coverage across domains.
risks.impact_description: If adequate engineering and architecture representation is not secured, the core team may lack the domain expertise and capacity to design and implement standards, integrations, and remediation at scale. This could delay Phase 1 deliverables, result in poorly designed solutions, and reduce adoption across engineering teams.
risks.mitigation: Follow up with Engineering leadership to identify and formally align additional engineering and architecture representatives to the core working group, ensuring coverage for key domains (e.g., Platform Engineering, Legal, Research, Content). Define roles, expectations, and engagement cadence for these resources.

risks.title: Delivery Quality measurement using AI Adoption Dashboard
risks.description: Until all data issues are resolved and platforms have consistent adoption reporting, delivery quality and efficiency tracking remains partially mixed and directional rather than definitive.
risks.mitigation: Getting all platforms on the AI adoption dashboard to enable automated tracking and measurement rather than manual tracking

risks.title: Missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads
risks.description: During progress on ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation reporting, the team identified that some ServiceNow payloads contain missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs. This gap affects the ability to correlate incidents to specific monitors and impacts the accuracy of the correlation MVP.
risks.impact_description: If missing or blank Monitor IDs are not resolved, ServiceNow incidents cannot be reliably linked to Datadog monitors. This breaks correlation dashboards, limits the ability to analyze alert effectiveness during incidents, and weakens the hygiene backlog derived from these insights. It may also erode stakeholder trust in reporting and slow down adoption of correlation tooling.
risks.mitigation: Investigate the sources of missing or blank Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads, identify whether issues arise in the Datadog–ServiceNow integration or upstream configurations, and remediate mapping or payload generation issues. Add validation checks to ensure Monitor IDs are present and correct before incidents are created or processed.

risks.title: Phase 1 backlog remains ungroomed and unprioritized
risks.description: April 14 notes and tracker actions indicate that the Phase 1 backlog (epics, features, and stories in Azure DevOps) requires cleanup and prioritization. Backlog grooming has been deferred to an offline working session.
risks.impact_description: If the Phase 1 backlog remains unstructured and unprioritized, teams may lack clarity on sequencing and dependencies, leading to inefficiencies, delays, and uneven focus. Status reporting may not accurately reflect progress, and high‑impact hygiene work may be delayed in favor of lower‑value items.
risks.mitigation: Schedule and complete an offline working session to groom and prioritize the Phase 1 backlog in Azure DevOps, ensuring each item has a clear owner, definition of done, and target timeframe. Use this prioritized backlog as the basis for status reporting and risk assessment.

risks.title: Event taxonomy for informational/warning/exception states may not be defined in time for Legal Tracker
risks.description: The target-state design depends on a clear event taxonomy that distinguishes informational, warning, and exception conditions so that ServiceNow Event Management can filter, classify, and prioritize events correctly. The Target Future State deck explicitly calls out that "Event taxonomy must be defined" as a dependency for filtering and classification rules. If this taxonomy is not defined and agreed before enabling broader AIOps behaviour for Legal Tracker, filtering and prioritization rules will be based on ad-hoc or inconsistent interpretations of monitor states.
risks.impact_description: Without a defined and adopted event taxonomy, ServiceNow Event Management will struggle to consistently determine which events are informational, which are warnings, and which are true exceptions. This will: (1) limit effective noise reduction because non-actionable events may still create alerts or incidents; (2) cause inconsistent incident creation behaviour across monitors and teams; (3) undermine trust in severity and priority because similar problems may be classified differently; and (4) complicate future scaling to other products that are expected to reuse Legal Tracker’s model. Overall, this jeopardizes the project’s objectives around incident volume reduction and improved MTTR.
risks.mitigation: Facilitate a focused working session (Damian, Chris, GCC, and Legal Tracker representatives) to define a minimal but clear event taxonomy for Legal Tracker covering at least: informational, warning, and exception states; how these map to Datadog monitor conditions; and how they drive ServiceNow severity and incident creation. Document this taxonomy and incorporate it into (a) Datadog monitor configuration standards, and (b) ServiceNow Event Management rules for filtering and classification. Validate the taxonomy during a limited observation/parallel period in production and adjust based on real alert behaviour before using it as a template for subsequent products.

risks.title: Data quality issues in correlation IDs and Datadog–ServiceNow mappings prevent reliable analytics
risks.description: Phase 1 discussions highlighted current data quality issues such as missing or inconsistent correlation IDs and gaps between Datadog alerts and ServiceNow incidents. These issues currently prevent reliable analysis and prioritization, and undermine the foundational analytics and dashboards needed for the program.
risks.impact_description: If correlation IDs, asset/service associations, and Datadog–ServiceNow mappings remain inconsistent or incomplete, analytics and dashboards used to drive remediation will be inaccurate or misleading. This will impede the ability to prioritize high‑impact hygiene work, reduce confidence in metrics, and may lead to misallocation of remediation effort and slower reduction in alert noise.
risks.mitigation: Develop a standard metrics dictionary and data quality standards for correlation IDs, asset IDs, and service associations. Implement validation rules and checks to detect missing or invalid IDs, create a prioritized remediation backlog for data quality issues, and standardize the Datadog–ServiceNow integration to preserve context. Use ongoing reporting to track improvements and prevent regression.

risks.title: HCL Vayusphere renewal decision may be misaligned with Agent Chat and Copilot timelines
risks.description: Jakub reminded the team that Vyas has a renewal with HCL this month and that HCL needs to know whether they should renew their existing Vayusphere chat solution. Kiran noted that Agent Chat as a Vayusphere replacement is "almost 95% done" and IVR work is also ongoing, while Shariq said they need a one-page view of options and impacts before deciding. If the Copilot and Agent Chat strategy is not clarified in time, HCL may either renew Vayusphere unnecessarily or face a gap without a supported chat solution.
risks.impact_description: If the decision on HCL's Vayusphere renewal is not aligned with the readiness of ServiceNow Agent Chat and the Copilot front end, HCL may renew Vayusphere and incur additional costs for a legacy solution while also investing in the new stack, reducing savings and complicating operations. Alternatively, if they do not renew and Agent Chat/Copilot are not yet production-ready, the service desk may experience a disruption in chat support, impacting user experience and potentially increasing call volumes.
risks.mitigation:
1) Prepare the one-page options and pros/cons table that Shariq and Mayank discussed, explicitly covering: (a) continuing with Vayusphere, (b) moving fully to ServiceNow Agent Chat with Copilot, and (c) hybrid or phased options.
2) Use this summary to support a decision meeting with Marc, AD, and HCL leadership (including Vyas) ahead of the renewal deadline.
3) Clearly communicate to HCL the expected go-live readiness of Agent Chat (currently ~95% complete) and any dependencies on Copilot or IVR work so they can make an informed renewal decision.
4) If there is a risk of delay in Agent Chat/Copilot go-live, consider a short-term extension of Vayusphere as a contingency, rather than a full renewal, and incorporate this into the negotiation with HCL.
5) Update project timelines and financial models to reflect the chosen path and ensure the PMO tracker and RAAID log capture any residual risk.

risks.title: Absence of minimum alert standards constrains remediation
risks.description: The March 17 meeting recap explicitly noted that minimum alert standards do not yet exist. Without defined standards (e.g., required fields, service/asset associations, runbooks, thresholds), remediation work in Phase 1 is constrained and may be inconsistent across teams.
risks.impact_description: If minimum alert standards are not defined, teams may remediate alerts in inconsistent ways, leaving critical gaps such as missing thresholds, incomplete associations, and absent runbooks. This will reduce the effectiveness of baseline hygiene efforts, prolong noisy or low‑value alerts, and make it harder to enforce consistent practices in later phases.
risks.mitigation: Define and document minimum alert standards covering thresholds, asset and service associations, correlation IDs, runbook linkage, and tagging. Socialize these standards with teams, integrate them into the Datadog–ServiceNow integration guidelines, and use the standards as a basis for Phase 1 remediation and Phase 2 enforcement and automation.

risks.title: Limited communication of the new monitoring review process beyond Problem Management
risks.description: April 14 meeting notes state that current communications about the new Datadog alert/monitoring review process have been internal to Problem Management. The need for broader communication to Service Management leadership, with cascade to their teams, was acknowledged.
risks.impact_description: If the new monitoring review process is not communicated beyond Problem Management, other stakeholders (e.g., Service Management leadership, Platform Engineering, GCC, product teams) may not follow the process, leading to inconsistent adoption, missed reviews, and incomplete feedback into the Datadog Hygiene backlog. This will limit the effectiveness of the review framework and slow improvement of alert quality.
risks.mitigation: Communicate the new monitoring review process to Service Management leadership, provide clear guidance and expectations, and ask leaders to cascade to their teams. Use pilot sessions with Legal and Corporate incidents to refine messaging and incorporate feedback before broader rollout.

risks.title: Monitoring effectiveness review process not yet fully operationalized
risks.description: The Datadog Alert & Monitor Effectiveness Review framework was introduced on April 7, with agreement to anchor it in Problem Tasks (P‑tasks). However, the review cadence is still being refined, and operationalization (including P‑task structure and review cadence) is pending alignment between Robin and Dominique.
risks.impact_description: If the monitoring effectiveness review process is not fully operationalized, the program may miss opportunities to learn from major incidents, improve alerts, and feed actionable items into the Datadog Hygiene backlog. Reviews may be ad‑hoc or inconsistent, reducing the impact of Phase 1 pilots and delaying broader adoption into BAU problem/post‑incident reviews.
risks.mitigation: Robin to align with Dominique on how to operationalize the review process, including defining the P‑task structure, specifying required inputs, and agreeing on a practical review cadence (e.g., grouped periodic reviews). Pilot the process with Legal and Corporate incidents in April and iterate based on feedback.

risks.title: Recurring mis-mapping of Datadog P3 alerts to critical severity/P1 incidents in ServiceNow production
risks.description: During the 24-Apr-2026 AIOps Event Management regular sync, the team confirmed that alerts coming from Datadog with P3 priority are being created in ServiceNow as critical severity, which then drives P1 incident creation. Doug identified that the custom Datadog-to-Severity event field mapping script that worked in dev is not behaving correctly in production, likely due to rule ordering and interaction with other event mappings (e.g., synthetics). Until this is fixed, enabling automatic incident creation from alerts would generate a large number of false P1 incidents.
risks.impact_description: If Datadog P3 (and other non-critical) alerts continue to be mapped to critical severity in ServiceNow, AIOps will generate P1 incidents for issues that are actually P3. This will flood on-call processes and Major Incident workflows with false P1s, distort incident metrics, and erode trust in AIOps-driven incident creation. Legal Tracker and other product teams may refuse to adopt the new pipeline, forcing continued reliance on legacy Datadog-direct incidents and delaying POV and scale-out milestones.
risks.mitigation:
1) Doug and Rodriguez, Luis Jorge to jointly review the Datadog-to-Severity event field mapping rule in production, comparing it to the working dev configuration.
2) Adjust rule execution order so the Datadog priority-to-severity mapping runs before other source-specific mappings (e.g., synthetic-specific rules), and ensure no other mappings override its result.
3) Temporarily set the "create incident" subflow to manual-only so incidents are created on demand for test alerts rather than automatically, preventing large volumes of mis-prioritized P1 incidents while the mapping is fixed.
4) Run controlled tests using known P3 Datadog alerts, verify that the resulting ServiceNow alerts and any manually created incidents show the correct non-critical severity/priority, and iterate until consistent.
5) Once mapping is correct, re-enable automatic incident creation and perform an additional short observation period to confirm that no unexpected P1 inflation occurs in production.
6) Document the final mapping logic and dependencies (including defaulting behaviour when Datadog sends no priority) so future changes to event rules do not inadvertently reintroduce this issue.

risks.title: SRE Agent: Unclear path to scaled benefits beyond initial scope
risks.description: The aggregate business value of the SRE Agent workstream is predicated on scaling beyond the initial product suite (LPP). There is currently no confirmed product roadmap or suitability assessment that provides a clear, sequenced line-of-sight into which additional products will benefit from automation, or when.
risks.impact_description: Without a defined scaling path, benefits remain constrained to a narrow initial scope, significantly reducing ROI and undermining stakeholder confidence. The workstream may be deprioritized before reaching the scale at which SRE-to-team coverage ratios improve materially across the portfolio.
risks.mitigation: Pillar LT to confirm the short-list of candidate products for the initial roadmap (noted as complete). Develop a detailed scaling plan that documents: (1) prioritization criteria for product suitability, (2) the sequencing logic that maximizes early benefit realization, and (3) a governance checkpoint at the end of each phase to validate the next tranche of candidates before expanding scope.

risks.title: SRE Agent: Unproven technology dependency
risks.description: The workstream places a strategic "big-bet" on AI agent technology that has not yet been validated in production SRE environments. The core automated remediation and runbook execution capabilities depend on cloud-native AI services (AWS) whose reliability, accuracy, and performance at scale remain unproven within the organization.
risks.impact_description: Failure to prove out the technology delays or eliminates SRE productivity gains, exposing the portfolio to material concentration risk. Teams continue operating at current capacity, preventing each SRE from supporting additional Product Engineering teams and eroding the business case for the investment.
risks.mitigation: Accelerate validation through a time-boxed proof-of-concept using AWS infrastructure with the embedded AI Squad on a long-term basis. Define clear technical pass/fail criteria up front. Run parallel runbook execution (manual and automated) during the trial to measure accuracy and reduction in mean time to recovery (MTTR) before full commitment.

risks.title: DevOps: Diamond Lane Scale Readiness Risk – Incomplete Automation and Criteria Frameworks
risks.description: With 4 of 11 core milestones still in progress and ServiceNow policy integration intentionally deferred, there is a risk that Diamond Lane's CI criteria, product contracts, scorecard v1, and pipeline-driven change automation will not reach sufficient maturity by the 30 Jun 2026 target. This could prevent the program from enforcing eligibility and routing decisions in an auditable, repeatable way before broader application onboarding begins.
risks.impact_description: If the pipeline automation, rollback patterns, and scorecard frameworks are not stabilized before expansion, Diamond Lane risks scaling ahead of proven templates and controls. This could result in ungoverned production changes, audit exposure, and potential rollback failures for onboarded applications — undermining the program's core value proposition of faster, compliant delivery.
risks.mitigation: Gate all new application onboarding behind defined readiness criteria tied to scorecard v1 and crawl-stage rollback completion. Prioritize the 30 Jun 2026 milestone for CI criteria, contracts, and pipeline automation. Maintain the deferral of ServiceNow policy integration to avoid scope creep. Conduct bi-weekly checkpoint reviews against the path-to-green plan to surface blockers early and allow resource reallocation if needed.

risks.title: DevOps Diamond Lane – Limited '26 Product Coverage and VC Benefit Realization
risks.impact_description: Without a product in the 2026 plan that delivers meaningful VC benefits, the Diamond Lane program risks being perceived as a capability buildout rather than a value driver. This could affect stakeholder confidence, funding continuity, and prioritization decisions heading into 2027 planning cycles — particularly if leadership expects demonstrable ROI from the DevOps Acceleration investment within the year.
risks.mitigation: Identify and evaluate whether any current or near-term candidate products could be onboarded to Diamond Lane in a way that surfaces measurable VC benefits without compromising pilot integrity. In parallel, develop a clear narrative that frames the 2026 crawl-stage work as the prerequisite to VC realization in 2027, with defined benefit milestones tied to the expansion and enablement phase. Establish leading indicators (e.g., deployment frequency, change failure rate, manual effort reduction) that can serve as proxy VC metrics while the full model matures.

risks.title: PLE Phased Benefits Realization Plan Delivery Pending
risks.description: A high-level benefits delivery plan is in place. A phased plan is in progress, with initial confirmed benefits realization expected in June. However, there is currently no period/quarter-level visibility into the benefits delivery schedule. The absence of granular planning creates uncertainty around tracking, reporting, and on-time realization of PLE program benefits.
risks.impact_description: Without period or quarterly breakdowns, it is not possible to monitor benefits delivery against plan milestones, assess progress in any given reporting period, or proactively identify and address delivery gaps. This limits stakeholder confidence and reduces the program's ability to course-correct in a timely manner.
risks.mitigation: Track completion of the phased benefits delivery plan by the June 15 deadline. Ensure the plan includes period-level or quarterly phasing for all key benefits. PLE, HR and Finance are partnering to confirm team funding for exits and address legal aspects of benefits realization. These actions are expected to inform and underpin the phased plan once delivered.

risks.title: Salesforce Coding Assistant / Agentforce licensing and low adoption
risks.description: As of June 1, 2026, Agentforce (Agent Force Vibes) became a licensed tool and all existing developer access was cut off, impacting ~45 Salesforce developers who had been using it for AI-assisted development. Licensing decisions (whether to purchase Agentforce licenses or standardize on an alternative such as GitHub Copilot or another TR-approved AI tool) remain unresolved, while teams temporarily experiment with GitHub Copilot and OpenArena. This compounds the existing low-adoption issue for the Salesforce Coding Assistant and creates uncertainty around a stable, approved AI coding tool for Salesforce.
risks.impact_description: If a clear, funded Salesforce AI coding tool strategy is not defined quickly (e.g., purchasing Agentforce licenses or standardising on GitHub Copilot or another approved tool), Salesforce development teams will lose sustained access to effective AI assistance. The  impacted developers will revert to manual work or fragmented tool usage, causing adoption levels to fall from prior baselines, undermining efficiency gains and benefits realisation for the CE2 Salesforce Coding Assistant use case and the broader CE AI Coding Agents Efficiency program. Metrics in the AI adoption dashboard will show a drop or stalled progress, the risk will remain Red for CIO reporting, and additional rework will be required to re-establish adoption once a final tool decision is made.
risks.mitigation: Tool strategy and licensing: Evaluate options and decide whether to (a) proceed with Agentforce licensing, including confirming cost and sourcing via Pierre’s/sourcing team, or (b) evaluate Claude AI and compare the outcome to Claude Vs Agentforce vibe to decide the right tool for future 3) Escalation: Angela will start a group chat with Linki and escalate to Jason so leadership is explicitly aware that licenses were removed on June 1 and that prior adoption progress is at risk of being lost. 4) Metrics and reporting: Preeti will mark the Salesforce AI coding stream as Red in the PMO tool and ensure this is called out in the June 9 CIO update, maintaining transparency until a stable tool and licensing decision is implemented and adoption can recover.

risks.title: Parallel onboarding of GTM4 and SIAM may overextend capacity and delay effective onboarding
risks.description: The team plans to onboard both ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel as the next AIOps adopters. During the 11 May 2026 sync, Mike Krause raised concern that GTM4 generates a high volume of alerts and will likely produce many findings and follow-up work. Although he is not opposed to onboarding two products in parallel, he is conscious that resource and attention demands could be significant, particularly while the team is still resolving early issues from the Legal Tracker pilot.
risks.impact_description: If GTM4 and SIAM are onboarded in parallel without sufficient capacity, the AIOps core team may be unable to address configuration issues, monitor cleanups, and follow-up items in a timely manner. This could result in prolonged QA observation windows, slower progression to production, inconsistent application of standards between the two products, and delayed realization of noise-reduction benefits. It may also lead to stakeholder frustration if teams see many findings but limited progress on remediation, and could stretch key individuals (e.g., Luis, Jot, Talia) across too many concurrent tasks while Legal Tracker is still in an observation and tuning phase.
risks.mitigation: Proceed with kickoff for both GTM4 and SIAM but explicitly manage scope and timing: (1) Use the QA observation approach described by Talia (pull all monitors into QA and run for one to two weeks) while timeboxing the overall onboarding to no more than three to four weeks per ADs guidance. (2) After the initial QA run, review the volume of findings and required monitor changes for each product using Luiss Datadog helper readiness assessment. (3) If GTM4 proves significantly more demanding than expected, temporarily sequence deeper remediation for SIAM after GTM4 reaches a stable baseline, rather than pushing both to production simultaneously. (4) Communicate the agreed timelines and scope back to AD, Mike, and the product teams by mid-week, and adjust if Legal Tracker feedback indicates further configuration changes are needed before scaling.

risks.title: ETS VC Targets

risks.title: Insufficient CI/CMDB data quality and CI binding for effective correlation and routing
risks.description: Many incoming events lack reliable CI bindings due to inconsistent or missing metadata, such as FQDNs for Azure VMs, host/node field gaps, and inconsistent tag usage. CI mapping is often at service level only, and HighQ and other products rely heavily on tags and Asset Insight IDs. If CI binding issues are not resolved, correlation, grouping, and routing in ServiceNow will be inaccurate.
risks.impact_description: Alerts may not bind to the correct CIs or application services, leading to poor correlation, fragmented alert groups, and mis-routed incidents. This will reduce the ability to understand blast radius, undermine service-level reporting, and limit the effectiveness of automated remediation and AI analysis. Workarounds such as manual assignment and analysis will persist. The May 12, 2026 onboarding sync also highlighted that current CI/service association behaviour appears constrained by a configurable limit of 1,000 CIs per service, forcing use of dynamic CI groups and preventing correct service association for large applications like Legal Tracker. Until this is resolved, Legal Tracker stakeholders (e.g., Elizabeth) view it as a showstopper for cutting over from Datadog-direct incidents to AIOps-driven incidents. During the 26-May-2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regular sync, Luis reiterated that CMDB configuration remains the primary blocker to onboarding additional applications at scale; attempting to onboard many apps before this is resolved would "create a mess of alerts" due to incorrect correlation and routing, and Talia estimated that resolving the CMDB/service mapping issues may take at least another month, further constraining rollout timelines.
risks.mitigation: Standardize on VM object ID as the unique identifier for virtual machines, ensure Datadog payloads include Asset Insight ID (AAID) and relevant tags, and update ServiceNow event rules to bind using these identifiers. Investigate and fix Azure discovery to populate FQDNs consistently, and validate CI binding by reviewing alerts for Legal Tracker (and later other apps) to confirm they bind to the correct CI/service. Consider deploying the Service Graph Connector for Datadog to enrich CMDB relationships. In addition, based on April 21, 2026 lessons learned: (1) work with the CMDB team (e.g., Ragash, Kavi) to identify and unretire Legal Tracker CIs that are incorrectly marked as retired so that CI binding and impacted services can populate; (2) introduce a CMDB/data-readiness check as a prerequisite in the AIOps onboarding checklist, including a dry run to confirm that critical resources for a product are discovered and in the correct operational state before enabling event ingestion and grouping. Following the May 12, 2026 onboarding sync, also: (3) work with ServiceNow (Doug and their CMDB expert) to analyse and remediate the apparent 1,000-CI-per-service association limit and to design appropriate traverse rules so that large applications like Legal Tracker can have all required CIs associated to their services without forcing dynamic CI groups; and (4) treat resolution of this CI association behaviour as a prerequisite for fully cutting off Datadog-direct incident creation for Legal Tracker.

risks.title: Insufficient CI/CMDB data quality and CI–service association may block broader onboarding despite ongoing remediation
risks.description: During the 28-May-2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, the team reconfirmed that unresolved CMDB health and CI–service association behaviour remain a gating factor for Legal Tracker and all downstream product onboardings. Talia reiterated that the new ServiceNow resource (Bill) has proposed an approach to address the CI/service association problem (including the current configurable ~1,000-CI-per-service parameter and overall service mapping strategy), and that a detailed pre-read and action plan are expected for the 4-June session. AD and Eric explicitly questioned whether the magnitude of the CMDB problem is being underestimated and noted that if the CI/service association issue is not understood and fixed, it will halt implementation for additional applications and jeopardize the September onboarding roadmap. Jot highlighted that any approach which relies on application teams to validate and reduce their CI sets could introduce significant lift and delay, because most teams lack mature documentation and would need to manually validate which CIs are actually consumed by their processes. The team agreed that CMDB health and service mapping must become an explicit prerequisite and part of the onboarding process for each application, and that the feasibility of the multimonth roadmap depends directly on the outcome of Bill’s design and the CMDB team’s capacity to execute it.
risks.impact_description: If the CMDB health and CI/service association problems (including the current ~1,000-CI-per-service configuration and oversized, poorly pruned CI sets for applications like Legal Tracker and SIAM) are not resolved with a clear, scalable approach: (1) Legal Tracker’s AIOps incidents will continue to carry incomplete or incorrect impacted service information, preventing safe cutover from Datadog-direct incidents; (2) onboarding of additional products on the FY26 roadmap (through September and beyond) will stall because each application will inherit the same CI/service association limitations and unclear data-readiness process; (3) the AIOps team will face a large manual burden to run CI reports, engage each application team, and negotiate CI reductions on a case-by-case basis, which could extend onboarding timelines well beyond leadership expectations; (4) machine-learning-based grouping will continue to learn from inconsistent or mis-associated CIs, reducing the effectiveness of AI-driven correlation and potentially requiring re-training once CMDB corrections are made; and (5) leadership may lose confidence in the program’s ability to scale, as the September roadmap and broader rollout become contingent on a complex CMDB remediation effort that spans platform, CMDB, and application teams.

raised_by.name: Loch, Talia (TR Technology) and Sand, Eric S. (TR Technology) in 28-May-2026 onboarding sync

mitigation_plan_owner.name: Bill (new ServiceNow CMDB/resource) in partnership with Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth (TR Technology)

risks.mitigation:
1) Bill (the newly assigned ServiceNow resource) will produce a concrete pre-read and action plan by the end of day Friday 30-May-2026, outlining exactly how to remediate CI/service association behaviour for Legal Tracker, including treatment of the ~1,000-CI-per-service configuration parameter, recommended service modelling changes, and any performance implications of raising or restructuring CI associations.
2) In the 4-June working session, Bill, the CMDB team (Ragesh, Kavya, Nitin), and the TR AIOps core team will review this plan and agree on a repeatable design that can be applied to other products, clarifying where CIs should be modelled as attributes rather than full CIs, and how to avoid overpopulating services with unused or irrelevant CIs.
3) Jot and Talia will incorporate the agreed CMDB health and service-mapping steps into the standardized onboarding runbook and checklist, explicitly defining CMDB prerequisites (reports, ownership, and validation steps) for each new product and identifying the CMDB representative required on the onboarding team.
4) The CMDB team will generate per-application CI reports (e.g., for Legal Tracker, SIAM, GTM4) that show current CI classes, counts, and usage, and will work with each application team to identify candidate CIs or classes that can be excluded without impacting existing incident or change processes.
5) The AIOps roadmap (through September 2026) will be revisited after the 4-June session to confirm whether the agreed CMDB approach and available CMDB capacity support the planned onboarding volume; if capacity is constrained, the roadmap will be adjusted explicitly rather than overcommitting.
6) Until the new CI/service association design is implemented and validated for Legal Tracker, the project will continue to treat CI/service association behaviour as a go/no-go gate for disabling Datadog-direct incidents and for aggressively onboarding additional products.

risks.title: Insufficient AIOps engineering capacity and access to scale onboarding to multiple applications
risks.description: Current AIOps onboarding and configuration work for Legal Tracker, ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM is heavily dependent on a single engineer (Rodriguez, Luis Jorge). During the 26-May-2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regular sync, Talia and Jot highlighted that scaling to 5–6 applications per month or per week is unrealistic with the existing capacity, even before addressing CMDB issues. Without increased and properly permissioned engineering capacity, onboarding timelines for the FY 2026 roadmap will slip and the program will not be able to meet leadership expectations for scale.

If AIOps engineering capacity and access are not increased beyond the current reliance on Luis Jorge Rodriguez, the program will be unable to onboard multiple applications in parallel or to respond quickly to application-specific requests (e.g., custom grouping for synthetics in SIAM). This will result in:
1) Slower than planned onboarding of the FY 2026 target applications, undermining commitments made in AI Reimagine leadership forums.
2) Burnout and single-point-of-failure risk for Luis, with limited coverage across time zones and shifts.
3) Inability to consistently apply and maintain event rules, correlation logic and onboarding runbooks across a larger portfolio, increasing configuration drift.
4) Delays in resolving AIOps issues for existing onboarded products when new products are added, eroding stakeholder confidence in both the platform and the programs scalability.
risks.mitigation:
1) Onboard additional engineering resources (e.g., Vijay, Mahesha, Owen, Erikipaty) into the AIOps/Event Management workstream with clearly defined technical responsibilities (monitor analysis, Datadog updates via Luiss tool, rule configuration) while ensuring they are not diverted into non-engineering tasks such as stakeholder chasing.
2) Coordinate with the ServiceNow platform team (e.g., Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth; Tim; Jazz) to provision appropriate Event Management admin or equivalent roles for these engineers, so they can safely configure and test event rules and respond rules in dev/QA and prod.
3) Use the emerging onboarding runbook and checklist to standardize tasks and enable parallel work across engineers, dividing applications between Luis and the additional resources once CMDB/service mapping issues are resolved.
4) Present the capacity constraint and resourcing plan to AD and other leaders (including Aaron and Eric) so that expectations on onboarding pace are aligned with available engineering capacity, and secure explicit support for prioritizing these resources on AIOps.
