risks.title: Machine-learning-based alert grouping may incorrectly group unrelated Legal Tracker alerts
risks.description: ServiceNow AIOps machine-learning (ML)–driven alert grouping is combining unrelated Legal Tracker alerts (e.g., a synthetic monitor and an infrastructure monitor) into the same alert group based on CI relationships, even when impacted services differ. These ML-created groups are not using the TR-defined correlation rules. If ML continues to group dissimilar alerts, incidents derived from these groups may represent multiple distinct issues, and teams will see inconsistent, hard-to-explain behaviour in Event Management.
risks.impact_description: If ML-based alert grouping continues to combine unrelated alerts: (1) Legal Tracker incidents may represent multiple, unrelated problems, confusing support teams and delaying triage; (2) Legal Tracker and GCC teams will be forced to inspect raw alerts more often instead of trusting incident-level signals, undermining the event-first model; (3) the team may feel compelled to disable or bypass ML capabilities, reducing the value of AIOps analytics and dashboards; and (4) onboarding of additional products could be delayed because platform behaviour appears inconsistent and not well understood, eroding stakeholder confidence in the AIOps solution.
risks.mitigation: Luis will analyse the specific alert group Andrea highlighted (synthetic + monitor grouped together) and confirm, with Doug, whether it was created by ServiceNow ML grouping rather than TR-defined rules. Together with Doug, he will: (1) review the current ML grouping configuration and CI-relationship-based rules; (2) adjust or restrict ML grouping so that it does not group alerts with different impacted services or clearly different monitor types unless explicitly desired; (3) ensure that TR-standard correlation rules remain the primary grouping mechanism for Legal Tracker; and (4) validate updated behaviour with Andrea and Elizabeth by reviewing new alert groups over several days. If necessary, ML-based grouping for Legal Tracker will be temporarily disabled while a safer configuration is designed.

risks.title: ServiceNow event forwarding limits may cause loss of events in lower environments
risks.description: ServiceNow event forwarding from production to lower environments (dev/QA) appears subject to a per-day forwarding limit and a one-hour event duration window. Yash raised a concern that, under the current configuration, older events outside the one-hour window may not be forwarded, creating a risk that some Datadog-originating events will never reach dev/QA for rule testing and correlation validation.
risks.impact_description: If event forwarding only sends a subset of recent events and is constrained by daily limits, dev and QA will not receive a complete or representative stream of production Datadog events. This will limit the team’s ability to test event rules, CI binding, and correlation changes using lower environments, potentially allowing misconfigurations to reach production unobserved or forcing more testing to occur directly in production.
risks.mitigation: Yash has opened a HiCase with ServiceNow Support and received confirmation that event forwarding does not backfill and is constrained by per-day and duration limits. Doug will review the HiCase details, including screenshots Yash shared in the 30-Apr-2026 sync, and investigate whether forwarding can be configured to target only Datadog-originated events and whether the time-window/limit behaviour can be adjusted. Depending on findings, the team may (1) tune forwarding parameters, (2) schedule periodic targeted forwarding windows to capture key test data, or (3) fall back to pointing selected Datadog monitors directly at dev/QA for specific test campaigns.

risks.title: Incident creation policy and notification tiers may not be agreed before event-first processing is enabled
risks.description: The Target Future State and capability prioritization highlight open design decisions around incident creation policy (which events should create incidents vs remain as events or trigger auto-remediation) and notification tiers (what severity warrants after-hours paging vs next-business-day notification). These are listed as later-phase design items, yet the routing and resolution stages of the target lifecycle depend on them. If incident creation policy and notification tiers are not agreed before enabling broader event-first processing for Legal Tracker, incidents and on-call pages may not reflect true business impact.
risks.impact_description: If the project proceeds without a clear incident creation policy and defined notification tiers, Legal Tracker and GCC could experience: (1) too many incidents being created for low-impact events, preserving the current 1:1 pattern and alert fatigue; (2) under-notification or missed pages for genuine service-impacting exceptions; (3) inconsistent paging behaviour between teams and shifts; and (4) confusion among engineers about when and why they are being paged. This will erode trust in AIOps, distort incident metrics, and reduce realized benefits in noise reduction and MTTR improvement.
risks.mitigation: Define an initial, explicit incident creation policy for Legal Tracker that specifies which correlated event types and severities will create incidents, which will remain as events only, and which (if any) can be handled via auto-remediation without incidents. In parallel, agree on notification tiers with Incident Management (Damian) and the Legal Tracker team so that only correlated incidents at agreed severities (e.g., P1/P2) drive after-hours paging, while lower-severity items generate next-business-day notifications or dashboards. Document these policies in the AIOps onboarding package and validate behaviour during the Legal Tracker observation/parallel period, adjusting rules before scaling to other products.

risks.mitigation:
1) Bill (the newly assigned ServiceNow resource) will produce a concrete pre-read and action plan by the end of day Friday 30-May-2026, outlining exactly how to remediate CI/service association behaviour for Legal Tracker, including treatment of the ~1,000-CI-per-service configuration parameter, recommended service modelling changes, and any performance implications of raising or restructuring CI associations.
2) In the 4-June working session, Bill, the CMDB team (Ragesh, Kavya, Nitin), and the TR AIOps core team will review this plan and agree on a repeatable design that can be applied to other products, clarifying where CIs should be modelled as attributes rather than full CIs, and how to avoid overpopulating services with unused or irrelevant CIs.
3) Jot and Talia will incorporate the agreed CMDB health and service-mapping steps into the standardized onboarding runbook and checklist, explicitly defining CMDB prerequisites (reports, ownership, and validation steps) for each new product and identifying the CMDB representative required on the onboarding team.
4) The CMDB team will generate per-application CI reports (e.g., for Legal Tracker, SIAM, GTM4) that show current CI classes, counts, and usage, and will work with each application team to identify candidate CIs or classes that can be excluded without impacting existing incident or change processes.
5) The AIOps roadmap (through September 2026) will be revisited after the 4-June session to confirm whether the agreed CMDB approach and available CMDB capacity support the planned onboarding volume; if capacity is constrained, the roadmap will be adjusted explicitly rather than overcommitting.
6) Until the new CI/service association design is implemented and validated for Legal Tracker, the project will continue to treat CI/service association behaviour as a go/no-go gate for disabling Datadog-direct incidents and for aggressively onboarding additional products.
risks.source_file_name: AIOps Onboarding Datadog Coverage App Prioritization and Resourcing.docx

assumptions.title: ServiceNow Event Management will be the central event processing and correlation engine
assumptions.description: The design assumes Datadog and other monitoring tools remain the detection layer, while ServiceNow Event Management becomes the central platform for ingestion, filtering, deduplication, correlation, classification, routing, and remediation orchestration for Legal Tracker and, eventually, other Tier 1 applications.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The target future state and workshop discussions explicitly position ServiceNow as the event‑first processing engine to replace direct‑to‑incident integrations from Datadog and Azure.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial integrations from Datadog to the ServiceNow dev environment are working, out‑of‑the‑box grouping and correlation rules are being tuned, and there is agreement that correlation should primarily occur in ServiceNow given Datadog’s lack of egress cost. However, full production validation is pending.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If ServiceNow cannot reliably handle core event processing for certain use cases, keep or enhance Datadog‑side correlation for those cases and restrict ServiceNow Event Management to aggregated or filtered events, while revisiting the longer‑term AIOps platform strategy.
assumptions.validation_method: Pilot Legal Tracker end‑to‑end in ServiceNow Event Management, including ingestion, grouping, incident creation, and initial playbooks, and compare performance and noise metrics versus the current Datadog‑only model.

assumptions.title: Datadog egress is free, enabling broad event forwarding into ServiceNow
assumptions.description: The team assumes Datadog does not charge for data egress to ServiceNow, so sending large volumes of events from Datadog into ServiceNow will not materially increase Datadog costs.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Jacob clarified during the workshop that Datadog charges primarily for data ingestion and storage, not for egress via APIs or webhooks to external systems such as ServiceNow.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Jacob stated clearly that Datadog’s billing is based on data ingest and type rather than egress, and no opposing evidence was raised in the workshops.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If unexpected Datadog egress costs are discovered, reduce the scope of events forwarded (e.g., filter at Datadog by severity or tag), or move some correlation logic back into Datadog to minimize outbound traffic.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm Datadog contractual terms and billing details with the Datadog account team, and monitor invoices after increasing webhook traffic to ServiceNow.

assumptions.title: Legal Tracker is representative of broader Tier 1 service management patterns
assumptions.description: The project planning assumes that Legal Tracker’s monitoring, incident patterns, and event management needs are broadly representative of other Tier 1 stability products, making it a suitable baseline for designing the Event Management process and technical implementation.
assumptions.rationale_basis: AD and the team selected Legal Tracker as a mature product with good observability, expecting its patterns to reflect common challenges and practices across Tier 1 services.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Workshop discussions treated Legal Tracker as a baseline but also highlighted outliers such as HighQ’s extreme noise, suggesting there is some variation. Validation will require examining additional products during later rollout phases.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If Legal Tracker proves atypical, treat its implementation as a specific reference pattern and design more generic, adjustable rule sets and governance frameworks that can be tuned per product. Prioritize an additional early adopter (e.g., HighQ) to refine cross‑product applicability.
assumptions.validation_method: Compare metrics and event patterns from Legal Tracker with those from other Tier 1 products, especially HighQ and a small sample of others, after Legal Tracker’s solution is in place. Use workshops with other product teams to validate that workflows and rules are applicable with minimal changes.

assumptions.title: A dual-run period with duplicate incidents is acceptable to stakeholders
assumptions.description: The plan assumes that stakeholders will accept a temporary period where both the legacy Datadog integration and the new AIOps Event Management path create incidents in parallel, to validate grouping, mapping, and priority logic.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Multiple working sessions agreed on a parallel‑run strategy (initially at least 24 hours, and for Legal Tracker a two‑week window) to avoid operational disruption while proving correlation value and preventing incident loss during transition.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Workshops explicitly called out parallel operation as the recommended approach, but acceptance will ultimately depend on real duplicate volumes and how well they are communicated and managed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If duplicate incidents become unmanageable, narrow the scope of parallel incident creation (e.g., limit AIOps incidents to primary group alerts only, or to specific severities) while continuing to ingest and group events silently. Alternatively, extend the observation period using alerts‑only (no AIOps incidents) to validate mapping before attempting a new dual‑run.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor actual duplicate incident volumes and operational impact during the agreed dual‑run, and solicit feedback from GCC, product teams, and Major Incident after the period. Confirm that the observed impact is acceptable and that comparison data are sufficient for decision‑making.

assumptions.title: Monitoring teams will reliably set monitor priority and required tags in Datadog
assumptions.description: The incident prioritization and grouping design assumes that Datadog monitor owners will correctly set monitor priority (e.g., P1P5) and required tags (such as Asset Insight ID and service tags) so that ServiceNow can map and route alerts accurately without excessive central overrides.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The chosen approach is to use monitor priority as the authoritative signal for incident priority and to rely on TRstandard tags (with TR_ prefixes) for correlation and service mapping. This pushes responsibility to monitor authors at source.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Workshops and pilot activity show that while tools and standards exist, actual practice is inconsistent: many monitors misuse priorities and are poorly tagged. The Datadog hygiene programme and AIOps onboarding checklists are intended to close this gap, but success depends on sustained adoption by product teams.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: Introduce automated governance checks and dashboards that flag monitors lacking required tags or using non-standard priorities; provide templates and training; and, where necessary, implement defaulting and correction logic in ServiceNow event rules while governance matures.
assumptions.validation_method: During and after the Legal Tracker rollout, audit a sample of monitors and resulting alerts to verify presence and correctness of priority and tags, and compare expected vs actual incident priority and routing. Extend this audit to additional teams as they are onboarded.

assumptions.title: Out-of-the-box ServiceNow AIOps rules are sufficient as MVP baseline
assumptions.description: The project is assuming that ServiceNow’s out‑of‑the‑box event correlation and incident‑creation logic, supplemented by a small number of TR‑specific rules, will be adequate as a first release for Legal Tracker, with further tuning to follow.
assumptions.rationale_basis: ServiceNow AIOps is delivered with standard event rules and incident mapping intended to work generically. The team wants to minimize customization and complexity at initial go‑live to reduce risk and ease maintenance, only extending rules where obviously necessary.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Through several working sessions, the team reviewed incoming events and built sample rules; they confirmed that the majority of scenarios look acceptable for an 80/20 MVP. Known gaps are documented and have clear tuning options (e.g., adjusting message keys, adding specific grouping rules) that can be applied post‑go‑live without fundamental redesign.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If actual production behaviour diverges significantly from expectations (e.g., too many or too few incidents, bad groupings), prioritize rapid rule tuning with Doug and GCC. In severe cases, temporarily disable incident creation from AIOps while continuing to use legacy Datadog‑driven incidents, then re‑enable after adjustments.
assumptions.validation_method: Run Legal Tracker in a controlled rollout using the out‑of‑the‑box rules and a few TR rules in dev/QA and then production, monitor resulting alerts and incidents closely with GCC and Legal Tracker SMEs, and compare behaviour and volume against expectations and legacy Datadog incidents.

assumptions.title: Teams onboarding to AIOps will be willing and able to adjust their Datadog monitors to TR standards
assumptions.description: The rollout plan assumes product teams (starting with Legal Tracker) will invest the time and effort to review and update their Datadog monitor configurations (priority, severity, tags, etc.) so they conform to TR standards needed for AIOps to work effectively.
assumptions.rationale_basis: AIOps effectiveness depends on well-configured monitors. Discussions recognized that many current monitors do not follow standards, but leadership (AD, Paul, Damian) signaled that standardization must improve and that AIOps is a forcing function for this.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Legal Tracker has already implemented monitor configuration changes as part of the pilot, and GTM4 and SIAM have provided monitor lists and are participating in readiness assessments. However, Luis stated that all GTM4 monitors will need to change, confirming significant effort remains. This reinforces the assumption that teams must be committed and may require close support to complete the work.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If some teams resist or lack capacity to adjust monitors, prioritize onboarding for teams that actively commit to the standards, provide additional tooling (e.g., Luiss readiness assessment, bulk-update scripts) and coaching to reduce effort, and consider more centralized management (monitoring-as-code) for critical products where local teams cannot keep up.
assumptions.validation_method: Track actual monitor changes completed by Legal Tracker, GTM4, and SIAM (using Terraform, scripts, or manual updates) and compare their Datadog configurations against the documented AIOps standards and readiness assessment results from Luiss Datadog helper tool.

assumptions.title: Future products will be onboarded using standardized AIOps rules directly in production
assumptions.description: For products beyond Legal Tracker (e.g., Westlaw), the team assumes onboarding will reuse the standardized event correlation, alert management, and incident creation rules already built and tuned, and that new products will send their event data directly into the production ServiceNow instance. Product teams will review events, alerts, and incidents in production during a defined observation period rather than performing lengthy, product-specific validations in dev/QA environments before using AIOps.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Chris stated that having each team validate behaviour in lower environments would prevent rapid onboarding and that the standardized rules were intentionally built to be reused. He proposed that new teams observe their data and incidents directly in production over a two-week window and provide feedback, adjusting platform rules only when necessary.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The Legal Tracker implementation has already gone through significant rule tuning, and Chris is confident these rules are broadly applicable. Leadership is explicitly seeking a scalable, "cookie-cutter" onboarding model, making it likely that this approach will be endorsed and followed, provided early follow-on products validate the pattern.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If production-first onboarding proves problematic for certain products (e.g., due to unusual patterns or risk appetite), fall back to a hybrid approach: still reuse standardized rules but allow limited, time-boxed lower-environment testing for specific rule adjustments while maintaining overall emphasis on shared platform configuration and minimizing per-product customisation.
assumptions.validation_method: Pilot the next selected products (e.g., from Steve T’s portfolio) by onboarding them directly into production using the existing rule set, running an observation/parallel period, and confirming with product teams that behaviour is acceptable without substantial lower-environment rule work.

assumptions.title: Product teams will adjust on-call paging configurations to align with the alert-centric AIOps model
assumptions.description: The onboarding approach assumes that each product team will review and adjust their on-call paging rules and schedules to work appropriately with AIOps, potentially paging on alerts as well as incidents, and reflecting changes in how priority and urgency are derived.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Chris highlighted that teams currently manage their own paging schedules and conditions based on incident priority and that these may need to change to react to alerts under AIOps. The onboarding checklist discussion explicitly called out on-call adjustment as something that must be included for successful operationalization.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Teams are already familiar with managing on-call and have autonomy over their paging rules. Including this work explicitly in onboarding and training increases the likelihood that they will make necessary adjustments rather than ignoring the change in signal sources.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If some teams do not adjust paging configurations despite guidance, provide targeted support (e.g., incident management coaching) to those teams, and consider temporary, centrally recommended paging templates for AIOps alerts. In extreme cases, maintain incident-based paging for those teams while gradually transitioning them as they become more comfortable with the alert-centric model.
assumptions.validation_method: During each product’s onboarding, confirm that on-call paging rules have been reviewed and updated as needed, and after go-live, monitor paging behaviour and gather feedback from on-call engineers about whether they are receiving appropriate notifications from alerts and incidents.

assumptions.title: Centralized Customer Trust Platform will improve engagement and enable long-term AI strategy
assumptions.description: A new centralized Customer Trust Platform, replacing the current ServiceNow solution, will improve engagement and efficiency and enable the long-term AI strategy.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The current legacy ServiceNow platform no longer meets Customer Trust engagement needs, and the AI strategy requires a single, integrated front door with better configurability, reporting, automation, and role-based experiences.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The problem statement identifies clear limitations with the legacy ServiceNow platform, and the project charter articulates a long-term vision for a single integrated front door for Sales and internal stakeholders. The initial implementation of a new Loopio instance and planned AI-enabled self-service milestones are already underway, indicating organizational commitment and technical feasibility. These factors make it reasonable to assume that a centralized Customer Trust Platform will improve engagement and support the AI strategy.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the centralized platform does not deliver the expected benefits, reassess platform requirements and consider alternative solutions or architectural adjustments (e.g., additional integrations, enhanced governance, or a different core AI platform) while maintaining continuity of service using transitional tools like Loopio.
assumptions.validation_method: Validate through phased deployment of the new platform (including Loopio and the long-term AI platform), measurement of engagement and operational metrics, and qualitative feedback from Sales and internal stakeholders.
assumptions.source_file_name: RAID Log – 2026 Customer Trust - AI Strategy.xlsx

assumptions.title: Availability of Platform Engineering development resources after CT MVP1 design
assumptions.description: Platform Engineering development team resources, led by Matthew Schlosser, will be available to assist with long term platform set up after the Customer Trust MVP1 technical design is completed.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Planning for MVP1 is scheduled in Q2 2026, including technical discussions about the current state and future development needs. The assumption is that once design work is complete, Platform Engineering resources will be able to support development for later phases.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current planning activities in Q2 2026 include technical discussions between Customer Trust and Platform Engineering about existing capabilities and future needs. These discussions typically precede formal resource assignments for development work, making it reasonable to assume that Platform Engineering will engage post-design, though competing priorities could still affect timing.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If Platform Engineering resources are not available as assumed, adjust the roadmap by re-sequencing scope, identifying alternative development resources, reducing initial feature scope, or extending timelines for MVP1 and subsequent phases. Escalate through governance forums to secure prioritized resourcing or to formalize revised timelines.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm resource allocation and timelines with Matthew Schlosser’s Platform Engineering team during Q2 2026 planning and through formal commitments in the project plan and PMO artifacts.

assumptions.title: Hybrid operating model combining central standards with active product and engineering engagement
assumptions.description: The program has decided to adopt a hybrid operating model in which central teams provide standards, governance, and visibility while product and engineering teams actively collaborate on implementation, rather than relying on purely top‑down enforcement or self‑serve models.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Stakeholder discussions revealed broad, non‑conflicting pain points across teams, and leadership agreed that a mix of centralized standards with local ownership is needed to achieve enterprise‑wide hygiene without over‑centralizing control.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The hybrid model balances centralized control of standards and metrics with local accountability for implementation, which aligns with how large enterprises typically manage cross‑cutting programs. The decision is supported by consensus (DL‑04) that the program should not be purely top‑down or purely self‑serve.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the hybrid model fails (e.g., persistent non‑engagement from product teams), shift toward stronger top‑down enforcement with clearer mandates, or alternatively, invest in more enablement resources and incentives to drive bottom‑up adoption.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor participation and responsiveness of product and engineering teams in Phase 1, review outcomes of pilot efforts, and solicit feedback in SteerCo and core team meetings.

assumptions.title: Datadog inventory exports, once validated, will be accurate enough to drive remediation outreach and tracking
assumptions.description: The program assumes that the Datadog inventory dataset, once refreshed and validated, will provide sufficiently accurate details (including Asset IDs and other fields) to support outreach to teams and tracking of hygiene remediation work.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Actions have been raised to establish recurring inventory refreshes, grant required permissions to developers, and validate exports before contacting teams, indicating reliance on this data as a core input to analytics and remediation.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Core team updates on 4/28 note that Eric Sand is joining to build the inventory refresh script and that validations will be performed before outreach. The June 1–5, 2026 summary further confirms that a live, daily refreshed Power BI report with current Datadog monitor data is now in place, indicating that the inventory is being actively maintained and used to provide accurate visibility into tagging compliance and AssetID coverage.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If exports cannot be sufficiently validated, limit their use to internal analytics and require teams to confirm details before acting, while in parallel exploring alternative data sources or integration enhancements to improve inventory quality.
assumptions.validation_method: Have the Datadog team and Eric Sand develop and run an inventory refresh script, validate sample exports against live Datadog and ServiceNow data, and obtain sign-off from data and architecture leads before using the dataset for outreach.

assumptions.title: Existing standards are sufficient; the main gap is enforcement, auditability, and governance
assumptions.description: The group concluded that standards largely exist and that the core problem is enforcement, auditability, and sustained governance, rather than a complete absence of standards.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Discussion in the March 20 kick‑off and decision DL‑05 indicated consensus that standards are already in place but are not consistently enforced or audited across Datadog organizations and teams.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Decision DL‑05 recorded consensus that standards exist, and early Phase 1 work is already leveraging these standards as a basis for enforcement planning.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If significant gaps are identified, add a workstream to define or refresh missing standards and adjust the program plan to include standard creation before or alongside enforcement activities.
assumptions.validation_method: Inventory existing standards from Architecture, Data, and Service Management teams, compare them against current practice and program needs, and identify any true gaps that must be filled.

assumptions.title: Synthetic monitors are expected to lack traditional alert thresholds and should be excluded from threshold-gap metrics
assumptions.description: During review of monitors without alert thresholds, Dominique and Nick agreed that many of the monitors counted as "missing thresholds" are actually synthetic monitors, for which the absence of a traditional threshold is expected behavior. The team is assuming that synthetic monitors generally do not require the same threshold configuration as other monitor types and therefore should be excluded from metrics and remediation backlogs that track missing alert thresholds.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Analysis with TRTA Tax showed that a large portion of monitors counted as lacking thresholds were synthetic monitors. Dominique noted that for these, the lack of a threshold is expected, suggesting that current counts are conflating valid synthetic configurations with genuine hygiene issues.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Current empirical review indicates that many no-threshold monitors are synthetic and that teams treat this configuration as normal. However, this behavior must be confirmed against Datadog best practices and internal standards before it is encoded into metrics and remediation logic, hence a medium confidence level.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation shows that synthetic monitors should be treated as having required threshold-like conditions, update the metrics and dashboards to include synthetics in threshold-gap counts, define clear minimum configuration standards for synthetics, and create targeted remediation stories for affected product teams, starting with Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ.
assumptions.validation_method: Have Zafar, Dominique, Eric, and LJ review Datadog documentation and a sample of synthetic monitor configurations across Tax, Corporate, and Legal/HighQ to confirm expected behavior and align on whether synthetic monitors should generally be excluded from threshold-gap metrics. Reflect the outcome in the monitoring hygiene metrics dictionary and dashboard logic.
assumptions.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

assumptions.title: ServiceNow vendor working sessions this week will resolve key conversational workflow blockers by 2026-05-15
assumptions.description: The team assumes that four working sessions with the ServiceNow vendor, scheduled between Tuesday and Friday of the week of May 11, 2026, will be sufficient to obtain guidance and configuration options needed to resolve the outstanding virtual agent conversational workflow issues—particularly the ability to provide a greeting even when users do not start with "hi"—and to confirm whether any required customizations are safe. This is expected to enable completion of all eight conversational feedback items by the agreed May 15 target date.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the May 11, 2026 sync, Kiran stated he was coordinating with ServiceNow (via John) to schedule working sessions from Tuesday to Friday to address conversational workflow issues. Ashima explicitly asked whether customization was feasible, and Vinay advised that high‑risk customization should only be considered after consulting ServiceNow. The team aligned on using these vendor sessions to work through the greeting behavior and related items.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The vendor sessions are being actively organized, with ownership by Kiran and clear participation from key technical and UX stakeholders (Vinay, Ashima, Mayank, Prithvi). However, the complexity of Now Assist / Virtual Agent internals and the explicit caution against customization mean there is some uncertainty about whether all blockers can be resolved within four sessions.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the vendor sessions do not resolve all blockers by May 15, the team should (1) prioritize a minimum viable set of conversational changes for production (e.g., greeting and handover only), (2) schedule additional vendor sessions or escalate within ServiceNow for deeper support, and (3) update project milestones and the associated risk to reflect a revised delivery date.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm that four working sessions with ServiceNow are scheduled and held between Tuesday and Friday and that they produce concrete configuration or design decisions for each of the eight conversational feedback items, especially greeting behavior when users do not start with "hi".
assumptions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

assumptions.title: Developers will complete backup of update sets and documentation before Zurich upgrade clone
assumptions.description: It is assumed that developers (primarily Srinu and Prashanth, with any contributions from Prudhvi or Mayank) will export all relevant ServiceNow update sets and document configuration changes not captured in update sets before the Zurich upgrade clone from production to the dev environment, as discussed in the May 11, 2026 sync.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Vinay explained the need to take backups of update sets before Friday and to document configuration-only changes so they can be re-applied after the clone. Srinu confirmed on the call that he and Prashanth would "take care of those" and that they are aware some items require manual rework.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Srinu and Prashanth have prior experience managing update sets and clones, and they explicitly acknowledged ownership for backups and documentation on the call. However, time constraints and competing upgrade testing tasks introduce moderate risk that some items may be missed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If, upon verification, some update sets or configuration steps were not backed up, the team should (1) immediately catalog what was lost, (2) allocate time for Srinu and Prashanth to re-implement those changes on the cloned dev instance, and (3) tighten the process for future upgrades by standardizing a backup checklist and sign-off step.
assumptions.validation_method: Verify by the end of Friday that (1) update sets containing recent conversational workflow and Agent Chat changes have been exported and stored, and (2) a document exists listing configuration-only changes that must be manually re-applied post-clone.
assumptions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

assumptions.title: Non-production development can continue during Zurich prod change freeze without impacting timelines
assumptions.description: The team assumes that the Zurich production change freeze does not prevent ongoing development and testing in non-production environments (Dev1 and QA) for virtual agent conversational workflows and Agent Chat, and that only promotions to production are restricted until after the upgrade window.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the May 11, 2026 sync, Vinay clarified that although there is a dev freeze period for production (May 8 to June 8), developers can continue to work on changes in Dev1 and QA, with only production deployments blocked until after the change freeze. Kiran explicitly sought confirmation that this would not stop their work, and Vinay confirmed it would not.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The assumption is grounded in standard ServiceNow upgrade procedures and explicit statements from the platform lead, but final enforcement depends on broader change management policy, which may impose additional constraints.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If non-prod development is restricted, the team should (1) adjust timelines for conversational workflow and Agent Chat changes, (2) explore using a separate sandbox or lower environment not subject to the freeze, and (3) communicate revised delivery dates and risks to stakeholders, updating the RAAID log accordingly.
assumptions.validation_method: Confirm with the ServiceNow upgrade/change management team that Dev1 and QA can be used for ongoing development and testing during the Zurich prod change freeze, and monitor whether any unexpected restrictions or repeated clones impact their usability.
assumptions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF  Sync (1).docx

assumptions.title: Azure DevOps (ADO) will be available and suitable as the system of record for the Datadog Hygiene backlog
assumptions.description: The team identified Azure DevOps as the likely system for tracking Phase 1 deliverables and the broader hygiene backlog, assuming it can support the needed epics, features, stories, and reporting.
assumptions.rationale_basis: ADO is already in use for other initiatives, and leadership directed that deliverables be entered into a formal backlog system for tracking and reporting.
assumptions.validity_explanation: March 17 notes explicitly mention ADO as the likely tracking system, and subsequent actions reference Phase 1 tasks created in Service Management ADO.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If ADO proves unsuitable, select an alternative enterprise‑approved tool (e.g., Jira) and migrate existing backlog items, ensuring minimal disruption by maintaining consistent IDs and references.
assumptions.validation_method: Configure the Datadog Hygiene backlog in ADO, verify that core fields and workflows meet program needs, and test basic reporting before committing to it as the system of record.

assumptions.title: Program can proceed through a four‑phase structure as proposed
assumptions.description: The program plan assumes that work will proceed through four phases: Baseline Hygiene, Enforcement & Automation, Outcome‑Driven Maturity, and Sustainability, with later phases building on the foundations established in earlier ones.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Stakeholder input showed the problem space is broad and best addressed via a phased approach rather than a single remediation effort. Each phase targets distinct but related outcomes that depend on prior work.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The March 17 recap documented group alignment on the four‑phase structure, and the Phase 1 plan is already being operationalized, suggesting organizational buy‑in to this approach.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If all four phases cannot be executed as planned, reprioritize and merge elements of later phases into ongoing operations or other initiatives, focusing on the most critical outcomes (e.g., enforcement and customer journey monitoring).
assumptions.validation_method: Review progress and feasibility at the end of each phase; confirm continued sponsorship, funding, and alignment with strategic priorities before progressing to subsequent phases.

assumptions.title: Anchoring monitoring effectiveness reviews in Problem Tasks (P‑tasks) will provide sufficient evidence without per‑incident meetings
assumptions.description: The process is designed to fold evidence gathering and conclusions into existing Problem Tasks, avoiding a dedicated review meeting for every incident. This assumes P‑tasks can be structured to capture the necessary monitoring evidence and outcomes.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Teams want to avoid creating an additional meeting for every major incident and instead leverage existing problem management workflows for efficiency and scalability.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The April 7 meeting highlighted strong agreement to avoid per‑incident meetings and to rely on P‑tasks, provided input expectations are clearly defined.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If P‑tasks prove insufficient, introduce a lightweight periodic review meeting (e.g., weekly) of completed P‑tasks or define a short template for supplemental documentation to capture missing details.
assumptions.validation_method: Pilot the P‑task‑anchored process with Legal and Corporate incidents, review a sample of completed P‑tasks for completeness, and adjust guidance based on gaps.

assumptions.title: Monitoring review scope limited to forward‑looking, net‑new major incidents
assumptions.description: The team agreed that the Datadog Alert & Monitor Effectiveness Review process will initially apply to new major incidents going forward and will not be retrospective (e.g., March incidents are out of scope for now).
assumptions.rationale_basis: Limiting scope to forward‑looking incidents keeps the process manageable for Phase 1 pilots and avoids overloading teams with retrospective analysis while the framework and tooling are still being established.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Forward‑only scope is a common way to pilot new review processes, and the team explicitly agreed to this in the April 7 meeting. It allows for real‑time learning while minimizing initial overhead.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If forward‑only scope is insufficient, selectively add high‑impact historical incidents (e.g., recent severe outages) into the review pipeline, prioritizing them based on business impact and available capacity.
assumptions.validation_method: Assess the volume and quality of insights produced from forward‑looking reviews during the pilot with Legal and Corporate incidents, and evaluate whether historical incidents need to be brought into scope.

assumptions.title: Legacy Datadog→ServiceNow incident integration will remain stable during AIOps rollout
assumptions.description: Planning assumes the existing direct Datadog→ServiceNow API integration that currently creates Legal Tracker incidents will continue functioning unchanged while Event Management/AIOps is introduced, allowing a safe parallel period.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The project is explicitly adding Event Management on top of, not replacing, the current incident integration initially. There is no planned change to the Datadog API path until after AIOps incidents are validated, and several team members emphasized that incidents will still be created "as we have today" during early rollout.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Elizabeth and Yash explicitly distinguished between the webhook used for events and the API path used for incidents, and the team proposed using cloned monitors or separate notifiers to send events only to dev/QA. As of the 6-May and 12-May daily updates, the project explicitly notes that they "can't cut off Datadog incident creation until" the service association issue is resolved, confirming that the legacy path remains in place and is a deliberate dependency during the stability phase.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If anomalies in legacy incident creation are detected, pause or roll back the latest AIOps-related changes (e.g., webhook endpoint updates, handler changes) and restore the last known good configuration. Use monitoring and logs to pinpoint interference, then redesign the rollout (for example, isolating test monitors) before attempting again.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitor incident creation through the existing Datadog API integration while enabling AIOps in parallel, checking that incident volume and types remain consistent with historical patterns until the planned cutover away from the legacy path.

assumptions.title: All applications will reuse the standardized Datadog webhook payload and tag schema defined for Legal Tracker
assumptions.description: The onboarding approach for ONESOURCE GTM4, CIAM, and future products assumes that all applications will use the same Datadog webhook payload structure and TR-standard tag schema that were defined during the Legal Tracker onboarding. Luis stated during the May 12, 2026 onboarding sync that the purpose of the standardized tags is to ensure that all applications send the same fields (e.g., TR API name for grouping synthetics, environment type, primary support group) and that the existing Legal Tracker webhook payload can be reused without requiring application-specific payload definitions.
assumptions.rationale_basis: To scale AIOps onboarding efficiently, the team designed a single standardized Datadog webhook payload and tag schema during the Legal Tracker pilot. Reusing this payload for GTM4, SIAM, and other products avoids per-application payload design and allows ServiceNow Event Management rules to remain generic.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Standardizing on a single webhook payload is a deliberate design choice, and the team has codified the required tags and fields in a shared slide deck and checklist. Legal Tracker demonstrates that this payload works in practice. However, each product has its own monitoring history and may have unique requirements, so there is a meaningful chance that some will request non-standard payload elements or have legacy monitors that cannot easily be aligned.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If application teams need non-standard payload elements or cannot align fully with the Legal Tracker schema, the platform team will: (1) require those teams to explicitly document their exceptions; (2) assess whether exceptions can be supported via generic fields (e.g., additional tags) rather than bespoke payloads; and (3) only as a last resort, introduce narrowly scoped, product-specific rules in ServiceNow. The onboarding checklist will also be updated to require teams to confirm they are not using non-standard payloads, and any exceptions will be tracked centrally to avoid uncontrolled divergence.
assumptions.validation_method: During each products onboarding sessions, Luis will present the expected tag and payload schema, review a sample of their Datadog monitors and webhook configurations, and confirm that no non-standard payload fields are required. Application teams will be asked to confirm that they are not relying on additional custom fields beyond the standardized set, or to explicitly identify any exceptions that need design.
assumptions.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 12 May 26.docx

assumptions.title: Future products will be onboarded using standardized AIOps rules with a short QA observation period before production
assumptions.description: For products beyond Legal Tracker, the team assumes onboarding will reuse the standardized event correlation, alert management, and incident creation rules already built and tuned, and that new products will first send their event data into a QA environment for a short observation period (about one to two weeks, timeboxed within a three-to-four-week onboarding window) before moving to production. Product teams will review events, alerts, and incidents in QA to understand grouping and rules behaviour, then proceed to production once behaviour is acceptable.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 11 May 2026 sync, Talia described an approach to pull all GTM4 and SIAM monitors into QA and let them run for one to two weeks to see how grouping and rules behave, while AD emphasized the need to timebox onboarding to no more than three to four weeks. This adapts the previously stated production-first reuse of standardized rules to include a short QA observation phase while still avoiding heavy, per-product customization.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The Legal Tracker implementation has established a standardized rule set, and GTM4 and SIAM are willing early adopters with significant alert volume. The team has agreed on a practical process (QA observation for one to two weeks, overall onboarding not exceeding three to four weeks) that balances risk and speed. However, GTM4s high alert volume and expected findings mean there is still uncertainty about how much tuning will be needed within that window.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If the QA observation period reveals that GTM4, SIAM, or later products need substantial rule customization or longer stabilization, the team will (1) prioritize one product at a time where necessary, (2) keep standardized rules as the default and tightly constrain any product-specific rules, and (3) adjust onboarding timelines and expectations with leadership rather than allowing open-ended QA runs.
assumptions.validation_method: Pilot the QA-first, timeboxed onboarding approach with GTM4 and SIAM by running their monitors in QA for approximately one to two weeks, using the existing standardized rules. Measure the amount of tuning required and whether behaviour is acceptable before promoting to production. Use these results to confirm the viability of this approach for subsequent products.

assumptions.title: QA observation of GTM4 and SIAM monitors will provide sufficient data within a timeboxed window
assumptions.description: The onboarding plan for GTM4 and SIAM assumes that pulling all of their Datadog monitors into QA and running them for approximately one to two weeks (within an overall onboarding window of no more than three to four weeks) will generate enough representative alert data to assess grouping, rule application, and required monitor changes before moving to production.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Talia proposed during the 11 May 2026 sync that all GTM4 and SIAM monitors be pulled into QA and run for a week or two to observe how rules and grouping behave. AD endorsed this approach but stressed the need to timebox onboarding and avoid long-running observation periods, suggesting a target of no more than three to four weeks. This plan assumes that the chosen timeframe will expose typical alert patterns and issues.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Past experience with Legal Tracker and knowledge of GTM4/SIAM alert volumes suggest that even short runs will produce ample data for analysis. However, some rare or edge-case scenarios may not appear within that window, and the team is still evolving its onboarding playbook, so the sufficiency of the timeframe remains to be proven.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If QA data proves insufficient, either extend the QA run modestly while keeping the overall onboarding window within leaderships three-to-four-week expectation, or supplement QA observation with targeted test alerts and simulations to cover missing scenarios. Communicate any deviations from the planned timeframe to AD and Mike and adjust downstream product onboarding schedules accordingly.
assumptions.validation_method: After the initial one-to-two-week QA run for GTM4 and SIAM, review alert and incident metrics, coverage of key monitor types, and findings from Luiss readiness assessment tool to determine whether the dataset is representative. Confirm with GTM4 and SIAM teams whether observed behaviour matches their expectations before deciding to move to production.

assumptions.title: Machine-learning-based AIOps grouping will be tuned to provide reliable incident reduction for Legal Tracker
assumptions.description: The team is assuming that ServiceNow’s AI/ML-based alert grouping can be configured and tuned so that it reliably groups only related alerts (e.g., by CI and service) and demonstrably reduces incident volume for Legal Tracker, instead of creating confusing or incorrect groups. This assumption underpins the decision to invest in AIOps features rather than disabling ML and relying solely on static rules.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 12 May 2026 sync, Elizabeth and Andrea highlighted that the only active AI functionality is machine-learning-based grouping and that it is not yet behaving as expected, while Jot stressed that "there’s no point in implementing AIOps if we cannot make use of it." The team wants to leverage AI-driven grouping and suppression for long-term value, and is planning further discussions with Doug on how to configure ML so it works "in our favour" rather than against us.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial ML behaviour has produced at least one incorrect group (synthetic + monitor with different impacted services), demonstrating that configuration is not yet correct. However, this appears to be a configuration/tuning issue rather than a fundamental product limitation. With direct engagement from ServiceNow (Doug) and access to AIOps dashboards and configuration options, the team believes it is feasible to iteratively tune ML grouping to acceptable behaviour, but acknowledges uncertainty until those changes are tested in production.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If ML-based grouping cannot be made reliable, the contingency is to (1) disable ML grouping for Legal Tracker and rely on deterministic, rule-based grouping only; (2) clearly communicate to stakeholders that AIOps will focus on rule-based correlation and automation rather than AI-driven grouping; (3) ensure incidents continue to be created correctly via deterministic mappings from Datadog (e.g., FinOpsDatadogAlerts configuration) so that Legal Tracker can still cut over from Datadog-direct incidents; and (4) re-evaluate the AIOps roadmap to emphasise other value areas (e.g., runbooks, dashboards) while deferring AI-driven grouping for future phases or specific use cases.
assumptions.validation_method: Collect and review examples of ML-generated alert groups with Doug and the ServiceNow AIOps team, adjust ML and correlation configurations as needed, and then monitor AIOps dashboards and production behaviour over a defined period to confirm that ML groupings align with expected CI/service relationships and that incident counts are reduced without mis-groupings. Legal Tracker and GCC operators will provide qualitative feedback on whether alert groups and incidents now make sense.

assumptions.title: CMDB/discovery data readiness checklist will be validated with CMDB team before onboarding new products
assumptions.description: For future products such as ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM, the team assumes that a CMDB and discovery data readiness checklist (covering discovery scope, CI existence and status, and service associations) will be reviewed and agreed with the CMDB team (Yash and colleagues) before Datadog webhooks are enabled and events are ingested into AIOps environments.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 6-May-2026 regular sync, Yash stressed that previous AIOps issues (e.g., Legal Tracker impacted-service gaps) stemmed from insufficient validation of discovered CI data and a lack of readiness checks. He recommended introducing a pre-checklist to verify discovery scope and data quality before onboarding new applications, and Talia/Jot agreed to review the existing checklist with him and to defer GTM4/SIAM calls until his input is incorporated.
assumptions.validity_explanation: There is clear intent and alignment among Jot, Talia, Luis and Yash to bake CMDB/data-readiness into the onboarding process, and they have agreed to postpone GTM4/SIAM calls until Yash reviews the checklist. However, competing priorities (e.g., production incidents, Zurich upgrade) and pressure to onboard new products mean the checklist might not always be applied rigorously without continued governance.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If products are onboarded without full checklist validation, introduce a remedial data readiness audit shortly after initial event ingestion: pause expansion of AIOps functionality for those products, involve the CMDB team to correct discovery scope and CI associations, and adjust the onboarding playbook to require explicit CMDB sign-off before any further products are added.
assumptions.validation_method: Schedule and complete a review session with Yash and the CMDB team to update the AIOps onboarding checklist with explicit data-readiness checks, then confirm for each new product (starting with GTM4 and SIAM) that the checklist has been applied and signed off before enabling Datadog webhooks.

assumptions.title: Partial-year ServiceNow incident data is sufficient to prioritize top AIOps onboarding candidates
assumptions.description: For selecting the first ~top 40 applications to onboard to AIOps/Event Management, the team will rely on incident data available only from the new ServiceNow instance (January 2026 onward), without merging or reconciling incident volumes from the legacy ServiceNow instance. The working belief is that 5 months of incident data is enough to reveal the main noise patterns and priority candidates (e.g., Plexus, HighQ, ONESOURCE GTM4), and that investing effort to pull and normalize legacy-instance data is not necessary for round-one prioritization.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 30-Apr-2026 AIOps Product Onboarding regional sync, Luis Jorge Rodriguez confirmed that he only has incident data from the new ServiceNow instance. Talia Loch asked whether legacy-instance data was needed for a like-for-like comparison, but Paul Berry argued that five months of current-instance data is adequate to see patterns and identify noisy applications, and that spending effort to extract and merge legacy data would be overkill for an initial prioritization pass.
assumptions.validity_explanation: In the meeting, Paul emphasized that the goal is to find signals, not a mathematically perfect ordering, and that anomalies between alert rankings and incident rankings can themselves be useful. Luis confirmed that the current ServiceNow data already aligns with known noisy applications. This provides reasonable but not absolute confidence that decisions based on the January-onward dataset will be directionally correct for round-one onboarding.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If later analysis or stakeholder feedback reveals that initial onboarding choices missed key noisy or critical applications due to relying only on January-onward data, adjust the roadmap by (1) inserting missed high-priority applications into upcoming waves, (2) using a combined historical view (including legacy-instance extracts) for future re-prioritization, and (3) documenting lessons learned so future planning cycles do not rely solely on partial-year data when legacy data is readily available.
assumptions.validation_method: Compare the top incident-volume applications from the January–current 2026 dataset against (a) GCC operational experience and (b) any sampled legacy-instance reports that can be obtained opportunistically. If significant discrepancies are found (e.g., major Tier 1 apps with high historical incident volume but low current ranking), revisit the prioritization and consider incorporating legacy data for the next planning cycle.
assumptions.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 30 Apr.docx

assumptions.title: Event forwarding between ServiceNow production and lower environments will function for test data
assumptions.description: The team is planning to use ServiceNow’s event forwarding from the production instance to dev and QA so that lower environments receive representative Datadog event traffic for testing rules and correlation without needing separate Datadog integrations for each environment.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Documentation and Doug’s guidance indicate that ServiceNow can forward events between instances using configured connectors and appropriate integration users, avoiding the need to maintain Datadog connections to each SNOW environment.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Yash has configured forwarding using an integration user with the required event management role and received a response from ServiceNow Support indicating that forwarding is working as expected, albeit without backfill and with per-day and time-window limits. Events are flowing, but the limitations introduce some uncertainty about completeness for testing purposes.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If forwarding proves unreliable or incomplete, the team will either (1) point specific Datadog test webhooks directly to dev/QA for targeted monitors, or (2) manually inject representative events into lower environments for rule testing. Event management plugins and configuration will be adjusted with Doug’s help if out-of-box forwarding behaviour is insufficient.
assumptions.validation_method: Enable the event forwarding configuration in production, trigger Datadog events into the SNOW prod instance after webhook cutover, and confirm that corresponding events appear in dev (and subsequently QA) according to the expected schedule.

assumptions.title: CI discovery fixes have restored reliable CI binding for Legal Tracker and will not block production enablement
assumptions.description: Planning for Legal Tracker’s AIOps go-live now assumes that recent fixes to Azure discovery and custom CI-handling logic have resolved the earlier problems with “dead” or retired VMs, so that CI binding from events/alerts to CMDB CIs works as expected. Any remaining limitation is expected to be in the service–CI association model (e.g., 1,000-CI-per-service limit), not in core CI discovery, and therefore should not by itself prevent moving to production.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 30-Apr-2026 regular sync, Yash explained that discovery failures caused by bit server transformation from LHR2 to LHR3 had been resolved, custom logic that was retaining incorrect data had been deactivated, and retired-status discrepancies for CIs had been remediated. He stated that Legal Tracker should now have active, correctly discovered CIs suitable for CI binding.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The discovery and data-quality fixes described by Yash directly address the previously known causes of failed CI binding (retired/“dead” VMs and custom logic). However, the team has not yet completed end-to-end validation of CI binding using fresh Legal Tracker events and incidents, so this remains an assumption until Luis and the product team confirm behaviour in the environment.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation shows that CI binding is still failing, delay or stage Legal Tracker’s production rollout, re-open investigation into discovery and mapping rules with Doug and the CMDB team, and, if necessary, rely temporarily on manual assignment or deterministic mappings while underlying issues are resolved. Communicate any delay to Legal Tracker stakeholders and adjust the onboarding timeline for subsequent products accordingly.
assumptions.validation_method: Have Luis perform sample checks on current Legal Tracker events and alerts in ServiceNow to confirm that CI binding is working as expected, then ask Elizabeth’s team to validate behaviour against real incidents before finalising production enablement.

assumptions.title: ServiceNow CI–service association limitations will not block Legal Tracker production go-live
assumptions.description: Planning for Legal Tracker assumes that the current ServiceNow limit on the number of CIs that can be associated to a service via tag-based association, and the resulting partial service-association behaviour, will not prevent enabling AIOps/Event Management in production. The team is assuming CI binding itself will function correctly for Legal Tracker and that service-association remediation can be handled in parallel without blocking production deployment.
assumptions.rationale_basis: During the 30-Apr-2026 regular sync, Yash confirmed that discovery issues and retired CI states for Legal Tracker have been resolved and that CI binding "should work as expected". He and Doug agreed that the remaining limitation primarily affects service associations (impacted service population) rather than CI binding. When Jot asked whether this issue should stop movement to production, both Yash and Doug indicated that it "shouldn’t" block production, implying that go-live can proceed while the service-association behaviour is investigated in more detail.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The technical team closest to the CMDB (Yash) has confirmed that underlying CI discovery issues are resolved and that CI records for Legal Tracker are in a healthy state. Doug, as the ServiceNow consultant, concurred that CI binding and asset behaviour "should" be fine for production, and proposed treating the CI–service association limit as a separate design topic rather than a go-live blocker. However, the Legal Tracker product team has previously flagged missing service associations as a blocker for disabling Datadog incidents, so this assumption remains tentative until validated with real incident behaviour and stakeholder feedback.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If validation shows that CI–service association issues materially impact operations or stakeholder confidence, the team will (1) pause or narrow the AIOps rollout for Legal Tracker (e.g., disable AIOps-driven incidents while continuing to ingest and group events), (2) prioritise remediation of the CI–service association behaviour with ServiceNow CMDB experts (tuning limits, traverse rules, or service modelling), and (3) maintain the legacy Datadog-direct incident path until Legal Tracker confirms that impacted service information in AIOps-generated incidents is reliable.
assumptions.validation_method: Doug and Yash will conduct a focused review of the CI–service association configuration (including the 1,000-CI limit and tag-based association behaviour) in a follow-up session, then validate end-to-end behaviour by inspecting recent Legal Tracker events and incidents in production to confirm that CIs bind correctly and that any service-association gaps are acceptable or have a clear remediation plan.

issues.title: Missing or blank Datadog Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads
issues.description: Some ServiceNow incidents generated from Datadog alerts are missing or have blank Datadog Monitor IDs in their payloads, causing gaps in incident‑to‑monitor correlation.
issues.impact_assessment: The project is building a ServiceNow–Datadog incident correlation MVP that relies on accurate Datadog Monitor IDs being present in ServiceNow payloads. Missing or blank Monitor IDs prevent reliable linkage between incidents and their originating monitors, which undermines analytics on monitor effectiveness, complicates root‑cause analysis, and reduces the value of the MVP for Phase 1. This issue also impairs the ability to feed monitoring gaps into the Datadog Hygiene backlog.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on completion and deployment of the ServiceNow–Datadog correlation MVP and on remediation of Datadog–ServiceNow integration mappings. Affects the alert and monitor effectiveness review process and reporting.
issues.resolution: Investigate root causes of missing or blank Monitor IDs in ServiceNow payloads, then remediate configuration issues in the Datadog–ServiceNow integration or payload mapping so Monitor IDs are consistently populated. The incident correlation MVP will be updated as needed once causes are addressed.

issues.title: ServiceNow CI binding not working as expected for Legal Tracker events
issues.description: Events ingested from Datadog into ServiceNow are not automatically associating to existing CIs in the CMDB, even when matching CI names exist, causing CI binding to fail for many events.
issues.impact_assessment: Without reliable CI binding, events and alerts cannot be accurately tied to infrastructure and application components, hampering incident routing, impact analysis, and remediation automation for the Legal Tracker AIOps implementation.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on CMDB data quality, ServiceNow out‑of‑the‑box CI association rules, and any custom responder rules configured by Doug.

issues.title: Governance difficulty with 110+ Datadog organizations
issues.description: The current landscape includes more than 110 Datadog organizations, making centralized governance significantly harder and raising questions about whether consolidation is needed.
issues.impact_assessment: During the March 20 discussions, the group acknowledged that operating more than 110 Datadog organizations makes consistent governance, standards enforcement, and reporting far more complex. It increases fragmentation of configuration, complicates access and oversight, and may limit the feasibility of unified maturity measurement. However, consolidation carries risks such as historical data loss and changes to anomaly detection behavior, so analysis is required before proceeding.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Linked to decisions DL‑02 and DL‑03 on Datadog org strategy and governance feasibility, and to the assessment of Datadog maturity scorecard usage (DL‑01).
issues.resolution: Conduct a detailed impact analysis of potential Datadog organization consolidation, including risks such as historical data loss, anomaly resets, and AI/MCP rate‑limit impacts, and define governance options that may include improved standards enforcement without consolidation. The analysis will inform the open decisions on Datadog org strategy and governance feasibility.

issues.title: Potential duplicate/incidental increase during AIOps cutover
issues.description: Enabling AIOps‑driven incident creation while leaving existing Datadog→ServiceNow incident integrations active could temporarily increase incident counts or create near‑duplicate incidents until Datadog incident creation is disabled.
issues.impact_assessment: Temporary duplicate or increased incidents could increase workload for GCC and Legal Tracker support teams and distort incident reporting metrics during the cutover period.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on clear cutover plan, QA parallel run, and ability to programmatically adjust Datadog monitor notification targets by product.
issues.resolution:

issues.title: AIOps-generated incident priorities are higher than corresponding alert priorities
issues.description: Incidents created by ServiceNow AIOps from group alerts are being assigned higher priorities (often P1) than expected based on the underlying alert severity and priority. Analysis of the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and related flow actions shows that incident impact and urgency are set to their highest values whenever the alert priority group or severity is 1 or 2, which forces the incident priority matrix to produce P1 incidents. In addition, the alert 'priority group' field is driven by an out-of-the-box priority score that may not align with Thomson Reuters expectations, and current event rules map Datadog monitor priority into alert severity but do not explicitly map priority into the alert priority group. As a result, Legal Tracker alerts with moderate priorities (e.g., P3) can still generate P1 incidents, causing misaligned incident priorities compared to direct Datadog-created incidents.
issues.impact_assessment: The mismatch between alert priority and AIOps-generated incident priority causes Legal Tracker incidents to be raised as P1 when the underlying monitor/alert priority is lower (e.g., P2 or P3). This over-escalation inflates the number of P1 incidents, drives unnecessary major incident engagement, and creates inconsistency between incidents created directly from Datadog and those created via AIOps. It undermines trust in the AIOps implementation, complicates incident reporting and metrics, and makes Legal Tracker and GCC reluctant to rely on AIOps-driven incidents until priority behavior is corrected.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on ServiceNow vendor configuration of the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and priority score thresholds; relies on correct Datadog monitor priority values and current event rules that map Datadog priority into alert severity; interacts with the ServiceNow incident priority matrix and incident management practice settings.
issues.resolution:
Review and adjust the incident creation flow and priority mapping so that incident impact and urgency are derived appropriately from alert severity and priority group without systematically elevating incidents to P1. This includes: (1) analysing the 'create incident TR presets' subflow and its scripted flow actions to change logic that currently sets incident impact/urgency to 1 when alert priority group or severity is 1 or 2; (2) confirming how the alert 'priority group' field is populated from the out-of-the-box priority score and whether threshold properties should be tuned instead of custom code changes; and (3) ensuring event rules that map Datadog monitor priority to alert severity and priority group produce incident priorities aligned with TR's incident priority matrix. Proposed changes will be validated on sample Legal Tracker alerts and incidents before wider rollout.  
*Datadog priority and service directly being transferred to the incident

issues.title: Datadog P3 alerts mapped as critical severity in ServiceNow alerts for Legal Tracker
issues.description: In the ServiceNow production instance, Legal Tracker alerts coming from Datadog with monitor priority P3 are being mapped to critical severity on the ServiceNow alert records. As a result, incidents created from these alerts appear as P1, even though the underlying Datadog monitors are configured as P3. The problem appears to originate in the custom ServiceNow event field mapping rule "Datadog map alert priority to severity" not behaving as it did in dev, potentially due to rule ordering or execution context.
issues.impact_assessment: Because P3 Datadog alerts for Legal Tracker are being mapped to critical severity in ServiceNow, any incidents generated from these alerts are incorrectly created as P1. This mis-prioritization would cause an excessive number of P1 incidents, distort SLAs and reporting, and could trigger unnecessary major incident workflows and on-call paging. The team has therefore disabled automatic incident creation and set the incident-creation subflow to manual to avoid flooding operations with false P1s, which in turn delays full end-to-end testing and cutover to the AIOps event-first model.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on the correct configuration and execution order of the ServiceNow event field mapping rule "Datadog map alert priority to severity" and on availability of representative Legal Tracker alerts from Datadog (including synthetics) for testing. Affects the ability to safely enable AIOps-driven incident creation for Legal Tracker without generating spurious P1 incidents.
issues.resolution:
Investigate and correct the ServiceNow event field mapping rule that converts Datadog alert_priority values (P1–P5) into ServiceNow alert severity. Specifically: (1) review the "Datadog map alert priority to severity" event field mapping script in production; (2) adjust the rule order so that it executes before other mapping rules (e.g., synthetic-related mappings at order 20/25); (3) rerun tests with known P3 Legal Tracker alerts (including synthetics) to confirm that alert severity is set correctly; and (4) only after the mapping is verified, re-enable automatic incident creation for Legal Tracker alerts, starting with manual creation from alerts and then switching back to automatic once behaviour is stable.
Refer to Issue#15
