issues.title: Synthetic monitors inflate reported count of monitors without alert thresholds
issues.description: Current analytics count monitors without alert thresholds without distinguishing synthetic monitors, leading to a reported figure of 20–30% of monitors lacking thresholds. The majority of these are synthetic monitors, for which the absence of a threshold is expected, causing the analytics to overstate the true threshold gap.
issues.impact_assessment: Analytics and dashboards used in the Datadog Hygiene program currently highlight a large percentage of monitors without alert thresholds (20–30%). However, May 5 discussions confirmed that most of these are synthetic monitors that are not expected to have thresholds. Treating these as defects misrepresents the scale of the problem, can misdirect remediation effort, and may erode stakeholder confidence in the reported metrics.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on availability of enriched Datadog monitor metadata (including monitor type) via scripts developed by Eric Sand and/or LJ's 'Data Doc Jacker' tool.
issues.resolution: Update analytics and reporting logic to filter out synthetic monitors when calculating monitors without alert thresholds so that reported threshold gaps reflect only monitors where thresholds are required. This will likely be implemented in the Datadog inventory Power BI report and underlying queries.
issues.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

issues.title: Lack of Datadog monitor metadata in inventory exports blocks team-level cleanup
issues.description: Current Datadog inventory exports (e.g., those produced by Jacob Kinsa) lack critical metadata such as who created each monitor, who it is assigned to, and when it last fired. Tax and Corporate stakeholders have stated that without this metadata they cannot practically group and address monitors with missing Asset IDs and other hygiene issues, calling it a showstopper for ongoing cleanup.
issues.impact_assessment: Tax and Corporate teams must remediate large numbers of Datadog monitors with missing Asset IDs and other hygiene defects. Without metadata indicating monitor creator, ownership and last-fired time, they cannot efficiently group monitors, prioritize work, or route questions to the correct owners. This significantly slows baseline hygiene remediation, risks leaving noisy or orphaned monitors in place, and undermines the usefulness of the Datadog inventory Power BI report as a driver for action.
issues.dependencies_affecting: Depends on Eric Sand obtaining necessary Datadog permissions, developing or integrating scripts to pull complete monitor metadata, and coordination with LJ's 'Data Doc Jacker' tool where applicable.
issues.resolution: Enhance the Datadog inventory extraction process (via scripts developed by Eric Sand and/or LJ's tooling) so that exports include key metadata fields (monitor creator, owner/assignee, last-fired timestamp, and relevant tags). Update the Power BI inventory report to surface this metadata for filtering and grouping, enabling teams such as Tax and Corporate to run targeted cleanup campaigns.
issues.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

decisions.title: Use out-of-the-box ServiceNow AIOps incident priority calculation instead of custom impact/urgency event fields
decisions.description: The team will not persist custom impact and urgency fields on ServiceNow event records to mirror Datadog values. Instead, Datadog monitors will be configured with appropriate severity and priority, and ServiceNow will use its out‑of‑the‑box logic (including severity and alert type) to calculate incident impact and urgency.
decisions.rationale: Custom impact/urgency fields add complexity and diverge from the out‑of‑the‑box product design. Using ServiceNow’s standard AIOps logic simplifies maintenance and ensures consistency as the solution scales across products, even though it requires additional work to train teams on correct use of severity and priority in Datadog.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Introduce custom impact/urgency fields on events populated directly from Datadog and map them to incidents.
2) Stay out-of-the-box by configuring severity/priority in Datadog and relying on ServiceNow’s AIOps engine to derive impact/urgency for incidents.
3) Hybrid approach using both custom fields and AIOps calculations.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow CI binding and incident creation behaviour; Datadog monitor configuration standards; removal of custom event fields added by Yash.

decisions.title: Legal Tracker AIOps to proceed using minimal rule set (out-of-the-box plus three TR rules)
decisions.description: For Legal Tracker go‑live, the team will rely primarily on out‑of‑the‑box ServiceNow event rules with a small set of three Thomson Reuters–specific rules, rather than waiting to design a comprehensive custom rule library.
decisions.rationale: Using a minimal rule set allows the team to start realizing AIOps value sooner and avoids over‑engineering for the first product. Additional rules can be added iteratively once real event data and behaviours are better understood.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Design extensive custom event and correlation rules for Legal Tracker before go‑live.
2) Use out-of-the-box rules only.
3) Use out-of-the-box rules plus a small number of TR-specific rules for initial go-live.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow vendor rule configuration; Datadog payload contents; cutover planning for incidents.

decisions.title: Event forwarding from ServiceNow production to dev/QA is not a go-live blocker
decisions.description: The team agreed that ServiceNow event forwarding from production to lower environments (dev and QA) is helpful for testing but is not required for the initial Legal Tracker go‑live.
decisions.rationale: Forwarding allows consistent test data across environments, but its absence does not prevent AIOps from functioning in production. Delaying go‑live until forwarding is perfect would unnecessarily slow delivery.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Make event forwarding a prerequisite for go-live.
2) Treat forwarding as a post-go-live improvement while focusing on production connectivity and incident behaviour.
decisions.dependencies_linked: ServiceNow event forwarding configuration managed by Yash; Datadog webhook pointing to production.

decisions.title: Pilot parallel incident run in QA before enabling AIOps incidents in production
decisions.description: Before AIOps begins creating incidents in production for Legal Tracker, the team plans a time‑boxed parallel run in a QA environment where AIOps incidents can be compared to existing Datadog‑driven incidents, to assess completeness and volume reduction.
decisions.rationale: A QA parallel run allows the team to validate that AIOps does not miss important incidents and provides incident volume reduction, without risking production operations or confusing support teams with duplicates.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Immediately enable AIOps incident creation in production and disable Datadog incidents.
2) Run AIOps alerts only in production and compare manually.
3) Run AIOps incidents in QA for a short period while keeping production unchanged, then decide on production enablement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: QA environment setup; ability to mirror event data into QA; cutover plan for disabling Datadog incidents per product.

decisions.title: Reassign interium CT AI project sponsorship from Lauren Clark to Anthony Rokis to now, Terry Hancock.
decisions.description: Customer Trust AI project sponsorship has been transferred from Lauren Clark to Anthony Rokis  to now, Terry Hancock while Jason Horowitz is out on leave for 3 months (3/23-6/28/26).
decisions.rationale: To ensure consistent sponsorship and leadership coverage for the Customer Trust AI project during broader leadership transitions and to support the expanded scope of the program.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain Lauren Clark as sponsor; transition sponsorship to another leader such as Anthony Rokis.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Risk R5 - Project sponsor out for ~3 months requiring temporary restructure of project team and decision-making model.

decisions.title: Position Loopio as transitional capability to be reevaluated by Q3 2026
decisions.description: Loopio is designated as a transitional capability to support current volume and immediate scalability needs but is not the long-term AI solution and will be reevaluated by Q3 2026.
decisions.rationale: Loopio can address near-term operational scalability needs, but the long-term AI strategy requires a broader, integrated platform. A reevaluation ensures alignment with evolving requirements and technology options.
decisions.options_considered: Use Loopio as the long-term AI platform; adopt a different platform immediately; treat Loopio as transitional and plan for a long-term AI platform selection.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependent on selection and implementation of the long-term AI platform; impacts content migration and governance processes.
decisions.source_file_name: RAID Log – 2026 Customer Trust - AI Strategy.xlsx

decisions.title: Implement new Loopio instance as Phase 1 of Customer Trust AI Strategy
decisions.description: Establish a new Loopio instance as Phase 1 of the Customer Trust AI Strategy to centralize trusted content, improve governance, and reduce response times.
decisions.rationale: A centralized trusted content repository within Loopio provides a foundational capability to support AI-driven responses, improve content governance, and accelerate ticket closure before the long-term AI platform is selected and implemented.
decisions.options_considered: Continue using ServiceNow; use another tool for content management; implement a new Loopio instance as an interim platform.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Dependent on content migration from ServiceNow, AI contract enablement, and future integration with the long-term Customer Trust platform.
decisions.source_file_name: RAID Log – 2026 Customer Trust - AI Strategy.xlsx

decisions.title: Use single NAVA pilot group for Agent Chat access and avoid creating additional groups
decisions.description: HCL pilot agents for Agent Chat will use the existing NAVA pilot users group for access. No additional groups will be created or granted access unless absolutely required, to keep access management simple and centralized.
decisions.rationale: Centralizing Agent Chat access through a single NAVA pilot group simplifies administration, reduces configuration complexity, and minimizes inconsistencies in role assignments. It also avoids proliferation of redundant groups that could cause access discrepancies.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Create separate groups for different HCL cohorts; 2) Reuse existing HCL service desk groups; 3) Use a single NAVA pilot group for all pilot users.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Agent Chat access configuration for HCL testers; NAVA pilot user group role assignments.
decisions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF Daily Sync.docx

decisions.title: Track Agent Chat issues and access problems in a shared Excel for continuous updates
decisions.description: All Agent Chat issues and access-related problems will be tracked in a shared Excel file, kept open for HCL testers to add new items continuously. TR (including Srinu and Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth) will use this tracker to prioritize and resolve items across UK and ISU hours.
decisions.rationale: Using a shared Excel tracker allows real-time capture of issues from multiple HCL testers without waiting for batch updates, enabling better prioritization and coordination between TR and HCL teams across time zones.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Collect issues via periodic emails; 2) Have HCL compile and send issues in batches; 3) Maintain a shared Excel tracker for continuous entry and prioritization.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Resolution of Agent Chat access issues; coordination between HCL testers and TR support (Srinu, Kolluru, Prudhvi Yaswanth).
decisions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF Daily Sync.docx

decisions.title: Define support process for UK and ISU hours via Gandikota, Srinu and escalation through L, Kiran Kumar
decisions.description: During UK and ISU hours, Gandikota, Srinu will be the primary support contact for Agent Chat issues. HCL testers can also reach out to L, Kiran Kumar, who will route issues to Srinu or Male, Prashanth as appropriate.
decisions.rationale: Assigning a clear support owner for UK and ISU hours ensures prompt resolution of Agent Chat issues encountered by HCL testers and clarifies escalation paths across time zones.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Ad-hoc support via whoever is available; 2) Dedicated UK/ISU support via Gandikota, Srinu with escalation through L, Kiran Kumar; 3) Route all issues only through daily sync meetings.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Timely resolution of HCL Agent Chat issues; effectiveness of the shared Excel issue tracker.
decisions.source_file_name: Service Desk AI automation WF Daily Sync.docx

decisions.title: Reduce number of Datadog organizations to improve governance
decisions.description: The program is considering whether to reduce the current number of Datadog organizations (approximately 110+) as a strategy to improve governance and consistency.
decisions.rationale: Operating with 110+ Datadog organizations creates high complexity for governance, makes it difficult to enforce standards, and complicates reporting. However, consolidation carries risks such as historical data loss, anomaly detection resets, and AI/MCP rate‑limit impacts, which must be weighed before deciding.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current number of organizations with improved governance vs. consolidate organizations to reduce complexity, accepting potential data and anomaly impacts.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to issues around governance feasibility, historical data retention, anomaly detection behavior, and AI/MCP rate limits.

decisions.title: Feasibility of governance with current number of Datadog organizations
decisions.description: The team is assessing whether effective governance is feasible with the current number of Datadog organizations or if structural changes such as consolidation are necessary.
decisions.rationale: During discussions on 2026-03-20, the group agreed that governance is significantly harder at the current scale. A more detailed architectural and governance analysis is required to understand whether process and tooling changes can address the issue without consolidation.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current multi‑org structure with improved governance processes vs. consolidate or restructure organizations to simplify governance.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Related to DL‑02 (Datadog Org Strategy) and impacts ongoing governance of standards enforcement and reporting.

decisions.title: Program operating model: enforcement vs. adoption approach
decisions.description: The Datadog Hygiene program will operate using a hybrid model: central standards and governance with active engagement of product and engineering teams, rather than purely top‑down enforcement or purely bottom‑up self‑service adoption.
decisions.rationale: Stakeholders agreed that standards already exist and need enforcement, but also that success requires engagement and ownership by product and engineering teams. A hybrid model balances the need for central governance with distributed implementation and avoids a purely self‑serve model that lacks accountability.
decisions.options_considered: Top‑down enforcement model vs. bottom‑up self‑serve adoption vs. hybrid model combining central governance with collaborative engagement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Influences governance structures, stakeholder engagement plans, and how enforcement mechanisms are designed in later phases.

decisions.title: Standards vs. enforcement and governance gap
decisions.description: The team concluded that standards for Datadog monitoring largely exist, and that the primary gap is in enforcement, auditability, and sustained governance rather than in the absence of standards.
decisions.rationale: Stakeholder input and core team discussions indicated that many standards are already documented, but they are not consistently enforced or auditable. Focusing on enforcement and governance is therefore more impactful than creating entirely new standards.
decisions.options_considered: Create new standards vs. improve enforcement and governance of existing standards.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Shapes Phase 2 (Enforcement & Automation) and informs how metrics and controls are designed.

decisions.title: Balance of customer journey monitoring vs. infrastructure alerting
decisions.description: Customer journey monitoring and infrastructure alerting will both be treated as required and must be explicitly connected so that infrastructure signals map to customer experience outcomes.
decisions.rationale: The group recognized that focusing solely on infrastructure health without connecting to customer experience would be insufficient, and that customer journeys must be first‑class monitoring priorities. At the same time, infrastructure signals are necessary inputs to understanding service health.
decisions.options_considered: Prioritize customer journey monitoring over infrastructure alerting vs. prioritize infrastructure alerting vs. treat both as required with explicit linkage.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Influences Phase 3 (Outcome‑Driven Maturity) and how monitors and alerts are designed across infrastructure and customer journeys.

decisions.title: Exclude synthetic monitors when measuring alert-threshold gaps
decisions.description: Analytics and reporting for monitors without alert thresholds will exclude synthetic monitors from the calculation so that metrics reflect only monitors where thresholds are expected.
decisions.rationale: May 5 discussions confirmed that the majority of monitors reported as lacking thresholds are synthetic monitors, for which missing thresholds are expected. Including them inflates the reported threshold gap (20–30%) and misrepresents the actual issue. Filtering synthetic monitors provides a more accurate picture of threshold hygiene.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Continue counting all monitors without thresholds, including synthetic monitors; 2) Exclude synthetic monitors from the threshold-gap metric; 3) Report both figures separately. The team opted to at least exclude synthetic monitors from the primary threshold-gap metric.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Depends on enriched Datadog inventory metadata (including monitor type) supplied by scripts and tools under development by Eric Sand and LJ.
decisions.source_file_name: May 5_Weekly Touch Base - Core team - Datadog Hygiene Project.docx

decisions.title: Use or customize existing Datadog maturity scorecards for observability measurement
decisions.description: The team is evaluating whether existing Datadog maturity scorecards can be used to measure observability maturity at Thomson Reuters. Initial assessment indicates that Datadog’s default scorecards are generic and likely not aligned to internal standards, so customization or redefinition may be required.
decisions.rationale: Datadog provides built‑in maturity scorecards, but they may not reflect Thomson Reuters’ governance standards and operational practices. Using them as‑is might misrepresent true maturity and misalign with internal expectations.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to the need for consistent program measurement and potentially to standards enforcement decisions.

decisions.title: Engineering and architecture resources aligned to core working group
decisions.description: Current attendees will form the core Datadog Hygiene program team, but additional engineering participation is needed to provide implementation depth, and specific resources must be identified and aligned.
decisions.rationale: The initial core team covers key roles, but additional engineering and architecture expertise is required to implement standards and remediation at scale. Aligning named individuals will improve execution capability.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain current core team membership vs. expand to include additional engineering and architecture resources.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Depends on action A4 and Masthanaiah’s follow‑up with Engineering leadership; impacts the delivery capacity for Phase 1 and beyond.

decisions.title: Define target timelines for Phase 1 and overall program delivery
decisions.description: The program acknowledged the need to define target timelines for Phase 1 and overall Datadog Hygiene delivery, time‑boxed via a backlog, but no dates were set during the initial discussions.
decisions.rationale: Timelines are required for reporting and to provide accountability for deliverables. However, the group wanted to better understand scope and scale before committing to dates.
decisions.options_considered: Set immediate timelines vs. defer timeline definition until after backlog creation and scope refinement.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to backlog creation and grooming actions (e.g., A15) and to program reporting requirements.

decisions.title: Define notification tiers for after-hours vs next-business-day alerts
decisions.description: The team must decide what severity levels and event types trigger after-hours paging versus next-business-day notification for Legal Tracker, based on correlated incidents and event severity.

decision_owner.name: Service Management / Incident Management leadership (e.g., Heymann, Damian)

decisions.rationale: Tiered notifications reduce alert fatigue by ensuring that teams are only paged for true service-impacting exceptions while less severe events are handled during business hours.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Only P1 (and possibly P2) incidents generated from primary correlated alerts trigger after-hours pages; others become next-business-day notifications.
2) Include some high-severity warnings in after-hours paging for specific services.
3) Maintain current incident-based paging behaviour initially and gradually introduce alert-driven paging tiers.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Incident creation policy, on-call configuration on the ServiceNow alert/incident tables, and Legal Tracker on-call agreements.

decisions.title: Timebox QA observation period for new AIOps product onboardings
decisions.description: For new products being onboarded to AIOps/Event Management (such as ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM), the QA observation period for running their monitors and alerts through ServiceNow will be timeboxed to no more than three to four weeks, with a target of one to two weeks, to avoid prolonged onboarding and encourage iterative movement towards production.
decisions.rationale: AD emphasized the need to avoid letting QA observation drag on, preferring short, iterative cycles so that teams can move to production quickly while still gaining sufficient insight into alert grouping and rule behaviour.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Run QA observation for an open-ended period until all issues are resolved.
2) Timebox QA observation to a maximum of three to four weeks with a target of one to two weeks before deciding on production onboarding.
3) Skip QA observation and onboard directly to production using enterprise rules.
decisions.dependencies_linked: AIOps onboarding plans for ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM; Legal Tracker lessons learned; QA data ingestion for GTM4 and SIAM.

decisions.title: Proceed with onboarding ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel with caution
decisions.description: The team will initiate AIOps/Event Management onboarding for both ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel, while closely monitoring the workload and alert volumes from GTM4 and leveraging QA observation to understand and manage the expected high volume of findings.
decisions.rationale: Both GTM4 and SIAM generate significant alert volume and their teams are ready to engage. Despite concerns about the effort required for GTM4, the group agreed that starting with both, with a cautious and timeboxed QA approach, provides maximum learning and impact.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Onboard only ONESOURCE GTM4 first, then onboard SIAM later.
2) Onboard only SIAM first.
3) Onboard both ONESOURCE GTM4 and SIAM in parallel, with a timeboxed QA observation period and readiness assessments.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Readiness assessments for GTM4 and SIAM monitors; Datadog webhooks and QA event flow; Legal Tracker feedback influencing configuration adjustments.

decisions.title: Prioritize AIOps capabilities in sequence: ingestion → correlation & prioritization → notification → root cause & resolutions
decisions.description: For Legal Tracker, capability rollout will follow a defined order: (1) Alert ingestion (event-first processing) as the foundation; (2) Intelligent correlation as the highest-value capability; (3) Event prioritization and notification reduction; and (4) later-phase root cause identification and AI-suggested resolutions once correlation and data volume are sufficient.
decisions.rationale: Sequencing capabilities ensures a stable foundation before introducing advanced features. Ingestion and correlation deliver the highest immediate value by breaking the 1:1 event-to-incident pattern, while notification reduction and advanced root cause/AI resolutions depend on stable correlation, prioritization, and sufficient historical data.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Implement all capabilities at once (ingestion, correlation, prioritization, notification, root cause, AI resolutions).
2) Focus only on ingestion and correlation for MVP and defer all other capabilities.
3) Implement capabilities in the chosen sequence: ingestion → correlation & prioritization → notification → root cause & resolutions.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Ingestion readiness (integration mechanism), correlation tuning, event taxonomy definition, KB/runbook quality, and sufficient historical incident data.

decisions.title: Adopt deterministic Datadog monitor priority as MVP incident priority for Legal Tracker
decisions.description: For the Legal Tracker MVP, ServiceNow’s out-of-the-box incident priority calculation has been disabled and Datadog monitor priority is passed deterministically through to the incident priority. This patch aligns incident priority with existing Legal Tracker practices while the team gains experience with AIOps and prepares to tune non-deterministic priority behaviour in lower environments.
decisions.rationale: Legal Tracker and GCC are accustomed to deterministic incident priority based directly on Datadog monitors. Early trials of AIOps-native, non-deterministic priority were perceived as too aggressive (e.g., raising priority after only two alerts). To avoid blocking the production MVP and to meet previously communicated timelines, the team agreed to a temporary deterministic configuration as an MVP, while planning a ‘laboratory’ effort in dev/QA to tune native AIOps scoring before reintroducing it.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Keep ServiceNow out-of-the-box non-deterministic incident priority (based on CI importance, blast radius, and alert state).
2) Temporarily disable AIOps-native priority and deterministically map Datadog monitor priority directly to incident priority for Legal Tracker.
3) Delay Legal Tracker MVP until non-deterministic behaviour is fully tuned and accepted by the product team.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to risk 'Reliance on temporary customizations for incident priority and CI binding instead of AIOps-native behaviour' and dependency 'ServiceNow vendor configuration of event rules, responder rules, and mappings'; also interacts with future tuning sessions in dev/QA for non-deterministic priority.

decisions.title: Use incident data from new ServiceNow instance (January 2026 onward) without backfilling legacy instance data for initial AIOps onboarding prioritization
decisions.description: For the first round of AIOps onboarding prioritization, the team will rely on incident data extracted from the new ServiceNow instance (approximately January 2026 onward) combined with existing alert data, and will not pursue extracting or merging historical incident data from the legacy ServiceNow instance at this stage.
decisions.rationale: Paul Berry judged that five months of incident data from the new ServiceNow instance is sufficient to reveal patterns and identify candidate applications for the top 40 AIOps migration list. Fetching and merging legacy incident data would consume additional effort without materially improving the directional signals needed for round-one prioritization. Any anomalies (e.g., applications with high recent incidents but lower historical alert ranking) will themselves be useful signals to investigate rather than reasons to delay decisions.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Extract and merge legacy ServiceNow incident data with new-instance data to create a full-year, like-for-like incident view.
2) Limit analysis to incident data from the new ServiceNow instance (January 2026 onward) and compare with existing alert data for prioritization.
3) Restrict both alert and incident datasets to a common time window starting January 2026, requiring additional re-extraction but still avoiding legacy system queries.
decisions.dependencies_linked: AIOps product prioritization spreadsheet; action for Rodriguez, Luis Jorge to add incident data column from new ServiceNow instance.
decisions.source_file_name: AIOps Product Onboarding Reg Sync 30 Apr.docx

decisions.title: Define ingestion scope for Legal Tracker monitors entering ServiceNow
decisions.description: The team needs to decide whether all Legal Tracker monitors will send events into the ServiceNow event table from the outset, or whether AIOps will start with a defined subset of monitors and expand in later phases.

decision_owner.name: TR AIOps leadership (e.g., Rutherford, Chris; AD Al-Ghourabi)

decisions.rationale: Ingestion scope affects both risk and value. Including all monitors maximizes observability and correlation opportunities but may introduce noise and configuration risk; starting with a subset reduces initial complexity but may limit early value and require additional rollout planning.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Route all Legal Tracker monitors into ServiceNow from day one.
2) Start with a defined subset of monitors (e.g., infrastructure and critical synthetics) and expand in Phase 2.
3) Pilot with only specific regions or monitor types before full ingestion.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Event ingestion dependencies (integration mechanism, monitor inventory) and filtering/correlation configuration for Legal Tracker.

decisions.title: Define Legal Tracker event taxonomy for informational, warning, and exception events
decisions.description: The project must agree on what constitutes informational, warning, and exception events for Legal Tracker monitors. This taxonomy will drive filtering, suppression, and classification rules in ServiceNow Event Management.

decision_owner.name: Incident Management and AIOps design leads (e.g., Heymann, Damian; Rutherford, Chris)

decisions.rationale: A clear event taxonomy is necessary to consistently suppress non-actionable events, classify exceptions that should create incidents, and align monitor configurations with business impact expectations.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Adopt a simple three-level taxonomy (informational, warning, exception) aligned with current incident severity definitions.
2) Use a more granular taxonomy (e.g., multiple warning levels) for synthetics versus infrastructure.
3) Defer to existing Datadog priority levels and map them directly to ServiceNow severities with minimal new taxonomy definition.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Event prioritization configuration, monitor classification standards, and Datadog hygiene programme alignment.

decisions.title: Set incident creation policy for AIOps-correlated events
decisions.description: A decision is required on whether every actionable event should create an incident or whether some remediation can occur at the event level without incident records, based on correlation and classification outcomes.

decision_owner.name: AD Al-Ghourabi (TR Technology) with Service Management leadership

decisions.rationale: Incident creation policy determines the balance between visibility and noise. Creating incidents for all actionable events maintains legacy visibility but risks retaining the 1:1 event-to-incident pattern; restricting incidents to true exceptions reduces noise but requires strong confidence in correlation and remediation processes.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Every actionable event creates an incident.
2) Only exception-level events (as defined by the event taxonomy) create incidents; informational and warning events remain as events.
3) Some remediations are executed and recorded at the event level only, with incidents created only if remediation fails or service impact is detected.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Correlation rule tuning, event taxonomy definition, and incident management SLAs for Legal Tracker.

decisions.title: No customization of interaction record for Amazon Connect CTI; use out-of-the-box interaction view
decisions.description: For the Amazon Connect–ServiceNow CTI integration, the interaction record opened for agents must remain the out-of-the-box interaction view (showing user details, recent tasks/interactions, and assigned assets). TR and HCL agreed that no new fields or layout customizations will be implemented on this interaction record as part of the CTI URL change; the focus is solely on providing a URL that opens the standard interaction record instead of an incident.
decisions.rationale: ServiceNow vendor (John) recommended using out-of-the-box CTI capabilities and the Amazon Connect connector rather than building custom APIs or customized interaction forms. Keeping the interaction record standard reduces maintenance, avoids high-risk customizations, and ensures future compatibility, while still meeting HCLs requirement to see user details and related records when a call is received.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Customize the interaction record (new fields/layout changes) to meet HCLs expectations; 2) Use the out-of-the-box interaction record and only adjust the CTI URL to open it; 3) Redesign the integration using the ServiceNow Amazon Connect connector and new flows in a future phase.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Amazon Connect (AWS) CTI integration with ServiceNow and Virtual Agent; Risk: Amazon Connect CTI URL misconfiguration may delay IVR demo and cutover; Action: Provide corrected CTI interaction URL for Amazon ConnectServiceNow integration.
decisions.source_file_name: Issue with Amazon CTI URL __ RITM0147285 & REQ0145658.docx

decisions.title: Prioritize minimal-change CTI URL fix for Amazon Connect migration and defer connector-based redesign
decisions.description: For the immediate Avaya-to-Amazon Connect migration, TR and HCL will prioritize a minimal-change solution that adjusts the existing CTI URL so it opens an interaction record (instead of an incident) using current architecture, rather than redesigning the integration around the ServiceNow Amazon Connect connector. A connector-based redesign and proof of concept (POC) may be pursued later once the basic migration is stable and time/resources permit.
decisions.rationale: HCL reported that almost all technical and UAT activities for the Amazon Connect migration are complete, with only the URL landing page behavior pending. ServiceNow vendor guidance and internal review indicated that re-architecting around the Amazon Connect connector would require additional time, effort, and POC work, which the team cannot afford before go-live. A minimal-change CTI URL fix enables timely migration while keeping open the option to adopt the connector later.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Redesign the integration using the ServiceNow Amazon Connect connector and perform a POC in sandbox before go-live; 2) Adjust the existing CTI URL and parameters to open an interaction record instead of an incident, keeping the current architecture; 3) Continue with the current incident-landing behavior and accept the UX gap.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Amazon Connect (AWS) CTI integration with ServiceNow and Virtual Agent; Action: Provide corrected CTI interaction URL for Amazon ConnectServiceNow integration.
decisions.source_file_name: Issue with Amazon CTI URL __ RITM0147285 & REQ0145658.docx

decisions.title: Prioritise maturing GCC coverage for existing products before onboarding additional applications
decisions.description: For GCC onboarding and AIOps adoption, the programme will first focus on making products already on GCC (such as Legal Tracker and other tier 1 services) fully onboarded and working correctly under the new event-first, AI Ops-enabled model before expanding aggressively to additional products. This includes stabilising Datadog monitor hygiene, CI/CMDB service associations, and routing rules so the formula is proven before scaling.
decisions.rationale: AD emphasised that continuing to add more products without a proven, repeatable formula for GCC + AIOps onboarding risks spreading issues across a larger footprint. Ensuring that current GCC products are correctly onboarded, with stable routing and service-mapping, will provide a reusable pattern and reduce operational risk when scaling to the broader portfolio.
decisions.options_considered:
1) Increase the overall number of products on GCC as quickly as possible, even if existing products are only partially onboarded.
2) Prioritise making products already on GCC (e.g., Legal Tracker) fully onboarded and stable before onboarding additional products.
3) Attempt to do both simultaneously by onboarding many new products while also stabilising existing ones.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to dependencies on Datadog hygiene programme alignment with AIOps and resolution of CI/service association behaviour by CMDB resource and ServiceNow consultant, as these are prerequisites for a repeatable GCC+AIOps onboarding formula.
decisions.source_file_name: AIOps Onboarding Datadog Coverage App Prioritization and Resourcing.docx

decisions.title: Extend overall Customer Trust AI program completion to Q2 2027
decisions.description: The overall program completion timeline for the Customer Trust AI Strategy has been extended to June 30, 2027 to reflect the full set of program activities beyond the initial Loopio implementation.
decisions.rationale: The scope of the Customer Trust AI program extends beyond Loopio implementation to include self-service AI capabilities and multiple phases; extending the LE date better reflects realistic delivery of all strategic activities.
decisions.options_considered: Maintain original completion date of December 11, 2025; extend completion date to align with phase milestones culminating in Q2 2027.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Linked to Phase 1 (Loopio implementation), Phase 2 (MVP1 self-service/automated response generation), and Phase 3 (Iteration 2) milestones.
decisions.source_file_name: RAID Log – 2026 Customer Trust - AI Strategy.xlsx

decisions.title: CT- AI Strategy Platform - Short term and long term use
decisions.description: Evaluating current Loopio AI enablement by Q3 2026 and planning ahead for future long-term platform use.
decisions.rationale: platform usage
decisions.options_considered: 6/1/26- CT Operational Team mentioned they narrowed down to 2 potential candidates for long term platform use and will need to evaluate criteria based off migration efforts.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Migration from Loopio to tool

decisions.title: Adopt M365 Copilot as interim conversational AI; pause Now Assist work and treat Employee Works as phase 2
decisions.description: The program will pause further investment in Now Assist conversational workflows and instead pursue M365 Copilot as the immediate conversational AI front end for the Service Desk, integrated with ServiceNow. Employee Works (MoveWorks) will be treated as a potential phase 2 solution, contingent on sourcing and licensing negotiations, and is not a current dependency for project milestones.
decisions.rationale: Now Assists LLM and conversational experience were assessed as not good enough for end users, and ServiceNow indicated that Employee Works is the longer-term answer. However, Employee Works timelines are uncertain and could significantly delay delivery. Copilot testing shows promising results, requires no Now Assist dependency, and can be integrated with ServiceNow while licensing and Employee Works negotiations proceed in parallel.
decisions.options_considered: 1) Continue investing in Now Assist conversational workflows; 2) Pause Now Assist and move directly to Employee Works when available; 3) Adopt M365 Copilot as the interim conversational AI integrated with ServiceNow, while treating Employee Works as a future phase; 4) Replace Now Assists LLM with a different LLM while keeping the ServiceNow front end.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Issue: ServiceNow license renewal and Now Assist license mapping blocking AI capabilities on new instance; Dependency: ServiceNow license renewal and Now Assist enablement on new instance; Copilot Integration Testing milestone.

decisions.title: Position Now Assist vs Employee Works licensing as non-blocking for SD Automation milestones
decisions.description: Licensing negotiations and strategy around moving from Now Assist to Employee Works (MoveWorks) will continue via sourcing and vendor discussions but are no longer treated as a dependency or blocker for Service Desk Automation milestones. AI delivery will proceed via Copilot, with Employee Works evaluated later as a separate phase.
decisions.rationale: Waiting for Employee Works licensing and implementation would introduce significant schedule risk and delay user experience improvements, while Copilot can fill the gap now. latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

Cloud Optimization is driving standardized FinOps practices, cloud modernization to AWS, and platform governance to reduce average cloud waste by 7%, improve forecast accuracy, and keep CIO cloud spend aligned to 2026 targets. The program also advances Windows-to-Linux and Graviton adoption to deliver structural cost savings and future-ready application architectures across key estates such as GTM4, GST, Onvio, and Cobalt.

Steady Amber status is mainly driven by the $2.4M shortfall of the $3.5M cloud savings target and the currently identified and executable savings pipeline and Modernization resource & competing priorities constraints. However, the program delivers tangible financial and operational value in that:

-   $220K in-year savings achieved through GTM4 AWS DB migrations, including UAT and PROD Wave 1; with a total of $360K annual savings.
    
-   Cobalt Modernization's Windows to Linux migration (Document Service) released May 28 supporting the run rate savings of $2.3M and estimated in year savings of $1.3M.
    
-   Governance established over ~$1.5M/month in AI/DevOps spend via a new cost & control dashboard, strengthening financial accountability
    
-   Released TRUCCR Bot, AI-powered FinOps Assistant to align with user queries on cloud usage & spend with TRUCCR & AWS source data, into production one month ahead of schedule.
    

Cloud savings performance is behind plan against a $3.5M target; potential $1.1M in -year savings to implement and $0.6M realized to date (~32%), leaving an estimated $2.4M gap. FinOps OKRs show mixed progress: Win-to-Linux modernization has ~20% of AWS Windows EC2 migrations in progress and 5% pending kickoff toward a 25% year-end goal, Graviton adoption is at 56% against the Q2 Target of 57%, actual to forecast cloud spend variance is at 4.8% against the 3% Q2 target, and 8 of 15 tech orgs are now within the 7% cloud-waste threshold, down 1 since April.

## **Path to Green**

Remove key Modernization production blockers and de-risk delivery by:

-   Secure Service Management Tech Ops resources across GST's FSx and GST Batch Services workstreams to address execution bottlenecks and competing priorities. Finalize GST Windows to Linux roadmap with Product Engineering leadership alignment.
    
-   GTM4 Reporting Services POC has been delayed to June 12 due to added scope. Initial findings confirm full automation is not feasible, with manual effort still required. Alignment is needed on the updated scope to operationalize the new reporting platform for new reports, while migrating 1,800 existing reports with AI-assisted tooling in 2026/2027. This delays Windows server decommissioning and reduces cloud run-rate savings by ~ $60K.
    
-   Progress the S3 Document store via a phased/gradual rollout approach, with final scope and savings profile to be confirmed.  Establish cross-team alignment (Product Engineering + Platform Engineering) for Website module and Elastic/Open Search modernizations to de-risk timelines and confirm execution models.
    

Finalize with priority the red lever opportunities of the CIO application team, given they are currently lagging behind Product teams (tracking at ~2% of their target due to PLE support as well as larger savings opportunity base), and align where required with Cloud SteerCo on visibility of risks and opportunities (30-June). Continue momentum on AWS NAT Gateway red lever execution for potential in-year savings of $400k by end of Q3.

## **Milestones**

-   Complete GST Modernization Phase 1B (Batch Services) and GST Phase 2A FSx Modernization by 30-June.
    
-   Migrate BRM/Lafi/Tax Return Live cutting over to UAT 5-June.
    
-   Complete GTM4 AMS to AWS Production DB Migration Wave 2 and associated decommissioning by 30-Jun
    
-   Complete Q2 EPC Business Case Tracker – Modernization reporting by 30-June.

risks.title: GTM4 Content PROD Cluster Migration
risks.description:
The GTM4 Content PROD environment includes three critical content clusters with high customer dependency. Migrating these clusters requires re‑initializing database replication from scratch, which is time‑consuming and highly sensitive to maintenance windows. There is a risk that replication may not complete within the agreed downtime window. Similar challenges were experienced during the earlier on‑prem to cloud migration, where replication delays caused operational issues.
Additionally, a future GCP content migration is already planned, which may require repeating the same replication process—potentially resulting in two customer downtimes if not carefully planned.
Risk Impact:
Potential extended PROD downtime impacting customers
Increased operational and reputational risk if replication fails or overruns
Need for multiple customer downtimes (current migration + future GCP migration)
Possible schedule changes to GTM4 Phase / Wave execution
Minor cost impact (~$4.5K/month) if clusters are retained longer as‑is, but operational risk outweighs cost considerations.
Risk Probability:
Medium – based on past replication challenges and dependency complexity, pending business decision. 
Current Status / Decision Pending:
Risk logged primarily as a decision risk
Business discussion scheduled to assess tolerance for downtime vs. deferring migration
Final approach may change based on Business Unit agreement
Mitigation / Next Steps:
Review and align with the Business Unit on acceptable downtime and migration approach
Explore deferring migration of these clusters to align with future GCP migration, avoiding double downtime
Document final business decision in ADO and update RAID accordingly (close or re‑categorize risk)

risks.title: GST Phase 1B - GST Batch Transfer Issue not resolved
risks.description: During GST Phase 1B migration from the AMS environment to native AWS, a critical defect was discovered: the GST batch transfer operation (moving tax return data and locators between internal systems or client sub-accounts) consistently fails in both AMS-to-AWS flows and in AWS (FSx-backed) environments. A potential fix is under development and testing, but until it is fully validated this remains a high-impact risk.
risks.impact_description: If the GST batch transfer issue is not fully resolved and validated before go-live, a core tax data transfer process will fail in production. This could cause widespread production system failures, incorrect or incomplete data transfers between systems and client sub-accounts, and serious customer impact during critical tax processing periods. The Phase 1B go-live would likely need to be delayed, undermining the modernization schedule and delaying realization of cloud cost savings.
risks.mitigation: Complete the GST batch transfer fix and validate it in lower environments, followed by full regression testing to ensure no critical defects remain. Once testing passes, finalize a cutover plan with stakeholder alignment and obtain leadership approval prior to production release. Maintain the decision to delay the Phase 1B go-live until after tax season if necessary, prioritizing customer stability and avoiding changes to critical systems during peak tax usage.

risks.title: Schedule risk due to expanded cloud expense forecast scope to Reuters and International

risks.impact_description: If Reuters and International finance teams cannot provide forecast data that is available, timely, and in a consumable format, the cloud expense forecasting and variance analysis feature in TRUCCR may not be delivered as designed and the revised end-of-June 2026 target date for the milestone may not be achievable. This would delay improved forecasting capabilities for Finance, Engineering, and Leadership and could impact 2026 planning and budget decisions that rely on these insights.
risks.mitigation: Pete will schedule and conduct sessions with Reuters and International finance teams to assess forecast data availability, structure, and forecasting approaches. Based on the findings, the team will adjust integration plans, timelines, or scope to align with what can be reliably delivered.

risks.title: GTM4 - Production Migration Capacity Constraint
risks.description: Capacity risk for GTM4 AMS to AWS database production migration waves. The number of production clusters to be included in each migration wave has not yet been finalized, so the overall migration schedule cannot be confirmed. If sufficient clusters cannot be migrated in each wave, the current plan to complete production migration in 2026 may not be achievable.
risks.impact_description: If the team cannot include enough production clusters in each migration wave, the GTM4 production database migration from AMS to AWS will extend beyond 2026. This would delay full decommissioning of AMS infrastructure, prolong dual-running costs, limit realization of cloud cost savings and performance benefits, and could create ongoing operational complexity managing two environments for longer than planned.
risks.mitigation: Finalize the number of production clusters per migration wave based on available capacity, adjust wave sizing and schedule to ensure all clusters can be migrated within 2026, and secure any additional resources needed to deliver the planned throughput. If required, re-baseline the migration plan with realistic wave sizes and timelines while maintaining risk controls for production stability.

risks.title: GTM4 Reporting Services Phase 3: Feasibility Risk – Jasper Reports vs Crystal Reports
risks.description: Feasibility risk for the GTM4 Windows to Linux Reporting Services modernization (Phase 3). The modernization depends on validating that Jasper Reports can fully replicate Crystal Reports functionality, including complex reporting logic and handling large datasets. There is a risk that the Proof of Concept (PoC) may be successful only for a limited set of manually converted reports and may not scale or be acceptable for full production rollout.
risks.impact_description: If Jasper Reports cannot match Crystal Reports capabilities at scale, or if the PoC results do not translate into a viable full-production solution for ~1,800 reports, the Reporting Services modernization to Linux may be delayed or fail. This would prevent decommissioning of Windows-based reporting infrastructure, extend licensing and infrastructure costs, and delay cloud modernization benefits. It may also require rework to identify and implement an alternative reporting technology, impacting the overall GTM4 Windows to Linux migration timeline and cost savings.
risks.mitigation: Execute the Reporting Services PoC using Jasper Reports to convert a representative subset of Crystal Reports, focusing on complex logic and high-volume datasets, and validate output parity, performance, usability, and business acceptance. Based on PoC outcomes, define a detailed migration plan for the full report set. In parallel, prepare contingency options (such as alternative reporting platforms or a hybrid approach) in case Jasper cannot fully replace Crystal Reports, and clarify next steps if the PoC is unsuccessful.

latest_report.content:
## Executive Summary

GCP Cloud Migration Program is a CIO‑sponsored strategic initiative, jointly aligned with Product Engineering, focused on demonstrating cloud portability while modernizing TR's application landscape. GCP Program targets the migration of ~59 applications across ~18 product families from AWS to GCP over a 30‑month, wave‑based roadmap. This matters because it consolidates platforms, enables cloud portability, and sets up AI-ready foundations while maintaining service reliability for customers using the GTM, IDT, DT, and Data Hub applications.

Program Initiation and Planning completed on 10 Apr 2026 as planned, and the Foundation Architecture and Landing Zone phase is in progress against a 16-week Google Foundations engagement targeting completion by 26 Jun 2026. Pilot preparation is on track, with Constellation confirmed as the first pilot targeting mid to late Aug 2026, supported by strong progress across Wave 1 deep-dives, application inventory validation, and GCP Foundations training.

Overall program status is Amber trending Green, driven by delay in the readiness of the project for turnover to Accenture. This delay stems from several contributing factors:

-   An elevated volume of internal conversations and decisions required within TR that are still in progress. These included designs conversations between TR teams and Google which directly impacted multiple areas.
    
-   The Technical Design Document (TDD) from Google has taken longer than anticipated to be reviewed, confirmed, and formally signed off.
    
-   Additional coordination overhead across workstreams has contributed to the overall schedule pressure.
    

## Path to Green

Our path back to Green status is well-defined and dependent on the following actions:

1.  **TR Internal Decisions** – TR stakeholders moving quickly on outstanding decisions in key areas to unblock downstream progress.
    
2.  **Google TDD Update** – Google providing a revised TDD that is clearly structured, contains accurate information, and fully reflects updates agreed upon during calls and email exchanges with the TR team.
    
3.  **Accenture Delivery Timeline** – Accenture maintaining their current expected delivery timeline for the pilot migration during mid/ late Aug.
    

## Milestones

-   Complete Foundation Architecture and Landing Zone Ready phase by 26 Jun 2026.
    
-   Complete pilot workload migration and have at least one pilot workload live on GCP by 31 Aug 2026.
    
-   Complete Wave 1 application deep-dive analysis and mandatory GCP Foundations training for program participants by 30 Jun 2026.
    
-   Subsequent Wave Migrations Completion July'26 - Sep'28.
    
-   Deliver full AWS to GCP migration program outcomes, covering all in-scope applications and customer onboarding, by 30 Sep 2028.

risks.title: Landing Zone build delay may impact pilot migration timelines and July deliverables
risks.description: GCP Landing Zone (LZ) build is currently forecasting a 2-week delay relative to the original plan. The exact completion date is pending confirmation from Thomson Reuters, and Accenture must assess how the revised LZ build plan will impact pilot migration activities and key July deliverables (D2 Pilot Migration Report, D3 Landing Zone Validation Report, D4 Volumetric Validation Report, and D5 Target State Architecture & Design) as well as milestone M2 (Landing Zone validation & Pilot Apps migrated).
risks.impact_description: If the Landing Zone build slips further or the 2-week delay is not absorbed, the pilot migration schedule could be pushed back, delaying completion of the Pilot Migration Report (D2), Landing Zone Validation Report (D3), Volumetric Validation Report (D4), and Target State Architecture & Design (D5). This in turn may delay milestone M2 (Landing Zone validation & Pilot Apps migrated), compress downstream migration wave timelines, and increase schedule risk against the 30-month AWS to GCP migration objective.
risks.mitigation: 1) Thomson Reuters to confirm the updated Landing Zone completion date and revised build plan by 2026-05-29. 2) Accenture to assess schedule and dependency impacts based on the confirmed LZ plan, including effects on pilot migration activities and deliverables D2–D5. 3) Adjust pilot and wave-1 schedules as needed (e.g., resequencing tasks, prioritizing critical pilot scope) and escalate any residual schedule risk through program governance. 4) Define and agree validation checkpoints and governance expectations for evaluating how LZ build timelines affect pilot migration readiness.

assumptions.title: Google funding and Professional Services support will be available as planned
assumptions.description: The program assumes that approximately $16M in Google funding for migration and modernization and an additional $14M in Google Professional Services support will be provided over the full 30‑month program period.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Funding commitments have been outlined as part of the CIO‑sponsored strategic initiative with Google as a key partner.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Google funding and PS support are core elements of the business case for the AWS to GCP migration and have been explicitly quantified in program documentation, but are still subject to detailed commercial agreements and ongoing governance.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If funding is reduced or delayed, reprioritize application families and customer onboarding scope, adjust wave content, and seek alternative TR funding or cost optimizations to preserve critical program outcomes.
assumptions.validation_method: Formal confirmation through executed contracts and ongoing financial governance reviews between TR, Accenture and Google.

assumptions.title: Program can complete AWS to GCP migration within the 30‑month timeline
assumptions.description: The program assumes that the pilot phase and four migration waves, covering 59 in‑scope applications and customer onboarding, can be completed within the April 2026 to October 2028 period.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The timeline has been set by the CIO‑sponsored initiative, aligned with resource forecasts and wave planning assumptions across Global Trade, Indirect Tax and Platform portfolios.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The initial high‑level plan allocates time for pilot and four waves, supported by governance and weekly RAID reviews, but the schedule depends on timely decisions, environment readiness and resource availability across all parties.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If schedule risk increases, resequence applications between waves, reduce or defer lower‑value scope, or extend the program with Executive Steering Board approval.
assumptions.validation_method: Integrated schedule reviews during Program Board sessions, with periodic re‑forecasting based on wave progress and dependency status.

assumptions.title: GCP Landing Zone validated for pilots will be suitable for broader portfolio
assumptions.description: The program assumes that the GCP Landing Zone and associated patterns validated during pilot migrations will be suitable for the majority of the 59 in‑scope applications across 18 families.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Landing Zone design is intended as a reusable, standardized foundation for all migrated workloads, with pilots used to validate key patterns.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Landing Zone designs are typically reusable, but this program spans diverse applications and regulatory requirements, so suitability must be validated through pilots and architecture governance.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If pilots reveal significant gaps, plan controlled Landing Zone enhancements and re‑baseline wave schedules to incorporate necessary changes before broad rollout.
assumptions.validation_method: Architecture Board reviews of pilot migration outcomes, Landing Zone validation assessment reports, and security/compliance sign‑offs before expanding to additional waves.

assumptions.title: TR will provide required VDI access and technical enablement to Accenture on time
assumptions.description: The program assumes that Thomson Reuters will provision VDI access with required tools, software and repository connectivity for Accenture teams according to agreed dates.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Accenture relies on TR‑provided VDI environments for secure access to application code and tools across all workstreams.
assumptions.validity_explanation: TR Platform Engineering has accountability for VDI provisioning and is engaged via program governance, but provisioning timelines are still being actively managed.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If VDI provisioning slips, prioritize critical teams and applications for access, explore interim access mechanisms where compliant, and escalate delays through program governance.
assumptions.validation_method: Tracking of VDI provisioning milestones and periodic status review in Workstream Steering and Program Board meetings.

assumptions.title: A program‑wide DevSecOps approach and CI/CD tooling will be agreed before major build activities
assumptions.description: The program assumes that a standard DevSecOps approach, including selection of CI/CD tools and network connectivity between AWS and GCP, will be agreed by TR Platform Engineering, Accenture and Google before intensive pilot and wave build work begins.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Consistent DevSecOps practices are required to support secure, repeatable deployments across all applications and waves.
assumptions.validity_explanation: All parties recognize the need for a unified DevSecOps approach, but final decisions on tools and connectivity are still pending.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If alignment is delayed, define a minimal common toolset for pilots and restrict divergence, while fast‑tracking final decisions through Architecture and Transformation Boards.
assumptions.validation_method: Architecture Board and Workstream Steering review and approval of the chosen DevSecOps tools, patterns and connectivity model.

assumptions.title: Wave planning and application sequencing will be agreed and baselined early in the program
assumptions.description: The program assumes that application sequencing into the four migration waves will be discussed, agreed and baselined between TR and Accenture early in WS1 Planning & Baselining.
assumptions.rationale_basis: A clear wave plan is needed to coordinate resources, manage dependencies and align workstreams across Global Trade, Indirect Tax, Platform and customer onboarding.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Initial preparation for wave planning is underway, but the final sequence requires cross‑portfolio agreement and governance sign‑off.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If agreement cannot be reached on time, adopt a phased approval (e.g., approve first two waves while refining later ones) and limit unplanned changes through strict change control.
assumptions.validation_method: Formal approval of the wave plan at the Program Board and incorporation into the integrated program schedule.

assumptions.title: Program governance forums will operate as defined in the governance framework
assumptions.description: The program assumes that all governance forums (Integrated Delivery Pods, Workstream Steering, Program Board, Architecture Board, Transformation Board, Executive Steering Board) will meet with the prescribed cadence, membership and escalation paths.
assumptions.rationale_basis: The RAID log and instructions define a multi‑tier governance model with specific responsibilities and escalation rules.
assumptions.validity_explanation: The governance model is agreed on paper, but its effectiveness depends on consistent participation and disciplined execution by all parties.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If governance forums under‑perform, rationalize or adjust the governance structure, clarify decision rights, and escalate persistent gaps to the Executive Steering Board.
assumptions.validation_method: Monitoring adherence to the governance calendar, meeting attendance, and timely resolution of escalated items.

assumptions.title: Planned customer onboarding volumes (800 GTM IP customers) are achievable within the program
assumptions.description: The program assumes that onboarding of approximately 800 GTM IP customers to the new GCP‑based services can be achieved within the program timeframe and capacity constraints.
assumptions.rationale_basis: Customer onboarding is explicitly defined as Workstream 3 and is integral to realizing business value from the migration.
assumptions.validity_explanation: Customer onboarding targets are set at a program level, but depend on customer readiness, internal capacity, and technical stability of migrated services.
assumptions.mitigation_contingency: If onboarding lags, reprioritize high‑value customers, adjust onboarding schedules, and consider additional resources or extended timelines with Executive Steering Board approval.
assumptions.validation_method: Detailed onboarding planning, capacity analysis, and tracking of customer onboarding KPIs through Workstream Steering and Program Board reviews.

decisions.title: Definition of program scope and wave-based delivery model
decisions.description: The program will migrate approximately 65 applications across 18 product families from AWS to GCP over a 30‑month timeline, using a wave-based approach that includes application migration, platform modernization, and customer onboarding.

decision_owner.name: Thomson Reuters Corporate Tax & Trade leadership with Program Ferrari governance

decisions.rationale: A wave-based scope and timeline enable manageable risk, phased learning, and coordinated customer onboarding while fitting within funding and resource constraints.
decisions.options_considered: Big‑bang migration of all applications; limiting scope to infrastructure-only migration without modernization; extending duration beyond 30 months with smaller waves.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Customer onboarding phases dependent on GTM IP migration; GCP landing zone readiness before large-scale application migrations.

decisions.title: Adoption of a three‑party strategic partnership model
decisions.description: The AWS to GCP Migration Program will be executed as a structured three‑party partnership with clear accountability: Thomson Reuters owns business outcomes, product priorities, security standards, and final acceptance; Google Cloud provides consultancy on platform, foundations, and architecture governance; Accenture executes migration and modernization activities under defined governance.

decision_owner.name: Matt Dimich (Program Sponsor, Thomson Reuters) with Google and Accenture executive leads

decisions.rationale: A three‑party model aligns each partner to their strengths—TR owning outcomes and risk, Google providing deep GCP expertise and foundations, and Accenture providing migration factory execution—reducing risk and improving delivery velocity across multiple workstreams.
decisions.options_considered: Single vendor responsible for both foundations and migration; internal-only migration using Thomson Reuters resources; two‑party partnership without a dedicated SI migration factory.
decisions.dependencies_linked: GCP landing zone readiness before large-scale application migrations; Completion of Google Foundations prior to full migration waves; Architecture governance model to support migration decisions.

decisions.title: Adoption of migration guiding principles for the program
decisions.description: The program will be guided by principles of minimum customer interruption, reliability from day one, cloud-native automation aligned with TR standards, combined migrate-and-modernize activities, and enabling future transformation and agentic AI.
decisions.rationale: Shared guiding principles provide consistent decision criteria across projects and vendors, ensuring that short‑term migration choices support long‑term resilience, automation, and AI‑ready capabilities.
decisions.options_considered: Focusing solely on lift‑and‑shift with minimal modernization; prioritizing speed over customer impact; deferring AI and automation considerations to a future program.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Infrastructure as Code modules availability for migration factory; Completion of Google Foundations prior to full migration waves.

decisions.title: Google Foundations scope limited to infrastructure and landing zone
decisions.description: Google Cloud Professional Services will focus on infrastructure-only scope: building the target-state GCP landing zone via IaC, conducting AWS architecture audits, and providing architecture governance. Manual workload migration, data transfer, and application code refactoring are explicitly out of scope and will be handled by the SI partner.

decision_owner.name: Google Cloud TR Account Lead (Hesham Rasmy Ali) with Thomson Reuters program leadership

decisions.rationale: Keeping Google PSO focused on foundations and governance maximizes leverage of GCP expertise while avoiding overlap with SI responsibilities, clarifying accountability and funding usage.
decisions.options_considered: Including workload migration and data transfer in Google PSO scope; a narrower advisory-only role for Google without IaC delivery; combining foundations and migration under a single vendor.
decisions.dependencies_linked: AWS environment inventory and service mapping for foundation design; Infrastructure as Code modules availability for migration factory; Completion of Google Foundations prior to full migration waves.

decisions.title: Establishment of architecture governance and escalation model
decisions.description: The program will operate with a structured architecture governance and escalation model: architecture decisions are owned at the lowest appropriate level, with defined escalation paths from Architecture Council to Program Governance to Joint Steering Committee, and a fast‑track mechanism for critical, time‑bound decisions affecting delivery, risk, or customer continuity.

decision_owner.name: Thomson Reuters Enterprise Architecture leadership in conjunction with Google and Accenture program leads

decisions.rationale: Clear governance and escalation reduce decision latency, align stakeholders, and ensure consistent architecture across multiple projects and vendors while protecting customer continuity.
decisions.options_considered: Ad‑hoc decision making without formal councils; centralized decision making only at executive level; vendor-specific governance without a joint model.
decisions.dependencies_linked: Architecture governance model to support migration decisions; GCP landing zone readiness before large-scale application migrations.

decisions.title: Use of a migration factory model for wave-based delivery
decisions.description: The program will use an Accenture-led migration factory to execute wave-based AWS to GCP migrations, including planning, assessments, wave design, migration execution, testing, cutover, hypercare, and coordination of customer onboarding.

decision_owner.name: Accenture Program Delivery Lead (Tejesh Nandyala) with Thomson Reuters program leadership

decisions.rationale: A factory model supports standardized processes, economies of scale, and repeatable patterns across many applications and product families, improving predictability of delivery.
decisions.options_considered: Individual project-by-project migrations led by separate teams; in-house only migration teams; fully automated tooling-only migration approach without a structured factory.
decisions.dependencies_linked: GCP landing zone readiness before large-scale application migrations; Infrastructure as Code modules availability for migration factory; Nomination of application and data owners for migrations.

Accenture SOW is finalized, awaiting confirmation.
